skills.search_text: cgmlst-core-locus-selection Use when you have a chewBBACA allelic profile matrix (results_alleles.tsv) over draft or complete assemblies and must reduce the wgMLST schema to loci present in ≥95% (or 95-99%) of strains for core-genome typing. Input is raw FASTA assemblies rather than a completed chewBBACA AlleleCall profile matrix — schema creation/allele calling must precede core-locus selection Paralogous loci from RepeatedLoci.txt have not yet been removed, so uncertain allele assignments would inflate the core-locus count A pre-defined cg/wgMLST schema already exists (it can be downloaded from Chewie-NS or adapted via PrepExternalSchema instead of being re-derived) http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Defines a cgMLST (core-genome) schema by selecting loci present in a chosen percentage of analysed strains (e.g. 95%) from a chewBBACA wgMLST allele-calling matrix, using TestGenomeQuality to explore thresholds and ExtractCgMLST to write the retained locus list. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000166
skills.summary: Defines a cgMLST (core-genome) schema by selecting loci present in a chosen percentage of analysed strains (e.g. 95%) from a chewBBACA wgMLST allele-calling matrix, using TestGenomeQuality to explore thresholds and ExtractCgMLST to write the retained locus list.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTA assemblies rather than a completed chewBBACA AlleleCall profile matrix — schema creation/allele calling must precede core-locus selection Paralogous loci from RepeatedLoci.txt have not yet been removed, so uncertain allele assignments would inflate the core-locus count A pre-defined cg/wgMLST schema already exists (it can be downloaded from Chewie-NS or adapted via PrepExternalSchema instead of being re-derived)

skills.description: Use when a chewBBACA schema (per-locus FASTA files with full allelic diversity) must be assessed locus-by-locus, e.g. to inspect allele variability before using the schema for cg/wgMLST strain identification.
skills.name: cgmlst-schema-evaluation
skills.search_text: cgmlst-schema-evaluation Use when a chewBBACA schema (per-locus FASTA files with full allelic diversity) must be assessed locus-by-locus, e.g. to inspect allele variability before using the schema for cg/wgMLST strain identification. Input is raw sequencing reads or draft assemblies without a schema — perform allele calling first (chewBBACA AlleleCall), not per-locus MSA/tree evaluation Only an allelic profile matrix is needed (e.g. core-genome extraction with ExtractCgMLST or paralog removal with RemoveGenes) — this skill builds per-locus alignments and trees, which is unnecessary The schema loci are known paralogs listed in RepeatedLoci.txt — such loci carry uncertainty in allele assignment and should be removed rather than evaluated for phylogenetic structure http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 Per-locus evaluation of a cg/wgMLST schema by reconstructing, for each locus, a MAFFT multiple sequence alignment of all identified alleles and a ClustalW2 neighbour-joining tree, enabling exploration of the consequences of allelic variability at each locus in the chewBBACA SchemaEvaluator workflow. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000166
skills.summary: Per-locus evaluation of a cg/wgMLST schema by reconstructing, for each locus, a MAFFT multiple sequence alignment of all identified alleles and a ClustalW2 neighbour-joining tree, enabling exploration of the consequences of allelic variability at each locus in the chewBBACA SchemaEvaluator workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads or draft assemblies without a schema — perform allele calling first (chewBBACA AlleleCall), not per-locus MSA/tree evaluation Only an allelic profile matrix is needed (e.g. core-genome extraction with ExtractCgMLST or paralog removal with RemoveGenes) — this skill builds per-locus alignments and trees, which is unnecessary The schema loci are known paralogs listed in RepeatedLoci.txt — such loci carry uncertainty in allele assignment and should be removed rather than evaluated for phylogenetic structure

skills.description: Use when calling alleles of query-genome CDSs against a pre-defined cg/wgMLST schema and interpreting classification tags (EXC, INF, ASM, ALM, NIPH, NIPHEM, PLOT, LNF) in the allelic profile.

It underpins gene-by-gene (cg/wgMLST) strain identification from draft assemblies.

skills.description: Use when you need to classify 16S rRNA sequences into seven taxonomic ranks (Domain–Species) with an existing published DeepTaxa checkpoint, without retraining, e.g. on the 69,335-sequence Greengenes2 2024.09 test FASTA.
skills.name: checkpoint-based-model-inference
skills.search_text: checkpoint-based-model-inference Use when you need to classify 16S rRNA sequences into seven taxonomic ranks (Domain–Species) with an existing published DeepTaxa checkpoint, without retraining, e.g. on the 69,335-sequence Greengenes2 2024.09 test FASTA. skills.search_text: checkv-quality-class-interpretation Use when a viral metagenomic contig library must be screened for viral sequences and CheckV quality-class output should be merged with VirSorter2, VIBRANT, DeepVirFinder, and MMseqs2 hits into a per-contig confidence label. skills.description: Use when reconstructing or re-implementing Kraken's taxonomic label assignment for metagenomic DNA reads, or when scoring query sequences against a k-mer LCA database built with Jellyfish and the NCBI taxonomy tree.
skills.name: classification-tree-path-scoring
skills.search_text: classification-tree-path-scoring Use when reconstructing or re-implementing Kraken's taxonomic label assignment for metagenomic DNA reads, or when scoring query sequences against a k-mer LCA database built with Jellyfish and the NCBI taxonomy tree. The task requires inexact alignment or quantifying abundance rather than per-read taxonomic classification — Kraken relies on exact-match k-mer database queries rather than inexact alignment of sequences. The query sequences are short k-mers containing ambiguous nucleotides spanning 'N' characters, which are ignored and cannot contribute classification evidence. The k-mer database does not contain the organism's k-mers — sequences with no k-mers in the database must be left unclassified, not force-labeled. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Reimplements Kraken's RTL path-scoring classification algorithm: each k-mer of a query sequence votes for its LCA taxon in a weighted classification tree, and the taxon of the maximum-scoring root-to-leaf path is assigned to the sequence. Ties are resolved by taking the LCA of tied leaves; sequences with no database k-mer hits are left unclassified. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/gb-2014-15-3-r46
skills.summary: Reimplements Kraken's RTL path-scoring classification algorithm: each k-mer of a query sequence votes for its LCA taxon in a weighted classification tree, and the taxon of the maximum-scoring root-to-leaf path is assigned to the sequence. Ties are resolved by taking the LCA of tied leaves; sequences with no database k-mer hits are left unclassified.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires inexact alignment or quantifying abundance rather than per-read taxonomic classification — Kraken relies on exact-match k-mer database queries rather than inexact alignment of sequences. The query sequences are short k-mers containing ambiguous nucleotides spanning 'N' characters, which are ignored and cannot contribute classification evidence. The k-mer database does not contain the organism's k-mers — sequences with no k-mers in the database must be left unclassified, not force-labeled.

skills.search_text: classifier-throughput-measurement Use when reproducing or verifying reads-per-minute throughput claims for a metagenomic classifier, or when comparing classifier speed on HiSeq/MiSeq/simBA-5 read sets. The goal is accuracy assessment (sensitivity/precision at genus or species rank), not speed — use the clade exclusion and rank-measurement experiments instead Only a single read set is available and no cache-priming or competitor runs can be performed, so no comparable speedup factor can be computed The workload is abundance estimation rather than full read classification — MetaPhlAn-style programs classify only a small percentage of reads, so rpm comparisons of the paper's type do not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmarks taxonomic classifier throughput (reads per minute) across the HiSeq, simBA-5, and MiSeq metagenomes using the paper's cache-priming protocol, and computes speedup factors over Megablast and MetaPhlAn to verify claims like 909x and 11x. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/gb-2014-15-3-r46
skills.summary: Benchmarks taxonomic classifier throughput (reads per minute) across the HiSeq, simBA-5, and MiSeq metagenomes using the paper's cache-priming protocol, and computes speedup factors over Megablast and MetaPhlAn to verify claims like 909x and 11x.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is accuracy assessment (sensitivity/precision at genus or species rank), not speed — use the clade exclusion and rank-measurement experiments instead Only a single read set is available and no cache-priming or competitor runs can be performed, so no comparable speedup factor can be computed The workload is abundance estimation rather than full read classification — MetaPhlAn-style programs classify only a small percentage of reads, so rpm comparisons of the paper's type do not apply

skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset has more than 199 expected clusters (e.g., ~5000 clusters) — --n_clusters is restricted to the range 0, 2-199, and the authors flag >200-cluster datasets as future work Sequences are shorter than the regime the paper evaluated (short reads <500 bp were excluded from the published evaluation and flagged for future testing) The goal is alignment-based sequence analysis — iDeLUCS clusters genomic signatures without sequence alignment or taxonomic identifiers

skills.description: Use when OTU/feature count tables (e.g., otu.tab.txt from the MiSurv Data folder) must be compositionally normalized before linear-regression differential abundance or Cox proportional hazards models that relate taxon abundance to survival outcomes.
skills.name: clr-compositional-data-transformation
skills.search_text: clr-compositional-data-transformation Use when OTU/feature count tables (e.g., otu.tab.txt from the MiSurv Data folder) must be compositionally normalized before linear-regression differential abundance or Cox proportional hazards models that relate taxon abundance to survival outcomes. The analysis target is alpha/beta diversity or survival modeling that consumes diversity measures rather than taxon-level compositional abundances. The response is a continuous or binary variable instead of a survival (time-to-event) response — MiSurv is designed for survival responses, while MiCloud handles continuous/binary outcomes. The count table has already been transformed (e.g., proportions or arcsine square root) and another normalization is inappropriate for the planned regression. Apply the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation to microbiome taxonomic count data as implemented in MiSurv's data transformations step, producing compositional normalized taxon abundances that serve as the basis for covariate-adjusted differential abundance testing (phylum-to-genus) and Cox-model association testing of microbial composition with survival responses. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Apply the centered log-ratio (CLR) transformation to microbiome taxonomic count data as implemented in MiSurv's data transformations step, producing compositional normalized taxon abundances that serve as the basis for covariate-adjusted differential abundance testing (phylum-to-genus) and Cox-model association testing of microbial composition with survival responses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis target is alpha/beta diversity or survival modeling that consumes diversity measures rather than taxon-level compositional abundances. The response is a continuous or binary variable instead of a survival (time-to-event) response — MiSurv is designed for survival responses, while MiCloud handles continuous/binary outcomes. The count table has already been transformed (e.g., proportions or arcsine square root) and another normalization is inappropriate for the planned regression.

skills.description: Use when raw genus/OTU count data (e.g. biom.Rdata or otu.tab.txt from the MiSurv Data folder) must be converted to compositional predictors before survival prediction modeling, such as feeding random survival forests in MiSurv Module 4.

The data have already been transformed in the Data Processing module (e.g. rarefaction, proportion, or arcsine square root applied) — applying CLR on top would double-transform. NOD mouse data. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Transforms genus-level OTU count tables into centered log-ratio (CLR) compositional predictors, as implemented in the MiSurv Data Processing module, so that taxon abundances can be used as covariates in Module 4 prediction modeling (random survival forests) of survival responses such as time-to-T1D-onset in the Zhang et al. NOD mouse data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data have already been transformed in the Data Processing module (e.g. rarefaction, proportion, or arcsine square root applied) — applying CLR on top would double-transform. The analysis goal is Module 1 (comparative survival analysis between treatment groups, not involving microbiome data) or Module 2 (comparative microbial composition analysis, not involving survival data), where CLR predictors for survival modeling are not the target. Input is alpha- or beta-diversity output (e.g. 'estimate_richness' in phyloseq or 'pd' from picante) rather than taxon-level count data.

skills.description: Use when you have run Minimap2 overlap scoring plus StrainXpress single-linkage clustering on metagenomic short reads and need to write or validate a per-read cluster assignment TSV as the deliverable of the 'Clustering Reads' stage.
skills.name: cluster-assignment-table-formatting
skills.search_text: cluster-assignment-table-formatting Use when you have run Minimap2 overlap scoring plus StrainXpress single-linkage clustering on metagenomic short reads and need to write or validate a per-read cluster assignment TSV as the deliverable of the 'Clustering Reads' stage. The input is third-generation long-read data (PacBio/Nanopore) rather than Illumina-type short reads — the workflow targets interleaved short-read FASTQ and high error rates remain unresolved. You need strain-resolved contigs rather than read-to-cluster groupings — the assignment TSV is only the pre-processing output feeding the subsequent 'Local Assembly' and 'Global Assembly' stages. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Emit and validate the read-to-cluster TSV (cluster_assignments.tsv) produced by StrainXpress's 'Clustering Reads' stage, which single-linkage merges reads from the interleaved FASTQ (all_reads.fq) after Minimap2 overlap scoring so that reads from the same species share a cluster ID. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac543
skills.summary: Emit and validate the read-to-cluster TSV (cluster_assignments.tsv) produced by StrainXpress's 'Clustering Reads' stage, which single-linkage merges reads from the interleaved FASTQ (all_reads.fq) after Minimap2 overlap scoring so that reads from the same species share a cluster ID.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is third-generation long-read data (PacBio/Nanopore) rather than Illumina-type short reads — the workflow targets interleaved short-read FASTQ and high error rates remain unresolved. You need strain-resolved contigs rather than read-to-cluster groupings — the assignment TSV is only the pre-processing output feeding the subsequent 'Local Assembly' and 'Global Assembly' stages.

skills.description: Use when a claimed clustering outcome (e.g. Metaclust's 424 million clusters) must be independently reproduced or validated from a published FASTA and reported Linclust parameters.
skills.name: cluster-count-verification
skills.search_text: cluster-count-verification Use when a claimed clustering outcome (e.g. Metaclust's 424 million clusters) must be independently reproduced or validated from a published FASTA and reported Linclust parameters. The sequence set is already redundant-reduced or the input is a precomputed cluster mapping rather than a FASTA of representatives or raw sequences The clustering was performed with approximate-only prefiltering whose cluster members were not verified with the exact similarity measure, since pair verification still requires quadratic time and counts may not be reproducible Available compute cannot hold the multi-billion-sequence input; Linclust can exceed main memory via the MMseqs2 suite but a full reproduction still needs a single server-class machine http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 Verifies large-scale protein sequence clustering results by counting cluster representatives in a FASTA set and reproducing Linclust/MMseqs2 clustering parameters, as done to confirm the Metaclust result of 424 million clusters from 1,595,926,152 input proteins clustered in 10 h. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Verifies large-scale protein sequence clustering results by counting cluster representatives in a FASTA set and reproducing Linclust/MMseqs2 clustering parameters, as done to confirm the Metaclust result of 424 million clusters from 1,595,926,152 input proteins clustered in 10 h.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequence set is already redundant-reduced or the input is a precomputed cluster mapping rather than a FASTA of representatives or raw sequences The clustering was performed with approximate-only prefiltering whose cluster members were not verified with the exact similarity measure, since pair verification still requires quadratic time and counts may not be reproducible Available compute cannot hold the multi-billion-sequence input; Linclust can exceed main memory via the MMseqs2 suite but a full reproduction still needs a single server-class machine

skills.description: Use when a published pipeline reports a specific number of sequence clusters at a stated identity threshold and you must independently reproduce and validate that cluster count from the same curated input set.

skills.search_text: cluster-count-verification-against-reported-results Use when a published pipeline reports a specific number of sequence clusters at a stated identity threshold and you must independently reproduce and validate that cluster count from the same curated input set. Input sequences are not the curated amoA-AOB reference set (e.g., raw unfiltered FunGene hits or metagenome reads), since the 60-cluster count was reported only for the filtered 1,205-sequence input The goal is de novo threshold selection rather than reproducing a published count — use the first-order difference optimization scan over 80–100% instead Clustering nucleotide rather than protein sequences — the 96% threshold and 60-cluster result apply to amino acid similarity http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3299 Reproduces a reported sequence-clustering result — clustering 1,205 curated FunGene amoA-AOB protein sequences with CD-HIT at 96% amino acid similarity and verifying that exactly 60 representative gene clusters are obtained, as described in the MetaFunPrimer pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00201-21

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are not the curated amoA-AOB reference set (e.g., raw unfiltered FunGene hits or metagenome reads), since the 60-cluster count was reported only for the filtered 1,205-sequence input The goal is de novo threshold selection rather than reproducing a published count — use the first-order difference optimization scan over 80–100% instead Clustering nucleotide rather than protein sequences — the 96% threshold and 60-cluster result apply to amino acid similarity

skills.description: Use when multiple trained networks have emitted cluster assignments for the same DNA sequence set (e.g. iDeLUCS mimic-based training with n_mimics augmentations) and a single final consensus cluster label per sequence is required.

skills.search_text: clustering-ensemble-aggregation Use when multiple trained networks have emitted cluster assignments for the same DNA sequence set (e.g. iDeLUCS mimic-based training with n_mimics augmentations) and a single final consensus cluster label per sequence is required. Only a single trained network is available — there is no ensemble to aggregate and majority voting or the ensemble is undefined The sequences require alignment-based comparison or taxonomic identifiers; iDeLUCS is explicitly alignment-free Labels are needed during training — GT files in iDeLUCS are used only for post-hoc analysis, not supervised learning http://edamontology.org/topic_3295 http://edamontology.org/topic_3307 Aggregate per-network cluster assignments produced by multiple iDeLUCS deep-learning runs using an information-theoretic clustering ensemble instead of the majority voting scheme of its predecessor (DeLUCS), reducing variance and boosting unsupervised clustering accuracy. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad508
skills.summary: Aggregate per-network cluster assignments produced by multiple iDeLUCS deep-learning runs using an information-theoretic clustering ensemble instead of the majority voting scheme of its predecessor (DeLUCS), reducing variance and boosting unsupervised clustering accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single trained network is available — there is no ensemble to aggregate and majority voting or the ensemble is undefined The sequences require alignment-based comparison or taxonomic identifiers; iDeLUCS is explicitly alignment-free Labels are needed during training — GT files in iDeLUCS are used only for post-hoc analysis, not supervised learning

skills.description: Use when two protein clustering methods (e.g. Snekmer AAR-kmer clustering vs MMseqs2 easy-cluster) have been run on the same protein FASTA set and you must benchmark them via V-scores and quantify overlap/union coverage of assigned proteins.
skills.name: clustering-method-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: clustering-method-benchmark-comparison Use when two protein clustering methods (e.g. Snekmer AAR-kmer clustering vs MMseqs2 easy-cluster) have been run on the same protein FASTA set and you must benchmark them via V-scores and quantify overlap/union coverage of assigned proteins. The goal is supervised family prediction with per-sequence confidence — use Snekmer's learn/apply mode, which outputs results/apply/snekmer_results.csv with Prediction, Score, delta, and Confidence columns instead of cluster partitions. Only one clustering method's assignments are available — both the V-score comparison and the overlap/union coverage analysis require two partitions over the same protein set. Input sequences are not proteins (e.g. nucleotide reads) — AAR kmer recoding and the UniProt annotation benchmark assume protein FASTA input. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmarks unsupervised protein clustering methods — Snekmer AAR-kmer agglomerative-jaccard clustering versus MMseqs2 easy-cluster — on the same dataset using V-scores (harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness) over functional annotations, and quantifies whether integrating both partitions increases protein-cluster coverage (here from ~50-60% per method to 85%). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad005
skills.summary: Benchmarks unsupervised protein clustering methods — Snekmer AAR-kmer agglomerative-jaccard clustering versus MMseqs2 easy-cluster — on the same dataset using V-scores (harmonic mean of homogeneity and completeness) over functional annotations, and quantifies whether integrating both partitions increases protein-cluster coverage (here from ~50-60% per method to 85%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is supervised family prediction with per-sequence confidence — use Snekmer's learn/apply mode, which outputs results/apply/snekmer_results.csv with Prediction, Score, delta, and Confidence columns instead of cluster partitions. Only one clustering method's assignments are available — both the V-score comparison and the overlap/union coverage analysis require two partitions over the same protein set. Input sequences are not proteins (e.g. nucleotide reads) — AAR kmer recoding and the UniProt annotation benchmark assume protein FASTA input.

skills.description: Use when a spectral networking/clustering step has produced a spectrum-to-cluster assignment and you must verify the number of distinct clusters (e.g. 8,071 families from ~10M spectra) before downstream interpretation.
skills.name: clustering-result-count-validation
skills.search_text: clustering-result-count-validation Use when a spectral networking/clustering step has produced a spectrum-to-cluster assignment and you must verify the number of distinct clusters (e.g. 8,071 families from ~10M spectra) before downstream interpretation. The goal is to validate peptide-spectrum match counts (e.g. the 38 RiPPs at 1% FDR) rather than the number of spectral families from the networking step Input is a raw mzML/MS2 file collection that has not yet been clustered by GNPS spectral networks — no family assignments exist to count The spectra come from datasets other than the eight analyzed genomic/metagenomic GNPS datasets, so the 8,071-family reference count does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 A validation skill for spectral-networking outputs: count the distinct clusters (spectral families) produced from a large tandem MS/MS dataset and check the number against a published reference value, e.g. MetaMiner's ~10 million GNPS spectra collapsing into only 8,071 families. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2019.09.004
skills.summary: A validation skill for spectral-networking outputs: count the distinct clusters (spectral families) produced from a large tandem MS/MS dataset and check the number against a published reference value, e.g. MetaMiner's ~10 million GNPS spectra collapsing into only 8,071 families.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to validate peptide-spectrum match counts (e.g. the 38 RiPPs at 1% FDR) rather than the number of spectral families from the networking step Input is a raw mzML/MS2 file collection that has not yet been clustered by GNPS spectral networks — no family assignments exist to count The spectra come from datasets other than the eight analyzed genomic/metagenomic GNPS datasets, so the 8,071-family reference count does not apply

skills.description: Use when clustering large protein sequence sets at ~50% sequence identity and Linclust's default m=20 k-mers per sequence yields more (smaller) clusters than a reference tool like UCLUST, prompting a test of whether --kmer-per-seq 80 closes the sensitivity gap at acceptable runtime.
skills.name: clustering-sensitivity-runtime-tradeoff-analysis
skills.search_text: clustering-sensitivity-runtime-tradeoff-analysis Use when clustering large protein sequence sets at ~50% sequence identity and Linclust's default m=20 k-mers per sequence yields more (smaller) clusters than a reference tool like UCLUST, prompting a test of whether --kmer-per-seq 80 closes the sensitivity gap at acceptable runtime. When the target clustering identity is 90% or 70% rather than 50% — the paper's sensitivity gap where Linclust produced 13% more clusters than UCLUST was characterized at the 50% identity level When the workload cannot absorb a 1.5–2x runtime increase over default Linclust, or when pairs are so costly to miscluster that exact quadratic-time pairwise verification is mandatory (Linclust's k-mer prefilter is approximate) When the input is not redundancy-reducible protein sequence sets but, e.g., already-clustered or profile data where k-mer shared-key assumptions do not hold http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmarks Linclust's k-mer-per-sequence parameter (m) to quantify the sensitivity/runtime tradeoff at 50% sequence identity: raising m from 20 to 80 recovers cluster sensitivity to a level similar to UCLUST at only 1.5–2x runtime cost. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Benchmarks Linclust's k-mer-per-sequence parameter (m) to quantify the sensitivity/runtime tradeoff at 50% sequence identity: raising m from 20 to 80 recovers cluster sensitivity to a level similar to UCLUST at only 1.5–2x runtime cost.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target clustering identity is 90% or 70% rather than 50% — the paper's sensitivity gap where Linclust produced 13% more clusters than UCLUST was characterized at the 50% identity level When the workload cannot absorb a 1.5–2x runtime increase over default Linclust, or when pairs are so costly to miscluster that exact quadratic-time pairwise verification is mandatory (Linclust's k-mer prefilter is approximate) When the input is not redundancy-reducible protein sequence sets but, e.g., already-clustered or profile data where k-mer shared-key assumptions do not hold

skills.description: Use when clustering a protein or nucleotide FASTA set to a target sequence identity (e.g. 50%, 70%, 90%) and the tool invocation parameters must be specified, tuned, and logged for reproducible runtime or cluster-quality comparisons.
skills.name: clustering-tool-command-line-parameterization
skills.search_text: clustering-tool-command-line-parameterization Use when clustering a protein or nucleotide FASTA set to a target sequence identity (e.g. 50%, 70%, 90%) and the tool invocation parameters must be specified, tuned, and logged for reproducible runtime or cluster-quality comparisons. The input is not a raw sequence set (e.g. already-clustered representatives or a feature/abundance table) and no clustering step is needed An exact full sensitivity alignment search is required rather than fast approximate redundancy reduction at a fixed identity threshold The dataset is small enough that clustering runtime is irrelevant and parameter benchmarking adds no value http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Selects and records the exact command-line parameters (identity thresholds, coverage mode, word sizes, thread/memory flags) needed to run sequence clustering tools — Linclust/MMseqs2, CD-HIT, UCLUST — at defined sequence identity levels so that benchmark or production runs are reproducible. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Selects and records the exact command-line parameters (identity thresholds, coverage mode, word sizes, thread/memory flags) needed to run sequence clustering tools — Linclust/MMseqs2, CD-HIT, UCLUST — at defined sequence identity levels so that benchmark or production runs are reproducible.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a raw sequence set (e.g. already-clustered representatives or a feature/abundance table) and no clustering step is needed An exact full sensitivity alignment search is required rather than fast approximate redundancy reduction at a fixed identity threshold The dataset is small enough that clustering runtime is irrelevant and parameter benchmarking adds no value

skills.description: Use when comparing de novo protein clusterings against reference functional annotations (GO, Pfam, InterPro, TIGRFAMs, COG) using V-scores, or when selecting AAR/kmer parameterizations by clustering quality.
skills.name: clustering-vscore-annotation-evaluation
skills.search_text: clustering-vscore-annotation-evaluation Use when comparing de novo protein clusterings against reference functional annotations (GO, Pfam, InterPro, TIGRFAMs, COG) using V-scores, or when selecting AAR/kmer parameterizations by clustering quality. The task is supervised family classification rather than de novo clustering — use Snekmer's learn/apply (or easy) modes with family-specific thresholds instead. Input is already a cluster assignment or feature table; this skill requires raw protein sequences in FASTA to generate the clusterings being compared. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark unsupervised protein sequence clusterings (e.g., Snekmer AAR-kmer agglomerative-jaccard clustering) against a reference clustering such as MMseqs2 easy-cluster by scoring cluster assignments against UniProt annotations (GO, Pfam, InterPro, TIGRFAMs, COG) with homogeneity, completeness, and their harmonic mean (V-score). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad005
skills.summary: Benchmark unsupervised protein sequence clusterings (e.g., Snekmer AAR-kmer agglomerative-jaccard clustering) against a reference clustering such as MMseqs2 easy-cluster by scoring cluster assignments against UniProt annotations (GO, Pfam, InterPro, TIGRFAMs, COG) with homogeneity, completeness, and their harmonic mean (V-score).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is supervised family classification rather than de novo clustering — use Snekmer's learn/apply (or easy) modes with family-specific thresholds instead. Input is already a cluster assignment or feature table; this skill requires raw protein sequences in FASTA to generate the clusterings being compared.

skills.description: Use when the analysis goal is to assess adaptation (alpha) for a whole gene set — e.g. genes grouped by recombination rate bins or chromosome localization — rather than gene-by-gene, and to test heterogeneity of selection among those genes.
skills.name: cmh-heterogeneity-testing
skills.search_text: cmh-heterogeneity-testing Use when the analysis goal is to assess adaptation (alpha) for a whole gene set — e.g. genes grouped by recombination rate bins or chromosome localization — rather than gene-by-gene, and to test heterogeneity of selection among those genes. The goal is to estimate alpha for each individual gene separately — the concatenate mode analyzes the selective regime for the whole gene set, not per gene The user has only a single gene or a single aggregated 2x2 MKT table and there is no per-gene stratification for the CMH statistic The question is which of the four MKT variants (standard MKT, FWWMKT, eMKT, aMKT) to run on one dataset without a multi-gene grouping hypothesis http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 iMKT's multi-gene (concatenate) analysis mode tests whether the selection regime is homogeneous across a user-selected set of protein-coding genes by applying the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic to per-gene MKT contingency tables, and quantifies uncertainty in the alpha estimate via a 100-replicate gene-resampling bootstrap 95% CI. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: iMKT's multi-gene (concatenate) analysis mode tests whether the selection regime is homogeneous across a user-selected set of protein-coding genes by applying the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel statistic to per-gene MKT contingency tables, and quantifies uncertainty in the alpha estimate via a 100-replicate gene-resampling bootstrap 95% CI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to estimate alpha for each individual gene separately — the concatenate mode analyzes the selective regime for the whole gene set, not per gene The user has only a single gene or a single aggregated 2x2 MKT table and there is no per-gene stratification for the CMH statistic The question is which of the four MKT variants (standard MKT, FWWMKT, eMKT, aMKT) to run on one dataset without a multi-gene grouping hypothesis

skills.description: Use when estimating abundances of de novo MAG clusters from shotgun metagenomics and needing to pick cluster-specific signature genes from a non-redundant gene count matrix before read-based abundance computation.
skills.name: co-abundance-correlation-ranking
skills.search_text: co-abundance-correlation-ranking Use when estimating abundances of de novo MAG clusters from shotgun metagenomics and needing to pick cluster-specific signature genes from a non-redundant gene count matrix before read-based abundance computation. Input is a database of pre-derived strain marker genes rather than de novo signature genes identified from the given data (cross-cohort transfer of signature genes can underestimate abundance, as seen for COPSAC2010 genes in the CHILD cohort). The MAG cluster is present in fewer than --min_samples samples, since signature gene refinement is not performed in that case. Fewer than --min_mapped_signature_genes signature genes are detected in a sample — the MAG cluster should be filtered from the analysis instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Ranks genes within each MAG cluster by co-abundance correlation across samples and selects an initial de novo signature gene set, then refines it with a rank-based negative binomial model of expected detected genes to enable accurate per-sample MAG abundance estimation. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-49958-8
skills.summary: Ranks genes within each MAG cluster by co-abundance correlation across samples and selects an initial de novo signature gene set, then refines it with a rank-based negative binomial model of expected detected genes to enable accurate per-sample MAG abundance estimation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a database of pre-derived strain marker genes rather than de novo signature genes identified from the given data (cross-cohort transfer of signature genes can underestimate abundance, as seen for COPSAC2010 genes in the CHILD cohort). The MAG cluster is present in fewer than --min_samples samples, since signature gene refinement is not performed in that case. Fewer than --min_mapped_signature_genes signature genes are detected in a sample — the MAG cluster should be filtered from the analysis instead.

skills.description: Use when you have assembled metagenomic contigs plus short reads from multiple samples grouped by the user and need to bin contigs into MAGs exploiting sample-wise co-abundance, or to estimate per-sample MAG abundances.
skills.name: co-abundance-genome-binning
skills.search_text: co-abundance-genome-binning Use when you have assembled metagenomic contigs plus short reads from multiple samples grouped by the user and need to bin contigs into MAGs exploiting sample-wise co-abundance, or to estimate per-sample MAG abundances. Input is raw reads without an assembly — this skill bins assembled contigs, it does not assemble them (nf-core/mag runs assembly upstream) Only a single sample with no group information is available, so no cross-sample co-abundance signal can be computed The goal is bin refinement or functional annotation — the article lists these as future additions, not part of this binning step http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstruct metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) by clustering assembled contigs with MetaBAT2, combining tetranucleotide nucleotide frequencies with co-abundance patterns computed across samples in the same group, as implemented in the nf-core/mag pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Reconstruct metagenome assembled genomes (MAGs) by clustering assembled contigs with MetaBAT2, combining tetranucleotide nucleotide frequencies with co-abundance patterns computed across samples in the same group, as implemented in the nf-core/mag pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads without an assembly — this skill bins assembled contigs, it does not assemble them (nf-core/mag runs assembly upstream) Only a single sample with no group information is available, so no cross-sample co-abundance signal can be computed The goal is bin refinement or functional annotation — the article lists these as future additions, not part of this binning step

skills.description: Use when multiple related metagenomic samples (e.g. a time series) should be assembled jointly per group rather than sample-wise, and assembly size, N50, or MAG counts are the target metrics.
skills.name: co-assembly-sample-grouping
skills.search_text: co-assembly-sample-grouping Use when multiple related metagenomic samples (e.g. a time series) should be assembled jointly per group rather than sample-wise, and assembly size, N50, or MAG counts are the target metrics. Samples are biologically unrelated and share no group information, so pooling would mix communities without depth benefit The analysis goal is per-sample genome-resolved profiles where sample-wise assembly (or binning using co-abundances) is required The input is already assembled contigs rather than raw FASTQ reads http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Pools metagenomic samples into user-defined groups for co-assembly with nf-core/mag, exploiting sample-wise group information to increase sequencing depth and improve assembly completeness and MAG recovery. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Pools metagenomic samples into user-defined groups for co-assembly with nf-core/mag, exploiting sample-wise group information to increase sequencing depth and improve assembly completeness and MAG recovery.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Samples are biologically unrelated and share no group information, so pooling would mix communities without depth benefit The analysis goal is per-sample genome-resolved profiles where sample-wise assembly (or binning using co-abundances) is required The input is already assembled contigs rather than raw FASTQ reads

skills.description: Use when starting from a genus-level OTU/counts table (otu_table.tsv with obs_metadata.tsv) and the goal is to infer interaction networks and quantify how much inferred edges/nodes agree across different NI methods.
skills.name: co-occurrence-network-inference
skills.search_text: co-occurrence-network-inference Use when starting from a genus-level OTU/counts table (otu_table.tsv with obs_metadata.tsv) and the goal is to infer interaction networks and quantify how much inferred edges/nodes agree across different NI methods. The input is raw 16S reads and denoising/clustering has not been performed — use the full or ta_op_ni workflow templates instead of 'ni' The analysis goal is comparing effects of upstream pipeline steps (DC, CC, TA, OP) rather than comparing NI methods on a fixed counts table Only a single inference method is desired with no cross-method comparison, in which case the ensemble bootstrap and intersection machinery is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Infer microbial co-occurrence networks from genus-level abundance tables by running multiple network inference (NI) tools under their defaults within the MiCoNE Nextflow pipeline, converting bootstrapped results into filtered networks at interaction_threshold 0.3 and pvalue_threshold 0.05 for downstream cross-method comparison. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00961-22
skills.summary: Infer microbial co-occurrence networks from genus-level abundance tables by running multiple network inference (NI) tools under their defaults within the MiCoNE Nextflow pipeline, converting bootstrapped results into filtered networks at interaction_threshold 0.3 and pvalue_threshold 0.05 for downstream cross-method comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is raw 16S reads and denoising/clustering has not been performed — use the full or ta_op_ni workflow templates instead of 'ni' The analysis goal is comparing effects of upstream pipeline steps (DC, CC, TA, OP) rather than comparing NI methods on a fixed counts table Only a single inference method is desired with no cross-method comparison, in which case the ensemble bootstrap and intersection machinery is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when you need to predict the isolate origins of novel insertion sequences (or other query sequences) by screening them against a large set of microbial genomes, and when you must attach ENA BioSample metadata and taxonomy to the hits.
skills.name: cobs-compact-index-querying
skills.search_text: cobs-compact-index-querying Use when you need to predict the isolate origins of novel insertion sequences (or other query sequences) by screening them against a large set of microbial genomes, and when you must attach ENA BioSample metadata and taxonomy to the hits. The goal is to discover novel ISs from metagenomic reads rather than trace known query sequences against genomes (use Palidis/pal-MEM discovery instead) The query sequences should be annotated against a curated reference IS database (ISfinder) rather than screened across raw isolate genomes Genomes of interest are not represented in the 661,405-genome ENA index, so absence of a hit would not be informative http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Query a FASTA catalogue of insertion sequences against a compact bit-sliced signature (COBS) index of 661,405 ENA microbial genomes to trace candidate origins of each IS, mapping positive genome hits back to ENA BioSample accessions and their taxonomic identities. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000917
skills.summary: Query a FASTA catalogue of insertion sequences against a compact bit-sliced signature (COBS) index of 661,405 ENA microbial genomes to trace candidate origins of each IS, mapping positive genome hits back to ENA BioSample accessions and their taxonomic identities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is to discover novel ISs from metagenomic reads rather than trace known query sequences against genomes (use Palidis/pal-MEM discovery instead) The query sequences should be annotated against a curated reference IS database (ISfinder) rather than screened across raw isolate genomes Genomes of interest are not represented in the 661,405-genome ENA index, so absence of a hit would not be informative

skills.description: Use when you have COBS query results (per-IS genome hit lists) against the 661,405 microbial isolate genomes and need to quantify how widely each IS is shared across genera/species or identify ISfinder coverage gaps.
skills.name: cobs-hit-table-parsing
skills.search_text: cobs-hit-table-parsing Use when you have COBS query results (per-IS genome hit lists) against the 661,405 microbial isolate genomes and need to quantify how widely each IS is shared across genera/species or identify ISfinder coverage gaps. Input is raw metagenomic reads or IS discovery output — use Palidis/palidis4 first to generate the ISC catalogue before querying COBS The ISs lack ITRs (Palidis/ISC only contains DDE-type ISs with ITRs of 25+ nucleotides), so COBS queries of such elements are out of scope You need de novo IS identification rather than prevalence/breadth statistics for already-identified ISs http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0798 Parse COBS sample-hits tables from the 661,405-genome index to compute taxonomic sharing breadth (distinct genera and species) for each ISC insertion sequence, using study metadata to map genome hits to taxonomy. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000917
skills.summary: Parse COBS sample-hits tables from the 661,405-genome index to compute taxonomic sharing breadth (distinct genera and species) for each ISC insertion sequence, using study metadata to map genome hits to taxonomy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw metagenomic reads or IS discovery output — use Palidis/palidis4 first to generate the ISC catalogue before querying COBS The ISs lack ITRs (Palidis/ISC only contains DDE-type ISs with ITRs of 25+ nucleotides), so COBS queries of such elements are out of scope You need de novo IS identification rather than prevalence/breadth statistics for already-identified ISs

skills.search_text: coefficient-of-determination-model-assessment Use when a fitted model (e.g. radar fixed-effects NMDS1 models) must be validated on independent external plots, and predicted-vs-observed agreement needs to be quantified as R² per taxon. Evaluating radar prediction of species richness or phylogenetic diversity for taxa driven by understorey development — C-band Sentinel-1 has weak permeability through overstorey layers and was shown to underperform for these biodiversity measures Extending the assessment to forest ecosystems outside temperate Central Europe — the five study regions only represent major temperate forest ecosystems of Central Europe, so generality elsewhere is untested Input is already a within-training-region model fit (use internal cross-validation there); this skill targets independent external validation data collected outside the training regions Assesses predictive performance of biodiversity models by computing the coefficient of determination (R²) between model-predicted and independently observed values — here, radar-model-predicted NMDS1 assemblage-composition scores against externally surveyed bird and saproxylic beetle plots outside the five training regions. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x

skills.search_text: cog-database-category-filtering Use when preparing the -nv (nonviral) and -v (viral) protein FASTA inputs for virMine 2.0, or when a bacterial-only protein reference with viral-origin sequences excluded is needed. When running virMine on long-read or pre-assembled contigs without needing to rebuild the reference databases — reuse the existing viral_aa.fasta and nonviral_aa.fasta instead When a nucleotide-level or RNA viral reference database is required — this skill produces protein FASTA only, from RefSeq eukaryotic viral/phage proteins and bacterial COG proteins http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Constructs the nonviral (bacterial) reference database used by virMine 2.0 by retrieving the 2020-release bacterial COG database and removing all sequences annotated as viral/phage origin (category X), yielding nonviral_aa.fasta; pairs with a RefSeq viral database (viral_aa.fasta) for contig origin scoring. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/mra.00107-22
skills.summary: Constructs the nonviral (bacterial) reference database used by virMine 2.0 by retrieving the 2020-release bacterial COG database and removing all sequences annotated as viral/phage origin (category X), yielding nonviral_aa.fasta; pairs with a RefSeq viral database (viral_aa.fasta) for contig origin scoring.

skills.description: Use when training or validating SVM phenotype predictors from comparative-genomics data: inputs are complete/partial bacterial genomes or COG presence/absence tables plus trait labels, and features must be assembled and completeness-screened.
skills.name: cog-feature-matrix-handling
skills.search_text: cog-feature-matrix-handling Use when training or validating SVM phenotype predictors from comparative-genomics data: inputs are complete/partial bacterial genomes or COG presence/absence tables plus trait labels, and features must be assembled and completeness-screened. Input is already a filtered, labeled feature table ready for the PICA/libSVM classifier — re-assembling matrices would be redundant. The trait cannot be learned from generic COG content: the article notes deeper interpretation requires additional specific models beyond the generic COG-based first layer. Genome completeness is far below the 60-70% level at which most traits remain reliably predictable and the 39/40 marker-COG screen fails. Build and prepare COG presence/absence feature matrices for SVM-based phenotypic trait prediction in the PICA framework, including applying marker-COG genome completeness screening before model training. The matrix rows are genomes and columns are COGs (e.g. 97 complete bacterial genomes against 30,455 COGs), with trait labels attached per genome. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Build and prepare COG presence/absence feature matrices for SVM-based phenotypic trait prediction in the PICA framework, including applying marker-COG genome completeness screening before model training. The matrix rows are genomes and columns are COGs (e.g. 97 complete bacterial genomes against 30,455 COGs), with trait labels attached per genome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered, labeled feature table ready for the PICA/libSVM classifier — re-assembling matrices would be redundant. The trait cannot be learned from generic COG content: the article notes deeper interpretation requires additional specific models beyond the generic COG-based first layer. Genome completeness is far below the 60-70% level at which most traits remain reliably predictable and the 39/40 marker-COG screen fails.

skills.description: Use when a trained PICA/libSVM linear-kernel phenotype model must be explained by ranking its COG features by signed weight, e.g. to test whether gene absence dominates a genome-reduction trait.
skills.name: cog-feature-sign-interpretation
skills.search_text: cog-feature-sign-interpretation Use when a trained PICA/libSVM linear-kernel phenotype model must be explained by ranking its COG features by signed weight, e.g. to test whether gene absence dominates a genome-reduction trait. Input is a raw genome sequence or metagenomic bin needing trait prediction rather than model interpretation (use phenotrex predict instead) The model uses a non-linear kernel, where a single interpretable signed weight vector per COG feature is not available Training data are incomplete genomes below the 60-70% completeness level the article reports as required for reliable prediction Extracts and interprets the signed SVM weight vector of a PICA (libSVM linear kernel) phenotype model to rank COG features by absolute weight, distinguishing presence-based (positive) from absence-based (negative) predictors of a trait such as obligate intracellular lifestyle. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Extracts and interprets the signed SVM weight vector of a PICA (libSVM linear kernel) phenotype model to rank COG features by absolute weight, distinguishing presence-based (positive) from absence-based (negative) predictors of a trait such as obligate intracellular lifestyle.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw genome sequence or metagenomic bin needing trait prediction rather than model interpretation (use phenotrex predict instead) The model uses a non-linear kernel, where a single interpretable signed weight vector per COG feature is not available Training data are incomplete genomes below the 60-70% completeness level the article reports as required for reliable prediction

skills.description: Use when applying a trained phenotype model (e.g. obligate intracellular prediction) to new species whose genomes are summarized as COG presence/absence profiles, and the model expects only its specific universal marker COG features (e.g. the 39/40 marker COGs) rather than the full eggNOG 4.
skills.name: cog-profile-feature-filtering
skills.search_text: cog-profile-feature-filtering Use when applying a trained phenotype model (e.g. obligate intracellular prediction) to new species whose genomes are summarized as COG presence/absence profiles, and the model expects only its specific universal marker COG features (e.g. the 39/40 marker COGs) rather than the full eggNOG 4. Input is already a filtered, model-compatible feature table containing only the universal marker COGs — re-filtering may drop or misalign required features. Genome completeness is below roughly 60-70%, since the paper reports most traits can only be reliably predicted in 60-70% complete genomes, so COG profiles will be too incomplete for reliable trait prediction. The goal is trait prediction from raw sequences or metagenomic bins rather than from COG presence/absence profiles of known species. http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Restricts COG presence/absence trait profiles (e.g. from eggNOG 4.0 core and periphery genomes) to the universal marker COGs used by a trained phenotype model, so that the PICA/libSVM classifier can score species consistently. This is the feature-space alignment step that enables applying a trained intracellular phenotype model across large genome databases. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Restricts COG presence/absence trait profiles (e.g. from eggNOG 4.0 core and periphery genomes) to the universal marker COGs used by a trained phenotype model, so that the PICA/libSVM classifier can score species consistently. This is the feature-space alignment step that enables applying a trained intracellular phenotype model across large genome databases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered, model-compatible feature table containing only the universal marker COGs — re-filtering may drop or misalign required features. Genome completeness is below roughly 60-70%, since the paper reports most traits can only be reliably predicted in 60-70% complete genomes, so COG profiles will be too incomplete for reliable trait prediction. The goal is trait prediction from raw sequences or metagenomic bins rather than from COG presence/absence profiles of known species.

skills.description: Use when assessing the robustness of COG/SVM-based phenotypic trait predictors to genome incompleteness, e.g. before applying trait models to incomplete metagenomic bins.
skills.name: cog-profile-perturbation
skills.search_text: cog-profile-perturbation Use when assessing the robustness of COG/SVM-based phenotypic trait predictors to genome incompleteness, e.g. before applying trait models to incomplete metagenomic bins. The input genomes are already complete reference genomes and the goal is final trait annotation rather than robustness assessment — near-complete genomes can be annotated directly with PICA without perturbation The features are not COG presence/absence profiles (e.g. raw FASTQ reads or un-annotated contigs); first map genes to eggNOG/COG to build profiles before thinning The prediction pipeline is not profile-based (e.g. sequence-homology or k-mer methods); removing random COG entries would not represent its natural incompleteness mode Simulates incomplete genomes by randomly deleting x% (x = 10–90, in steps of 10) of the eggNOG 4.0 COG presence/absence entries per genome profile (3 replicates per level), producing PICA-compatible thinned profiles used to test SVM-based phenotypic trait prediction on partial genomes such as metagenomic bins. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Simulates incomplete genomes by randomly deleting x% (x = 10–90, in steps of 10) of the eggNOG 4.0 COG presence/absence entries per genome profile (3 replicates per level), producing PICA-compatible thinned profiles used to test SVM-based phenotypic trait prediction on partial genomes such as metagenomic bins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input genomes are already complete reference genomes and the goal is final trait annotation rather than robustness assessment — near-complete genomes can be annotated directly with PICA without perturbation The features are not COG presence/absence profiles (e.g. raw FASTQ reads or un-annotated contigs); first map genes to eggNOG/COG to build profiles before thinning The prediction pipeline is not profile-based (e.g. sequence-homology or k-mer methods); removing random COG entries would not represent its natural incompleteness mode

skills.description: Use when you have sample-level metadata (continent, country, sample source, disease status) plus paired fungal and bacterial taxonomic profiles and need to isolate a specific cohort before per-cohort modeling or network analysis.
skills.name: cohort-stratified-sample-subsetting

The input table already contains only a single pre-defined cohort and no further stratification is needed The metadata lacks any of the stratification fields (continent, country, sample source, disease status), making cohort definition ambiguous The goal is a pan-cohort (all 2,679 samples) analysis rather than a cohort-specific comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 Stratifies the 2,679-sample human metagenome collection into well-defined clinical/demographic cohorts (e.g. healthy Danish gut, healthy Spanish gut) by filtering sample metadata, so that downstream per-cohort analyses such as SparCC inter-kingdom correlation are run on matched fungal (FunOMIC-T) and bacterial (MetaPhlAn) profile tables. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: Stratifies the 2,679-sample human metagenome collection into well-defined clinical/demographic cohorts (e.g. healthy Danish gut, healthy Spanish gut) by filtering sample metadata, so that downstream per-cohort analyses such as SparCC inter-kingdom correlation are run on matched fungal (FunOMIC-T) and bacterial (MetaPhlAn) profile tables.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input table already contains only a single pre-defined cohort and no further stratification is needed The metadata lacks any of the stratification fields (continent, country, sample source, disease status), making cohort definition ambiguous The goal is a pan-cohort (all 2,679 samples) analysis rather than a cohort-specific comparison

skills.description: Use when raw nanopore signal seed matches (hash-table lookup hits) must be converted into a single mapping position for a read, i.e., when reconstructing the RawHash mapping step over seed matches from a hash index like ref.ind.
skills.name: colinear-seed-chaining
skills.search_text: colinear-seed-chaining Use when raw nanopore signal seed matches (hash-table lookup hits) must be converted into a single mapping position for a read, i.e., when reconstructing the RawHash mapping step over seed matches from a hash index like ref.ind. When no reference-genome hash index exists yet — the chaining step requires seed matches retrieved from the index built in the indexing step. When overlaps between raw signals are needed without a reference genome (all-vs-all overlapping) — use Rawsamble instead of reference-guided chaining. When base-level alignment of the raw signal is required — chaining yields only approximate mapping coordinates, not signal-level DTW alignment. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Converts matching seed hash values between a raw nanopore signal and a reference genome into a mapped region by chaining them into the best colinear chain, using Sigmap's chaining algorithm with the distance coefficient disabled. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Converts matching seed hash values between a raw nanopore signal and a reference genome into a mapped region by chaining them into the best colinear chain, using Sigmap's chaining algorithm with the distance coefficient disabled.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When no reference-genome hash index exists yet — the chaining step requires seed matches retrieved from the index built in the indexing step. When overlaps between raw signals are needed without a reference genome (all-vs-all overlapping) — use Rawsamble instead of reference-guided chaining. When base-level alignment of the raw signal is required — chaining yields only approximate mapping coordinates, not signal-level DTW alignment.

skills.description: Use when comparing metagenomic sample groups (e.g., healthy vs adenoma vs carcinoma) to identify taxa, genes, KOs, EC numbers, or reactions that differ significantly across phenotypes in a mapping-based analysis.
skills.name: colorectal-cancer-metagenome-phenotype-comparison
skills.search_text: colorectal-cancer-metagenome-phenotype-comparison Use when comparing metagenomic sample groups (e.g., healthy vs adenoma vs carcinoma) to identify taxa, genes, KOs, EC numbers, or reactions that differ significantly across phenotypes in a mapping-based analysis. Input is raw unmapped reads or assemblies — normalization and frequency tables from the mapping/CSS stages of CAMAMED must already exist The study design is single-cohort with no case-control group structure to compare across A compositional-bias-aware differential method suited to the specific hypothesis is required but the data have not passed through CSS correction; the article found results from the two colorectal cancer datasets were not consistent without applying the CSS http://edamontology.org/topic_3941 Reconstructs CAMAMED's comparative case-control analysis stage: loading CSS-normalized five-level frequency tables (taxon, gene, KO, EC number, reaction), testing each feature across healthy/adenoma/carcinoma groups with the Kruskal-Wallis H test (or ANOVA when normality is acceptable), and applying Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to flag significantly changed components and potential biomarkers. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa107
skills.summary: Reconstructs CAMAMED's comparative case-control analysis stage: loading CSS-normalized five-level frequency tables (taxon, gene, KO, EC number, reaction), testing each feature across healthy/adenoma/carcinoma groups with the Kruskal-Wallis H test (or ANOVA when normality is acceptable), and applying Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction to flag significantly changed components and potential biomarkers.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw unmapped reads or assemblies — normalization and frequency tables from the mapping/CSS stages of CAMAMED must already exist The study design is single-cohort with no case-control group structure to compare across A compositional-bias-aware differential method suited to the specific hypothesis is required but the data have not passed through CSS correction; the article found results from the two colorectal cancer datasets were not consistent without applying the CSS

skills.description: Use when building a compact pangenome/colored de Bruijn graph from a panel of highly similar FASTA sequences (e.g., the 12 human mitogenomes, or 5k/20k simulated panels) as the input substrate for cSupB decomposition and variant detection.
skills.name: colored-de-bruijn-graph-construction
skills.search_text: colored-de-bruijn-graph-construction Use when building a compact pangenome/colored de Bruijn graph from a panel of highly similar FASTA sequences (e.g., the 12 human mitogenomes, or 5k/20k simulated panels) as the input substrate for cSupB decomposition and variant detection. Input sequences have insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number), which the article states makes the variant detection model inapplicable The dataset contains highly repetitive sequences (especially tandem repeats), where the sequence-cutting/graph reconstruction step fragments sequences too much The goal requires handling degeneracy or structural variants such as large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications, which the method cannot address efficiently http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Constructs a colored de Bruijn graph from multiple haplotype sequences (e.g., human mitochondrial genomes) using VARI-merge at a k-mer size chosen to exceed the maximum longest repeat segment length, yielding a directed, acyclic, nondegenerate graph with unique start and end nodes suitable for downstream cSupB decomposition. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Constructs a colored de Bruijn graph from multiple haplotype sequences (e.g., human mitochondrial genomes) using VARI-merge at a k-mer size chosen to exceed the maximum longest repeat segment length, yielding a directed, acyclic, nondegenerate graph with unique start and end nodes suitable for downstream cSupB decomposition.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences have insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number), which the article states makes the variant detection model inapplicable The dataset contains highly repetitive sequences (especially tandem repeats), where the sequence-cutting/graph reconstruction step fragments sequences too much The goal requires handling degeneracy or structural variants such as large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications, which the method cannot address efficiently

skills.description: Use when a colored de Bruijn graph built from highly similar sequences (e.g., mitochondrial pangenomes) must be decomposed into nested, population-specific superbubble structures to enable coordinate assignment or variant detection.
skills.name: colored-superbubble-decomposition
skills.search_text: colored-superbubble-decomposition Use when a colored de Bruijn graph built from highly similar sequences (e.g., mitochondrial pangenomes) must be decomposed into nested, population-specific superbubble structures to enable coordinate assignment or variant detection. The input samples are not highly similar (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on cSupB is not applicable when sequence similarity is insufficient Sequences are highly repetitive, especially tandem repeats — the cutting-based reconstruction fragments sequences excessively, increasing computational difficulty and error The graph contains degeneracy or the gene elements are shorter than k — degeneracy cannot be handled efficiently and short elements map to multiple ambiguous nodes http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Decomposition of a colored de Bruijn graph into colored superbubbles (cSupBs) via a postorder-like traversal, reorganized into a hierarchical cSupB tree. This overcomes graph complexity and organizes species- or population-specific haplotype sequences into a tri-tuple coordinate system (position, bubid, basecolor). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Decomposition of a colored de Bruijn graph into colored superbubbles (cSupBs) via a postorder-like traversal, reorganized into a hierarchical cSupB tree. This overcomes graph complexity and organizes species- or population-specific haplotype sequences into a tri-tuple coordinate system (position, bubid, basecolor).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input samples are not highly similar (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on cSupB is not applicable when sequence similarity is insufficient Sequences are highly repetitive, especially tandem repeats — the cutting-based reconstruction fragments sequences excessively, increasing computational difficulty and error The graph contains degeneracy or the gene elements are shorter than k — degeneracy cannot be handled efficiently and short elements map to multiple ambiguous nodes

skills.description: Use when a VARI-merge constructed colored de Bruijn graph (.dbg + .colors.sd_vector) must be decomposed into sample-specific colored superbubbles and organized into a tree to support a tri-tuple coordinate system or nested variant detection.
skills.name: colored-superbubble-matching
skills.search_text: colored-superbubble-matching Use when a VARI-merge constructed colored de Bruijn graph (.dbg + .colors.sd_vector) must be decomposed into sample-specific colored superbubbles and organized into a tree to support a tri-tuple coordinate system or nested variant detection. The input is not a colored directed graph usable as directed, acyclic, nondegenerate with unique start and end nodes (e.g. degeneracy must be resolved elsewhere; the paper states 'we cannot handle degeneracy efficiently') Sample similarity is insufficient (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on the cSupB tree is not applicable You need to detect large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications — the downstream variant detection only addresses small indels (< 50 bp) in highly similar samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3678 Implements the cSupB decomposition of a colored de Bruijn graph: a single postorder-like traversal pairs source/sink nodes by the colored-edge intersection matching principle, then reorganizes the resulting colored superbubbles into the hierarchical cSupB tree that underlies the tri-tuple coordinate system (offset value, topological structure, sample information). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Implements the cSupB decomposition of a colored de Bruijn graph: a single postorder-like traversal pairs source/sink nodes by the colored-edge intersection matching principle, then reorganizes the resulting colored superbubbles into the hierarchical cSupB tree that underlies the tri-tuple coordinate system (offset value, topological structure, sample information).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not a colored directed graph usable as directed, acyclic, nondegenerate with unique start and end nodes (e.g. degeneracy must be resolved elsewhere; the paper states 'we cannot handle degeneracy efficiently') Sample similarity is insufficient (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on the cSupB tree is not applicable You need to detect large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications — the downstream variant detection only addresses small indels (< 50 bp) in highly similar samples

skills.description: Use when a two-group microbiome abundance table must be tested for association robustness across progressively mixed label permutations rather than a single global permutation test.
skills.name: combinatorial-scenario-enumeration
skills.search_text: combinatorial-scenario-enumeration Use when a two-group microbiome abundance table must be tested for association robustness across progressively mixed label permutations rather than a single global permutation test. The grouping factor has more than two levels — the progressive label-exchange scheme (bin_exchange, K=min(n1,n2)) is defined for binary outcomes only You need formal inference such as FDR-controlled adjusted p-values — the paper states the method 'does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values' Input is not a raw feature-by-sample count table with a binary outcome (e.g. already-permuted or summarized results) — scenario enumeration requires the original group labels http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Enumerates progressive label-mixing permutation scenarios for a two-group microbiome dataset, computing scenario bounds K=min(n1,n2) and Kf=ceil((n1*n2-1)/(n1+n2+2)) via the Vandermonde identity, and drawing label exchanges per scenario to enable differential testing under controlled mixing. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Enumerates progressive label-mixing permutation scenarios for a two-group microbiome dataset, computing scenario bounds K=min(n1,n2) and Kf=ceil((n1*n2-1)/(n1+n2+2)) via the Vandermonde identity, and drawing label exchanges per scenario to enable differential testing under controlled mixing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The grouping factor has more than two levels — the progressive label-exchange scheme (bin_exchange, K=min(n1,n2)) is defined for binary outcomes only You need formal inference such as FDR-controlled adjusted p-values — the paper states the method 'does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values' Input is not a raw feature-by-sample count table with a binary outcome (e.g. already-permuted or summarized results) — scenario enumeration requires the original group labels

skills.search_text: command-line-pipeline-execution Use when a large FASTA protein set (thousands to >190,000 (meta)genomic records) must be screened from the command line against an HMM library, with configurable output separator, prefixes, threads, and sequence extraction. skills.search_text: command-line-pipeline-execution Use when a task requires running the STEMSim simulator end-to-end from the command line, or reproducing its reported throughput benchmark (~1 million reads in ~3 minutes on a 2.40 GHz server CPU). The goal is de novo community abundance simulation — use CAMISIM itself; STEMSim consumes CAMISIM output rather than generating communities. The input is real metagenomic data from species with low depth or poorly characterized genomes — the README warns STEMSim 'only works well on species with high depth and well-characterized genomes'.
