skills.search_text: command-line-r-script-development Use when building reproducible R analysis scripts that consume ranked abundance summary tables and must emit statistical result tables (p-value, log2FoldChange) plus graphical outputs, invoked via Rscript from a shell. Input is still per-read DIAMOND annotation output — it must first be condensed into ranked abundance summaries by DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py The goal is raw read preprocessing (adaptor trimming, rRNA removal) — that belongs to the Trimmomatic/SortMeRNA preprocessing stage, not the R analysis stage The analysis must run under Python 3 only — SAMSA2's aggregation scripts require Python 2, though the R stage itself is independent http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Develop R scripts that run from the command line to perform statistical and graphical analysis of abundance count tables, as exemplified by the SAMSA2 analysis stage where DESeq-based scripts produce p-values, log2FoldChange scores, PCA plots, heatmaps, and stacked-bar graphs. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: Develop R scripts that run from the command line to perform statistical and graphical analysis of abundance count tables, as exemplified by the SAMSA2 analysis stage where DESeq-based scripts produce p-values, log2FoldChange scores, PCA plots, heatmaps, and stacked-bar graphs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is still per-read DIAMOND annotation output — it must first be condensed into ranked abundance summaries by DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py The goal is raw read preprocessing (adaptor trimming, rRNA removal) — that belongs to the Trimmomatic/SortMeRNA preprocessing stage, not the R analysis stage The analysis must run under Python 3 only — SAMSA2's aggregation scripts require Python 2, though the R stage itself is independent

skills.description: Use when several de novo assemblers (e.g. PEHaplo, SPAdes, SAVAGE, SGA) have been run on the same input reads and their contigs must be benchmarked against known reference haplotypes with MetaQUAST.
skills.name: comparative-assembly-table-compilation
skills.search_text: comparative-assembly-table-compilation Use when several de novo assemblers (e.g. PEHaplo, SPAdes, SAVAGE, SGA) have been run on the same input reads and their contigs must be benchmarked against known reference haplotypes with MetaQUAST. The contigs come from different, non-identical read sets — cross-assembler comparison on unequal inputs invalidates the benchmark The goal is abundance or variant calling rather than strain-level assembly quality benchmarking No reference haplotypes are available, so MetaQUAST coverage/completeness metrics cannot be computed http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Compiles MetaQUAST evaluation metrics (N50, genome coverage, contig count, mismatch rate) from multiple de novo assemblers run on the identical recruited read set into a single comparative TSV table, so assembler performance can be judged side-by-side. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2878-2
skills.summary: Compiles MetaQUAST evaluation metrics (N50, genome coverage, contig count, mismatch rate) from multiple de novo assemblers run on the identical recruited read set into a single comparative TSV table, so assembler performance can be judged side-by-side.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The contigs come from different, non-identical read sets — cross-assembler comparison on unequal inputs invalidates the benchmark The goal is abundance or variant calling rather than strain-level assembly quality benchmarking No reference haplotypes are available, so MetaQUAST coverage/completeness metrics cannot be computed

skills.description: Use when predicting biological phenotypes or ecological roles of uncharacterized microbial genomes or metagenomic bins from COG presence/absence profiles, or when benchmarking SVM-only vs CPAR2SVM phenotype classifiers.
skills.name: comparative-genomics-cog-profile-classification
skills.search_text: comparative-genomics-cog-profile-classification Use when predicting biological phenotypes or ecological roles of uncharacterized microbial genomes or metagenomic bins from COG presence/absence profiles, or when benchmarking SVM-only vs CPAR2SVM phenotype classifiers. Genome completeness is well below 60-70% — the article reports most traits can be reliably predicted only in 60-70% complete genomes Sufficient training data are unavailable for the ecologically important trait of interest — the article notes performance for further traits is pending availability of training data Input is already a raw phenotype annotation requiring no COG-profile-based inference http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Predicts microbial phenotypic traits (e.g. aerobe, motile, thermophile) from eggNOG COG presence/absence profiles using the PICA framework's machine-learning plug-ins, comparing pure libSVM classification against CPAR association-rule feature selection followed by SVM. Purely SVM-based classification achieves equal predictive quality at roughly three times lower runtime than the CPAR2SVM hybrid. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Predicts microbial phenotypic traits (e.g. aerobe, motile, thermophile) from eggNOG COG presence/absence profiles using the PICA framework's machine-learning plug-ins, comparing pure libSVM classification against CPAR association-rule feature selection followed by SVM. Purely SVM-based classification achieves equal predictive quality at roughly three times lower runtime than the CPAR2SVM hybrid.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Genome completeness is well below 60-70% — the article reports most traits can be reliably predicted only in 60-70% complete genomes Sufficient training data are unavailable for the ecologically important trait of interest — the article notes performance for further traits is pending availability of training data Input is already a raw phenotype annotation requiring no COG-profile-based inference

skills.description: Use when placing 16S/SSU rRNA sequences (e.g. assembled metagenome contigs or SILVA records) into a reference structural alignment, detecting insertions as alignment gaps, or preparing intron-stripped rRNA sequences for phylogeny.
skills.name: comparative-rna-structural-alignment
skills.search_text: comparative-rna-structural-alignment Use when placing 16S/SSU rRNA sequences (e.g. assembled metagenome contigs or SILVA records) into a reference structural alignment, detecting insertions as alignment gaps, or preparing intron-stripped rRNA sequences for phylogeny. Aligning protein-coding or non-rRNA sequences — the covariance model and gap-based insertion logic are specific to SSU rRNA structure When the goal is amplicon primer coverage estimation rather than structural placement or insertion detection (use primer binding analysis instead) Sequences shorter than the ≥800 bp aligned-residue cutoff used for phylogenetic analysis in this study http://edamontology.org/topic_0097 Align rRNA gene sequences against a manually curated structural (covariance-model) alignment to place them accurately despite divergent or intron-disrupted sequences. In this study it underpins both reliable CPR phylogeny and the survey of ≥10 bp insertions in bacterial 16S rRNA genes. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486
skills.summary: Align rRNA gene sequences against a manually curated structural (covariance-model) alignment to place them accurately despite divergent or intron-disrupted sequences. In this study it underpins both reliable CPR phylogeny and the survey of ≥10 bp insertions in bacterial 16S rRNA genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Aligning protein-coding or non-rRNA sequences — the covariance model and gap-based insertion logic are specific to SSU rRNA structure When the goal is amplicon primer coverage estimation rather than structural placement or insertion detection (use primer binding analysis instead) Sequences shorter than the ≥800 bp aligned-residue cutoff used for phylogenetic analysis in this study

skills.description: Use when a new host-depletion or filtering tool must be validated against an existing comparator on identical inputs, and retention/precision metrics such as microbial reads retained must be quantified and compared.
skills.name: comparator-tool-performance-evaluation
skills.search_text: comparator-tool-performance-evaluation Use when a new host-depletion or filtering tool must be validated against an existing comparator on identical inputs, and retention/precision metrics such as microbial reads retained must be quantified and compared. Evaluating host-read removal sensitivity on real human reads (e.g. 1000 Genomes Project samples) rather than microbial retention on simulated bacterial reads Benchmarking masked-index variants (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985) where the expected retention differs (≥99.997%) from the unmasked-index comparator values Scenarios where input reads are not held fixed across tools, making retention percentages non-comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark a candidate host-read removal tool (e.g. Hostile) against an established comparator (NCBI HRRT/sra-human-scrubber) by running both on the same read set and computing microbial read retention, as done for simulated ONT reads from 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial genomes. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Benchmark a candidate host-read removal tool (e.g. Hostile) against an established comparator (NCBI HRRT/sra-human-scrubber) by running both on the same read set and computing microbial read retention, as done for simulated ONT reads from 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial genomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluating host-read removal sensitivity on real human reads (e.g. 1000 Genomes Project samples) rather than microbial retention on simulated bacterial reads Benchmarking masked-index variants (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985) where the expected retention differs (≥99.997%) from the unmasked-index comparator values Scenarios where input reads are not held fixed across tools, making retention percentages non-comparable

skills.description: Use when computing core genomes from MAGs/SAGs of diverse completeness: completeness priors must be supplied so the Bayesian estimator can weigh presence/absence patterns per genome.
skills.name: completeness-estimation-from-mags
skills.search_text: completeness-estimation-from-mags Use when computing core genomes from MAGs/SAGs of diverse completeness: completeness priors must be supplied so the Bayesian estimator can weigh presence/absence patterns per genome. Genomes are high-quality complete isolates only — Roary or PPanGGOLiN are validated comparators for high-quality genomes No completeness information is available and genomes are of unknown, potentially wildly wrong quality — the prior drives the core/accessory likelihoods, so a bad prior corrupts the partitioning The goal is OTU clustering rather than core-genome estimation — use mOTUlize.py instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Establishes genome completeness priors (e.g. from CheckM output or fixed values) for MAGs/SAGs of varying quality, which mOTUpan uses as the basis of its iterative Bayesian core/accessory likelihood estimation. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac060
skills.summary: Establishes genome completeness priors (e.g. from CheckM output or fixed values) for MAGs/SAGs of varying quality, which mOTUpan uses as the basis of its iterative Bayesian core/accessory likelihood estimation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Genomes are high-quality complete isolates only — Roary or PPanGGOLiN are validated comparators for high-quality genomes No completeness information is available and genomes are of unknown, potentially wildly wrong quality — the prior drives the core/accessory likelihoods, so a bad prior corrupts the partitioning The goal is OTU clustering rather than core-genome estimation — use mOTUlize.py instead

skills.description: Use when estimating core genomes from genome sets of mixed or low quality (e.g. CheckM-estimated MAG completeness along a completeness scale) and you need the completeness prior refined from the data rather than fixed.
skills.name: completeness-prior-iterative-refinement
skills.search_text: completeness-prior-iterative-refinement Use when estimating core genomes from genome sets of mixed or low quality (e.g. CheckM-estimated MAG completeness along a completeness scale) and you need the completeness prior refined from the data rather than fixed. Genome set consists only of high-quality complete genomes where simpler presence/absence tools like Roary's default core-definition suffice You need OTU clustering and genome quality statistics rather than core-genome partitioning — use mOTUlize.py instead You have no completeness prior available (no CheckM output or fixed value) and cannot justify the Bayesian prior assumption http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 An iterative Bayesian scheme in mOTUpan where the gene-cluster core/accessory partitioning is used to update each genome's completeness prior, which is then re-fed into the likelihood computation until convergence, making core-genome estimation robust to incomplete MAGs/SAGs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac060
skills.summary: An iterative Bayesian scheme in mOTUpan where the gene-cluster core/accessory partitioning is used to update each genome's completeness prior, which is then re-fed into the likelihood computation until convergence, making core-genome estimation robust to incomplete MAGs/SAGs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Genome set consists only of high-quality complete genomes where simpler presence/absence tools like Roary's default core-definition suffice You need OTU clustering and genome quality statistics rather than core-genome partitioning — use mOTUlize.py instead You have no completeness prior available (no CheckM output or fixed value) and cannot justify the Bayesian prior assumption

skills.description: Use when phased, filtered biallelic SNP VCFs split by chromosome are available and you need single-population selective-sweep scans that complement haplotype-based iHS/XP-EHH analyses.
skills.name: composite-likelihood-ratio-sweep-detection
skills.search_text: composite-likelihood-ratio-sweep-detection Use when phased, filtered biallelic SNP VCFs split by chromosome are available and you need single-population selective-sweep scans that complement haplotype-based iHS/XP-EHH analyses. The goal is pair-wise population-comparison-based sweep detection (XP-EHH) rather than single-population scans — XP-EHH is computed with selscan instead Data are unphased multiallelic variants — the sub-workflow requires biallelic SNPs phased with Beagle/SHAPEIT5 before the selection scans No population structure/mapping is available — SweepFinder2 is run per population, so a sample.map of individual-to-population assignments is required http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3056 Run SweepFinder2 v1.0.0 per population within the scalepopgen signatures-of-selection sub-workflow to compute the composite likelihood ratio (Kim and Stephan 2002) along the genome, detecting recent selective sweeps from biallelic SNP data. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/molbev/msae057
skills.summary: Run SweepFinder2 v1.0.0 per population within the scalepopgen signatures-of-selection sub-workflow to compute the composite likelihood ratio (Kim and Stephan 2002) along the genome, detecting recent selective sweeps from biallelic SNP data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is pair-wise population-comparison-based sweep detection (XP-EHH) rather than single-population scans — XP-EHH is computed with selscan instead Data are unphased multiallelic variants — the sub-workflow requires biallelic SNPs phased with Beagle/SHAPEIT5 before the selection scans No population structure/mapping is available — SweepFinder2 is run per population, so a sample.map of individual-to-population assignments is required

skills.description: Use when you have a genus-level OTU/counts table and need to compare networks inferred by multiple compositional-aware inference methods, e.g. to quantify shared vs. unique nodes and edges (UpSet overlap) across methods.
skills.name: compositional-correlation-network-construction
skills.search_text: compositional-correlation-network-construction Use when you have a genus-level OTU/counts table and need to compare networks inferred by multiple compositional-aware inference methods, e.g. to quantify shared vs. unique nodes and edges (UpSet overlap) across methods. Input is raw 16S sequencing reads requiring demultiplexing, trimming, chimera checking, or OTU assignment — use the MiCoNE 'full' pipeline instead of the 'ni' template. Only a single inference method is required and cross-method robustness/consensus assessment is not a goal. The dataset lacks the taxonomy columns needed to group nodes at the genus level. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Construct microbial co-occurrence networks from genus-level OTU/count tables using eight network inference methods (SparCC, propr, SpiecEasi, FlashWeave, COZINE, HARMONIES, SPRING, mLDM) within the MiCoNE pipeline, then quantify node/edge agreement across methods with UpSet-style intersection analysis to expose method-driven rewiring. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00961-22
skills.summary: Construct microbial co-occurrence networks from genus-level OTU/count tables using eight network inference methods (SparCC, propr, SpiecEasi, FlashWeave, COZINE, HARMONIES, SPRING, mLDM) within the MiCoNE pipeline, then quantify node/edge agreement across methods with UpSet-style intersection analysis to expose method-driven rewiring.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw 16S sequencing reads requiring demultiplexing, trimming, chimera checking, or OTU assignment — use the MiCoNE 'full' pipeline instead of the 'ni' template. Only a single inference method is required and cross-method robustness/consensus assessment is not a goal. The dataset lacks the taxonomy columns needed to group nodes at the genus level.

skills.description: Use when selecting or validating a longitudinal differential-abundance method for high-dimensional microbiome count data with multiple covariates, and you need empirical runtime/memory/accuracy comparisons against ANCOM, lgpr, ZIBR or MaAsLin2.
skills.name: compositional-count-data-tool-comparison
skills.search_text: compositional-count-data-tool-comparison Use when selecting or validating a longitudinal differential-abundance method for high-dimensional microbiome count data with multiple covariates, and you need empirical runtime/memory/accuracy comparisons against ANCOM, lgpr, ZIBR or MaAsLin2. The dataset is cross-sectional with no time or repeated-measurement dimension — this skill is specific to longitudinal designs where time proxies treatment The goal is to compare tool statistical accuracy alone without profiling runtime/memory cost — the benchmarking machinery here centers on the 96 h timeout and memory bottlenecks Data are not compositional count/abundance microbiome measurements (e.g. raw RNA-seq or imaging data) since the compared tools assume OTU/SV-style absolute abundance tables Benchmark LongDat against competing longitudinal differential-abundance tools (MaAsLin2, ANCOM, lgpr, ZIBR) on microbiomeDASim-simulated multi-covariate count data, profiling accuracy alongside runtime and memory bottlenecks (e.g. ANCOM ~350 GB, ZIBR ~55 h, lgpr ~65 h). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad063
skills.summary: Benchmark LongDat against competing longitudinal differential-abundance tools (MaAsLin2, ANCOM, lgpr, ZIBR) on microbiomeDASim-simulated multi-covariate count data, profiling accuracy alongside runtime and memory bottlenecks (e.g. ANCOM ~350 GB, ZIBR ~55 h, lgpr ~65 h).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is cross-sectional with no time or repeated-measurement dimension — this skill is specific to longitudinal designs where time proxies treatment The goal is to compare tool statistical accuracy alone without profiling runtime/memory cost — the benchmarking machinery here centers on the 96 h timeout and memory bottlenecks Data are not compositional count/abundance microbiome measurements (e.g. raw RNA-seq or imaging data) since the compared tools assume OTU/SV-style absolute abundance tables

skills.description: Use when you have two compositional taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. fungal profiles from FunOMIC-T and bacterial profiles from MetaPhlAn) over matched samples and need statistically filtered cross-kingdom correlation edges.
skills.name: compositional-data-correlation-estimation
skills.search_text: compositional-data-correlation-estimation Use when you have two compositional taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. fungal profiles from FunOMIC-T and bacterial profiles from MetaPhlAn) over matched samples and need statistically filtered cross-kingdom correlation edges. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than taxonomic profile tables — profile first with FunOMIC (bowtie2 vs FunOMIC-T) and MetaPhlAn before correlating The analysis targets within-kingdom (fungus–fungus or bacterium–bacterium) correlations rather than the inter-kingdom fungus–bacterium networks this skill builds Samples include diseased or mixed-disease cohorts — the reported 4,184 and 3,471 edge counts are specific to the healthy Danish and healthy Spanish gut subsets; do not expect these counts outside them http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Estimate inter-kingdom (fungal–bacterial) correlations from compositional taxonomic profiles using SparCC, as applied in FunOMIC to healthy Danish and Spanish gut cohorts to build correlation networks of mycobiome–bacteriome interactions. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: Estimate inter-kingdom (fungal–bacterial) correlations from compositional taxonomic profiles using SparCC, as applied in FunOMIC to healthy Danish and Spanish gut cohorts to build correlation networks of mycobiome–bacteriome interactions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than taxonomic profile tables — profile first with FunOMIC (bowtie2 vs FunOMIC-T) and MetaPhlAn before correlating The analysis targets within-kingdom (fungus–fungus or bacterium–bacterium) correlations rather than the inter-kingdom fungus–bacterium networks this skill builds Samples include diseased or mixed-disease cohorts — the reported 4,184 and 3,471 edge counts are specific to the healthy Danish and healthy Spanish gut subsets; do not expect these counts outside them

skills.description: Use when metagenomic count data (taxa or gene-level abundance tables from case-control studies) is sparse and compositional, and differential abundance markers must be comparable or reproducible across independent datasets.
skills.name: compositional-data-css-normalization
skills.search_text: compositional-data-css-normalization Use when metagenomic count data (taxa or gene-level abundance tables from case-control studies) is sparse and compositional, and differential abundance markers must be comparable or reproducible across independent datasets. Input data is not sparse compositional count data (e.g., already normalized relative abundances or non-metagenomic expression tables) — CSS correction targets compositional bias in metagenomic count tables No differential abundance or biomarker identification is intended and only raw mapping/gene frequency computation is needed — run the CAMAMED taxonomic/functional profiling stages without the CSS+metagenomeSeq step The sample size is very small and high metagenomeSeq false-positive rates are a concern; the article notes metagenomeSeq has a high false-positive rate for differential abundance analysis when the sample size is small http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 A compositional data analysis (CoDA) skill from CAMAMED that applies cumulative sum-scaling (CSS) normalization to sparse metagenomic abundance tables at taxon, gene, KO, EC number, and reaction levels before zero-inflated metagenomeSeq differential abundance testing, correcting composition bias that otherwise makes case-control biomarker findings irreproducible across datasets. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa107
skills.summary: A compositional data analysis (CoDA) skill from CAMAMED that applies cumulative sum-scaling (CSS) normalization to sparse metagenomic abundance tables at taxon, gene, KO, EC number, and reaction levels before zero-inflated metagenomeSeq differential abundance testing, correcting composition bias that otherwise makes case-control biomarker findings irreproducible across datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data is not sparse compositional count data (e.g., already normalized relative abundances or non-metagenomic expression tables) — CSS correction targets compositional bias in metagenomic count tables No differential abundance or biomarker identification is intended and only raw mapping/gene frequency computation is needed — run the CAMAMED taxonomic/functional profiling stages without the CSS+metagenomeSeq step The sample size is very small and high metagenomeSeq false-positive rates are a concern; the article notes metagenomeSeq has a high false-positive rate for differential abundance analysis when the sample size is small

skills.description: Use when KO-level read-count or relative-abundance tables from shotgun metagenomic annotation must be converted to compositionally meaningful per-genome copy numbers before downstream functional comparisons.
skills.name: compositional-data-normalization
skills.search_text: compositional-data-normalization Use when KO-level read-count or relative-abundance tables from shotgun metagenomic annotation must be converted to compositionally meaningful per-genome copy numbers before downstream functional comparisons. When the goal is plain relative-abundance normalization rather than per-genome copy-number correction — MetaLAFFA supports switching the 'method' parameter from MUSiCC to 'relative' When input is already a MUSiCC-corrected copy-number table; re-running correction would double-correct When annotating at the pathway or module aggregation level rather than the KO orthology-group level http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Normalize metagenomic functional ortholog (KO) abundances using MUSiCC, MetaLAFFA's default ortholog abundance-correction method, which converts ortholog read counts into average copy number per genome via inter-sample normalization and intra-sample correction rather than leaving simple relative abundances. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Normalize metagenomic functional ortholog (KO) abundances using MUSiCC, MetaLAFFA's default ortholog abundance-correction method, which converts ortholog read counts into average copy number per genome via inter-sample normalization and intra-sample correction rather than leaving simple relative abundances.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is plain relative-abundance normalization rather than per-genome copy-number correction — MetaLAFFA supports switching the 'method' parameter from MUSiCC to 'relative' When input is already a MUSiCC-corrected copy-number table; re-running correction would double-correct When annotating at the pathway or module aggregation level rather than the KO orthology-group level

skills.search_text: compositional-microbiome-data-simulation Use when benchmarking a variable-selection or mediation-selection method for compositional count data and you need simulated data with known truth (e.g., which taxa, covariates, or balances are truly active) to score sensitivity/specificity of the selection. skills.when_to_use_negative: You need inference on real observational microbiome data with unknown truth — simulation provides synthetic benchmarks, not biological findings Your model is not a Dirichlet(-tree) multinomial or joint DM-linear/mediation model of compositional counts; the embedded ground truth of these simulators is tailored to those MicroBVS model classes You need phylogenetically structured trees or compositional data generated under mechanisms outside the vignette's default simulation settings

skills.description: Use when regressing genus-level OTU/taxon counts (compositional data with or without a known phylogenetic tree) on covariates such as FFQ dietary variables, and you need Bayesian sparse variable selection with FDR control at the branch level.
skills.name: compositional-microbiome-regression
skills.search_text: compositional-microbiome-regression Use when regressing genus-level OTU/taxon counts (compositional data with or without a known phylogenetic tree) on covariates such as FFQ dietary variables, and you need Bayesian sparse variable selection with FDR control at the branch level. When the outcome is a phenotypic outcome requiring joint prediction rather than covariate-branch association screening — the README separates the joint AOAS model (with corrected MH updates for auxiliary parameters c_ij) from the DTM variable-selection package, so pick the corresponding model code instead When the data lack any compositional/taxa-count structure and are plain tabular features; the DTM likelihood and branch-based priors would be inappropriate When a penalized (frequentist grouped-lasso) DTM fit with AIC selection is specifically required rather than Bayesian posterior inference http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression with Bayesian variable selection, implemented in the MicroBVS R package, to identify covariate (e.g., dietary factor) associations with phylogenetically structured microbiome abundance data. skills.summary: Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression with Bayesian variable selection, implemented in the MicroBVS R package, to identify covariate (e.g., dietary factor) associations with phylogenetically structured microbiome abundance data. skills.when_to_use_negative: When the outcome is a phenotypic outcome requiring joint prediction rather than covariate-branch association screening — the README separates the joint AOAS model (with corrected MH updates for auxiliary parameters c_ij) from the DTM variable-selection package, so pick the corresponding model code instead When the data lack any compositional/taxa-count structure and are plain tabular features; the DTM likelihood and branch-based priors would be inappropriate When a penalized (frequentist grouped-lasso) DTM fit with AIC selection is specifically required rather than Bayesian posterior inference

skills.when_to_use_negative: When features have genuine non-zero time effects — this skill is designed for negative-control (null) data and only estimates false positive rates, not power or true discovery When the data are already relative-abundance/TSS-normalized tables rather than raw counts — LongDat's negative-binomial count mode and rarefaction assume count input When the question is tool benchmarking for accuracy or runtime against MaAsLin2, ANCOM, lgpr or ZIBR rather than normalization-induced FPR under depth bias

skills.search_text: contig-length-filtering Use when preparing metagenomic or isolate assembly contigs/scaffolds (e.g. SPAdes output) as input for PlasFlow or other kmer-signature classifiers that perform poorly on short sequences. Input sequences are already short reads or already length-filtered below 1 kb targets — filtering would discard most data rather than improve classification The downstream tool does not depend on kmer coverage of contigs (e.g. read-based or assembly-graph methods such as Recycler or PlasmidSpades) — the length filter is a PlasFlow-specific preprocessing recommendation http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Filter an assembly (FASTA) by sequence length, retaining only contigs longer than a 1000 bp threshold, using the PlasFlow-provided Perl script filter_sequences_by_length.pl. This is a prerequisite step because kmer-based plasmid classifiers such as PlasFlow produce unreliable predictions on short contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321

skills.search_text: contig-n50-benchmark-computation Use when comparing two or more assembly runs (e.g. sparse_pregraph vs pregraph builds) and you need a single continuity metric such as contig N50 to quantify how a graph-construction choice affects assembly length. When the goal is per-base accuracy or misassembly detection rather than assembly continuity — N50 alone rewards longer contigs regardless of correctness (the article separately reports structural error, substitution error, and copy number error reductions). When scaffold-level continuity is the quantity of interest — use scaffold N50 from the *.scafSeq output instead of contig N50 from *.contig. When assemblies were built from different read sets or different k-mer settings without an explicit tradeoff rationale — N50 comparison is only meaningful for builds on identical input. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Computes contig N50 from assembled contig sequences to quantify assembly continuity, used here to measure the assembly tradeoff introduced by SOAPdenovo2's sparse de Bruijn graph mode versus the standard dense pregraph build. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/2047-217x-1-18

skills.description: Use when a strain-oblivious long-read metagenome assembly (FASTA) and a coordinate-sorted long-read alignment (BAM) exist and strain-separated contigs must be joined into longer, more complete strain scaffolds.
skills.name: contig-scaffold-path-tracing-with-median-gap-estimation
skills.search_text: contig-scaffold-path-tracing-with-median-gap-estimation Use when a strain-oblivious long-read metagenome assembly (FASTA) and a coordinate-sorted long-read alignment (BAM) exist and strain-separated contigs must be joined into longer, more complete strain scaffolds. The input is a single-isolate genome or a high-complexity metagenome rather than a single-sample low-complexity metagenome, which is Strainberry's stated scope No long reads or read-to-contig alignment are available — the scaffolding graph depends entirely on dovetail read alignments spanning contig ends The contigs already come as finished scaffolds and no further joining is needed — this step adds no information over the existing read alignment http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 A strain-aware scaffolding method from Strainberry that aligns long reads to strain-separated contigs, builds a bi-directed weighted string graph over contig ends using dovetail read alignments, trims weak/transitive edges, and traces maximal unambiguous paths to join strain-separated contigs into longer scaffolds with median-estimated gaps. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-021-24515-9
skills.summary: A strain-aware scaffolding method from Strainberry that aligns long reads to strain-separated contigs, builds a bi-directed weighted string graph over contig ends using dovetail read alignments, trims weak/transitive edges, and traces maximal unambiguous paths to join strain-separated contigs into longer scaffolds with median-estimated gaps.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a single-isolate genome or a high-complexity metagenome rather than a single-sample low-complexity metagenome, which is Strainberry's stated scope No long reads or read-to-contig alignment are available — the scaffolding graph depends entirely on dovetail read alignments spanning contig ends The contigs already come as finished scaffolds and no further joining is needed — this step adds no information over the existing read alignment

skills.description: Use when you have assembled contigs (or virMine assembly output) and need to classify which contigs are likely viral using gene-content origin scoring rather than homology alone.
skills.name: contig-viral-origin-scoring
skills.search_text: contig-viral-origin-scoring Use when you have assembled contigs (or virMine assembly output) and need to classify which contigs are likely viral using gene-content origin scoring rather than homology alone. Input is raw short-read sequencing data that has not yet been quality-controlled and assembled — use virMine's read QC and assembly steps (-a spades/metaspades/megahit) first instead of the -A contig-scoring path. You need to identify nonviral (e.g. bacterial) genomic content — this skill explicitly excludes nonviral matches and scores only viral likelihood. Contigs fail the optional filters (minimum/maximum contig size via -m/-M, minimum coverage via -c, minimum SPAdes coverage via -cov) and should be removed before scoring. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Scores assembled contigs for their likelihood of being viral in origin by predicting genes and classifying each gene's origin as cellular, viral, or unknown via an exclusion-based BLAST strategy against user-supplied viral and nonviral protein databases. This avoids relying solely on direct homology to known viruses, enabling detection of novel viral contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/mra.00107-22
skills.summary: Scores assembled contigs for their likelihood of being viral in origin by predicting genes and classifying each gene's origin as cellular, viral, or unknown via an exclusion-based BLAST strategy against user-supplied viral and nonviral protein databases. This avoids relying solely on direct homology to known viruses, enabling detection of novel viral contigs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw short-read sequencing data that has not yet been quality-controlled and assembled — use virMine's read QC and assembly steps (-a spades/metaspades/megahit) first instead of the -A contig-scoring path. You need to identify nonviral (e.g. bacterial) genomic content — this skill explicitly excludes nonviral matches and scores only viral likelihood. Contigs fail the optional filters (minimum/maximum contig size via -m/-M, minimum coverage via -c, minimum SPAdes coverage via -cov) and should be removed before scoring.

skills.description: Use when the grouping/clinical variable is continuous (not binary) and you want to gauge the overall strength of the microbiome-outcome association and rank feature robustness via a progressive-permutation U-curve.
skills.name: continuous-outcome-progressive-permutation
skills.search_text: continuous-outcome-progressive-permutation Use when the grouping/clinical variable is continuous (not binary) and you want to gauge the overall strength of the microbiome-outcome association and rank feature robustness via a progressive-permutation U-curve. The grouping outcome is binary or categorical — use the binary driver bin_permute_all with the default Wilcoxon rank sum test instead of con_permute_all. skills.search_text: cosine-similarity-metagenome-distance-computation Use when an all-vs-all distance matrix must be computed across many metagenome samples from full k-mer abundance vectors (no sketching or presence/absence reduction), and scale demands a single-pass, MapReduce-based sweep over an inverted k-mer index. Input is a pre-computed distance matrix or feature table rather than raw metagenome reads/indexed k-mer vectors The analysis requires a different distance metric explicitly supported by the paper's contrast (e.g., Bray-Curtis or Jensen-Shannon were Libra's alternative scoring algorithms, not the cosine sweep being reconstructed) Data reduction, read count normalization, or presence/absence distance metrics are acceptable for the analysis — the article states these greatly diminish resolution for large-scale comparisons http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstructs Libra's all-vs-all pairwise metagenome distance computation, which uses a sweep-line algorithm over an inverted k-mer index to accumulate cosine similarity terms (dot products D and per-sample magnitudes M) for every sample pair in a single scan rather than scanning each vector pair separately. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Reconstructs Libra's all-vs-all pairwise metagenome distance computation, which uses a sweep-line algorithm over an inverted k-mer index to accumulate cosine similarity terms (dot products D and per-sample magnitudes M) for every sample pair in a single scan rather than scanning each vector pair separately.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a pre-computed distance matrix or feature table rather than raw metagenome reads/indexed k-mer vectors The analysis requires a different distance metric explicitly supported by the paper's contrast (e.g., Bray-Curtis or Jensen-Shannon were Libra's alternative scoring algorithms, not the cosine sweep being reconstructed) Data reduction, read count normalization, or presence/absence distance metrics are acceptable for the analysis — the article states these greatly diminish resolution for large-scale comparisons

skills.description: Use when you have raw MG-RAST or DIAMOND-derived abundance summary counts (organism or functional category files) from ≥2 sample groups and need normalized differential transcript-activity calls with corrected p-values.

skills.search_text: count-data-normalization-and-multiple-testing-correction Use when you have raw MG-RAST or DIAMOND-derived abundance summary counts (organism or functional category files) from ≥2 sample groups and need normalized differential transcript-activity calls with corrected p-values. The data are shotgun metagenomic (DNA) rather than metatranscriptomic counts — mRNA-based analysis measures transcriptional activity, not population size shifts, which it cannot measure as accurately as metagenomics. The input is already a normalized or pre-tested result table rather than raw per-sample abundance summary counts. skills.description: Use when building a counting Approximate Membership Query (cAMQ) index from k-mer abundance files (e.g. KMC output) where k-mers must be indexed as s-mers with counts, typically with k=31 or 35, b=5, and z=3.
skills.name: counting-bloom-filter-construction
skills.search_text: counting-bloom-filter-construction Use when building a counting Approximate Membership Query (cAMQ) index from k-mer abundance files (e.g. KMC output) where k-mers must be indexed as s-mers with counts, typically with k=31 or 35, b=5, and z=3. Input is raw FASTA/FASTQ reads rather than a k-mer abundance file — fimpera_index requires a pre-counted k-mer file (e.g. from KMC) as input. The task is presence/absence membership without counts, where a plain (non-counting) Bloom filter or exact k-mer set would suffice and fimpera's s-mer machinery adds complexity. The downstream query tool cannot consume fimpera's index format or you need a different AMQ without adapting the templated fimpera-lib interfaces. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Constructs a counting Bloom filter (cBF) index of s-mer abundances derived from k-mer counts, using fimpera's indexing step (k≥s>0) so that the index can later be wrapped by fimpera for low-false-positive abundance queries. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad305
skills.summary: Constructs a counting Bloom filter (cBF) index of s-mer abundances derived from k-mer counts, using fimpera's indexing step (k≥s>0) so that the index can later be wrapped by fimpera for low-false-positive abundance queries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTA/FASTQ reads rather than a k-mer abundance file — fimpera_index requires a pre-counted k-mer file (e.g. from KMC) as input. The task is presence/absence membership without counts, where a plain (non-counting) Bloom filter or exact k-mer set would suffice and fimpera's s-mer machinery adds complexity. The input is a whole metagenome rather than virus-predicted scaffolds, or contains non-viral microbial genomes — vRhyme is built for viral sequences and is not meant to bin microbes, and performance on whole metagenomes has not been fully evaluated The community contains multiple inactive (non-replicating) prophages from the same host genome — vRhyme had difficulties separating these despite coverage comparisons Only one coverage sample is available for a highly redundant dataset where coverage variance is the sole discriminating signal — vRhyme performs optimally with multiple input samples http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 vRhyme's core binning signal: single- or multi-sample read coverage abundance effect sizes are compared between viral scaffolds to weight binning networks, separating scaffolds with similar nucleotide features (GC, tetranucleotide frequencies) that are actually different genomes. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac341
skills.summary: vRhyme's core binning signal: single- or multi-sample read coverage abundance effect sizes are compared between viral scaffolds to weight binning networks, separating scaffolds with similar nucleotide features (GC, tetranucleotide frequencies) that are actually different genomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a whole metagenome rather than virus-predicted scaffolds, or contains non-viral microbial genomes — vRhyme is built for viral sequences and is not meant to bin microbes, and performance on whole metagenomes has not been fully evaluated The community contains multiple inactive (non-replicating) prophages from the same host genome — vRhyme had difficulties separating these despite coverage comparisons Only one coverage sample is available for a highly redundant dataset where coverage variance is the sole discriminating signal — vRhyme performs optimally with multiple input samples

skills.description: Use when input is a phyloseq object (biom.Rdata) or its four component files with survival time, censoring indicator, treatment, and covariate columns, and the goal is a covariate-adjusted Cox model of treatment or CLR-transformed microbial abundance on survival.

skills.search_text: cox-proportional-hazards-survival-analysis Use when input is a phyloseq object (biom.Rdata) or its four component files with survival time, censoring indicator, treatment, and covariate columns, and the goal is a covariate-adjusted Cox model of treatment or CLR-transformed microbial abundance on survival. Input is raw 16S sequence data still needing QIIME 2.0 processing — use MiSurv's Data Processing module first (quality control, 97% OTU picking, ChimeraSlayer, rarefaction via rarefy_even_depth) The analysis goal is comparative microbial composition between treatment groups without survival data (Module 2) or prediction modeling of survival from microbial taxa (Module 4) The response is continuous or binary rather than a survival (time-to-event) response — MiCloud, not MiSurv, is the appropriate platform http://edamontology.org/topic_3334 Fits covariate-adjusted Cox proportional hazards models for microbiome survival studies via MiSurv's Module 1 (comparative survival analysis between treatment groups) or Module 3 (microbiome–survival association testing), reproducing results like the tylosin T1D trial (HR = 1.692, P = 0.005). metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22

skills.description: Use when inferring strain-type mixtures or allele compositions from MLST allele distributions requires solving an NP-hard optimization (ADP or SDP) with mixed integer linear programming, and when solver gap/time limits must be configured to balance accuracy against runtime.
skills.name: cplex-optimization-solving
skills.search_text: cplex-optimization-solving Use when inferring strain-type mixtures or allele compositions from MLST allele distributions requires solving an NP-hard optimization (ADP or SDP) with mixed integer linear programming, and when solver gap/time limits must be configured to balance accuracy against runtime. When the data are whole genomes rather than MLST allele sequences — the ILP formulations are specific to multi-locus allele/proportion structure When reference strain types are entirely unavailable, since the SDP objective requires weights based on edit distance to known strains When a de novo mixture method is preferred and no known allele database exists (e.g. DESMAN-style approaches) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3305 Formulating and solving the mixed integer linear programs (MILP/ILP) underlying the Allele Diversity Problem and Strain Diversity Problem for MLST-based strain deconvolution, using the Python API of IBM CPLEX 12.6.3.0. It converts combinatorial strain-mixture inference into constrained optimization with binary strain-usage variables, allele proportion variables, and error linearization. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3204-8
skills.summary: Formulating and solving the mixed integer linear programs (MILP/ILP) underlying the Allele Diversity Problem and Strain Diversity Problem for MLST-based strain deconvolution, using the Python API of IBM CPLEX 12.6.3.0. It converts combinatorial strain-mixture inference into constrained optimization with binary strain-usage variables, allele proportion variables, and error linearization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the data are whole genomes rather than MLST allele sequences — the ILP formulations are specific to multi-locus allele/proportion structure When reference strain types are entirely unavailable, since the SDP objective requires weights based on edit distance to known strains When a de novo mixture method is preferred and no known allele database exists (e.g. DESMAN-style approaches)

skills.description: Use when a metagenomic or 16S amplicon study asks which bacterial lineages would be missed by common 16S primers (e.g. 515F/806R), especially for divergent CPR phyla like Microgenomates, Saccharibacteria, WWE3, or WS6.
skills.name: cpr-lineage-16s-divergence-interpretation
skills.search_text: cpr-lineage-16s-divergence-interpretation Use when a metagenomic or 16S amplicon study asks which bacterial lineages would be missed by common 16S primers (e.g. 515F/806R), especially for divergent CPR phyla like Microgenomates, Saccharibacteria, WWE3, or WS6. The input is already a 16S amplicon feature table or OTU abundance matrix — this skill evaluates primer binding on assembled 16S gene sequences, not count data The sequences have not had introns/insertions removed — 31% of CPR 16S genes carry ≥10 bp insertions (up to 2,004 bp), so unspliced sequences will falsely appear primer-incompatible The question is about shotgun-relative abundance of CPR organisms rather than amplicon-survey detectability http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Interprets how divergent 16S rRNA gene sequences in candidate phyla radiation (CPR) lineages cause evasion of amplicon-survey primers, quantifying per-lineage and overall detection loss for primers like 515F/806R from the Brown et al. 2015 Rifle groundwater study. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486
skills.summary: Interprets how divergent 16S rRNA gene sequences in candidate phyla radiation (CPR) lineages cause evasion of amplicon-survey primers, quantifying per-lineage and overall detection loss for primers like 515F/806R from the Brown et al. 2015 Rifle groundwater study.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a 16S amplicon feature table or OTU abundance matrix — this skill evaluates primer binding on assembled 16S gene sequences, not count data The sequences have not had introns/insertions removed — 31% of CPR 16S genes carry ≥10 bp insertions (up to 2,004 bp), so unspliced sequences will falsely appear primer-incompatible The question is about shotgun-relative abundance of CPR organisms rather than amplicon-survey detectability

skills.description: Use when bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences contain large insertions (≥10 bp) that would corrupt multiple sequence alignment, and the goal is a defensible phylogeny to test whether CPR lineages form a monophyletic group.
skills.name: cpr-monophyly-tree-validation
skills.search_text: cpr-monophyly-tree-validation Use when bacterial 16S rRNA gene sequences contain large insertions (≥10 bp) that would corrupt multiple sequence alignment, and the goal is a defensible phylogeny to test whether CPR lineages form a monophyletic group. The input alignment is a ribosomal-protein (rp16) phylogeny — that workflow uses a ≥1,000 aligned-residue filter on protein SCGs, not intron-stripped 16S sequences 16S rRNA genes have no large insertions (rare outside CPR, per SILVA v115 screening) and a standard nucleotide alignment without intron removal is appropriate Sequences are short-read amplicons that cannot provide ≥800 bp of aligned 16S sequence for phylogeny http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Builds an intron-corrected 16S rRNA maximum-likelihood phylogeny in which the candidate phyla radiation (CPR) can be tested for monophyly: strip rRNA insertions ≥10 bp, structurally realign with SSUAlign, and infer a rooted RAxML tree. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486
skills.summary: Builds an intron-corrected 16S rRNA maximum-likelihood phylogeny in which the candidate phyla radiation (CPR) can be tested for monophyly: strip rRNA insertions ≥10 bp, structurally realign with SSUAlign, and infer a rooted RAxML tree.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input alignment is a ribosomal-protein (rp16) phylogeny — that workflow uses a ≥1,000 aligned-residue filter on protein SCGs, not intron-stripped 16S sequences 16S rRNA genes have no large insertions (rare outside CPR, per SILVA v115 screening) and a standard nucleotide alignment without intron removal is appropriate Sequences are short-read amplicons that cannot provide ≥800 bp of aligned 16S sequence for phylogeny

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify parallel-scaling behaviour of a CPU-parallelized bioinformatics tool (e.g. chewBBACA AlleleCall) by wall-clock timing the same workload across several --cpu values and identifying an I/O bottleneck.
skills.name: cpu-parallelization-runtime-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cpu-parallelization-runtime-benchmarking Use when you need to quantify parallel-scaling behaviour of a CPU-parallelized bioinformatics tool (e.g. chewBBACA AlleleCall) by wall-clock timing the same workload across several --cpu values and identifying an I/O bottleneck. The tool you are benchmarking uses a single CPU core (e.g. Genome Profiler), which 'making it unsuitable for large-scale analyses' — a CPU-scaling benchmark would be meaningless. You only need one allelic profile matrix and already know the machine's optimal core count — simply run AlleleCall with that --cpu value instead of a full sweep. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than draft/complete genome FASTA assemblies — AlleleCall takes FASTA assemblies, not FASTQ. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmarks how the runtime of chewBBACA's BLAST-based AlleleCall module scales with CPU count (multiprocessing) by timing repeated allele-calling runs on 100 S. agalactiae draft assemblies, revealing near-linear speedup up to 32 CPUs followed by a disk/I/O-bound plateau. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000166
skills.summary: Benchmarks how the runtime of chewBBACA's BLAST-based AlleleCall module scales with CPU count (multiprocessing) by timing repeated allele-calling runs on 100 S. agalactiae draft assemblies, revealing near-linear speedup up to 32 CPUs followed by a disk/I/O-bound plateau.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tool you are benchmarking uses a single CPU core (e.g. Genome Profiler), which 'making it unsuitable for large-scale analyses' — a CPU-scaling benchmark would be meaningless. You only need one allelic profile matrix and already know the machine's optimal core count — simply run AlleleCall with that --cpu value instead of a full sweep. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than draft/complete genome FASTA assemblies — AlleleCall takes FASTA assemblies, not FASTQ.

skills.description: Use when raw unassembled FASTQ reads must be recruited around known seed reads (HMM-derived or user-provided FASTA seeds) to capture a complete CRISPR/Cas operon for targeted assembly without assembling the full dataset.
skills.name: crispr-cas-targeted-read-capture
skills.search_text: crispr-cas-targeted-read-capture Use when raw unassembled FASTQ reads must be recruited around known seed reads (HMM-derived or user-provided FASTA seeds) to capture a complete CRISPR/Cas operon for targeted assembly without assembling the full dataset. The goal is whole-genome or whole-metagenome assembly rather than targeted recovery of a specific gene set — CasCollect is designed to avoid complete assembly of the raw read dataset No seed material is available: the expansion stage requires a seed set from cas-gene HMM matches or a user-defined FASTA of seed/CRISPR-array repeat reads The target gene family falls outside what the supplied HMM profiles or user reference sequences can seed — the pipeline is only reconfigurable for user-provided HMMs and/or reference nucleotide sequences http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Iteratively expands an initial set of 'seed' reads (cas-gene or CRISPR-array matches) into a larger read subset from raw Illumina FASTQ data using cycles of VSEARCH identity matching, priming targeted assembly of only CRISPR/Cas loci instead of the whole genome. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: Iteratively expands an initial set of 'seed' reads (cas-gene or CRISPR-array matches) into a larger read subset from raw Illumina FASTQ data using cycles of VSEARCH identity matching, priming targeted assembly of only CRISPR/Cas loci instead of the whole genome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is whole-genome or whole-metagenome assembly rather than targeted recovery of a specific gene set — CasCollect is designed to avoid complete assembly of the raw read dataset No seed material is available: the expansion stage requires a seed set from cas-gene HMM matches or a user-defined FASTA of seed/CRISPR-array repeat reads The target gene family falls outside what the supplied HMM profiles or user reference sequences can seed — the pipeline is only reconfigurable for user-provided HMMs and/or reference nucleotide sequences

skills.description: Use when raw unassembled FASTQ reads must be searched for CRISPR array repeat sequences by nucleotide identity to seed targeted assembly, especially where repeat-only arrays without cas genes would be missed by protein HMM screening.
skills.name: crispr-repeat-nucleotide-identity-matching
skills.search_text: crispr-repeat-nucleotide-identity-matching Use when raw unassembled FASTQ reads must be searched for CRISPR array repeat sequences by nucleotide identity to seed targeted assembly, especially where repeat-only arrays without cas genes would be missed by protein HMM screening. Input is already an assembled contig or genome — the skill is designed for short unassembled sequencing reads and loses purpose on assemblies. The target is protein-coding cas genes rather than CRISPR array repeats — protein mode (FragGeneScanPlus translation + HMMER against the 120 Cas profile HMMs) is the appropriate search. The user already has a defined seed FASTA and wants to bypass all searching — use the --seed -define mode to supply seeds directly. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 CasCollect's DNA-mode seed generation: identify raw sequencing reads containing CRISPR array repeats by VSEARCH identity matching against a user-defined FASTA of repeat sequences, adding the matching reads to the seed pool. This complements protein-mode HMMER screening of cas genes so that repeat-only arrays lacking cas genes are still captured. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: CasCollect's DNA-mode seed generation: identify raw sequencing reads containing CRISPR array repeats by VSEARCH identity matching against a user-defined FASTA of repeat sequences, adding the matching reads to the seed pool. This complements protein-mode HMMER screening of cas genes so that repeat-only arrays lacking cas genes are still captured.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an assembled contig or genome — the skill is designed for short unassembled sequencing reads and loses purpose on assemblies. The target is protein-coding cas genes rather than CRISPR array repeats — protein mode (FragGeneScanPlus translation + HMMER against the 120 Cas profile HMMs) is the appropriate search. The user already has a defined seed FASTA and wants to bypass all searching — use the --seed -define mode to supply seeds directly.

skills.name: crispr-spacer-prediction-from-viral-contigs
skills.search_text: crispr-spacer-prediction-from-viral-contigs Use when a metagenomic Hi-C pipeline (e.g. ViralCC + HiCBin) has produced draft viral bins and host MAGs, and you need sequence-level CRISPR spacer evidence to validate the inferred virus-host pairs or build an infection-spectrum summary like Fig. 6b. When the contigs are prokaryotic MAGs rather than viral bins — the skill targets CRISPR arrays within vMAGs; TAXAassign-type workflows 'can hardly annotate viral contigs', so do not substitute host-side workflows When no Hi-C-inferred virus-host pairs exist yet — the skill's validation logic (overlap fraction vs Hi-C linkages) requires the pair list from ViralCC/HiCBin as an input When contigs are already taxonomically classified viral sequences needing classification (use Demovir for Order/Family classification instead — it 'should not be used for discriminating viral contigs from bacterial/archael/eukaryotic sequences') http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Predicts CRISPR arrays in viral MAG (vMAG) contigs with PILER-CR, aligns extracted spacers against host MAG contigs with BLAST, and uses the resulting spacer-protospacer hits as an orthogonal, sequence-based validation of Hi-C-inferred virus-host pairs from ViralCC/HiCBin. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-023-35945-y
skills.summary: Predicts CRISPR arrays in viral MAG (vMAG) contigs with PILER-CR, aligns extracted spacers against host MAG contigs with BLAST, and uses the resulting spacer-protospacer hits as an orthogonal, sequence-based validation of Hi-C-inferred virus-host pairs from ViralCC/HiCBin.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the contigs are prokaryotic MAGs rather than viral bins — the skill targets CRISPR arrays within vMAGs; TAXAassign-type workflows 'can hardly annotate viral contigs', so do not substitute host-side workflows When no Hi-C-inferred virus-host pairs exist yet — the skill's validation logic (overlap fraction vs Hi-C linkages) requires the pair list from ViralCC/HiCBin as an input When contigs are already taxonomically classified viral sequences needing classification (use Demovir for Order/Family classification instead — it 'should not be used for discriminating viral contigs from bacterial/archael/eukaryotic sequences')
