skills.name: cross-tool-comparison-intersection
skills.search_text: cross-tool-comparison-intersection Use when per-sample metagenomic assemblies have been profiled by both SynTracker (APSS) and inStrain (popANI), and the goal is to detect species whose within-species diversity is preferentially point-mutation- or structurally-driven. Tracking phages or plasmids, where SynTracker alone achieved a significantly higher AUC than inStrain and an SNP-based comparison set is unnecessary Classifying pairs as same/different strain for delineation, which the authors recommend avoiding in favor of continuous genomic difference measures because thresholds like APSS 0.95 or popANI 99.999% are subjective and species-dependent Datasets where only one tool was run or where the two comparison sets share too few sample pairs to define a meaningful intersected background http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Intersects strain-comparison sets produced by a synteny-based tool (SynTracker APSS) and an SNP-based tool (inStrain popANI) per species, then uses hypergeometric tests on each tool's most-similar 5% comparisons to classify species as hypermutators (point mutations) or hyper-recombinants (structural differences). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-024-02276-2
skills.summary: Intersects strain-comparison sets produced by a synteny-based tool (SynTracker APSS) and an SNP-based tool (inStrain popANI) per species, then uses hypergeometric tests on each tool's most-similar 5% comparisons to classify species as hypermutators (point mutations) or hyper-recombinants (structural differences).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Tracking phages or plasmids, where SynTracker alone achieved a significantly higher AUC than inStrain and an SNP-based comparison set is unnecessary Classifying pairs as same/different strain for delineation, which the authors recommend avoiding in favor of continuous genomic difference measures because thresholds like APSS 0.95 or popANI 99.999% are subjective and species-dependent Datasets where only one tool was run or where the two comparison sets share too few sample pairs to define a meaningful intersected background

skills.description: Use when reproducing or extending a runtime/speedup claim, e.g. quantifying how much faster a parallel pipeline is than its sequential version and whether it matches a tool's runtime on the same input dataset.
skills.name: cross-tool-computational-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-computational-performance-comparison Use when reproducing or extending a runtime/speedup claim, e.g. quantifying how much faster a parallel pipeline is than its sequential version and whether it matches a tool's runtime on the same input dataset. When INDEL detection throughput is the benchmark target — the parallel HARC-based pipeline works for SNPs only When datasets differ between the candidate and competitor runs — runtime comparison is only valid on identical inputs and hardware When comparing space efficiency rather than speed — ebwt2InDel's headline improvement is memory, measured separately from wall-clock time http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks a candidate pipeline's wall-clock runtime against both a sequential baseline of the same tool and a state-of-the-art competitor (here, ebwt2InDel's parallel vs sequential pipelines and DISCOSNP++) on a shared dataset to demonstrate speedup and parity claims. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03586-3
skills.summary: Benchmarks a candidate pipeline's wall-clock runtime against both a sequential baseline of the same tool and a state-of-the-art competitor (here, ebwt2InDel's parallel vs sequential pipelines and DISCOSNP++) on a shared dataset to demonstrate speedup and parity claims.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When INDEL detection throughput is the benchmark target — the parallel HARC-based pipeline works for SNPs only When datasets differ between the candidate and competitor runs — runtime comparison is only valid on identical inputs and hardware When comparing space efficiency rather than speed — ebwt2InDel's headline improvement is memory, measured separately from wall-clock time

skills.description: Use when comparing pangenome/core-genome predictions from multiple tools (mOTUpan, Roary, PPanGGOLiN) on the same genome sets, especially MAGs spanning a wide completeness range.
skills.name: cross-tool-core-genome-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-core-genome-comparison Use when comparing pangenome/core-genome predictions from multiple tools (mOTUpan, Roary, PPanGGOLiN) on the same genome sets, especially MAGs spanning a wide completeness range. When only one pangenome tool's core-genome estimate is needed — no cross-tool benchmarking is required When genomes span such broad phylogenetic distances that a 95% ANI species cutoff cannot form coherent mOTUs (the method is for closely related genome sets) When GFF annotations are unavailable, since Roary and PPanGGOLiN require GFF-annotated genomes http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark core-genome estimates from mOTUpan against Roary and PPanGGOLiN by converting each tool's gene-cluster definitions into mOTUpan's genome-to-trait format and recomputing partitionings on the same genome sets, quantifying agreement via normalized residues. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac060
skills.summary: Benchmark core-genome estimates from mOTUpan against Roary and PPanGGOLiN by converting each tool's gene-cluster definitions into mOTUpan's genome-to-trait format and recomputing partitionings on the same genome sets, quantifying agreement via normalized residues.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When only one pangenome tool's core-genome estimate is needed — no cross-tool benchmarking is required When genomes span such broad phylogenetic distances that a 95% ANI species cutoff cannot form coherent mOTUs (the method is for closely related genome sets) When GFF annotations are unavailable, since Roary and PPanGGOLiN require GFF-annotated genomes

skills.description: Use when comparing detection performance (FDR, TPR) of longitudinal high-dimensional tools like LongDat and MaAsLin2 across varying numbers of covariates on simulated microbiome count data.
skills.name: cross-tool-detection-performance-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-detection-performance-comparison Use when comparing detection performance (FDR, TPR) of longitudinal high-dimensional tools like LongDat and MaAsLin2 across varying numbers of covariates on simulated microbiome count data. The data are cross-sectional with no time dimension — LongDat and MaAsLin2 are being applied here to longitudinal multivariable cohort data Only one tool is of interest and no identically simulated replicate set exists for a fair head-to-head comparison The analysis goal is single-dataset inference rather than method benchmarking; use the tool's own pipeline and inspect its Signal column instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark longitudinal feature-detection tools head-to-head on identically simulated replicates, computing false discovery rate (FDR) and true positive rate (TPR) per covariate setting. This skill operationalizes the LongDat paper's finding that LongDat stays stable while MaAsLin2's FDR escalates and TPR diminishes as covariates increase. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad063
skills.summary: Benchmark longitudinal feature-detection tools head-to-head on identically simulated replicates, computing false discovery rate (FDR) and true positive rate (TPR) per covariate setting. This skill operationalizes the LongDat paper's finding that LongDat stays stable while MaAsLin2's FDR escalates and TPR diminishes as covariates increase.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are cross-sectional with no time dimension — LongDat and MaAsLin2 are being applied here to longitudinal multivariable cohort data Only one tool is of interest and no identically simulated replicate set exists for a fair head-to-head comparison The analysis goal is single-dataset inference rather than method benchmarking; use the tool's own pipeline and inspect its Signal column instead

skills.description: Use when comparing multiple metagenome distance tools (Libra, Mash, Simka) on the same sample set to assess how data reduction, read-count normalization, or presence/absence metrics distort clustering by a known metadata factor such as body site.
skills.name: cross-tool-metagenomic-distance-normalization
skills.search_text: cross-tool-metagenomic-distance-normalization Use when comparing multiple metagenome distance tools (Libra, Mash, Simka) on the same sample set to assess how data reduction, read-count normalization, or presence/absence metrics distort clustering by a known metadata factor such as body site. Input is assembled contigs when the goal is to demonstrate Libra's abundance-aware clustering — Libra requires reads to calculate k-mer abundance and shows reduced resolution on contigs Samples have wildly unequal sizes and the chosen tool normalizes counts to the minimum sample count (Simka behavior), which collapses all pairwise distances to the maximum The analysis goal is presence/absence comparison only and abundance-driven separation is the expected signal http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark how distance metrics and count-normalization choices (Libra Cosine Similarity/Bray-Curtis on all reads, Mash MinHash sketches, Simka Jaccard-ab/Bray-Curtis with minimum-count normalization) affect all-vs-all metagenome clustering, e.g. demonstrating that assembled contigs strip abundance and collapse Simka distances. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Benchmark how distance metrics and count-normalization choices (Libra Cosine Similarity/Bray-Curtis on all reads, Mash MinHash sketches, Simka Jaccard-ab/Bray-Curtis with minimum-count normalization) affect all-vs-all metagenome clustering, e.g. demonstrating that assembled contigs strip abundance and collapse Simka distances.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is assembled contigs when the goal is to demonstrate Libra's abundance-aware clustering — Libra requires reads to calculate k-mer abundance and shows reduced resolution on contigs Samples have wildly unequal sizes and the chosen tool normalizes counts to the minimum sample count (Simka behavior), which collapses all pairwise distances to the maximum The analysis goal is presence/absence comparison only and abundance-driven separation is the expected signal

skills.description: Use when comparing mapping throughput/speed of raw-signal nanopore mappers across tools on the same FAST5 datasets and reference genomes, e.g., verifying whether each tool exceeds nanopore sequencing throughput on the human genome.
skills.name: cross-tool-performance-ratio-analysis
skills.search_text: cross-tool-performance-ratio-analysis Use when comparing mapping throughput/speed of raw-signal nanopore mappers across tools on the same FAST5 datasets and reference genomes, e.g., verifying whether each tool exceeds nanopore sequencing throughput on the human genome. The task is accuracy/precision evaluation of mappings rather than speed or throughput comparison — this skill measures CPU/real time and bases-per-second only. Only one mapping tool is being evaluated with no second tool to form a comparative ratio. Input data is not legacy R9.4.1 raw signal data, since UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Benchmark multiple raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) under identical conditions (same FAST5 datasets, references, thread counts), extract per-tool CPU/real time and throughput with UNCALLED's pafstats, and compute average throughput ratios against the published baselines (25.8x vs UNCALLED, 3.4x vs Sigmap). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Benchmark multiple raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) under identical conditions (same FAST5 datasets, references, thread counts), extract per-tool CPU/real time and throughput with UNCALLED's pafstats, and compute average throughput ratios against the published baselines (25.8x vs UNCALLED, 3.4x vs Sigmap).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is accuracy/precision evaluation of mappings rather than speed or throughput comparison — this skill measures CPU/real time and bases-per-second only. Only one mapping tool is being evaluated with no second tool to form a comparative ratio. Input data is not legacy R9.4.1 raw signal data, since UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data.

skills.description: Use when two plasmid-prediction tools have been run on identical contig/fragment sets and you must quantify error rates, agreement, and plasmid:chromosome separation ratios to decide which classifier to trust.
skills.name: cross-tool-prediction-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-prediction-comparison Use when two plasmid-prediction tools have been run on identical contig/fragment sets and you must quantify error rates, agreement, and plasmid:chromosome separation ratios to decide which classifier to trust. Inputs are raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs/fragments — kmer-based classifiers are unreliable on short sequences Only one classifier's output exists and there is no ground truth or second tool to compare against The goal is replicon typing of known plasmids in isolate assemblies (use PlasmidFinder) rather than metagenomic plasmid/chromosome separation http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Benchmark plasmid-classification tools (PlasFlow vs cBar) against each other and ground truth by computing false-positive/false-negative rates, prediction concordance, and plasmid-to-chromosome ratios on the same fragment sets and plasmidome assemblies. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321
skills.summary: Benchmark plasmid-classification tools (PlasFlow vs cBar) against each other and ground truth by computing false-positive/false-negative rates, prediction concordance, and plasmid-to-chromosome ratios on the same fragment sets and plasmidome assemblies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Inputs are raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs/fragments — kmer-based classifiers are unreliable on short sequences Only one classifier's output exists and there is no ground truth or second tool to compare against The goal is replicon typing of known plasmids in isolate assemblies (use PlasmidFinder) rather than metagenomic plasmid/chromosome separation

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify and compare false-removal rates (off-target loss of bacterial reads) of host-decontamination tools such as Hostile vs HRRT on simulated bacterial Illumina data.
skills.name: cross-tool-retention-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-tool-retention-comparison Use when you need to quantify and compare false-removal rates (off-target loss of bacterial reads) of host-decontamination tools such as Hostile vs HRRT on simulated bacterial Illumina data. The goal is decontaminating real (meta)genomic data rather than evaluating or benchmarking tool precision — in that case run `hostile clean` directly on the sample FASTQs. The primary question is human read removal sensitivity (percent of real human reads removed, e.g. the 1000 Genomes Project >99.5% benchmark), not microbial read retention on simulated bacterial data. Input reads are non-Illumina (e.g. ONT long reads) or not derived from the FDA-ARGOS bacterial assemblies, so the published retention figures and ≥99.989% validation threshold do not apply. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark how precisely host-read decontamination tools retain microbial sequence by simulating paired Illumina reads from the 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial assemblies (BioProject 231221) with DWGSIM, cleaning them with Hostile and HRRT, and tabulating bacterial read retention per tool. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Benchmark how precisely host-read decontamination tools retain microbial sequence by simulating paired Illumina reads from the 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial assemblies (BioProject 231221) with DWGSIM, cleaning them with Hostile and HRRT, and tabulating bacterial read retention per tool.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is decontaminating real (meta)genomic data rather than evaluating or benchmarking tool precision — in that case run `hostile clean` directly on the sample FASTQs. The primary question is human read removal sensitivity (percent of real human reads removed, e.g. the 1000 Genomes Project >99.5% benchmark), not microbial read retention on simulated bacterial data. Input reads are non-Illumina (e.g. ONT long reads) or not derived from the FDA-ARGOS bacterial assemblies, so the published retention figures and ≥99.989% validation threshold do not apply.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking multiple phylogenomic marker-mining tools (e.g. Patchwork vs ALiBaSeq vs aTRAM 2) for both accuracy and runtime across a sequencing-coverage gradient on a Slurm-managed HPC cluster.
skills.name: cross-tool-runtime-profiling-on-hpc
skills.search_text: cross-tool-runtime-profiling-on-hpc Use when benchmarking multiple phylogenomic marker-mining tools (e.g. Patchwork vs ALiBaSeq vs aTRAM 2) for both accuracy and runtime across a sequencing-coverage gradient on a Slurm-managed HPC cluster. If the goal is to retrieve markers for phylogeny from a single data set rather than to compare tool performance — use Patchwork directly instead of the benchmark harness If your data are not paired-end short reads with a computable genome-size-based coverage target, the 1x–40x subsampling gradient is meaningless If a candidate tool cannot run within the imposed wall-clock cap (aTRAM 2 failed to finish the 40x arm within 5 days), runtime figures will be dominated by non-completion rather than comparative speed http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A benchmarking protocol that profiles marker-retrieval accuracy and wall-clock runtime of Patchwork, ALiBaSeq v.1.2, and aTRAM 2 v.2.4.3 across D. gyrociliatus short-read data subsampled to 1x–40x coverage, with per-tool Slurm-elapsed times compiled into benchmark_comparison.tsv. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: A benchmarking protocol that profiles marker-retrieval accuracy and wall-clock runtime of Patchwork, ALiBaSeq v.1.2, and aTRAM 2 v.2.4.3 across D. gyrociliatus short-read data subsampled to 1x–40x coverage, with per-tool Slurm-elapsed times compiled into benchmark_comparison.tsv.
skills.when_to_use_negative: If the goal is to retrieve markers for phylogeny from a single data set rather than to compare tool performance — use Patchwork directly instead of the benchmark harness If your data are not paired-end short reads with a computable genome-size-based coverage target, the 1x–40x subsampling gradient is meaningless If a candidate tool cannot run within the imposed wall-clock cap (aTRAM 2 failed to finish the 40x arm within 5 days), runtime figures will be dominated by non-completion rather than comparative speed

skills.description: Decision support for choosing between longitudinal differential-abundance tools when multiple covariates (e.g. medications) may confound a time/treatment effect in high-dimensional microbiome data.
skills.name: cross-tool-significance-overlap-quantification
skills.search_text: cross-tool-significance-overlap-quantification Decision support for choosing between longitudinal differential-abundance tools when multiple covariates (e.g. medications) may confound a time/treatment effect in high-dimensional microbiome data. Data are cross-sectional with no time or repeated-measure structure — LongDat's longitudinal pipelines (longdat_cont/longdat_disc) and this comparison assume longitudinal design You only need a single tool's differential-abundance output rather than a tool-vs-tool concordance assessment The feature table is not count data and you cannot supply the matching data_type; LongDat requires the correct data_type (count, proportion, binary, ordinal, continuous) for valid signal calls http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 A skill for benchmarking differential-abundance calls by running two longitudinal tools (LongDat and MaAsLin2) on the same species-level abundance table and metadata, with and without medication covariates, then tabulating significant species counts per tool per condition and quantifying their overlap. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad063
skills.summary: A skill for benchmarking differential-abundance calls by running two longitudinal tools (LongDat and MaAsLin2) on the same species-level abundance table and metadata, with and without medication covariates, then tabulating significant species counts per tool per condition and quantifying their overlap.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are cross-sectional with no time or repeated-measure structure — LongDat's longitudinal pipelines (longdat_cont/longdat_disc) and this comparison assume longitudinal design You only need a single tool's differential-abundance output rather than a tool-vs-tool concordance assessment The feature table is not count data and you cannot supply the matching data_type; LongDat requires the correct data_type (count, proportion, binary, ordinal, continuous) for valid signal calls

skills.description: Use when a newly proposed MAG/prokaryotic genome taxonomy classifier must be validated against established gold standards (GTDBtk, CAMITAX) on a common benchmark set with known NCBI taxonomic labels.
skills.name: cross-tool-taxonomic-benchmarking
skills.search_text: cross-tool-taxonomic-benchmarking Use when a newly proposed MAG/prokaryotic genome taxonomy classifier must be validated against established gold standards (GTDBtk, CAMITAX) on a common benchmark set with known NCBI taxonomic labels. The goal is functional or compositional profiling of shotgun reads rather than classification of assembled genomes/MAGs — kMetaShot and this benchmark target bins/MAG FASTA inputs Only one classifier is to be run with no comparison baseline — cross-tool benchmarking requires at least two tools evaluated on the identical genome set Expected taxonomy is not in NCBI space and no conversion table exists (GTDBtk outputs must be converted to NCBI via ncbi_vs_gtdb_r89 for fair comparison) http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Head-to-head benchmarking of taxonomic classifiers (kMetaShot vs GTDBtk and CAMITAX) on a curated genome set such as the 939 HMP genomes, comparing strain-, species-, and genus-level classification using set-based sensitivity, precision, FPR, balanced accuracy, and F1-score. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bib/bbae680
skills.summary: Head-to-head benchmarking of taxonomic classifiers (kMetaShot vs GTDBtk and CAMITAX) on a curated genome set such as the 939 HMP genomes, comparing strain-, species-, and genus-level classification using set-based sensitivity, precision, FPR, balanced accuracy, and F1-score.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is functional or compositional profiling of shotgun reads rather than classification of assembled genomes/MAGs — kMetaShot and this benchmark target bins/MAG FASTA inputs Only one classifier is to be run with no comparison baseline — cross-tool benchmarking requires at least two tools evaluated on the identical genome set Expected taxonomy is not in NCBI space and no conversion table exists (GTDBtk outputs must be converted to NCBI via ncbi_vs_gtdb_r89 for fair comparison)

skills.description: Use when fitting a regularized (L1/Lasso) mixture model — e.g., STENSL source selection with sink profile x vs. Y^T*α — and the sparsity level must be chosen from data rather than fixed arbitrarily.
skills.name: cross-validated-hyperparameter-grid-search
skills.search_text: cross-validated-hyperparameter-grid-search Use when fitting a regularized (L1/Lasso) mixture model — e.g., STENSL source selection with sink profile x vs. Y^T*α — and the sparsity level must be chosen from data rather than fixed arbitrarily. When the number of candidate sources is small and full (non-sparse) source tracking is adequate — the paper notes existing methods like FEAST/SourceTracker2 are sufficient in low-source-count settings, and STENSL's sparsity targets large candidate sets. When no hyperparameter is tunable or the model has already been fit with a validated fixed λ (e.g., the authors' λ = 1 × 10−6) — a grid search would add cost without benefit. When the input is already a mixing-proportion output (S1 × S2 matrix P); the grid search operates on the count matrix and metadata, not on downstream contribution tables. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Determines an optimal Lasso regularization hyperparameter λ for sparse microbial source tracking (STENSL) by cross-validation over a candidate grid, then running expectation-maximization at each fixed λ and returning the α, γ parameter set with the highest likelihood. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00995-21
skills.summary: Determines an optimal Lasso regularization hyperparameter λ for sparse microbial source tracking (STENSL) by cross-validation over a candidate grid, then running expectation-maximization at each fixed λ and returning the α, γ parameter set with the highest likelihood.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the number of candidate sources is small and full (non-sparse) source tracking is adequate — the paper notes existing methods like FEAST/SourceTracker2 are sufficient in low-source-count settings, and STENSL's sparsity targets large candidate sets. When no hyperparameter is tunable or the model has already been fit with a validated fixed λ (e.g., the authors' λ = 1 × 10−6) — a grid search would add cost without benefit. When the input is already a mixing-proportion output (S1 × S2 matrix P); the grid search operates on the count matrix and metadata, not on downstream contribution tables.

skills.description: Use when predicting phenotypic traits (e.g. aerobe, anaerobe, gramneg, thermophile) from comparative-genomics feature matrices (COG/eggNOG presence-absence profiles) and need cross-validated, kernel-comparable SVM accuracy and runtime figures.
skills.name: cross-validated-phenotype-trait-prediction
skills.search_text: cross-validated-phenotype-trait-prediction Use when predicting phenotypic traits (e.g. aerobe, anaerobe, gramneg, thermophile) from comparative-genomics feature matrices (COG/eggNOG presence-absence profiles) and need cross-validated, kernel-comparable SVM accuracy and runtime figures. Input genomes are far below 60-70% completeness — the article notes most traits can only be reliably predicted at 60-70% completeness, so incomplete bins below this range will yield unreliable predictions The target trait lacks sufficient labeled training data — the article states good performance for further ecologically important traits is pending availability of sufficient training data The goal is a detailed functional analysis of individual genome features rather than genome-level phenotypic trait classification http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Trains and evaluates microbial phenotypic trait predictors from COG presence/absence profiles using PICA's SVM plug-in (libSVM) with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times, scoring balanced accuracy per trait. It supports both kernel comparisons (linear vs RBF/sigmoid/polynomial) and SVM-only vs CPAR2SVM feature-selection comparisons. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Trains and evaluates microbial phenotypic trait predictors from COG presence/absence profiles using PICA's SVM plug-in (libSVM) with 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times, scoring balanced accuracy per trait. It supports both kernel comparisons (linear vs RBF/sigmoid/polynomial) and SVM-only vs CPAR2SVM feature-selection comparisons.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input genomes are far below 60-70% completeness — the article notes most traits can only be reliably predicted at 60-70% completeness, so incomplete bins below this range will yield unreliable predictions The target trait lacks sufficient labeled training data — the article states good performance for further ecologically important traits is pending availability of sufficient training data The goal is a detailed functional analysis of individual genome features rather than genome-level phenotypic trait classification

skills.description: Use when evaluating whether combining models from k-fold cross-validation splits raises protein contact prediction accuracy over a single model, and when comparing accuracy across fold counts (e.g., 3/5/7/10) on CASP-style benchmark sets.
skills.name: cross-validation-fold-count-comparison
skills.search_text: cross-validation-fold-count-comparison Use when evaluating whether combining models from k-fold cross-validation splits raises protein contact prediction accuracy over a single model, and when comparing accuracy across fold counts (e.g., 3/5/7/10) on CASP-style benchmark sets. You only need a single-model prediction without benchmarking ensemble gains — running pipeline.py once suffices The model/MSA input is not one of the DeepECA multitask cross-validation models; the averaging result is specific to models trained on split datasets of the same architecture http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0082 Reproduce DeepECA's ensemble-averaging protocol: average residue-pair contact probabilities over models trained on cross-validation splits of the training set, and quantify how the number of folds (3-, 5-, 7-, 10-fold) affects top-L/L/2/L/5/L/10 contact accuracy on CASP11 and CASP12 targets. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3190-x
skills.summary: Reproduce DeepECA's ensemble-averaging protocol: average residue-pair contact probabilities over models trained on cross-validation splits of the training set, and quantify how the number of folds (3-, 5-, 7-, 10-fold) affects top-L/L/2/L/5/L/10 contact accuracy on CASP11 and CASP12 targets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need a single-model prediction without benchmarking ensemble gains — running pipeline.py once suffices The model/MSA input is not one of the DeepECA multitask cross-validation models; the averaging result is specific to models trained on split datasets of the same architecture

skills.description: Use when inferring population structure from genome-wide biallelic SNP data (VCF- or PLINK-derived BED files) and the number of ancestral populations (K) is unknown and must be estimated.
skills.name: cross-validation-k-selection
skills.search_text: cross-validation-k-selection Use when inferring population structure from genome-wide biallelic SNP data (VCF- or PLINK-derived BED files) and the number of ancestral populations (K) is unknown and must be estimated. The number of ancestral populations (K) is already known or fixed by the study design — run ADMIXTURE at the chosen K only. The goal is phylogenetic relationship inference or migration-edge analysis — use the TreeMix sub-workflow instead. The SNP set is not LD-pruned and no recoding of non-integer chromosome IDs to integers has been done, so tools expecting integer chromosome IDs or linkage equilibrium cannot read the data correctly. http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3299 Select the optimal number of ancestral clusters (K) in ADMIXTURE by running ADMIXTURE over a user-defined range of K on a LD-pruned PLINK BED file, parsing each run's log for the cross-validation (CV) error, and choosing the K with the lowest CV error for downstream Q-matrix visualization. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/molbev/msae057
skills.summary: Select the optimal number of ancestral clusters (K) in ADMIXTURE by running ADMIXTURE over a user-defined range of K on a LD-pruned PLINK BED file, parsing each run's log for the cross-validation (CV) error, and choosing the K with the lowest CV error for downstream Q-matrix visualization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The number of ancestral populations (K) is already known or fixed by the study design — run ADMIXTURE at the chosen K only. The goal is phylogenetic relationship inference or migration-edge analysis — use the TreeMix sub-workflow instead. The SNP set is not LD-pruned and no recoding of non-integer chromosome IDs to integers has been done, so tools expecting integer chromosome IDs or linkage equilibrium cannot read the data correctly.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking supervised protein family classifiers built on amino acid recoding kmer vectors, and you need cross-validated ROC AUC/PR AUC to compare alphabets and kmer lengths.
skills.name: cross-validation-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: cross-validation-model-evaluation Use when benchmarking supervised protein family classifiers built on amino acid recoding kmer vectors, and you need cross-validated ROC AUC/PR AUC to compare alphabets and kmer lengths. The task is unsupervised de novo family determination — use Snekmer's 'cluster' mode with agglomerative/density Jaccard clustering instead of model-mode cross-validation. skills.description: Use when a reference genome database (e.g. AFS31RS90, ~135 GB in RAM) exceeds single-node or single-executor memory and you need to quantify the time/memory/speed trade-off of splitting it into partitions or distributing it over Spark executors.
skills.name: database-partitioning-scalability-benchmarking
skills.search_text: database-partitioning-scalability-benchmarking Use when a reference genome database (e.g. AFS31RS90, ~135 GB in RAM) exceeds single-node or single-executor memory and you need to quantify the time/memory/speed trade-off of splitting it into partitions or distributing it over Spark executors. The database already fits comfortably in workstation memory (e.g. ≤128 GB for the default RefSeq build), since partitioning only costs query speed without necessity. The task is tool accuracy benchmarking against CLARK, Kraken2, or Kraken2+Bracken rather than memory/time scaling of partitioned database construction. Query speed, not peak memory, is the binding constraint — partitioning degraded throughput from 7.2 to 2.5 MR/m in the paper's measurements. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark how partitioning a large minhashing reference database (AFS31RS90) affects build time, peak memory, and query speed for the C++ workstation tool AFS-MetaCache and the Spark-based MetaCacheSpark, reproducing the paper's Table 8 scaling behaviour. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-3429-6
skills.summary: Benchmark how partitioning a large minhashing reference database (AFS31RS90) affects build time, peak memory, and query speed for the C++ workstation tool AFS-MetaCache and the Spark-based MetaCacheSpark, reproducing the paper's Table 8 scaling behaviour.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The database already fits comfortably in workstation memory (e.g. ≤128 GB for the default RefSeq build), since partitioning only costs query speed without necessity. skills.description: Use when a Kraken database (e.g., the ~70-GB standard RefSeq build) exceeds available RAM and a reduced-memory variant must be created by record subsampling, and the resulting sensitivity/precision deltas need to be measured.
skills.name: database-shrinking-record-subsampling
skills.search_text: database-shrinking-record-subsampling Use when a Kraken database (e.g., the ~70-GB standard RefSeq build) exceeds available RAM and a reduced-memory variant must be created by record subsampling, and the resulting sensitivity/precision deltas need to be measured. The database already fits in available RAM — subsampling only removes k-mers and strictly reduces sensitivity on real metagenomes. The goal is maximum precision per classified read on high-error data — MiniKraken is more precise, but if sensitivity on high-error simulated reads (simBA-5) matters, the full database is required. You need species- or strain-level resolution from a low-memory build — the article's validation is framed at the genus level only. http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reduce a large Kraken k-mer/LCA database to fit memory-constrained machines (MiniKraken) by deterministically removing records in fixed-size blocks, then quantify the accuracy trade-off as genus-level sensitivity loss versus precision gain compared to the full database. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/gb-2014-15-3-r46
skills.summary: Reduce a large Kraken k-mer/LCA database to fit memory-constrained machines (MiniKraken) by deterministically removing records in fixed-size blocks, then quantify the accuracy trade-off as genus-level sensitivity loss versus precision gain compared to the full database.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The database already fits in available RAM — subsampling only removes k-mers and strictly reduces sensitivity on real metagenomes. The goal is maximum precision per classified read on high-error data — MiniKraken is more precise, but if sensitivity on high-error simulated reads (simBA-5) matters, the full database is required. You need species- or strain-level resolution from a low-memory build — the article's validation is framed at the genus level only.

skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-baseline-variant-calling Use when benchmarking a reference-free variant caller against the de Bruijn graph on simulated or real WGS reads, needing an independent baseline call set for hap.py validation. You need to call variants from a BWT/eBWT of the read collection alone without a de Bruijn graph — that is ebwt2InDel's role, not the baseline's Input is not raw reads (e.g. already an aligned BAM or an existing VCF call set) — DISCOSNP++ in this workflow operates on raw read sets The comparison targets INDEL detection with the parallel pipeline's external pre-processing tool, which does not take into account the presence of INDELs in the read set http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Run DISCOSNP++, the de Bruijn graph-based variant caller, on the same read set as the eBWT-based tool to provide the state-of-the-art baseline for SNP/INDEL sensitivity and precision comparison. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03586-3

skills.description: Use when assembling Illumina short reads de novo and peak memory during de Bruijn graph construction is limiting, or when benchmarking sparse-vs-dense DBG memory tradeoffs.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-construction
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-construction Use when assembling Illumina short reads de novo and peak memory during de Bruijn graph construction is limiting, or when benchmarking sparse-vs-dense DBG memory tradeoffs. Input is metagenomic or single-cell data better served by MEGAHIT, which the SOAPdenovo2 README notes generates longer contigs with less memory The goal is finished scaffolding only and read layout is already assembled into contigs — use the map/scaff or SOAPdenovo-fusion steps instead of rebuilding the graph The read set is so small that memory during graph construction is not a constraint, removing the sparse mode's rationale http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Constructs a de Bruijn graph from short reads, either with the standard pregraph module or SOAPdenovo2's sparse de Bruijn graph mode, which groups linear unique k-mers to cut memory consumption during graph construction at the cost of a shorter k-mer length. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/2047-217x-1-18
skills.summary: Constructs a de Bruijn graph from short reads, either with the standard pregraph module or SOAPdenovo2's sparse de Bruijn graph mode, which groups linear unique k-mers to cut memory consumption during graph construction at the cost of a shorter k-mer length.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is metagenomic or single-cell data better served by MEGAHIT, which the SOAPdenovo2 README notes generates longer contigs with less memory The goal is finished scaffolding only and read layout is already assembled into contigs — use the map/scaff or SOAPdenovo-fusion steps instead of rebuilding the graph The read set is so small that memory during graph construction is not a constraint, removing the sparse mode's rationale

skills.description: Use when assembling Illumina GA short reads (FASTA/FASTQ/BAM, paired-end or mate-pair libraries) into a de novo draft genome for large plant/animal or human-sized genomes and you need scaffold N50 and error metrics comparable to SOAPdenovo1, ALLPATHS-LG, or Assemblathon1/GAGE benchmarks.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-contig-scaffolding
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-contig-scaffolding Use when assembling Illumina GA short reads (FASTA/FASTQ/BAM, paired-end or mate-pair libraries) into a de novo draft genome for large plant/animal or human-sized genomes and you need scaffold N50 and error metrics comparable to SOAPdenovo1, ALLPATHS-LG, or Assemblathon1/GAGE benchmarks. Input is single-cell or metagenomics data — the README directs such data to MEGAHIT, which generates longer contigs with less memory Only a few CPUs/memory available — the README requires a 64-bit Linux system with at least 5 GB physical memory (~150 GB for human-sized genomes) The goal is comparing against published baseline assemblies rather than producing a new one — use evaluation-focused skills on existing Assemblathon1/GAGE assemblies instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Assembles Illumina GA short reads into contigs and scaffolds using SOAPdenovo2's six-module de Bruijn graph pipeline (read error correction, DBG construction, contig assembly, PE reads mapping, scaffold construction, gap closure with GapCloser), with reduced memory consumption and improved continuity/accuracy over SOAPdenovo1. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/2047-217x-1-18
skills.summary: Assembles Illumina GA short reads into contigs and scaffolds using SOAPdenovo2's six-module de Bruijn graph pipeline (read error correction, DBG construction, contig assembly, PE reads mapping, scaffold construction, gap closure with GapCloser), with reduced memory consumption and improved continuity/accuracy over SOAPdenovo1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell or metagenomics data — the README directs such data to MEGAHIT, which generates longer contigs with less memory Only a few CPUs/memory available — the README requires a 64-bit Linux system with at least 5 GB physical memory (~150 GB for human-sized genomes) The goal is comparing against published baseline assemblies rather than producing a new one — use evaluation-focused skills on existing Assemblathon1/GAGE assemblies instead

skills.description: Use when raw FASTQ reads (Illumina MiSeq or high-error-rate ONT MinION) from S. aureus or M. tuberculosis isolates must be converted directly into an antibiotic-resistance call set without assembly or SNP-calling pipelines.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-genotype-calling
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-genotype-calling Use when raw FASTQ reads (Illumina MiSeq or high-error-rate ONT MinION) from S. aureus or M. tuberculosis isolates must be converted directly into an antibiotic-resistance call set without assembly or SNP-calling pipelines. skills.summary: Predict species identity and antibiotic-resistance profiles from raw sequence data by genotyping known resistance determinants against a de Bruijn graph representation of bacterial diversity, implemented in Mykrobe predictor and demonstrated on both Illumina MiSeq and Oxford Nanopore MinION reads.

skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-kmer-parameterization Use when assembling metagenomic (environmental) FASTQ reads with MetaCortex and a maximum k-mer size must be chosen and baked in at compile time before building the de Bruijn graph. If you need to explore multiple k-mer values post-hoc on the same installation: the max k-mer is a compile-time choice, so you must recompile (or install a different Conda build) rather than pass k as a runtime flag If the required kmer exceeds the Conda build limit of 127: compile from source with make MAXK=160 or 192 instead of using the bioconda package If the data are not short-read metagenomic sequence data: MetaCortex is built on the consensus Cortex assembler (cortex_con) for environmental sequence data, not for other data modalities http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Selects and compiles MetaCortex with an appropriate maximum k-mer size (one of 31/63/95/127/160/192) so the de Bruijn graph construction captures strain-level variation in metagenomic viral read data. The k-mer choice is a compile-time parameter, so it must be fixed before assembly. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad020
skills.summary: Selects and compiles MetaCortex with an appropriate maximum k-mer size (one of 31/63/95/127/160/192) so the de Bruijn graph construction captures strain-level variation in metagenomic viral read data. The k-mer choice is a compile-time parameter, so it must be fixed before assembly.

skills.description: Use when assembling metagenomic (environmental) FASTQ reads from samples with high strain-level diversity — e.g. viral mock communities, HIV lab mixes, or gut microbiomes — and both a consensus contig set and per-strain graph paths are needed.
skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-metagenomic-assembly
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-metagenomic-assembly Use when assembling metagenomic (environmental) FASTQ reads from samples with high strain-level diversity — e.g. viral mock communities, HIV lab mixes, or gut microbiomes — and both a consensus contig set and per-strain graph paths are needed. The input is not raw metagenomic reads but already-assembled contigs or a feature/bin table — this skill operates on FASTQ reads via de Bruijn graph construction. Only a single-isolate genome with no strain-level variation is targeted; a consensus-only isolate assembler is more appropriate than MetaCortex's sequence-graph output. Only an LLVM toolchain is available on macOS and the conda build is unsuitable — MetaCortex source compilation requires GCC ('LLVM will not compile MetaCortex'). http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Two-stage de Bruijn graph metagenomic assembly with MetaCortex: reads are imported in parallel into CTX binary graph files, then combined to output consensus contigs and sequence graphs (GFA) that retain intra-species variation for strain-level reconstruction. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad020
skills.summary: Two-stage de Bruijn graph metagenomic assembly with MetaCortex: reads are imported in parallel into CTX binary graph files, then combined to output consensus contigs and sequence graphs (GFA) that retain intra-species variation for strain-level reconstruction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is not raw metagenomic reads but already-assembled contigs or a feature/bin table — this skill operates on FASTQ reads via de Bruijn graph construction. Only a single-isolate genome with no strain-level variation is targeted; a consensus-only isolate assembler is more appropriate than MetaCortex's sequence-graph output. Only an LLVM toolchain is available on macOS and the conda build is unsuitable — MetaCortex source compilation requires GCC ('LLVM will not compile MetaCortex').

skills.name: de-bruijn-graph-postorder-traversal
skills.search_text: de-bruijn-graph-postorder-traversal Use when you must decompose a colored (multi-sample) de Bruijn graph into sample-specific superbubbles, assign offset values per node, and build the cSupB tree used for graph coordinates and variant detection. Sequences with insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on the traversal is not applicable Highly repetitive sequences, especially tandem repeats — the cutting method fragments the sequence, increasing computational difficulty and error Cases requiring large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications — the method only addresses small indels (< 50 bp) and cannot handle degeneracy efficiently http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 A single postorder-like traversal of a colored de Bruijn graph (as implemented in VARI-cSupB/C++) that uses four visiting states and a color-intersection matching principle to identify all colored superbubbles (cSupBs) in one pass, then reorganizes them into the hierarchical cSupB tree underlying the tri-tuple coordinate system. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: A single postorder-like traversal of a colored de Bruijn graph (as implemented in VARI-cSupB/C++) that uses four visiting states and a color-intersection matching principle to identify all colored superbubbles (cSupBs) in one pass, then reorganizes them into the hierarchical cSupB tree underlying the tri-tuple coordinate system.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sequences with insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number) — the variant detection model built on the traversal is not applicable Highly repetitive sequences, especially tandem repeats — the cutting method fragments the sequence, increasing computational difficulty and error Cases requiring large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications — the method only addresses small indels (< 50 bp) and cannot handle degeneracy efficiently

skills.search_text: de-novo-metagenome-assembly Use when input is raw paired-end metagenomic (or spiked-in isolate) Illumina FASTQ reads and the goal is to recover cas operons/CRISPR arrays while measuring runtime against a complete-assembly baseline. Input is already assembled contigs or a genome — use annotation/detection tools directly rather than targeted re-assembly The goal is a whole-community taxonomic/functional profile rather than recovery of CRISPR/Cas loci — targeted assembly discards the vast majority of the metagenome Reads are long-read or non-Illumina data; the pipeline is designed for unassembled raw Illumina short reads http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Assemble CRISPR/Cas regions from pooled metagenomic FASTQ reads either via targeted assembly (CasCollect: HMMER seed reads against 120 Cas protein HMMs, VSEARCH expansion at 95% identity, metaSPAdes, CRISPRCasFinder) or via complete metaSPAdes assembly, benchmarking runtime and contig output. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: Assemble CRISPR/Cas regions from pooled metagenomic FASTQ reads either via targeted assembly (CasCollect: HMMER seed reads against 120 Cas protein HMMs, VSEARCH expansion at 95% identity, metaSPAdes, CRISPRCasFinder) or via complete metaSPAdes assembly, benchmarking runtime and contig output.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already assembled contigs or a genome — use annotation/detection tools directly rather than targeted re-assembly The goal is a whole-community taxonomic/functional profile rather than recovery of CRISPR/Cas loci — targeted assembly discards the vast majority of the metagenome Reads are long-read or non-Illumina data; the pipeline is designed for unassembled raw Illumina short reads

skills.description: Use when you have trimmed paired-end Illumina reads from an isolate genome (e.g., E. coli K-12 MG1655, ~4.6-4.8 Mb) and need de novo contig assemblies from several widely-cited short-read assemblers for downstream quality comparison.
skills.name: de-novo-short-read-genome-assembly
skills.search_text: de-novo-short-read-genome-assembly Use when you have trimmed paired-end Illumina reads from an isolate genome (e.g., E. coli K-12 MG1655, ~4.6-4.8 Mb) and need de novo contig assemblies from several widely-cited short-read assemblers for downstream quality comparison. Long-read or hybrid sequencing data is the input — these assemblers were shortlisted and benchmarked as short-read assemblers only A high-quality reference genome is available and a reference-guided assembly or variant-aware evaluation (e.g., against a close substrain such as W3110) is the actual goal The goal is assembly quality assessment rather than assembly generation — use QUAST/WebQUAST for evaluation instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Assemble trimmed paired-end short reads into a contig FASTA using multiple short-read assemblers (ABySS, MEGAHIT, SPAdes, Velvet installed via Bioconda), as demonstrated on the E. coli K-12 MG1655 dataset (SRA ERR008613) used to build WebQUAST's sample evaluation dataset. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad406
skills.summary: Assemble trimmed paired-end short reads into a contig FASTA using multiple short-read assemblers (ABySS, MEGAHIT, SPAdes, Velvet installed via Bioconda), as demonstrated on the E. coli K-12 MG1655 dataset (SRA ERR008613) used to build WebQUAST's sample evaluation dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Long-read or hybrid sequencing data is the input — these assemblers were shortlisted and benchmarked as short-read assemblers only A high-quality reference genome is available and a reference-guided assembly or variant-aware evaluation (e.g., against a close substrain such as W3110) is the actual goal The goal is assembly quality assessment rather than assembly generation — use QUAST/WebQUAST for evaluation instead

skills.description: Use when evaluating a deep unsupervised clustering tool for unlabeled DNA sequences (e.g. FASTA mitochondrial genomes) against k-means++, GMM, DeLUCS, and MeShClust v3.0 with ground-truth cluster_id TSV labels available for posthoc scoring.
skills.name: deep-learning-baseline-algorithm-comparison
skills.search_text: deep-learning-baseline-algorithm-comparison Use when evaluating a deep unsupervised clustering tool for unlabeled DNA sequences (e.g. FASTA mitochondrial genomes) against k-means++, GMM, DeLUCS, and MeShClust v3.0 with ground-truth cluster_id TSV labels available for posthoc scoring. The sequences are already labeled or a supervised classifier is the goal — the ground-truth TSV must not be used during iDeLUCS training, only for posthoc comparison The input is a feature table or aligned sequences — iDeLUCS clusters raw DNA sequences via genomic signatures without alignment The number of clusters is unknown and fine-grained — although --n_clusters=0 launches iDeLUCS + HDBSCAN to infer cluster count automatically, this comparison workflow assumes the true cluster count is provided http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Benchmark a deep-learning clustering method (iDeLUCS, PyTorch) against two classical baselines (k-means++, GMM) and two DNA-specialized algorithms (DeLUCS, MeShClust v3.0) on alignment-free DNA sequence clustering, scoring every method x dataset cell with intrinsic (DBI, silhouette) and external (Homogeneity, Completeness, ACC) metrics. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad508
skills.summary: Benchmark a deep-learning clustering method (iDeLUCS, PyTorch) against two classical baselines (k-means++, GMM) and two DNA-specialized algorithms (DeLUCS, MeShClust v3.0) on alignment-free DNA sequence clustering, scoring every method x dataset cell with intrinsic (DBI, silhouette) and external (Homogeneity, Completeness, ACC) metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequences are already labeled or a supervised classifier is the goal — the ground-truth TSV must not be used during iDeLUCS training, only for posthoc comparison The input is a feature table or aligned sequences — iDeLUCS clusters raw DNA sequences via genomic signatures without alignment The number of clusters is unknown and fine-grained — although --n_clusters=0 launches iDeLUCS + HDBSCAN to infer cluster count automatically, this comparison workflow assumes the true cluster count is provided

skills.description: Use when benchmarking a multi-status microbiome classifier (e.g. 3 oral labels Control/Periodontitis/Gingivitis or 5 gut labels) and needing convolution-based deep learning baselines that were originally designed for a different output task.
skills.name: deep-learning-baseline-output-layer-adaptation
skills.search_text: deep-learning-baseline-output-layer-adaptation Use when benchmarking a multi-status microbiome classifier (e.g. 3 oral labels Control/Periodontitis/Gingivitis or 5 gut labels) and needing convolution-based deep learning baselines that were originally designed for a different output task. The baseline model is already configured for the target number of classes — no output-layer adaptation is needed The task is binary or the label schema matches the baseline's original design, so retraining with identical splits without layer modification is sufficient Only conventional ML baselines (KNN, DT, SVM, XGBoost, RF) are being benchmarked and no convolution deep baseline is required http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Adapts single-branch convolution deep learning baselines (regular CNN, MDeep) to multi-status microbiome classification by widening their output layers to the number of status classes, so they can be benchmarked fairly against PM-CNN using identical cross-validation splits. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae013
skills.summary: Adapts single-branch convolution deep learning baselines (regular CNN, MDeep) to multi-status microbiome classification by widening their output layers to the number of status classes, so they can be benchmarked fairly against PM-CNN using identical cross-validation splits.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The baseline model is already configured for the target number of classes — no output-layer adaptation is needed The task is binary or the label schema matches the baseline's original design, so retraining with identical splits without layer modification is sufficient Only conventional ML baselines (KNN, DT, SVM, XGBoost, RF) are being benchmarked and no convolution deep baseline is required

skills.description: Use when reproducing or extending the DeepECA Feature Added Model for long-range contact prediction from MSAs, particularly to test whether sequential features improve accuracy when homologous sequence depth is small.
skills.name: deep-neural-network-contact-prediction-training
skills.search_text: deep-neural-network-contact-prediction-training Use when reproducing or extending the DeepECA Feature Added Model for long-range contact prediction from MSAs, particularly to test whether sequential features improve accuracy when homologous sequence depth is small. The goal is contact prediction from a single sequence or from non-MSA-derived covariance features (e.g. PDB structures directly) — this skill requires a multiple sequence alignment as input The task is MSA construction quality improvement itself; the article leaves improving MSA construction and collecting evolutionary information for shallow MSAs as future work GPU memory cannot accommodate the 60-layer network, which the authors chose because of GPU memory limitations http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0128 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train the Feature Added deep neural network from DeepECA to predict protein residue-residue contacts directly from a multiple sequence alignment, augmenting weighted-MSA covariance features with sequential features (one-hot query, PSSM, entropy, mutual information, sequence separations) to boost long-range contact accuracy, especially for shallow MSAs. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3190-x
skills.summary: Train the Feature Added deep neural network from DeepECA to predict protein residue-residue contacts directly from a multiple sequence alignment, augmenting weighted-MSA covariance features with sequential features (one-hot query, PSSM, entropy, mutual information, sequence separations) to boost long-range contact accuracy, especially for shallow MSAs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is contact prediction from a single sequence or from non-MSA-derived covariance features (e.g. PDB structures directly) — this skill requires a multiple sequence alignment as input The task is MSA construction quality improvement itself; the article leaves improving MSA construction and collecting evolutionary information for shallow MSAs as future work GPU memory cannot accommodate the 60-layer network, which the authors chose because of GPU memory limitations

skills.description: Use when labeled whole-genome sequences (FASTA with training labels in sequence IDs) must be turned into a DNN read classifier and architecture variants (one-hot CNN, hybrid, LSTM, self-attention) need to be compared by read-level precision and recall.
skills.name: deep-neural-network-training-on-genomes
skills.search_text: deep-neural-network-training-on-genomes Use when labeled whole-genome sequences (FASTA with training labels in sequence IDs) must be turned into a DNN read classifier and architecture variants (one-hot CNN, hybrid, LSTM, self-attention) need to be compared by read-level precision and recall. The input reads come from long-read platforms or have error profiles strongly different from the training data — retraining is required in that case per the discussion. The goal is to add new species to an already-trained classifier without retraining — the current framework requires retraining the entire deep neural network. A reference-free or alignment-free abundance-only estimate is needed without species-level read classification (e.g. genus-level profiling with a chosen confidence threshold may suffice). http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Trains deep neural network architectures (e.g. k-mer embedding + BiLSTM + self-attention) on labeled genome sequences converted to TFRecord, to classify short shotgun metagenomic reads at species rank, as done in DeepMicrobes with the 2505-genome human gut bacterial repertoire. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa009
skills.summary: Trains deep neural network architectures (e.g. k-mer embedding + BiLSTM + self-attention) on labeled genome sequences converted to TFRecord, to classify short shotgun metagenomic reads at species rank, as done in DeepMicrobes with the 2505-genome human gut bacterial repertoire.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input reads come from long-read platforms or have error profiles strongly different from the training data — retraining is required in that case per the discussion. The goal is to add new species to an already-trained classifier without retraining — the current framework requires retraining the entire deep neural network. A reference-free or alignment-free abundance-only estimate is needed without species-level read classification (e.g. genus-level profiling with a chosen confidence threshold may suffice).

skills.description: Use when training a DNN to predict protein contacts and secondary structure from raw MSAs end-to-end, rather than from precomputed covariance or precision-matrix features.
skills.name: deep-residual-network-training
skills.search_text: deep-residual-network-training Use when training a DNN to predict protein contacts and secondary structure from raw MSAs end-to-end, rather than from precomputed covariance or precision-matrix features. When a pre-trained DeepECA model suffices — use pipeline.py for prediction instead of retraining from scratch When only shallow MSAs are available without the option to add sequential/derived features, since the paper notes accuracy gains depend on MSA depth and weighting When input is already a covariance or precision matrix (e.g., PSICOV output) — DeepECA takes the raw MSA as its input feature source http://edamontology.org/topic_0128 http://edamontology.org/topic_2275 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train DeepECA's deep residual network (up to 60 residual layers with batch normalization) end-to-end on multiple sequence alignments for protein contact, secondary structure, and solvent accessibility prediction, using the multitask.py training script. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3190-x
skills.summary: Train DeepECA's deep residual network (up to 60 residual layers with batch normalization) end-to-end on multiple sequence alignments for protein contact, secondary structure, and solvent accessibility prediction, using the multitask.py training script.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a pre-trained DeepECA model suffices — use pipeline.py for prediction instead of retraining from scratch When only shallow MSAs are available without the option to add sequential/derived features, since the paper notes accuracy gains depend on MSA depth and weighting When input is already a covariance or precision matrix (e.g., PSICOV output) — DeepECA takes the raw MSA as its input feature source

skills.description: Use when classifying assembled metagenomic contigs as viral in ViroProfiler, specifically to apply DeepVirFinder's score/p-value threshold as one of the per-tool detection criteria.
skills.name: deepvirfinder-score-thresholding
skills.search_text: deepvirfinder-score-thresholding Use when classifying assembled metagenomic contigs as viral in ViroProfiler, specifically to apply DeepVirFinder's score/p-value threshold as one of the per-tool detection criteria. When ViroProfiler is applied to samples with isolated viruses only — the pipeline is specifically designed for classifying viruses in samples with isolated viruses, and environmental contamination can lower precision. When contigs are already classified (e.g., binned vMAGs from vRhyme or phamb) and only annotation or taxonomy is needed. When you need a standalone viral verdict — a single DeepVirFinder pass alone yields only a 'low confident' label under the multi-tool rule. http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 A ViroProfiler decision rule that flags contigs as putatively viral when DeepVirFinder's deep-learning score exceeds 0.9 with p < 0.01, feeding this criterion into the multi-tool confidence scoring used to classify viral contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1080/19490976.2023.2192522
skills.summary: A ViroProfiler decision rule that flags contigs as putatively viral when DeepVirFinder's deep-learning score exceeds 0.9 with p < 0.01, feeding this criterion into the multi-tool confidence scoring used to classify viral contigs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When ViroProfiler is applied to samples with isolated viruses only — the pipeline is specifically designed for classifying viruses in samples with isolated viruses, and environmental contamination can lower precision. When contigs are already classified (e.g., binned vMAGs from vRhyme or phamb) and only annotation or taxonomy is needed. When you need a standalone viral verdict — a single DeepVirFinder pass alone yields only a 'low confident' label under the multi-tool rule.

skills.description: Use when aligned nucleotide sequences of target functional genes (e.g., amoA-AOB FASTA from ranked/clustered gene sets) must be converted into a minimal set of primer pairs that captures maximal diversity of a reference gene set.
skills.name: degenerate-primer-design
skills.search_text: degenerate-primer-design Use when aligned nucleotide sequences of target functional genes (e.g., amoA-AOB FASTA from ranked/clustered gene sets) must be converted into a minimal set of primer pairs that captures maximal diversity of a reference gene set. Input sequences are unaligned or not in FASTA format — EcoFunPrimer's select subcommand requires aligned nucleotide sequences The goal is ranking/prioritizing gene targets from metagenomes rather than designing primers (use the upstream ranking stage instead) Only a handful of closely related sequences must be targeted and a single degenerate consensus primer suffices; the high-throughput minimal-set machinery is unnecessary http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Designs thermodynamically stable degenerate and nondegenerate primer pairs from aligned nucleotide sequences of environmentally abundant target genes using EcoFunPrimer within MetaFunPrimer, then enumerates nondegenerate forms and evaluates them via in silico PCR against a reference gene set. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00201-21
skills.summary: Designs thermodynamically stable degenerate and nondegenerate primer pairs from aligned nucleotide sequences of environmentally abundant target genes using EcoFunPrimer within MetaFunPrimer, then enumerates nondegenerate forms and evaluates them via in silico PCR against a reference gene set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are unaligned or not in FASTA format — EcoFunPrimer's select subcommand requires aligned nucleotide sequences The goal is ranking/prioritizing gene targets from metagenomes rather than designing primers (use the upstream ranking stage instead) Only a handful of closely related sequences must be targeted and a single degenerate consensus primer suffices; the high-throughput minimal-set machinery is unnecessary

skills.description: Use when two DA methods have been applied to the same samples with known ground-truth labels and you need a statistically valid paired comparison of their ROC AUCs (e.g., 800 simulated bacterial species, 400 null / 400 differential).
skills.name: delong-correlated-roc-comparison
skills.search_text: delong-correlated-roc-comparison Use when two DA methods have been applied to the same samples with known ground-truth labels and you need a statistically valid paired comparison of their ROC AUCs (e.g., 800 simulated bacterial species, 400 null / 400 differential). The two methods were run on DIFFERENT datasets or taxa sets (curves are not correlated, so paired DeLong is inappropriate) The task is calibration, effect-size, or FDR-power assessment rather than ranking/discrimination via ROC (p-values and effect estimates need other summaries) Data are not relative abundances resembling a zero-inflated beta distribution (e.g., raw counts or compositional data transformed to log-ratios) — the simulation context here assumes zero-inflated beta relative abundance A benchmarking skill for comparing two differential-abundance classifiers that score the SAME simulated taxa (correlated/paired predictions): compute ROC curves and AUCs with pROC in R, then compare paired AUCs with DeLong's test. Used in metamicrobiomeR's simulation to show GAMLSS-BEZI (AUC 95.6) significantly outperforms LMAS (AUC 92.9) on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for comparing two differential-abundance classifiers that score the SAME simulated taxa (correlated/paired predictions): compute ROC curves and AUCs with pROC in R, then compare paired AUCs with DeLong's test. Used in metamicrobiomeR's simulation to show GAMLSS-BEZI (AUC 95.6) significantly outperforms LMAS (AUC 92.9) on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The two methods were run on DIFFERENT datasets or taxa sets (curves are not correlated, so paired DeLong is inappropriate) The task is calibration, effect-size, or FDR-power assessment rather than ranking/discrimination via ROC (p-values and effect estimates need other summaries) Data are not relative abundances resembling a zero-inflated beta distribution (e.g., raw counts or compositional data transformed to log-ratios) — the simulation context here assumes zero-inflated beta relative abundance

skills.description: Reference for reproducing the Sentinel-1 GRDH-to-gamma0 chain when input is uncalibrated DN in slant-range coordinates and output must be calibrated, terrain-normalized gamma_0 at 10 m pixel spacing.
skills.name: dem-based-sar-geocoding
skills.search_text: dem-based-sar-geocoding Reference for reproducing the Sentinel-1 GRDH-to-gamma0 chain when input is uncalibrated DN in slant-range coordinates and output must be calibrated, terrain-normalized gamma_0 at 10 m pixel spacing. Data are already gamma_0 in geographic coordinates (e.g. temporal gamma_0 stacks like ALB_gamma0_VH.tif used downstream in R) — only pixel/neighborhood statistics are needed A spatial speckle filter is required before single-scene analysis — this chain deliberately omits spatial speckle filtering because median compositing over acquisitions suppresses speckle implicitly Working from SLC products requiring full SLC-level processing, since the study used only backscatter coefficients available in GRDH Converts Sentinel-1 GRDH backscatter from slant-range image coordinates to terrain-flattened, orthorectified gamma_0 in geographic coordinates by combining radiometric terrain flattening and range-Doppler terrain correction with the SRTM 1 sec DEM and precise orbits in SNAP's GPT. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x
skills.summary: Converts Sentinel-1 GRDH backscatter from slant-range image coordinates to terrain-flattened, orthorectified gamma_0 in geographic coordinates by combining radiometric terrain flattening and range-Doppler terrain correction with the SRTM 1 sec DEM and precise orbits in SNAP's GPT.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are already gamma_0 in geographic coordinates (e.g. temporal gamma_0 stacks like ALB_gamma0_VH.tif used downstream in R) — only pixel/neighborhood statistics are needed A spatial speckle filter is required before single-scene analysis — this chain deliberately omits spatial speckle filtering because median compositing over acquisitions suppresses speckle implicitly Working from SLC products requiring full SLC-level processing, since the study used only backscatter coefficients available in GRDH

skills.description: Use when multiple binary clinical/grouping factors are available for the same microbiome feature table and the goal is a quantitative, comparable measure (AUMC/AOI) of which factor identifies differences in microbial communities.
skills.name: descriptive-association-metric-quantification
skills.search_text: descriptive-association-metric-quantification Use when multiple binary clinical/grouping factors are available for the same microbiome feature table and the goal is a quantitative, comparable measure (AUMC/AOI) of which factor identifies differences in microbial communities. The question is formal inference (p-value adjustment or FDR control) — the paper states the method does not control the false discovery rate and AOI/AUMC are descriptive only The grouping factor is not binary (multi-class or continuous factors need regrouping first, as done for SmitsData 1/2) The goal is to validate individual feature hits robustly (use fragility index or the full-permutation best-feature workflow instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quantify the overall association between the microbiome and binary grouping factors by computing the AUMC (area under the U-curve of significant features vs. proportion of mixing) from progressive permutation, then rank factors by decreasing AUMC (bigger AUMC = stronger association). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Quantify the overall association between the microbiome and binary grouping factors by computing the AUMC (area under the U-curve of significant features vs. proportion of mixing) from progressive permutation, then rank factors by decreasing AUMC (bigger AUMC = stronger association).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question is formal inference (p-value adjustment or FDR control) — the paper states the method does not control the false discovery rate and AOI/AUMC are descriptive only The grouping factor is not binary (multi-class or continuous factors need regrouping first, as done for SmitsData 1/2) The goal is to validate individual feature hits robustly (use fragility index or the full-permutation best-feature workflow instead)

skills.search_text: detection-curve-visualization Use when you need to determine how many raw MinION reads are required before a baseLess abundance-mode classifier's MSRD plateau is reached, e.g. plotting MSRD-vs-reads curves for multiple target species on a single figure. You need per-read target detection output — in abundance mode baseLess retains no reads, so read-level filtering plots are not applicable. You are using read_detection mode on 16S data where the relevant metric is the >66% k-mer fraction threshold per read, not an MSRD stability curve. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Visualizes MSRD (model stability metric) as a function of the number of MinION reads processed by baseLess abundance-mode models, to identify the read count at which each species classification stabilizes. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad017
skills.summary: Visualizes MSRD (model stability metric) as a function of the number of MinION reads processed by baseLess abundance-mode models, to identify the read count at which each species classification stabilizes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need per-read target detection output — in abundance mode baseLess retains no reads, so read-level filtering plots are not applicable.
