skills.description: Use when calling fecal source presence/absence in short-read metagenomes from SourceApp's genome-equivalent-normalized cell fraction estimates, where spurious low-level signal must be filtered before computing apportionment portions.
skills.name: detection-limit-threshold-filtering
skills.search_text: detection-limit-threshold-filtering Use when calling fecal source presence/absence in short-read metagenomes from SourceApp's genome-equivalent-normalized cell fraction estimates, where spurious low-level signal must be filtered before computing apportionment portions. Inputs are long reads or non-FASTQ data — SourceApp's mapping filters were tuned for short 2x150-bp Illumina NovaSeq 6000 reads The goal is a mass balance of fecal contamination — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of prokaryotic cells based on genome equivalents, not mass balance Estimating contamination age or detecting growth-capable (nonconservative) populations — the tool explicitly cannot do this http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Applies SourceApp's detection thresholds — a per-source limit of detection (LOD, 0.01% cell fraction by default) plus read-mapping filters (93% identity, 70% query coverage, sequence breadth limit) — to decide whether a fecal source is present in a shotgun metagenome before apportioning cell fractions among present sources. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Applies SourceApp's detection thresholds — a per-source limit of detection (LOD, 0.01% cell fraction by default) plus read-mapping filters (93% identity, 70% query coverage, sequence breadth limit) — to decide whether a fecal source is present in a shotgun metagenome before apportioning cell fractions among present sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Inputs are long reads or non-FASTQ data — SourceApp's mapping filters were tuned for short 2x150-bp Illumina NovaSeq 6000 reads The goal is a mass balance of fecal contamination — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of prokaryotic cells based on genome equivalents, not mass balance Estimating contamination age or detecting growth-capable (nonconservative) populations — the tool explicitly cannot do this

skills.description: Use when estimating the minimum detectable minor-population frequency for a genotype-based resistance or species caller on Illumina data, e.g. benchmarking mecA or plasmid-borne tetracycline/erythromycin detection in in silico S. aureus/CoNS mixtures.
skills.name: detection-power-evaluation
skills.search_text: detection-power-evaluation Use when estimating the minimum detectable minor-population frequency for a genotype-based resistance or species caller on Illumina data, e.g. benchmarking mecA or plasmid-borne tetracycline/erythromycin detection in in silico S. aureus/CoNS mixtures. The caller being evaluated has no JSON output mode and cannot be run in --format json, so per-sample structured parsing is impossible The question is per-isolate resistance prediction accuracy (sensitivity/specificity against a phenotype gold standard, e.g. the n=470 S. aureus validation set) rather than minor-population detection power in mixtures Input is a single isolate rather than pooled/simulated mixtures — detection power as a function of minor frequency is undefined Quantifies how reliably Mykrobe predictor detects low-frequency resistant populations in simulated mixed infections, by pooling FASTQ reads from St_B1 S. aureus and St_B2 CoNS samples across a controlled frequency gradient and computing the fraction of correct calls per frequency. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms10063
skills.summary: Quantifies how reliably Mykrobe predictor detects low-frequency resistant populations in simulated mixed infections, by pooling FASTQ reads from St_B1 S. aureus and St_B2 CoNS samples across a controlled frequency gradient and computing the fraction of correct calls per frequency.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The caller being evaluated has no JSON output mode and cannot be run in --format json, so per-sample structured parsing is impossible The question is per-isolate resistance prediction accuracy (sensitivity/specificity against a phenotype gold standard, e.g. the n=470 S. aureus validation set) rather than minor-population detection power in mixtures Input is a single isolate rather than pooled/simulated mixtures — detection power as a function of minor frequency is undefined

skills.description: Use when you need to predict or budget DIAMOND annotation compute time for metatranscriptome samples by measuring how SAMSA2's DIAMOND runtime scales with the number of input sequences under a fixed CPU/memory allocation.
skills.name: diamond-aligner-benchmarking
skills.search_text: diamond-aligner-benchmarking Use when you need to predict or budget DIAMOND annotation compute time for metatranscriptome samples by measuring how SAMSA2's DIAMOND runtime scales with the number of input sequences under a fixed CPU/memory allocation. The goal is annotation accuracy or genus-level classification quality rather than runtime scaling — use SAMSA2's accuracy comparison workflow instead Input reads have not passed SAMSA2 preprocessing (PEAR merging, Trimmomatic cleaning, SortMeRNA ribosomal filtering), so annotated size would not reflect the mRNA fraction being benchmarked Compute resources vary between runs, since non-constant CPU/RAM allocation would confound the linear scaling measurement http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks DIAMOND-based annotation runtime scaling in SAMSA2 by running DIAMOND (version 0.8.3) over metatranscriptome input files of increasing sequence count under fixed compute resources, then verifying that wall-clock annotation time grows approximately linearly with input size so runtime can be estimated from file size. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: Benchmarks DIAMOND-based annotation runtime scaling in SAMSA2 by running DIAMOND (version 0.8.3) over metatranscriptome input files of increasing sequence count under fixed compute resources, then verifying that wall-clock annotation time grows approximately linearly with input size so runtime can be estimated from file size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is annotation accuracy or genus-level classification quality rather than runtime scaling — use SAMSA2's accuracy comparison workflow instead Input reads have not passed SAMSA2 preprocessing (PEAR merging, Trimmomatic cleaning, SortMeRNA ribosomal filtering), so annotated size would not reflect the mRNA fraction being benchmarked Compute resources vary between runs, since non-constant CPU/RAM allocation would confound the linear scaling measurement

skills.description: Use when you have DIAMOND tabular alignment hits of shotgun metagenomic reads against a microbial gene database (e.g. UniRef90) and must refine them to hits per read for gene abundance estimation.
skills.name: diamond-alignment-output-parsing
skills.search_text: diamond-alignment-output-parsing Use when you have DIAMOND tabular alignment hits of shotgun metagenomic reads against a microbial gene database (e.g. UniRef90) and must refine them to hits per read for gene abundance estimation. Input is already a gene count or gene abundance table rather than raw DIAMOND alignment hits Alignments are in SAM/BAM or other formats not produced by MetaLAFFA's DIAMOND tabular output A different hit-refinement strategy (not best-e-value per read) is required by the analysis design http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0114 Parse DIAMOND tabular alignment output from MetaLAFFA's read-mapping phase and reduce it to best matches per read using the hit-refinement (best e-value hit filtering) strategy, yielding a gzipped read-gene hit table that feeds fractional gene counting. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Parse DIAMOND tabular alignment output from MetaLAFFA's read-mapping phase and reduce it to best matches per read using the hit-refinement (best e-value hit filtering) strategy, yielding a gzipped read-gene hit table that feeds fractional gene counting.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a gene count or gene abundance table rather than raw DIAMOND alignment hits Alignments are in SAM/BAM or other formats not produced by MetaLAFFA's DIAMOND tabular output A different hit-refinement strategy (not best-e-value per read) is required by the analysis design

skills.description: Use when DIAMOND-based retrieval of phylogenetic markers yields low query coverage, particularly with low-coverage read data as query, and masking or sensitivity settings may be limiting alignments.
skills.name: diamond-alignment-parameter-tuning
skills.search_text: diamond-alignment-parameter-tuning Use when DIAMOND-based retrieval of phylogenetic markers yields low query coverage, particularly with low-coverage read data as query, and masking or sensitivity settings may be limiting alignments. Query coverage is already high (e.g. the high-quality-assembly benchmark reached 92.2% mean query coverage), so masking has little room to help The analysis goal is maximizing percent identity only; disabling tantan can slightly reduce identity while raising coverage The aligner or pipeline does not expose DIAMOND's tantan masking option (the skill is specific to DIAMOND-driven searches) http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Tunes DIAMOND alignment parameters used inside alignment-based marker retrieval (e.g. Patchwork), specifically disabling tantan masking with --masking 0 to improve query coverage of recovered markers, especially for read-based queries. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Tunes DIAMOND alignment parameters used inside alignment-based marker retrieval (e.g. Patchwork), specifically disabling tantan masking with --masking 0 to improve query coverage of recovered markers, especially for read-based queries.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Query coverage is already high (e.g. the high-quality-assembly benchmark reached 92.2% mean query coverage), so masking has little room to help The analysis goal is maximizing percent identity only; disabling tantan can slightly reduce identity while raising coverage The aligner or pipeline does not expose DIAMOND's tantan masking option (the skill is specific to DIAMOND-driven searches)

skills.description: Use when raw FASTQ metatranscriptome reads need organism or functional annotation against a local protein database, and speed or reproducibility rules out BLAST or web services such as MG-RAST.
skills.name: diamond-protein-database-alignment
skills.search_text: diamond-protein-database-alignment Use when raw FASTQ metatranscriptome reads need organism or functional annotation against a local protein database, and speed or reproducibility rules out BLAST or web services such as MG-RAST. Input is already an aggregated abundance/annotation summary table — the alignment step operates on per-read FASTQ data The analysis requires rRNA or 16S-based community profiling — SortMeRNA-filtered reads exclude ribosomal sequences, which DIAMOND protein alignment is not designed to annotate Only a web service with no local database control is acceptable — this skill requires local, DIAMOND-indexed databases and Python 2.7 for aggregation http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Annotate metatranscriptome reads by translating and aligning them to a local, DIAMOND-indexed protein reference database (e.g. RefSeq for organisms, SEED Subsystems for functions) using the DIAMOND aligner, as implemented in the SAMSA2 pipeline. This replaces BLAST and web services like MG-RAST, yielding per-read annotations orders of magnitude faster and reproducibly on a cluster. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: Annotate metatranscriptome reads by translating and aligning them to a local, DIAMOND-indexed protein reference database (e.g. RefSeq for organisms, SEED Subsystems for functions) using the DIAMOND aligner, as implemented in the SAMSA2 pipeline. This replaces BLAST and web services like MG-RAST, yielding per-read annotations orders of magnitude faster and reproducibly on a cluster.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aggregated abundance/annotation summary table — the alignment step operates on per-read FASTQ data The analysis requires rRNA or 16S-based community profiling — SortMeRNA-filtered reads exclude ribosomal sequences, which DIAMOND protein alignment is not designed to annotate Only a web service with no local database control is acceptable — this skill requires local, DIAMOND-indexed databases and Python 2.7 for aggregation

skills.description: Use when you have unassembled NGS shotgun-read FASTA metagenomes (extensions '.fasta', '.fa' or '.fna') with host diet or phenotype metadata and want to test whether alignment-free d2S distances recapitulate those groups.
skills.name: dietary-group-separation-analysis-of-metagenomes
skills.search_text: dietary-group-separation-analysis-of-metagenomes Use when you have unassembled NGS shotgun-read FASTA metagenomes (extensions '.fasta', '.fa' or '.fna') with host diet or phenotype metadata and want to test whether alignment-free d2S distances recapitulate those groups. Input is already a k-mer count matrix, OTU/ASV table, or precomputed dissimilarity matrix — the d2S computation step is redundant; proceed directly to clustering. The goal is alignment-based reconstruction of host phylogeny rather than testing phenotype (diet) concordance; the paper's premise is that alignment-based methods are not appropriate for NGS short reads, so mixing goals confuses the acceptance criterion. Sequences require substitution-model-aware evolutionary distances with assembled references rather than background-adjusted k-mer count statistics on raw reads. http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Reproduce separation of mammalian dietary groups (hindgut fermenters, foregut fermenters, carnivores) from 28 NGS gut metagenomic shotgun-read samples by computing alignment-free d2S dissimilarities (k = 5, Markov order 0) with CAFE/JELLYFISH and clustering them into a UPGMA dendrogram. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx351
skills.summary: Reproduce separation of mammalian dietary groups (hindgut fermenters, foregut fermenters, carnivores) from 28 NGS gut metagenomic shotgun-read samples by computing alignment-free d2S dissimilarities (k = 5, Markov order 0) with CAFE/JELLYFISH and clustering them into a UPGMA dendrogram.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a k-mer count matrix, OTU/ASV table, or precomputed dissimilarity matrix — the d2S computation step is redundant; proceed directly to clustering. The goal is alignment-based reconstruction of host phylogeny rather than testing phenotype (diet) concordance; the paper's premise is that alignment-based methods are not appropriate for NGS short reads, so mixing goals confuses the acceptance criterion. Sequences require substitution-model-aware evolutionary distances with assembled references rather than background-adjusted k-mer count statistics on raw reads.

skills.description: Use when comparing phenotype-enrichment methods for species/pathway abundance tables (16S or metagenomic), especially with limited cohort sizes, or when reproducing the VTwins-vs-conventional sensitivity/10-fold-sample-size benchmark.
skills.name: differential-abundance-benchmarking
skills.search_text: differential-abundance-benchmarking Use when comparing phenotype-enrichment methods for species/pathway abundance tables (16S or metagenomic), especially with limited cohort sizes, or when reproducing the VTwins-vs-conventional sensitivity/10-fold-sample-size benchmark. Input is raw counts or already-normalized compositions not suited to decostand 'total' relative-abundance normalization, or the table is not a sample-by-feature data frame as required by pair_find Fewer than 10 eligible sample pairs exist across the two phenotype groups — pair_find returns nothing in that case The goal is generic multi-software benchmarking with tools other than VTwins beyond the article's 16-software benchmark scope, or samples are not clustered and ordered by grp1/grp2 as the method requires http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark causal-feature detection in metagenomic data by running VTwins, which pairs samples across phenotypes to eliminate confounder effects, against a conventional unpaired differential-abundance approach on simulated and empirical datasets. VTwins reportedly matches conventional recall with a 10-fold smaller sample size. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.scib.2023.10.024
skills.summary: Benchmark causal-feature detection in metagenomic data by running VTwins, which pairs samples across phenotypes to eliminate confounder effects, against a conventional unpaired differential-abundance approach on simulated and empirical datasets. VTwins reportedly matches conventional recall with a 10-fold smaller sample size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw counts or already-normalized compositions not suited to decostand 'total' relative-abundance normalization, or the table is not a sample-by-feature data frame as required by pair_find Fewer than 10 eligible sample pairs exist across the two phenotype groups — pair_find returns nothing in that case The goal is generic multi-software benchmarking with tools other than VTwins beyond the article's 16-software benchmark scope, or samples are not clustered and ordered by grp1/grp2 as the method requires

skills.description: Use when you need to quantitatively compare two or more differential abundance testing methods on simulated microbiome relative abundance data with known differential/null species labels, to decide which method has detection power.
skills.name: differential-abundance-method-benchmarking
skills.search_text: differential-abundance-method-benchmarking Use when you need to quantitatively compare two or more differential abundance testing methods on simulated microbiome relative abundance data with known differential/null species labels, to decide which method has detection power. Input is real observational data without known ground truth (null vs differential taxa) — ROC/AUC benchmarking requires true labels from simulation The goal is a single-method differential abundance analysis rather than comparing competing methods Data are absolute counts or compositional data you do not intend to model as zero-inflated beta relative abundances http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A simulation-based benchmarking workflow that compares differential abundance methods (GAMLSS-BEZI via metamicrobiomeR vs LMAS) on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data with known ground truth, using ROC/AUC and DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: A simulation-based benchmarking workflow that compares differential abundance methods (GAMLSS-BEZI via metamicrobiomeR vs LMAS) on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data with known ground truth, using ROC/AUC and DeLong's test for correlated ROC curves.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real observational data without known ground truth (null vs differential taxa) — ROC/AUC benchmarking requires true labels from simulation The goal is a single-method differential abundance analysis rather than comparing competing methods Data are absolute counts or compositional data you do not intend to model as zero-inflated beta relative abundances

skills.summary: Render error-bar plots of PICRUSt2 predicted pathway differential abundance results with ggpicrust2::pathway_errorbar(), showing group mean relative abundances with error bars annotated with log2 fold change and P-values per pathway.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw KO abundance table with no DA results yet — run differential abundance analysis first You want GSEA result visuals (enrichment plots, ridge plots) rather than DA error bars — use visualize_gsea() or pathway_ridgeplot() You need a per-taxa contribution view of which organisms drive pathway shifts — use the taxa contribution workflow (taxa_contribution_bar/heatmap) instead

skills.summary: Statistical identification of significantly differing features (organisms or functions) between metatranscriptome sample groups using DESeq in R, followed by graphical summaries such as PCA plots, heatmaps, and stacked-bar abundance graphs within the SAMSA2 pipeline.

skills.description: Use when you must reproduce or verify that metagenomeSeq improves differential abundance calling on sparse, undersampled marker-gene survey data relative to default DESeq, edgeR, Metastats, and LEfSe workflows.

skills.search_text: differential-abundance-tool-benchmarking Use when you must reproduce or verify that metagenomeSeq improves differential abundance calling on sparse, undersampled marker-gene survey data relative to default DESeq, edgeR, Metastats, and LEfSe workflows. skills.summary: Benchmark metagenomeSeq's normalization plus under-sampling (zero-inflated) statistical model against standard differential-abundance tools (DESeq, edgeR, Metastats, LEfSe) on sparse OTU/marker-gene count data with simulated ground truth.

skills.search_text: differential-gene-expression-analysis Use when you have a raw bulk RNA-seq count matrix (csv/txt) plus optional sample metadata and need per-gene differential expression results (log2FoldChange, Benjamini-Hochberg adjusted p-values) without scripting R/DESeq2 directly. skills.description: Use when preparing metagenomic/virome FASTQ reads for de-novo assembly where read depth is uneven and deep coverage would inflate assembly time or contig composition, e.g. prior to Virmap.pl or MEGAHIT.
skills.name: digital-normalization-of-reads
skills.search_text: digital-normalization-of-reads Use when preparing metagenomic/virome FASTQ reads for de-novo assembly where read depth is uneven and deep coverage would inflate assembly time or contig composition, e.g. prior to Virmap.pl or MEGAHIT. skills.summary: Generate two haploid reference FASTA files by inserting SNVs from a VCF into the hg38 reference genome using gen_fasta.py, creating a diploid ground truth for simulating Linked-Read data with LRTK-SIM and for validating diploid assemblies.

skills.description: Use when you need to measure what fraction of the genome a 10x Linked-Read de novo assembly (Supernova2) recovers in a diploid (both-homologs-covered) state, rather than a haploid contiguity metric such as N50.
skills.name: diploid-region-window-classification
skills.search_text: diploid-region-window-classification Use when you need to measure what fraction of the genome a 10x Linked-Read de novo assembly (Supernova2) recovers in a diploid (both-homologs-covered) state, rather than a haploid contiguity metric such as N50. When the goal is haploid contiguity or accuracy assessment (e.g. N50, NA50, GIAB variant comparison) rather than diploid-state recovery. When the assembly was not produced with Supernova2 phase blocks / megabubble haplotypes — the classification depends on per-haplotype scaffold pairs from mkoutput. When no reference genome with good coordinates exists to which haplotype scaffolds can be aligned (window coordinates are defined on hg38). http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A window-based classification method that quantifies the diploid fraction of Supernova2 assemblies built from 10x Linked-Read data by sliding 500-bp windows over the hg38 reference and labeling each window as diploid, hemizygous, or uncovered based on haplotype-scaffold alignment coverage. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz141
skills.summary: A window-based classification method that quantifies the diploid fraction of Supernova2 assemblies built from 10x Linked-Read data by sliding 500-bp windows over the hg38 reference and labeling each window as diploid, hemizygous, or uncovered based on haplotype-scaffold alignment coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is haploid contiguity or accuracy assessment (e.g. N50, NA50, GIAB variant comparison) rather than diploid-state recovery. When the assembly was not produced with Supernova2 phase blocks / megabubble haplotypes — the classification depends on per-haplotype scaffold pairs from mkoutput. When no reference genome with good coordinates exists to which haplotype scaffolds can be aligned (window coordinates are defined on hg38).

skills.description: Use when you have an alignment of short NGS reads (BAM/CRAM or FASTA MSA) from a genetically heterogeneous sample and need error correction plus local haplotype reconstruction before global assembly or frequency estimation.
skills.name: dirichlet-process-read-clustering
skills.search_text: dirichlet-process-read-clustering Use when you have an alignment of short NGS reads (BAM/CRAM or FASTA MSA) from a genetically heterogeneous sample and need error correction plus local haplotype reconstruction before global assembly or frequency estimation. You already need global (full-length) haplotype reconstruction rather than local windowed reconstruction — ShoRAH2 disables global mode; use v1.1.3 or V-pipe global options instead The input is unassembled raw reads not yet aligned to a reference — alignment is the prerequisite step 1 of the ShoRAH pipeline You only need single nucleotide variant detection with strand-bias accounting — invoke shorah snv directly rather than the full clustering stage http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Corrects sequencing errors and reconstructs local haplotypes from deep-sequencing reads of a mixed viral sample by clustering reads that overlap the same genomic window with a Dirichlet-process mixture Gibbs sampler (ShoRAH's diri_sampler). Each cluster consensus represents the original haplotype, and the read count per cluster estimates that haplotype's prevalence. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-12-119
skills.summary: Corrects sequencing errors and reconstructs local haplotypes from deep-sequencing reads of a mixed viral sample by clustering reads that overlap the same genomic window with a Dirichlet-process mixture Gibbs sampler (ShoRAH's diri_sampler). Each cluster consensus represents the original haplotype, and the read count per cluster estimates that haplotype's prevalence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already need global (full-length) haplotype reconstruction rather than local windowed reconstruction — ShoRAH2 disables global mode; use v1.1.3 or V-pipe global options instead The input is unassembled raw reads not yet aligned to a reference — alignment is the prerequisite step 1 of the ShoRAH pipeline You only need single nucleotide variant detection with strand-bias accounting — invoke shorah snv directly rather than the full clustering stage

skills.description: Use when the input is compositional count data (e.g., microbiome taxa) paired with covariates, and the goal is variable selection of covariate-by-branch associations while respecting a known or unknown phylogenetic/graph structure.
skills.name: dirichlet-tree-multinomial-regression
skills.search_text: dirichlet-tree-multinomial-regression Use when the input is compositional count data (e.g., microbiome taxa) paired with covariates, and the goal is variable selection of covariate-by-branch associations while respecting a known or unknown phylogenetic/graph structure. The response data are not compositional counts (e.g., already normalized/relative abundance feature tables) — the DTM likelihood expects count compositions No covariates are of interest and the goal is purely unsupervised ordination or clustering rather than covariate-branch association selection A known phylogenetic tree is unavailable and MRF/DM structure is not the target — the DTM models accommodate tree-like structure between the compositional data http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Fit Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression models with Bayesian variable selection via the MicroBVS R package to identify covariates associated with compositional microbial abundance data, accommodating phylogenetic tree structure and alternative inclusion priors (Beta-Binomial or MRF-based). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03640-0
skills.summary: Fit Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression models with Bayesian variable selection via the MicroBVS R package to identify covariates associated with compositional microbial abundance data, accommodating phylogenetic tree structure and alternative inclusion priors (Beta-Binomial or MRF-based).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The response data are not compositional counts (e.g., already normalized/relative abundance feature tables) — the DTM likelihood expects count compositions No covariates are of interest and the goal is purely unsupervised ordination or clustering rather than covariate-branch association selection A known phylogenetic tree is unavailable and MRF/DM structure is not the target — the DTM models accommodate tree-like structure between the compositional data

skills.description: Use when paired-end shotgun NGS reads have been uniquely mapped to metagenomic reference genomes with BWA and junction pairs spanning two different references must be grouped into candidate HGT breakpoints.
skills.name: discordant-read-pair-junction-selection
skills.search_text: discordant-read-pair-junction-selection Use when paired-end shotgun NGS reads have been uniquely mapped to metagenomic reference genomes with BWA and junction pairs spanning two different references must be grouped into candidate HGT breakpoints. You already need exact breakpoint nucleotide positions — that requires the subsequent split-read refinement stage (get_acc_bkp), not this candidate-generation step. Input reads are not paired-end shotgun reads or the BAM contains multi-mapped/non-unique alignments; LEMON's junction-pair selection assumes unique-mapping BAM input. Breakpoints are already available (e.g. from LUMPY output) and only downstream strain reconstruction is needed. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 In LEMON's raw-breakpoint stage, discordant read pairs whose two ends map to two different references are converted to 2D points and clustered with DBSCAN (Euclidean distance, eps = average insert size, minsample = 1) to generate candidate HGT breakpoints before split-read refinement. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3301-8
skills.summary: In LEMON's raw-breakpoint stage, discordant read pairs whose two ends map to two different references are converted to 2D points and clustered with DBSCAN (Euclidean distance, eps = average insert size, minsample = 1) to generate candidate HGT breakpoints before split-read refinement.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You already need exact breakpoint nucleotide positions — that requires the subsequent split-read refinement stage (get_acc_bkp), not this candidate-generation step. Input reads are not paired-end shotgun reads or the BAM contains multi-mapped/non-unique alignments; LEMON's junction-pair selection assumes unique-mapping BAM input. Breakpoints are already available (e.g. from LUMPY output) and only downstream strain reconstruction is needed.

skills.description: Use when d2* oligonucleotide-frequency dissimilarity values have been computed with Jie Ren's tools but the downstream model (ILMF-VH on the virus-host heterogeneous network, or SNF host network fusion) requires similarity matrices instead.
skills.name: dissimilarity-to-similarity-transformation
skills.search_text: dissimilarity-to-similarity-transformation Use when d2* oligonucleotide-frequency dissimilarity values have been computed with Jie Ren's tools but the downstream model (ILMF-VH on the virus-host heterogeneous network, or SNF host network fusion) requires similarity matrices instead. The input matrix is already a similarity (e.g., the Gaussian interaction profile kernel similarity computed by similarity_os.py/main.py) — re-transforming it would distort the host network used by SNF The downstream method consumes dissimilarity directly (e.g., raw d2* distances for ranking hosts by oligonucleotide frequency alone) — transformation is only required because ILMF-VH's matrix factorization expects similarity A different k-mer size or a non-d2* dissimilarity measure is required by the analysis protocol; the paper's pipeline is calibrated on d2* with k=6 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Transforms pairwise d2* oligonucleotide-frequency dissimilarity matrices (k=6, computed with Jie Ren's alignment-free tools) into the symmetric, bounded [0,1] similarity matrices that ILMF-VH's kernelized logistic matrix factorization and similarity network fusion require as virus-virus (Sv) and host-host network inputs. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3082-0
skills.summary: Transforms pairwise d2* oligonucleotide-frequency dissimilarity matrices (k=6, computed with Jie Ren's alignment-free tools) into the symmetric, bounded [0,1] similarity matrices that ILMF-VH's kernelized logistic matrix factorization and similarity network fusion require as virus-virus (Sv) and host-host network inputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input matrix is already a similarity (e.g., the Gaussian interaction profile kernel similarity computed by similarity_os.py/main.py) — re-transforming it would distort the host network used by SNF The downstream method consumes dissimilarity directly (e.g., raw d2* distances for ranking hosts by oligonucleotide frequency alone) — transformation is only required because ILMF-VH's matrix factorization expects similarity A different k-mer size or a non-d2* dissimilarity measure is required by the analysis protocol; the paper's pipeline is calibrated on d2* with k=6

skills.description: Use when choosing among metagenome comparison tools/metrics and you need evidence on which metric preserves body-site or community-composition structure rather than collapsing resolution.
skills.name: distance-metric-resolution-benchmarking
skills.search_text: distance-metric-resolution-benchmarking Use when choosing among metagenome comparison tools/metrics and you need evidence on which metric preserves body-site or community-composition structure rather than collapsing resolution. When the goal is a single tool's output quality rather than a head-to-head metric comparison — use the tool's own validation workflow instead When samples lack a known grouping (e.g., body site) against which clustering resolution can be judged; benchmarking resolution requires a ground-truth label When the input is not raw reads (e.g., already-computed distance matrices or sketch files) — re-running Mash/Libra/Simka on derived objects would not reproduce the read-level abundance comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark how alternative metagenome distance metrics (Mash MinHash, Libra Cosine Similarity on k-mer abundance, Simka Jaccard-ab and Bray-Curtis) resolve biological structure — here, clustering of 48 HMP whole-genome shotgun read samples by body site — by running each tool on identical inputs and comparing the resulting sample clusterings. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Benchmark how alternative metagenome distance metrics (Mash MinHash, Libra Cosine Similarity on k-mer abundance, Simka Jaccard-ab and Bray-Curtis) resolve biological structure — here, clustering of 48 HMP whole-genome shotgun read samples by body site — by running each tool on identical inputs and comparing the resulting sample clusterings.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a single tool's output quality rather than a head-to-head metric comparison — use the tool's own validation workflow instead When samples lack a known grouping (e.g., body site) against which clustering resolution can be judged; benchmarking resolution requires a ground-truth label When the input is not raw reads (e.g., already-computed distance matrices or sketch files) — re-running Mash/Libra/Simka on derived objects would not reproduce the read-level abundance comparison

skills.description: Use when you must reproduce or verify runtime-scaling claims for an all-vs-all metagenome comparison tool, or quantify the per-metric runtime share of Libra's scoring algorithms across increasing input volumes.
skills.name: distance-metric-runtime-comparison
skills.search_text: distance-metric-runtime-comparison Use when you must reproduce or verify runtime-scaling claims for an all-vs-all metagenome comparison tool, or quantify the per-metric runtime share of Libra's scoring algorithms across increasing input volumes. The goal is clustering accuracy or distance-metric quality on real microbiomes (e.g. HMP 16S/WGS or CAMI toy datasets) rather than runtime scaling — use Libra's validation benchmarks instead Datasets are far smaller than the benchmark scale, where per-run times are too short to distinguish linear from quadratic scaling The scoring/k-mer index has not yet been built — this skill times the core scoring stage only, not FASTA/FASTQ preprocessing http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmarks how Libra's all-vs-all metagenome comparison runtime scales with input volume and how much runtime each scoring algorithm (COSINESIMILARITY, BRAYCURTIS, JENSENSHANNON) consumes, using synthetic 9.3 GB/sample datasets run on Hadoop. This validates the claim that Libra scales linearly despite the quadratically growing number of all-vs-all sample pairs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Benchmarks how Libra's all-vs-all metagenome comparison runtime scales with input volume and how much runtime each scoring algorithm (COSINESIMILARITY, BRAYCURTIS, JENSENSHANNON) consumes, using synthetic 9.3 GB/sample datasets run on Hadoop. This validates the claim that Libra scales linearly despite the quadratically growing number of all-vs-all sample pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is clustering accuracy or distance-metric quality on real microbiomes (e.g. HMP 16S/WGS or CAMI toy datasets) rather than runtime scaling — use Libra's validation benchmarks instead Datasets are far smaller than the benchmark scale, where per-run times are too short to distinguish linear from quadratic scaling The scoring/k-mer index has not yet been built — this skill times the core scoring stage only, not FASTA/FASTQ preprocessing

skills.description: Use when inStrain has called SNVs on read pairs mapped to a reference genome and you need per-gene synonymous/nonsynonymous classification and dN/dS to compare variation within versus between hosts.
skills.name: dn-ds-calculation-from-metagenomic-snvs
skills.search_text: dn-ds-calculation-from-metagenomic-snvs Use when inStrain has called SNVs on read pairs mapped to a reference genome and you need per-gene synonymous/nonsynonymous classification and dN/dS to compare variation within versus between hosts. Coverage is too low to meet the inStrain SNP criteria (>=5 reads per position, >5% variant base, FDR 1e-6); minor-allele detection is coverage-dependent (Supplemental Figure S2), so dN/dS from sparse SNVs will be noise The goal is strain-level genome comparison (ConANI/popANI) rather than gene-level selection statistics; use 'inStrain compare' instead No annotated reference exists — synonymous/nonsynonymous assignment requires a reference .fasta with Prodigal open reading frame calls http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Computes per-gene dN/dS from biallelic metagenomic SNVs called by inStrain, labeling each variant synonymous or nonsynonymous against Prodigal gene calls to test whether diversity within hosts differs from variation between hosts (e.g., the E. faecalis phage 482_10.ph tail fiber gene, Figure 6). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Computes per-gene dN/dS from biallelic metagenomic SNVs called by inStrain, labeling each variant synonymous or nonsynonymous against Prodigal gene calls to test whether diversity within hosts differs from variation between hosts (e.g., the E. faecalis phage 482_10.ph tail fiber gene, Figure 6).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Coverage is too low to meet the inStrain SNP criteria (>=5 reads per position, >5% variant base, FDR 1e-6); minor-allele detection is coverage-dependent (Supplemental Figure S2), so dN/dS from sparse SNVs will be noise The goal is strain-level genome comparison (ConANI/popANI) rather than gene-level selection statistics; use 'inStrain compare' instead No annotated reference exists — synonymous/nonsynonymous assignment requires a reference .fasta with Prodigal open reading frame calls

skills.description: Use when a FASTA of 16S rRNA sequences (full-length ~1,500 bp or in-silico amplicons such as ~420 bp V3-V4) must be converted into fixed-length token inputs for a DNABERT-2-vocabulary transformer classifier.
skills.name: dna-bpe-tokenization
skills.search_text: dna-bpe-tokenization Use when a FASTA of 16S rRNA sequences (full-length ~1,500 bp or in-silico amplicons such as ~420 bp V3-V4) must be converted into fixed-length token inputs for a DNABERT-2-vocabulary transformer classifier. Input is already model-ready (pre-tokenized tensor batches or checkpoint logits), so re-tokenizing would duplicate work The downstream classifier is k-mer based (SINTAX, Kraken 2) or alignment based (BLAST, MMseqs2, VSEARCH), which expects raw nucleotide sequences rather than BPE subword IDs Sequences are not DNA (e.g., protein or 18S/metagenomic reads) and were not tokenized on the DNA BPE vocabulary used to train the released DeepTaxa checkpoints http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Encodes 16S rRNA gene sequences as subword tokens using the DNABERT-2 byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer so that the DeepTaxa HybridCNNBERTClassifier can consume them; from-scratch training on this vocabulary lets the transformer learn DNA-specific subword patterns rather than amino-acid or word-level units. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbag166
skills.summary: Encodes 16S rRNA gene sequences as subword tokens using the DNABERT-2 byte-pair-encoding (BPE) tokenizer so that the DeepTaxa HybridCNNBERTClassifier can consume them; from-scratch training on this vocabulary lets the transformer learn DNA-specific subword patterns rather than amino-acid or word-level units.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already model-ready (pre-tokenized tensor batches or checkpoint logits), so re-tokenizing would duplicate work The downstream classifier is k-mer based (SINTAX, Kraken 2) or alignment based (BLAST, MMseqs2, VSEARCH), which expects raw nucleotide sequences rather than BPE subword IDs Sequences are not DNA (e.g., protein or 18S/metagenomic reads) and were not tokenized on the DNA BPE vocabulary used to train the released DeepTaxa checkpoints

skills.search_text: dna-sequence-clustering-benchmark-evaluation Decision support for choosing a clustering-quality metric when ground-truth labels are unavailable: apply when benchmark tables exist for multiple clustering algorithms/datasets and you need to know if silhouette or Davies-Bouldin can proxy ACC. skills.summary: Assigns 16S rRNA amplicon gut microbiome samples to enterotypes via PAM-style clustering on dominant-genus community profiles, and quantifies how gene copy number (GCN) correction with CopyRighter changes that classification. In the CopyRighter twin cohort, uncorrected profiles split into two enterotypes while GCN-corrected profiles are better partitioned into three, with 23.9% of samples misclassified without correction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is raw reads or an unclassified OTU table — enterotype clustering requires genus-level assignments on Greengenes taxonomy, not OTU IDs alone Samples have fewer than 1,000 reads, below the cohort's depth threshold for reliable enterotype assignment Your data are shotgun metagenomes or non-gut communities where the enterotype framework and dominant-genus clustering do not apply

skills.description: Use when relative abundance estimates per reference genome (values in [0,1]) have been produced from mapped-read counts and must be scored against known mock-community mixing proportions by Euclidean distance.
skills.name: euclidean-distance-error-computation
skills.search_text: euclidean-distance-error-computation Use when relative abundance estimates per reference genome (values in [0,1]) have been produced from mapped-read counts and must be scored against known mock-community mixing proportions by Euclidean distance. Input lacks ground-truth mixing proportions for the mock community, so no distance can be computed. Abundance estimates are not normalized to the [0,1] range per genome, which would make Euclidean distances incomparable across tools. http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Computes Euclidean distance between a tool's estimated per-genome relative abundance vector and the ground-truth mixing proportions of a mock community, providing a single accuracy metric to rank raw-signal mappers such as RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Computes Euclidean distance between a tool's estimated per-genome relative abundance vector and the ground-truth mixing proportions of a mock community, providing a single accuracy metric to rank raw-signal mappers such as RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input lacks ground-truth mixing proportions for the mock community, so no distance can be computed. Abundance estimates are not normalized to the [0,1] range per genome, which would make Euclidean distances incomparable across tools.

skills.search_text: evolutionary-model-based-benchmarking Use when evaluating a strain-composition or haplotype-reconstruction method on simulated samples where ground-truth strain type distributions and mutation/recombination events must be generated under defined evolutionary models. skills.description: Use when a quality-filtered FASTQ/FNA amplicon dataset must be dereplicated before OTU inference and you need a deterministic exact-match collapse (or a fast runtime baseline to benchmark against VSEARCH-style dereplication).
skills.name: exact-string-matching-sequence-collapsing
skills.search_text: exact-string-matching-sequence-collapsing Use when a quality-filtered FASTQ/FNA amplicon dataset must be dereplicated before OTU inference and you need a deterministic exact-match collapse (or a fast runtime baseline to benchmark against VSEARCH-style dereplication). Input is already dereplicated or is a unique-sequence/abundance table rather than raw reads. Reads contain substantial sequencing errors and you need error-tolerant collapsing of near-identical reads; exact string matching will not merge single-base variants. The goal is similarity-threshold OTU clustering itself (e.g. de-novo greedy clustering) rather than the exact-identity dereplication step that precedes centroid selection. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Collapses identical amplicon reads into unique sequences with abundance counts using an exact string-matching dereplication algorithm, as implemented by MICCA-FAST as an alternative to the VSEARCH-based dereplication inside the MICCA OTU inference pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/srep09743
skills.summary: Collapses identical amplicon reads into unique sequences with abundance counts using an exact string-matching dereplication algorithm, as implemented by MICCA-FAST as an alternative to the VSEARCH-based dereplication inside the MICCA OTU inference pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already dereplicated or is a unique-sequence/abundance table rather than raw reads. Reads contain substantial sequencing errors and you need error-tolerant collapsing of near-identical reads; exact string matching will not merge single-base variants. The goal is similarity-threshold OTU clustering itself (e.g. de-novo greedy clustering) rather than the exact-identity dereplication step that precedes centroid selection.

skills.description: Decision support for identifying viral contigs from assembled sequences when direct homology to known viruses is insufficient, e.g., novel phages in metagenomic assemblies needing gene-content-based viral classification.
skills.name: exclusion-based-nonviral-data-filtering
skills.search_text: exclusion-based-nonviral-data-filtering Decision support for identifying viral contigs from assembled sequences when direct homology to known viruses is insufficient, e.g., novel phages in metagenomic assemblies needing gene-content-based viral classification. Input is raw short-read data where you want virMine's full QC-and-assembly pipeline (this skill presumes contigs already exist or are assembled by virMine) The goal is taxonomic classification of reads rather than scoring whole assembled contigs for viral origin No user-supplied nonviral database is available, since the exclusion step requires the -nv nonviral protein database http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 A contig-scoring strategy from virMine 2.0 that removes matches to a user-supplied nonviral database (exclusion technique) before scoring each contig by the origin of its gene content (cellular, viral, or unknown), eliminating sole dependency on homology to known viruses. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/mra.00107-22
skills.summary: A contig-scoring strategy from virMine 2.0 that removes matches to a user-supplied nonviral database (exclusion technique) before scoring each contig by the origin of its gene content (cellular, viral, or unknown), eliminating sole dependency on homology to known viruses.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw short-read data where you want virMine's full QC-and-assembly pipeline (this skill presumes contigs already exist or are assembled by virMine) The goal is taxonomic classification of reads rather than scoring whole assembled contigs for viral origin No user-supplied nonviral database is available, since the exclusion step requires the -nv nonviral protein database

skills.description: Use when you have globally reconstructed viral haplotypes (e.g., from ShoRAH's mm.py) and need maximum-likelihood estimates of their population frequencies, including low-frequency variants.
skills.name: expectation-maximization-frequency-estimation
skills.search_text: expectation-maximization-frequency-estimation Use when you have globally reconstructed viral haplotypes (e.g., from ShoRAH's mm.py) and need maximum-likelihood estimates of their population frequencies, including low-frequency variants. Running ShoRAH2 for global analysis: global haplotype reconstruction (and hence EM frequency estimation of global haplotypes) is disabled there; use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global options Only local haplotype/SNV calling is needed (shorah shotgun, shorah amplicon, or shorah snv) — frequency estimation of global haplotypes is unnecessary The sample is not genetically heterogeneous, so there is no mixed population to deconvolve http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Estimates population frequencies of reconstructed global haplotypes from a mixed deep-sequencing sample using freqEst, an Expectation Maximization algorithm that finds maximum-likelihood haplotype abundances, the final step of the ShoRAH pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-12-119
skills.summary: Estimates population frequencies of reconstructed global haplotypes from a mixed deep-sequencing sample using freqEst, an Expectation Maximization algorithm that finds maximum-likelihood haplotype abundances, the final step of the ShoRAH pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Running ShoRAH2 for global analysis: global haplotype reconstruction (and hence EM frequency estimation of global haplotypes) is disabled there; use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global options Only local haplotype/SNV calling is needed (shorah shotgun, shorah amplicon, or shorah snv) — frequency estimation of global haplotypes is unnecessary The sample is not genetically heterogeneous, so there is no mixed population to deconvolve

skills.description: Use when an m-by-n microbiome count matrix (rows = SampleID, taxa as columns) plus 3-column metadata (Env, SourceSink, id) must be decomposed into per-sink source contributions, especially with many noncontributing sources or an unknown source.
skills.name: expectation-maximization-mixing-proportion-inference
skills.search_text: expectation-maximization-mixing-proportion-inference Use when an m-by-n microbiome count matrix (rows = SampleID, taxa as columns) plus 3-column metadata (Env, SourceSink, id) must be decomposed into per-sink source contributions, especially with many noncontributing sources or an unknown source. When the true number of candidate sources is small and all are known contributors — plain FEAST suffices and STENSL's sparsity/unknown-source machinery is unnecessary overhead When the goal is source exploration with an unknown source using Aitchison-distance preselection only — the article shows this strategy has very low accuracy in the presence of an unknown source When inputs are not count tables in the required SampleID-by-taxa, 3-column metadata format — column order and 'Env'/'SourceSink'/'id' names must be respected http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Estimate microbial source-to-sink mixing proportions with FEAST/STENSL, expectation-maximization algorithms that model a sink community as a convex combination of contributing, nuisance, and unknown sources. STENSL adds L1-regularized sparsity so accuracy holds even with hundreds of candidate sources. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00995-21
skills.summary: Estimate microbial source-to-sink mixing proportions with FEAST/STENSL, expectation-maximization algorithms that model a sink community as a convex combination of contributing, nuisance, and unknown sources. STENSL adds L1-regularized sparsity so accuracy holds even with hundreds of candidate sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the true number of candidate sources is small and all are known contributors — plain FEAST suffices and STENSL's sparsity/unknown-source machinery is unnecessary overhead When the goal is source exploration with an unknown source using Aitchison-distance preselection only — the article shows this strategy has very low accuracy in the presence of an unknown source When inputs are not count tables in the required SampleID-by-taxa, 3-column metadata format — column order and 'Env'/'SourceSink'/'id' names must be respected

skills.description: Use when a microbial source tracking sink must be decomposed against many candidate sources (e.g., hundreds of environments from public repositories like HMP or EMP), where prior methods add considerable error and only a small subset of sources truly contribute.
skills.name: expectation-maximization-sparse-source-selection
skills.search_text: expectation-maximization-sparse-source-selection Use when a microbial source tracking sink must be decomposed against many candidate sources (e.g., hundreds of environments from public repositories like HMP or EMP), where prior methods add considerable error and only a small subset of sources truly contribute. When the full set of contributing sources is already known and small (simple source tracking without source exploration), where FEAST or SourceTracker2 suffice without sparsity-based selection When the input is raw sequence data or an unprocessed feature table requiring upstream taxonomy assignment and count-matrix construction http://edamontology.org/topic_0610 Apply STENSL, an expectation-maximization algorithm with sparsity (L1-regularized Lasso source selection inside the FEAST codebase), to estimate mixing proportions of contributing sources and an unknown source in a microbial sink even when hundreds of candidate source environments are considered. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00995-21
skills.summary: Apply STENSL, an expectation-maximization algorithm with sparsity (L1-regularized Lasso source selection inside the FEAST codebase), to estimate mixing proportions of contributing sources and an unknown source in a microbial sink even when hundreds of candidate source environments are considered.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the full set of contributing sources is already known and small (simple source tracking without source exploration), where FEAST or SourceTracker2 suffice without sparsity-based selection When the input is raw sequence data or an unprocessed feature table requiring upstream taxonomy assignment and count-matrix construction

skills.description: Use when profiling metagenomic read mappings against a reference .fasta and you need to distinguish low breadth caused by low coverage from breadth loss caused by strain absence or contamination.
skills.name: expected-breadth-coverage-modeling
skills.search_text: expected-breadth-coverage-modeling Use when profiling metagenomic read mappings against a reference .fasta and you need to distinguish low breadth caused by low coverage from breadth loss caused by strain absence or contamination. Input is raw reads or an unsorted .bam that has not been mapped to a reference .fasta — breadth modeling requires per-position depth on a reference You only need raw coverage/abundance numbers without breadth-vs-coverage interpretation; a fast tool like CoverM's 'coverm genome' suffices Comparing genomes across samples at strain level (use inStrain compare's ConANI/popANI instead of single-profile breadth metrics) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Models the expected fraction of a reference genome covered by at least one read as a monotonic function of mean mapping depth, using inStrain's expectedBreadth = -1*e^(-0.883*coverage)+1, so that observed scaffold breadth can be judged against coverage-implied expectations. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Models the expected fraction of a reference genome covered by at least one read as a monotonic function of mean mapping depth, using inStrain's expectedBreadth = -1*e^(-0.883*coverage)+1, so that observed scaffold breadth can be judged against coverage-implied expectations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads or an unsorted .bam that has not been mapped to a reference .fasta — breadth modeling requires per-position depth on a reference You only need raw coverage/abundance numbers without breadth-vs-coverage interpretation; a fast tool like CoverM's 'coverm genome' suffices Comparing genomes across samples at strain level (use inStrain compare's ConANI/popANI instead of single-profile breadth metrics)

skills.description: Use when evaluating a probabilistic 16S rRNA taxonomic classifier whose confidence must be verified against reported calibration numbers — e.g. reproducing DeepTaxa's per-rank ECE (domain 0.0002 → species 0.0242) on the 69,335-sequence Greengenes2 2024.09 test set.
skills.name: expected-calibration-error-estimation
skills.search_text: expected-calibration-error-estimation Use when evaluating a probabilistic 16S rRNA taxonomic classifier whose confidence must be verified against reported calibration numbers — e.g. reproducing DeepTaxa's per-rank ECE (domain 0.0002 → species 0.0242) on the 69,335-sequence Greengenes2 2024.09 test set. Only point-predictions or FASTA sequences without labels are available — ECE requires paired predictions and true taxonomic labels, so plain `deeptaxa predict` without a --taxonomy-file cannot produce it The input is a k-mer or alignment-based classifier (SINTAX, Kraken 2, DADA2) that does not emit calibrated softmax probabilities over all seven ranks Sequences come from reference databases outside the training vocabulary regime (e.g. SILVA, RDP) — the article notes cross-database performance remains untested, so calibration numbers would not be comparable to the 0.0242 reference http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Quantifies how well a hierarchical 16S rRNA classifier's softmax confidences match empirical correctness by binning confidence scores and computing expected calibration error (ECE) per taxonomic rank, alongside accuracy and F1. In DeepTaxa this yields species-level ECE ≈ 0.0242 on the Greengenes2 2024.09 test set. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbag166
skills.summary: Quantifies how well a hierarchical 16S rRNA classifier's softmax confidences match empirical correctness by binning confidence scores and computing expected calibration error (ECE) per taxonomic rank, alongside accuracy and F1. In DeepTaxa this yields species-level ECE ≈ 0.0242 on the Greengenes2 2024.09 test set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only point-predictions or FASTA sequences without labels are available — ECE requires paired predictions and true taxonomic labels, so plain `deeptaxa predict` without a --taxonomy-file cannot produce it The input is a k-mer or alignment-based classifier (SINTAX, Kraken 2, DADA2) that does not emit calibrated softmax probabilities over all seven ranks Sequences come from reference databases outside the training vocabulary regime (e.g. SILVA, RDP) — the article notes cross-database performance remains untested, so calibration numbers would not be comparable to the 0.0242 reference

skills.search_text: explained-variance-loss-quantification Use when you need to know how much of a predictor set's (e.g., ALS vs Sentinel-1 radar) explanatory power for many response variables depends on between-region variation rather than within-region structure. skills.search_text: extended-haplotype-homozygosity-selection-scanning Use when scanning phased biallelic SNP VCF (or PLINK binary) data, split by chromosome and indexed with tabix, for single-population (iHS) and pairwise population-comparison (XP-EHH) haplotype-based signals of selection. skills.when_to_use_negative: Input VCFs are not biallelic SNP data split by chromosome and tabix-indexed (chromosome names must not contain punctuation marks), or only PLINK non-binary formats are available The analysis goal is genetic structure (PCA, ADMIXTURE with optimal K via CV error) or phylogeny (TreeMix), not signatures of selection — use the corresponding scalepopgen sub-workflows instead A quick single-tool run is desired without intermediate transformations; the scalepopgen framework exists because many tools require nonstandard input formats and multistep transformations

skills.name: external-validation-of-species-composition-models
skills.search_text: external-validation-of-species-composition-models Use when testing whether a fitted radar (Sentinel-1 gamma_0) assemblage-composition model generalizes to independent, georeferenced field plots outside the training regions, e.g. bird or saproxylic beetle NMDS1 scores. Validation plots lie inside the five training forest regions — that is model fitting / internal validation, not the independent external test this skill performs The response of interest is species richness or phylogenetic diversity — Sentinel-1 performed poorly for taxa driven by understorey development (C-band weak permeability through overstorey layers) No independent, georeferenced, well-stratified species-composition data exist for the target area — the paper names this lack as the major barrier to larger-scale application http://edamontology.org/topic_3318 Reproduces the paper's external validation of Sentinel-1 radar assemblage-composition models: the fitted radar fixed-effects models (Supplementary Software 1) are applied, unchanged, to per-plot mean VH/VV gamma_0 backscatter statistics from independent plots outside the five training regions, and predicted vs observed NMDS1 scores are correlated (R² 0.26 for 72 bird plots, 0.22 for 91 saproxylic beetle plots). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x

skills.description: Use when running mbQTL's Approach B: you have estimated taxa-taxa correlation (R) values with coringTaxa and need to retain only the most extreme pairwise correlations before estimating taxa-SNP rho values with taxaSnpCor.
skills.name: extreme-quantile-correlation-filtering
skills.search_text: extreme-quantile-correlation-filtering Use when running mbQTL's Approach B: you have estimated taxa-taxa correlation (R) values with coringTaxa and need to retain only the most extreme pairwise correlations before estimating taxa-SNP rho values with taxaSnpCor. Input is not taxa-taxa correlation output but raw abundance or genotype data — coringTaxa must be run first. The goal is unadjusted pairwise correlation exploration without the taxa-SNP association step; the extreme-quantile filter exists specifically to support adjusted rho estimation in Approach B. http://edamontology.org/topic_3053 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 A filtering step from the mbQTL Approach B workflow in which all pairwise taxa-taxa correlations (R values, estimated with coringTaxa) are reduced to only the most extreme associations using allToAllProduct with probs = c(0.0001, 0.9999), so that subsequent taxa-SNP rho estimation (taxaSnpCor) is adjusted for extreme taxa-taxa correlation structure and can flag linkage disequilibrium (LD) SNPs/regions. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad565
skills.summary: A filtering step from the mbQTL Approach B workflow in which all pairwise taxa-taxa correlations (R values, estimated with coringTaxa) are reduced to only the most extreme associations using allToAllProduct with probs = c(0.0001, 0.9999), so that subsequent taxa-SNP rho estimation (taxaSnpCor) is adjusted for extreme taxa-taxa correlation structure and can flag linkage disequilibrium (LD) SNPs/regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Running mbQTL Approach A (linear regression via the MatrixeQTL core model) or the logistic regression analysis for presence/absence (categorical) taxa — these do not involve taxa-taxa R filtering. skills.description: Use when benchmarking read classifiers in a mock-community depletion setting: you have per-read target/non-target calls from SPUMONI or minimap2 over multiple index strategies and need F1 scores comparable to the paper's Table 1.
skills.name: f1-score-computation
skills.search_text: f1-score-computation Use when benchmarking read classifiers in a mock-community depletion setting: you have per-read target/non-target calls from SPUMONI or minimap2 over multiple index strategies and need F1 scores comparable to the paper's Table 1. The task is throughput, index-size, or memory benchmarking rather than classification accuracy — the paper measures speed and RSS separately from F1. You already have a predefined signal set or taxa-set (e.g. taxa-sets with at least five taxa at genus/family/order/class/phylum level) and do not need data-driven screening You are running a competing method such as aMiSPU, OMiRKAT, OMiAT, LDM or MiHC that tests the full clade without feature selection Your outcome-feature relationship is purely linear and well captured by marginal score statistics, where distance-correlation screening adds little http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Implements AMAT's data-adaptive screening guarantee: features are selected by comparing observed distance correlations with permuted null means, and if no feature passes, the single feature with maximum distance correlation to the adjusted response is force-selected so the testing subset S is never empty. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab120
