skills.description: Use when a large FASTA of predicted CDSs (e.g. ~5.5 million from assembled vaginal metagenomes) must be collapsed to a non-redundant gene set before annotation or read mapping.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-filtering
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-filtering Use when a large FASTA of predicted CDSs (e.g. ~5.5 million from assembled vaginal metagenomes) must be collapsed to a non-redundant gene set before annotation or read mapping. Input is already a non-redundant gene catalog (e.g. the published VIRGO 0.95-million-gene database) rather than raw predicted CDSs. Protein-level clustering is the goal; this nucleotide-level procedure (CD-HIT-EST) is for CDS de-redundancy, while VIRGO's VOGs are built separately by Jaccard clustering of all-vs-all BLASTP results. Reads rather than assembled/predicted sequences need filtering; read-level cutoffs in VIRGO (e.g. minimum 2 reads per gene hit, bowtie -l 25 seed length) are a different filter layer. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 De-redundify predicted coding sequences from assembled vaginal metagenomes with CD-HIT-EST at 95% identity over 90% of the shorter sequence, retaining only CDSs longer than 99 bp, to build a non-redundant gene catalog such as VIRGO's 948,158-gene catalog. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-14677-3
skills.summary: De-redundify predicted coding sequences from assembled vaginal metagenomes with CD-HIT-EST at 95% identity over 90% of the shorter sequence, retaining only CDSs longer than 99 bp, to build a non-redundant gene catalog such as VIRGO's 948,158-gene catalog.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a non-redundant gene catalog (e.g. the published VIRGO 0.95-million-gene database) rather than raw predicted CDSs. Protein-level clustering is the goal; this nucleotide-level procedure (CD-HIT-EST) is for CDS de-redundancy, while VIRGO's VOGs are built separately by Jaccard clustering of all-vs-all BLASTP results. Reads rather than assembled/predicted sequences need filtering; read-level cutoffs in VIRGO (e.g. minimum 2 reads per gene hit, bowtie -l 25 seed length) are a different filter layer.

skills.description: Use when a metagenomic assembly needs coverage-based edge correction of contigs — e.g. FASTA contigs plus a k-mer depth table where terminal regions of suspected interspecies misjoins show coverage deviating from the contig median.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-manipulation
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-manipulation Use when a metagenomic assembly needs coverage-based edge correction of contigs — e.g. FASTA contigs plus a k-mer depth table where terminal regions of suspected interspecies misjoins show coverage deviating from the contig median. Input is raw short reads rather than assembled contig FASTA — this skill operates on contig records, not read-level data Misassemblies must be corrected using long-range links (mate-pair/long reads) rather than coverage depth — MetaPlatanus' scaffolding/link modules, not edge trimming, are the right mechanism Coverage depth table is absent, so the 1.5x median-deviation condition cannot be evaluated for any contig http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Split and trim contig FASTA records by per-contig k-mer coverage depth, implementing MetaPlatanus' contig edge-correction: edge regions whose local coverage deviates more than 1.5x from the contig median are deleted to remove interspecies misjoinings within contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab831
skills.summary: Split and trim contig FASTA records by per-contig k-mer coverage depth, implementing MetaPlatanus' contig edge-correction: edge regions whose local coverage deviates more than 1.5x from the contig median are deleted to remove interspecies misjoinings within contigs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw short reads rather than assembled contig FASTA — this skill operates on contig records, not read-level data Misassemblies must be corrected using long-range links (mate-pair/long reads) rather than coverage depth — MetaPlatanus' scaffolding/link modules, not edge trimming, are the right mechanism Coverage depth table is absent, so the 1.5x median-deviation condition cannot be evaluated for any contig

skills.description: Use when merging overlapping DIAMOND BLASTX hits into continuous per-reference sequences or trimming noncoding regions, and the resulting marker sequences must be emitted as FASTA for phylogenetic use.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-output-writing
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-output-writing Use when merging overlapping DIAMOND BLASTX hits into continuous per-reference sequences or trimming noncoding regions, and the resulting marker sequences must be emitted as FASTA for phylogenetic use. The data are raw DIAMOND tabular BLASTX hits that have not yet been stitched or masked — FASTA emission should happen after overlap resolution, not on raw HSP tables The input is unassembled short reads (FASTQ); Patchwork can search raw reads, but this FASTA-writing step applies to the resulting stitched/trimmed marker sequences, not the read files http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Serialize the nucleotide/translated sequences produced by Patchwork's hit-stitching and sliding-window alignment-trimming stages into FASTA files (stitched_hits.fasta, trimmed_sequence.fasta), one continuous sequence per reference. This is the terminal output step that makes retrieved phylogenetic markers usable downstream. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Serialize the nucleotide/translated sequences produced by Patchwork's hit-stitching and sliding-window alignment-trimming stages into FASTA files (stitched_hits.fasta, trimmed_sequence.fasta), one continuous sequence per reference. This is the terminal output step that makes retrieved phylogenetic markers usable downstream.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are raw DIAMOND tabular BLASTX hits that have not yet been stitched or masked — FASTA emission should happen after overlap resolution, not on raw HSP tables The input is unassembled short reads (FASTQ); Patchwork can search raw reads, but this FASTA-writing step applies to the resulting stitched/trimmed marker sequences, not the read files

skills.description: Use when the input is archived raw FASTA files (genomics or proteomics omic-type) that must be parsed into individual sequences before embedding, vectorization, or tabular conversion in a time-series multi-omics pipeline.
skills.name: fasta-sequence-parsing
skills.search_text: fasta-sequence-parsing Use when the input is archived raw FASTA files (genomics or proteomics omic-type) that must be parsed into individual sequences before embedding, vectorization, or tabular conversion in a time-series multi-omics pipeline. The input is already a tabular data set (CSV/TSV feature table) — the filtering step applies only to tabular data and FASTA parsing is unnecessary. The data are raw microarray-based data, which cannot be used directly as input and require separate preprocessing before the analysis core. The data have not been quality controlled and filtered — the data analysis core presupposes preprocessed data. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3170 Parse archived FASTA sequence files (e.g., the Example 1 BWWTP metaproteomics raw FASTA data in MOVIS) with Biopython's SeqIO to extract individual sequences, which are then tokenized and embedded (e.g., via Gensim Word2Vec into 100-dimensional vectors) for downstream clustering. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.02.012
skills.summary: Parse archived FASTA sequence files (e.g., the Example 1 BWWTP metaproteomics raw FASTA data in MOVIS) with Biopython's SeqIO to extract individual sequences, which are then tokenized and embedded (e.g., via Gensim Word2Vec into 100-dimensional vectors) for downstream clustering.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a tabular data set (CSV/TSV feature table) — the filtering step applies only to tabular data and FASTA parsing is unnecessary. The data are raw microarray-based data, which cannot be used directly as input and require separate preprocessing before the analysis core. The data have not been quality controlled and filtered — the data analysis core presupposes preprocessed data.

skills.description: Use when raw paired-end FASTQ metatranscriptome reads contain adaptor contamination or low-quality bases and must be trimmed and mate-joined before annotation, e.g. preparing 100 bp paired-end stool RNA-seq files for MG-RAST submission.
skills.name: fastq-adaptor-trimming
skills.search_text: fastq-adaptor-trimming Use when raw paired-end FASTQ metatranscriptome reads contain adaptor contamination or low-quality bases and must be trimmed and mate-joined before annotation, e.g. preparing 100 bp paired-end stool RNA-seq files for MG-RAST submission. Input reads are already long (>100 bp) single-end sequences that satisfy the pipeline's minimum-length requirement, so paired-end joining with FLASH/PEAR is unnecessary Reads have already been adaptor-trimmed and quality-filtered, and you would only be re-running Trimmomatic redundantly You are running SAMSA2's local pipeline and want its recommended merge tool (PEAR with multithreading, plus SortMeRNA ribosomal filtering) rather than the SAMSA v1 Trimmomatic+FLASH step http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Preprocessing phase of the SAMSA metatranscriptome pipeline: raw FASTQ reads are cleaned of adaptor contamination and low-quality bases with Trimmomatic, then paired-end mates are joined with FLASH (PEAR in SAMSA2) so reads exceed the 100 bp minimum needed for downstream MG-RAST annotation. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1270-8
skills.summary: Preprocessing phase of the SAMSA metatranscriptome pipeline: raw FASTQ reads are cleaned of adaptor contamination and low-quality bases with Trimmomatic, then paired-end mates are joined with FLASH (PEAR in SAMSA2) so reads exceed the 100 bp minimum needed for downstream MG-RAST annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are already long (>100 bp) single-end sequences that satisfy the pipeline's minimum-length requirement, so paired-end joining with FLASH/PEAR is unnecessary Reads have already been adaptor-trimmed and quality-filtered, and you would only be re-running Trimmomatic redundantly You are running SAMSA2's local pipeline and want its recommended merge tool (PEAR with multithreading, plus SortMeRNA ribosomal filtering) rather than the SAMSA v1 Trimmomatic+FLASH step

skills.description: Use when raw paired-end RNA-seq/metatranscriptome FASTQ files must be cleaned before annotation: mates need merging, low-quality bases and adapters removed, and rRNA reads filtered to speed up annotation.
skills.name: fastq-quality-control
skills.search_text: fastq-quality-control Use when raw paired-end RNA-seq/metatranscriptome FASTQ files must be cleaned before annotation: mates need merging, low-quality bases and adapters removed, and rRNA reads filtered to speed up annotation. Input reads are single-end only — the standard SAMSA2 preprocessing begins with PEAR merging of paired-end mates (use the master_script_preserving_unmerged variant if unmerged reads must be retained) Reads are already trimmed and rRNA-filtered and only annotation (DIAMOND), aggregation, or DESeq analysis is needed The goal is taxonomic identification from 16S rRNA sequencing rather than mRNA functional profiling from metatranscriptomes http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 SAMSA2's preprocessing stage that converts raw paired-end metatranscriptome FASTQ reads into a cleaned, ribosome-filtered FASTQ ready for DIAMOND annotation, by merging mate pairs with PEAR, trimming low-quality bases and adapters with Trimmomatic, and removing rRNA reads with SortMeRNA. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: SAMSA2's preprocessing stage that converts raw paired-end metatranscriptome FASTQ reads into a cleaned, ribosome-filtered FASTQ ready for DIAMOND annotation, by merging mate pairs with PEAR, trimming low-quality bases and adapters with Trimmomatic, and removing rRNA reads with SortMeRNA.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are single-end only — the standard SAMSA2 preprocessing begins with PEAR merging of paired-end mates (use the master_script_preserving_unmerged variant if unmerged reads must be retained) Reads are already trimmed and rRNA-filtered and only annotation (DIAMOND), aggregation, or DESeq analysis is needed The goal is taxonomic identification from 16S rRNA sequencing rather than mRNA functional profiling from metatranscriptomes

skills.description: Use when shotgun metagenomic FASTQs (host-filtered paired and singleton .fastq.gz) must be quality-trimmed before read mapping, and low-quality bases at read ends and overly short reads need removal.
skills.name: fastq-quality-trimming
skills.search_text: fastq-quality-trimming Use when shotgun metagenomic FASTQs (host-filtered paired and singleton .fastq.gz) must be quality-trimmed before read mapping, and low-quality bases at read ends and overly short reads need removal. Input data are already post-quality-control (e.g. post-HMP QC), where minimal additional trimming is expected and the step may add little value Reads still require host read removal or duplicate read filtering first — MetaLAFFA orders host filtering (Bowtie 2 vs. hs37d5) and duplicate filtering (PICARD MarkDuplicates) before quality trimming http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 MetaLAFFA's quality trimming and filtering step uses Trimmomatic with the MAXINFO criterion to trim low-quality bases from read ends and discard reads falling below a 60bp minimum length threshold, preparing quality-controlled FASTQs for read mapping. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: MetaLAFFA's quality trimming and filtering step uses Trimmomatic with the MAXINFO criterion to trim low-quality bases from read ends and discard reads falling below a 60bp minimum length threshold, preparing quality-controlled FASTQs for read mapping.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are already post-quality-control (e.g. post-HMP QC), where minimal additional trimming is expected and the step may add little value Reads still require host read removal or duplicate read filtering first — MetaLAFFA orders host filtering (Bowtie 2 vs. hs37d5) and duplicate filtering (PICARD MarkDuplicates) before quality trimming

skills.description: Use when you have run a MetaLAFFA QC step (e.g., Bowtie 2 host filtering against the hs37d5 reference) and need per-sample read counts plus average read length and base-quality summaries to document how many reads were removed.
skills.name: fastq-read-count-summary-statistics
skills.search_text: fastq-read-count-summary-statistics Use when you have run a MetaLAFFA QC step (e.g., Bowtie 2 host filtering against the hs37d5 reference) and need per-sample read counts plus average read length and base-quality summaries to document how many reads were removed. Your input is already a reduced result (gene counts, KO/pathway abundances) rather than FASTQ reads — there are no per-read counts to summarize. You need to modify reads (e.g., Trimmomatic MAXINFO quality trimming or PICARD MarkDuplicates duplicate removal) — this skill only summarizes counts, lengths, and qualities. You want the percentage of reads with a match in the UniRef90 database or per-gene abundances — that comes from the read mapping and gene counting phase, not per-step FASTQ summaries. http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes per-sample FASTQ summary statistics — number of reads, average read length, and average base quality — at MetaLAFFA pipeline steps such as host read filtering, so users can see exactly how many reads each quality-control operation removed and judge pre-processing quality. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Computes per-sample FASTQ summary statistics — number of reads, average read length, and average base quality — at MetaLAFFA pipeline steps such as host read filtering, so users can see exactly how many reads each quality-control operation removed and judge pre-processing quality.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a reduced result (gene counts, KO/pathway abundances) rather than FASTQ reads — there are no per-read counts to summarize. You need to modify reads (e.g., Trimmomatic MAXINFO quality trimming or PICARD MarkDuplicates duplicate removal) — this skill only summarizes counts, lengths, and qualities. You want the percentage of reads with a match in the UniRef90 database or per-gene abundances — that comes from the read mapping and gene counting phase, not per-step FASTQ summaries.

skills.description: Use when simulating ONT-like sequencing datasets to benchmark mutation detection, requiring FASTQ read-length and base-quality distributions (e.g. 1020–3968 bp, Q10–Q42) matched to the study's Methods parameters.
skills.name: fastq-read-length-distribution-modeling
skills.search_text: fastq-read-length-distribution-modeling Use when simulating ONT-like sequencing datasets to benchmark mutation detection, requiring FASTQ read-length and base-quality distributions (e.g. 1020–3968 bp, Q10–Q42) matched to the study's Methods parameters. Input is real nanopore FASTQ data (NA12878 or experimental ONT runs) — no simulation is needed; apply the detection pipeline directly Simulated ONT-like data are required to match actual experimental and sequencing platforms — the article notes the simulated data 'were not generated on the same experimental and sequencing platforms' The goal is metagenomic taxonomic classification simulation — that is the Nano2NGS-Meta module, not hotspot mutation benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Generates simulated nanopore FASTQ reads whose lengths are drawn from a specified normal distribution (as in Nano2NGS-Muta benchmarking: mean 2467 bp, sd 783 bp, range 1020–3968 bp) so that downstream hotspot-mutation callers are evaluated on realistic ONT-like data rather than fixed-length synthetic reads. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac033
skills.summary: Generates simulated nanopore FASTQ reads whose lengths are drawn from a specified normal distribution (as in Nano2NGS-Muta benchmarking: mean 2467 bp, sd 783 bp, range 1020–3968 bp) so that downstream hotspot-mutation callers are evaluated on realistic ONT-like data rather than fixed-length synthetic reads.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real nanopore FASTQ data (NA12878 or experimental ONT runs) — no simulation is needed; apply the detection pipeline directly Simulated ONT-like data are required to match actual experimental and sequencing platforms — the article notes the simulated data 'were not generated on the same experimental and sequencing platforms' The goal is metagenomic taxonomic classification simulation — that is the Nano2NGS-Meta module, not hotspot mutation benchmarking

skills.description: Use when reconstructing StrainXpress's read-overlap scoring: you have an interleaved FASTQ of Illumina-type short reads and Minimap2 all-vs-all alignments with CIGAR strings, and need per-pair scores D with >=30 bp / >=0.9 identity filtering.
skills.name: fastq-read-pair-handling
skills.search_text: fastq-read-pair-handling Use when reconstructing StrainXpress's read-overlap scoring: you have an interleaved FASTQ of Illumina-type short reads and Minimap2 all-vs-all alignments with CIGAR strings, and need per-pair scores D with >=30 bp / >=0.9 identity filtering. Input reads are third-generation long reads — the article notes the high error rate of such reads introduces issues that still need to be resolved Input is separate R1/R2 FASTQ files rather than the required single interleaved FASTQ Input is already assembled contigs — this skill operates on raw quality-controlled reads to seed the overlap graph http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes a weighted overlap score for each Minimap2-identified suffix-prefix overlap between quality-controlled NGS read pairs, combining alignment identity (weight 0.9) with relative overlap length (weight 0.1). This scoring feeds the overlap graph that StrainXpress builds for strain-aware metagenome assembly. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac543
skills.summary: Computes a weighted overlap score for each Minimap2-identified suffix-prefix overlap between quality-controlled NGS read pairs, combining alignment identity (weight 0.9) with relative overlap length (weight 0.1). This scoring feeds the overlap graph that StrainXpress builds for strain-aware metagenome assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are third-generation long reads — the article notes the high error rate of such reads introduces issues that still need to be resolved Input is separate R1/R2 FASTQ files rather than the required single interleaved FASTQ Input is already assembled contigs — this skill operates on raw quality-controlled reads to seed the overlap graph

skills.description: Use when input is paired-end Illumina FASTQ (or CASAVA/QSEQ) reads whose forward and reverse mates overlap an amplicon (e.g. 16S rRNA hypervariable regions) and reads are being discarded (~40%) due to uncalled or miscalled bases under naive perfect-match merging.
skills.name: fastq-read-pair-processing
skills.search_text: fastq-read-pair-processing Use when input is paired-end Illumina FASTQ (or CASAVA/QSEQ) reads whose forward and reverse mates overlap an amplicon (e.g. 16S rRNA hypervariable regions) and reads are being discarded (~40%) due to uncalled or miscalled bases under naive perfect-match merging. Read pairs do not overlap (adapter-only libraries with little expected overlap) — the probabilistic overlap search is wasted and pairs will be discarded Single-end reads or long-read data where no paired-end overlap signal exists Data already processed by a paired-end assembler (e.g. already-merged contigs or a feature table) http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Probabilistically assembles overlapping Illumina paired-end FASTQ reads (as in PANDAseq) by scoring every candidate overlap with base-error probabilities derived from Phred quality values, selecting the maximum-likelihood overlap, and correcting mismatches and uncalled bases in the overlap region. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-13-31
skills.summary: Probabilistically assembles overlapping Illumina paired-end FASTQ reads (as in PANDAseq) by scoring every candidate overlap with base-error probabilities derived from Phred quality values, selecting the maximum-likelihood overlap, and correcting mismatches and uncalled bases in the overlap region.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Read pairs do not overlap (adapter-only libraries with little expected overlap) — the probabilistic overlap search is wasted and pairs will be discarded Single-end reads or long-read data where no paired-end overlap signal exists Data already processed by a paired-end assembler (e.g. already-merged contigs or a feature table)

skills.description: Use when you have a small FASTA/FASTQ seed read set (e.g. cas-gene or CRISPR-repeat matches) and a large raw FASTQ dataset, and you need to recruit neighboring reads to prime targeted assembly without assembling the whole dataset.
skills.name: fastq-read-subset-management
skills.search_text: fastq-read-subset-management Use when you have a small FASTA/FASTQ seed read set (e.g. cas-gene or CRISPR-repeat matches) and a large raw FASTQ dataset, and you need to recruit neighboring reads to prime targeted assembly without assembling the whole dataset. The full genome/metagenome is small enough that complete assembly and annotation is acceptable — CasCollect's targeted expansion exists to avoid complete assembly Input is already an assembly (contigs/FASTA assemblies) rather than raw unassembled reads; the skill operates on FASTQ read datasets Protein-level or local-alignment recruitment is required — VSEARCH in this pipeline performs nucleotide identity matching only http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Iteratively expands a set of seed FASTQ reads into a targeted subset by cycling VSEARCH identity matching at 95%, removing matched reads from the search database each cycle so no read is searched twice. This is the read subset expansion stage that primes CasCollect's targeted assembly. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: Iteratively expands a set of seed FASTQ reads into a targeted subset by cycling VSEARCH identity matching at 95%, removing matched reads from the search database each cycle so no read is searched twice. This is the read subset expansion stage that primes CasCollect's targeted assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The full genome/metagenome is small enough that complete assembly and annotation is acceptable — CasCollect's targeted expansion exists to avoid complete assembly Input is already an assembly (contigs/FASTA assemblies) rather than raw unassembled reads; the skill operates on FASTQ read datasets Protein-level or local-alignment recruitment is required — VSEARCH in this pipeline performs nucleotide identity matching only

skills.description: Use when raw pooled/subsampled ONT long-read FASTQs (e.g. .fastq.gz from a MinION run) must be quality-trimmed before plasmid assembly, and every retained record must meet a length and Q-score cutoff.
skills.name: fastq-record-length-and-phred-thresholding
skills.search_text: fastq-record-length-and-phred-thresholding Use when raw pooled/subsampled ONT long-read FASTQs (e.g. .fastq.gz from a MinION run) must be quality-trimmed before plasmid assembly, and every retained record must meet a length and Q-score cutoff. Input is Illumina short-read FASTQ — the Plassembler pipeline handles short reads with fastp (>=0.24.2), not chopper. Reads are already error-corrected or subsampled assemblies/contigs, not raw long-read FASTQ records. A different length/quality regime is required by the upstream assembler (e.g. canu -correct subsampling to 100x depth) — thresholds must be re-derived rather than reusing the 500 bp/Q9 defaults. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Filters a long-read FASTQ by dropping records below a minimum length and minimum average Phred score, using chopper as Plassembler's quality-control step (defaults of 500 bp and Q9). It prevents low-quality, very short ONT reads from entering assembly or mapping. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad409
skills.summary: Filters a long-read FASTQ by dropping records below a minimum length and minimum average Phred score, using chopper as Plassembler's quality-control step (defaults of 500 bp and Q9). It prevents low-quality, very short ONT reads from entering assembly or mapping.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is Illumina short-read FASTQ — the Plassembler pipeline handles short reads with fastp (>=0.24.2), not chopper. Reads are already error-corrected or subsampled assemblies/contigs, not raw long-read FASTQ records. A different length/quality regime is required by the upstream assembler (e.g. canu -correct subsampling to 100x depth) — thresholds must be re-derived rather than reusing the 500 bp/Q9 defaults.

skills.description: Use when feeding FASTQ or FASTA metagenomic reads (e.g. simulated gut-MAG reads or iHMP gut metagenomes) into DeepMicrobes for training or prediction, since the LSTM/embedding models only consume TFRecord input.
skills.name: fastq-to-tfrecord-conversion
skills.search_text: fastq-to-tfrecord-conversion Use when feeding FASTQ or FASTA metagenomic reads (e.g. simulated gut-MAG reads or iHMP gut metagenomes) into DeepMicrobes for training or prediction, since the LSTM/embedding models only consume TFRecord input. skills.summary: Converts FASTQ/FASTA metagenomic reads into the TFRecord format required by the DeepMicrobes deep learning framework, encoding sequences as k-mer token IDs from the framework's vocabulary (12-mers for the pre-trained models).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not short-read metagenomic sequence (e.g. long-read data) — the article notes retraining may be required for reads with strongly different lengths and error profiles You plan to use an alignment- or k-mer-index-based classifier such as Kraken or Kaiju, which do not consume TFRecords A custom model with a k-mer length other than the default 12 is being trained without generating a matching (merged) vocabulary

skills.description: Use when raw Illumina metagenomic FASTQ/fastq.gz reads enter a QC stage and per-file FastQC reports plus a consolidated MultiQC summary are needed before and after adapter/quality trimming with bbduk.
skills.name: fastqc-quality-reporting

Input reads are long PacBio/Nanopore reads — nf-core/mag handles those with long-read tools (e.g. Filtlong, minimap2 alignment), not the fastp/FastQC short-read module Data are already quality-assessed feature outputs (e.g. assembled contigs or MAG bins) rather than raw/trimmed FASTQ The goal is de novo quality correction of reads — FastQC only profiles and reports; filtering is performed by fastp (and Bowtie2 contaminant removal) http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Interprets FastQC quality-control reports generated on both raw and pre-processed (fastp-trimmed, Bowtie2 host/PhiX-filtered) Illumina paired-end reads within the nf-core/mag metagenomics workflow, to verify each cleaning stage improved read quality before assembly and binning. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Interprets FastQC quality-control reports generated on both raw and pre-processed (fastp-trimmed, Bowtie2 host/PhiX-filtered) Illumina paired-end reads within the nf-core/mag metagenomics workflow, to verify each cleaning stage improved read quality before assembly and binning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are long PacBio/Nanopore reads — nf-core/mag handles those with long-read tools (e.g. Filtlong, minimap2 alignment), not the fastp/FastQC short-read module Data are already quality-assessed feature outputs (e.g. assembled contigs or MAG bins) rather than raw/trimmed FASTQ The goal is de novo quality correction of reads — FastQC only profiles and reports; filtering is performed by fastp (and Bowtie2 contaminant removal)

skills.description: Use when benchmarking host-decontamination precision on known bacterial content: you need reference-grade complete bacterial assemblies (FDA-ARGOS, BioProject 231221) to simulate reads or to mask a human index against bacterial sequence.
skills.name: fda-argos-reference-genome-handling
skills.search_text: fda-argos-reference-genome-handling Use when benchmarking host-decontamination precision on known bacterial content: you need reference-grade complete bacterial assemblies (FDA-ARGOS, BioProject 231221) to simulate reads or to mask a human index against bacterial sequence. The goal is removing real human reads from clinical metagenomes rather than benchmarking retention on known bacterial content — use Hostile's default human-t2t-hla index directly. Viral or phage sequence retention is the priority — the human-t2t-hla-argos985 masking covers only the 985 bacterial genomes, not the 18,719 RefSeq viral or 26,928 Millard Lab phage genomes. The input taxa are mycobacteria beyond the FDA-ARGOS set — use human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140, which additionally masks 140 mycobacterial genomes. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Handling of the 985 reference-grade FDA-ARGOS bacterial genomes (BioProject 231221) as ground-truth inputs for benchmarking host read removal tools, including their use in simulating bacterial reads with DWGSIM and in building masked Hostile indexes such as human-t2t-hla-argos985. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Handling of the 985 reference-grade FDA-ARGOS bacterial genomes (BioProject 231221) as ground-truth inputs for benchmarking host read removal tools, including their use in simulating bacterial reads with DWGSIM and in building masked Hostile indexes such as human-t2t-hla-argos985.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is removing real human reads from clinical metagenomes rather than benchmarking retention on known bacterial content — use Hostile's default human-t2t-hla index directly. Viral or phage sequence retention is the priority — the human-t2t-hla-argos985 masking covers only the 985 bacterial genomes, not the 18,719 RefSeq viral or 26,928 Millard Lab phage genomes. The input taxa are mycobacteria beyond the FDA-ARGOS set — use human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140, which additionally masks 140 mycobacterial genomes.

skills.description: Use when comparing longitudinal differential-abundance tools on simulated count data and you need per-setting FDR, TPR, and accuracy aggregated over replicate simulations with known ground truth.
skills.name: fdr-estimation-across-simulation-replicates
skills.search_text: fdr-estimation-across-simulation-replicates Use when comparing longitudinal differential-abundance tools on simulated count data and you need per-setting FDR, TPR, and accuracy aggregated over replicate simulations with known ground truth. Data are real experimental data without known ground truth — FDR and TPR cannot be computed against simulated truth Datasets contain multiple covariates — the article's core result is that LongDat's advantage (accuracy, runtime, memory) is greatest with multiple covariates, so a covariate-free benchmark does not represent that regime Single non-replicated comparison — FDR medians across 100 replicates per setting are the basis of the conclusion; a one-off run cannot support distributional claims http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark-method skill for estimating the false discovery rate (and TPR/accuracy) of longitudinal feature-detection tools by aggregating results across replicate microbiomeDASim simulations, as used to compare LongDat against MaAsLin2 (NEGBIN mode). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad063
skills.summary: Benchmark-method skill for estimating the false discovery rate (and TPR/accuracy) of longitudinal feature-detection tools by aggregating results across replicate microbiomeDASim simulations, as used to compare LongDat against MaAsLin2 (NEGBIN mode).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are real experimental data without known ground truth — FDR and TPR cannot be computed against simulated truth Datasets contain multiple covariates — the article's core result is that LongDat's advantage (accuracy, runtime, memory) is greatest with multiple covariates, so a covariate-free benchmark does not represent that regime Single non-replicated comparison — FDR medians across 100 replicates per setting are the basis of the conclusion; a one-off run cannot support distributional claims

skills.description: Use when tandem mass spectra must be searched against predicted RiPP structures and an FDR estimate is needed at a given p-value threshold via a target-decoy strategy.
skills.name: fdr-estimation-from-psm-p-values
skills.search_text: fdr-estimation-from-psm-p-values Use when tandem mass spectra must be searched against predicted RiPP structures and an FDR estimate is needed at a given p-value threshold via a target-decoy strategy. Spectra without paired genomics/metagenomics data — 99% of GNPS spectra cannot be searched, so no target-decoy FDR estimation is possible Cyclic peptides requiring blind modification searches, which MetaMiner does not perform due to inherent computational complexity General peptide ID where decoys should be sequence-only: here decoys must be shuffled BEFORE applying modifications, so the decoy database mirrors the target modification/mass profile rather than being a plain sequence scramble Target-decoy false discovery rate estimation for RiPP identifications in MetaMiner: decoy RiPP structures are built by randomly shuffling target precursor peptide sequences before applying the same post-translational modifications, and decoy-vs-target peptide-spectrum matches at MS-DPR p-value thresholds are used to estimate FDR. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2019.09.004
skills.summary: Target-decoy false discovery rate estimation for RiPP identifications in MetaMiner: decoy RiPP structures are built by randomly shuffling target precursor peptide sequences before applying the same post-translational modifications, and decoy-vs-target peptide-spectrum matches at MS-DPR p-value thresholds are used to estimate FDR.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Spectra without paired genomics/metagenomics data — 99% of GNPS spectra cannot be searched, so no target-decoy FDR estimation is possible Cyclic peptides requiring blind modification searches, which MetaMiner does not perform due to inherent computational complexity General peptide ID where decoys should be sequence-only: here decoys must be shuffled BEFORE applying modifications, so the decoy database mirrors the target modification/mass profile rather than being a plain sequence scramble

skills.description: Use when interpreting HashSeq's per-variant inference-test P values (e.g. deciding which one-mismatch children are true variants) and you need FDR-adjusted significance across many clusters tested simultaneously.
skills.name: fdr-multiple-hypothesis-correction
skills.search_text: fdr-multiple-hypothesis-correction Use when interpreting HashSeq's per-variant inference-test P values (e.g. deciding which one-mismatch children are true variants) and you need FDR-adjusted significance across many clusters tested simultaneously. The task requires detecting true low-abundance sequence variants — the paper states HashSeq is not sensitive for these and recommends more sensitive algorithms such as DADA2. The variant calls must capture indels or two-or-more-mismatch differences relative to a parent — HashSeq considers only one-mismatch variants and treats indels as separate parent sequences. Data come from long-read technologies (e.g. PacBio) where the assumption of rarity of multiple-mismatch sequences may not hold. http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 Apply Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction to the inference-test P values produced by HashSeq so that one-mismatch children flagged as significant are controlled for multiple testing across the large number of sequence-variant clusters. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Apply Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction to the inference-test P values produced by HashSeq so that one-mismatch children flagged as significant are controlled for multiple testing across the large number of sequence-variant clusters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires detecting true low-abundance sequence variants — the paper states HashSeq is not sensitive for these and recommends more sensitive algorithms such as DADA2. The variant calls must capture indels or two-or-more-mismatch differences relative to a parent — HashSeq considers only one-mismatch variants and treats indels as separate parent sequences. Data come from long-read technologies (e.g. PacBio) where the assumption of rarity of multiple-mismatch sequences may not hold.

skills.description: Use when testing differential relative abundances of many taxa (phylum to genus level, e.g. l2/l5/l6 tables) or pooling taxa estimates across studies, and raw p-values must be FDR-adjusted before calling significant taxa.
skills.name: fdr-multiple-testing-correction
skills.search_text: fdr-multiple-testing-correction Use when testing differential relative abundances of many taxa (phylum to genus level, e.g. l2/l5/l6 tables) or pooling taxa estimates across studies, and raw p-values must be FDR-adjusted before calling significant taxa. Only a single pre-specified hypothesis test is run (no multiplicity across taxa), so correction is unnecessary The comparison table has fewer taxa than needed for FDR to be meaningful after taxa.filter (percent.filter=0.05, relabund.filter=0.00005) removed rare taxa, and the practitioner wants family-wise rather than FDR error control P-values come from heterogeneous, non-comparable tests across studies that were not pooled via meta.taxa with a common id and study label, so readjustment across them is invalid http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Apply Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction to p-values from GAMLSS-BEZI differential abundance tests and random-effects meta-analysis of microbiome relative abundances, both within a single study comparison (via taxa.compare) and as a re-adjustment on displayed result tables (taxcomtab.show, metatab.show) and pooled meta-analysis results (meta.taxa). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: Apply Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction to p-values from GAMLSS-BEZI differential abundance tests and random-effects meta-analysis of microbiome relative abundances, both within a single study comparison (via taxa.compare) and as a re-adjustment on displayed result tables (taxcomtab.show, metatab.show) and pooled meta-analysis results (meta.taxa).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single pre-specified hypothesis test is run (no multiplicity across taxa), so correction is unnecessary The comparison table has fewer taxa than needed for FDR to be meaningful after taxa.filter (percent.filter=0.05, relabund.filter=0.00005) removed rare taxa, and the practitioner wants family-wise rather than FDR error control P-values come from heterogeneous, non-comparable tests across studies that were not pooled via meta.taxa with a common id and study label, so readjustment across them is invalid

skills.description: Use when abundance summary tables from DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py have already been tested with DESeq in the SAMSA2 pipeline and a heatmap of top significantly differing features is needed.
skills.name: feature-abundance-heatmap-rendering
skills.search_text: feature-abundance-heatmap-rendering Use when abundance summary tables from DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py have already been tested with DESeq in the SAMSA2 pipeline and a heatmap of top significantly differing features is needed. Input is raw DIAMOND per-read output that has not yet been condensed by DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py into ranked abundance summaries No differential statistics have been computed yet — run run_DESeq_stats.R first to identify which features to display The goal is sample-level variance structure rather than feature-level abundance patterns — a PCA plot (make_DESeq_PCA.R) is the appropriate output http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Render heatmaps of the most significantly differing features (organisms or functions) from SAMSA2's DESeq differential abundance results, providing a visual matrix view of per-sample abundance for top features. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: Render heatmaps of the most significantly differing features (organisms or functions) from SAMSA2's DESeq differential abundance results, providing a visual matrix view of per-sample abundance for top features.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw DIAMOND per-read output that has not yet been condensed by DIAMOND_analysis_counter.py into ranked abundance summaries No differential statistics have been computed yet — run run_DESeq_stats.R first to identify which features to display The goal is sample-level variance structure rather than feature-level abundance patterns — a PCA plot (make_DESeq_PCA.R) is the appropriate output

skills.description: Use when a raw 16S OTU count table (e.g. otu.tab.txt) and taxonomy table (tax.tab.txt) must be quality-controlled before survival-response microbiome analysis and the MiSurv default QC criteria need to be reproduced.
skills.name: feature-table-taxonomy-preprocessing
skills.search_text: feature-table-taxonomy-preprocessing Use when a raw 16S OTU count table (e.g. otu.tab.txt) and taxonomy table (tax.tab.txt) must be quality-controlled before survival-response microbiome analysis and the MiSurv default QC criteria need to be reproduced. The input is already the deposited post-QC data (biom.Rdata or the deposited post-QC otu.tab.txt/tax.tab.txt) — re-filtering would alter the feature/sample counts The analysis goal is raw read-level QC (Phred <20 trimming, chimera removal, 97% OTU picking) rather than feature-table-level filtering after OTU picking Survival data or analytic plans (survival time, censored/event, follow-up period) need processing rather than the abundance/taxonomy tables http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstructs MiSurv's default microbiome quality control, which filters an OTU/feature count table and taxonomy table by kingdom annotation, sample library size, and mean relative abundance. On the example T1D gut microbiome dataset these defaults retain 294 features across 172 subjects. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Reconstructs MiSurv's default microbiome quality control, which filters an OTU/feature count table and taxonomy table by kingdom annotation, sample library size, and mean relative abundance. On the example T1D gut microbiome dataset these defaults retain 294 features across 172 subjects.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already the deposited post-QC data (biom.Rdata or the deposited post-QC otu.tab.txt/tax.tab.txt) — re-filtering would alter the feature/sample counts The analysis goal is raw read-level QC (Phred <20 trimming, chimera removal, 97% OTU picking) rather than feature-table-level filtering after OTU picking Survival data or analytic plans (survival time, censored/event, follow-up period) need processing rather than the abundance/taxonomy tables

skills.description: Use when gzipped shotgun metagenomic FASTQ reads (e.g., from impaired waterways) must be attributed to and apportioned among fecal source categories (human, sewage, septage, cow, dog, bird) using a curated source-associated genome database.
skills.name: fecal-source-apportionment-estimation
skills.search_text: fecal-source-apportionment-estimation Use when gzipped shotgun metagenomic FASTQ reads (e.g., from impaired waterways) must be attributed to and apportioned among fecal source categories (human, sewage, septage, cow, dog, bird) using a curated source-associated genome database. When the goal is to infer the age of contamination or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations — SourceApp cannot do either When a strict mass balance of source contributions is required — SourceApp portions are genome-equivalent-based cell proportion estimates, not mass-balance results When the source category of interest is poorly represented at the genomic level (e.g., cow feces) — false negatives were observed across all samples for cows due to under-sampling of cow fecal microbiomes http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework, implemented in SourceApp, that infers which fecal sources are present and apportioned in water metagenomes by mapping shotgun reads to source-associated genome databases and normalizing mapped depths by genome equivalents to approximate prokaryotic cell fractions. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: A metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework, implemented in SourceApp, that infers which fecal sources are present and apportioned in water metagenomes by mapping shotgun reads to source-associated genome databases and normalizing mapped depths by genome equivalents to approximate prokaryotic cell fractions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to infer the age of contamination or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations — SourceApp cannot do either When a strict mass balance of source contributions is required — SourceApp portions are genome-equivalent-based cell proportion estimates, not mass-balance results When the source category of interest is poorly represented at the genomic level (e.g., cow feces) — false negatives were observed across all samples for cows due to under-sampling of cow fecal microbiomes

skills.description: Use when metagenomic read-mapping counts against source-associated genome databases must be converted into cell-fraction-like abundance units (genome equivalents) for fecal source attribution/apportionment.
skills.name: fecal-source-cell-fraction-estimation
skills.search_text: fecal-source-cell-fraction-estimation Use when metagenomic read-mapping counts against source-associated genome databases must be converted into cell-fraction-like abundance units (genome equivalents) for fecal source attribution/apportionment. When the goal is a mass-balance of mass inputs — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of cells based on genome equivalents and do not represent a mass balance When reads have not been mapped to source-associated genome databases (e.g., input is already a taxonomic profile or 16S table) — GEQ normalization requires per-genome sequence depth When contamination sources lack representative genomes in the database, e.g., cow feces where false negatives across all samples reflect a poor understanding of cow fecal prokaryotic genomic content http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Normalizes per-genome mapped read counts (from CoverM) into genome-copy-based relative abundances by estimating average genome size and total genome equivalents (GEQ) with MicrobeCensus, yielding prokaryotic cell fractions per fecal source category as used by SourceApp. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Normalizes per-genome mapped read counts (from CoverM) into genome-copy-based relative abundances by estimating average genome size and total genome equivalents (GEQ) with MicrobeCensus, yielding prokaryotic cell fractions per fecal source category as used by SourceApp.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a mass-balance of mass inputs — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of cells based on genome equivalents and do not represent a mass balance When reads have not been mapped to source-associated genome databases (e.g., input is already a taxonomic profile or 16S table) — GEQ normalization requires per-genome sequence depth When contamination sources lack representative genomes in the database, e.g., cow feces where false negatives across all samples reflect a poor understanding of cow fecal prokaryotic genomic content

skills.name: fecal-source-tracking-read-mapping
skills.search_text: fecal-source-tracking-read-mapping Use when assigning short-read shotgun metagenomic reads (e.g., 2 × 150-bp Illumina NovaSeq 6000) from waterway samples to curated genome databases with known source-associations to quantify fecal signal per source category. Input is long-read data or an already-assembled metagenome rather than short paired-end reads — SourceApp is designed to apportion fecal signal in short read metagenomes The goal is taxonomic profiling against a general database rather than attribution to genomes with known source-associations (e.g., fecal vs. lake water categories) Potential fecal sources must be distinguished solely from marker genes without reference genomes — this framework requires a genome-to-source-association database http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Maps shotgun metagenomic reads to source-associated reference genome databases with bwa mem and summarizes per-genome mapped read counts/depth with CoverM, the read-mapping core of SourceApp's metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Maps shotgun metagenomic reads to source-associated reference genome databases with bwa mem and summarizes per-genome mapped read counts/depth with CoverM, the read-mapping core of SourceApp's metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is long-read data or an already-assembled metagenome rather than short paired-end reads — SourceApp is designed to apportion fecal signal in short read metagenomes The goal is taxonomic profiling against a general database rather than attribution to genomes with known source-associations (e.g., fecal vs. lake water categories) Potential fecal sources must be distinguished solely from marker genes without reference genomes — this framework requires a genome-to-source-association database

skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have raw GWAS SNP-level summary statistics — pathway-level GWAS enrichment must first be produced (e.g. via PASCAL) before overlap testing is meaningful You want to test overlap of taxa/clade-level phylogenetic associations rather than biological pathway enrichment results No MWAS pathway enrichment results are available because the gene-level association and pathway annotation steps (OMARU_Func_AS.sm / OMARU_Func_permutation.sm) have not been run

skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is phenotype prediction for new genomes (use 'traitar phenotype' from nucleotides/genes instead) rather than inspecting or verifying phenotype model protein families. skills.description: Use when you have draft GSMMs/GEMs (e.g. from MAGs via CarveMe or gapseq) and need to quantify metabolic capabilities via exchange-reaction flux ranges, or to measure how annotation expansion closes the phenotype-prediction gap toward complete-genome models.
skills.name: flux-variability-analysis-phenotype-prediction
skills.search_text: flux-variability-analysis-phenotype-prediction Use when you have draft GSMMs/GEMs (e.g. from MAGs via CarveMe or gapseq) and need to quantify metabolic capabilities via exchange-reaction flux ranges, or to measure how annotation expansion closes the phenotype-prediction gap toward complete-genome models. Input is raw sequence or annotation data and no metabolic model has been reconstructed yet — reconstruct GSMMs first (CarveMe/gapseq) before FVA is possible. The goal is KEGG Module completeness evaluation or KO recovery alone — use KEMET with --skip_gsmm instead, since FVA requires a fully built model. Network gap-fill reactions lack genomic evidence — article warns such reactions 'are not always supported by genomic evidence, possibly resulting in erroneous predictions', so FVA capabilities from evidence-free gap-filling should not be treated as validated. http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 Use flux variability analysis (FVA) at fixed maximal growth rate on genome-scale metabolic models (MAG-derived, annotation-expanded, and complete-genome) to compare predicted metabolite production/consumption capabilities against wet-lab observed phenotypes. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.03.015
skills.summary: Use flux variability analysis (FVA) at fixed maximal growth rate on genome-scale metabolic models (MAG-derived, annotation-expanded, and complete-genome) to compare predicted metabolite production/consumption capabilities against wet-lab observed phenotypes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequence or annotation data and no metabolic model has been reconstructed yet — reconstruct GSMMs first (CarveMe/gapseq) before FVA is possible. The goal is KEGG Module completeness evaluation or KO recovery alone — use KEMET with --skip_gsmm instead, since FVA requires a fully built model. Network gap-fill reactions lack genomic evidence — article warns such reactions 'are not always supported by genomic evidence, possibly resulting in erroneous predictions', so FVA capabilities from evidence-free gap-filling should not be treated as validated.

skills.description: Use when you have plot-mean structural metrics from two remote-sensing sources (e.g. VH/VV gamma_0 temporal stacks vs ALS point clouds) and need to test whether the cheaper/spaceborne dataset captures the same forest-structure information.
skills.name: forest-structural-metric-comparison-radar-vs-als
skills.search_text: forest-structural-metric-comparison-radar-vs-als Use when you have plot-mean structural metrics from two remote-sensing sources (e.g. VH/VV gamma_0 temporal stacks vs ALS point clouds) and need to test whether the cheaper/spaceborne dataset captures the same forest-structure information. Input is already a single feature table — no second metric set exists to correlate against, so CCoA is undefined Goal is biodiversity modelling of taxa (species composition/richness) rather than comparing remote-sensing structural datasets Plots cannot be spatially matched 1:1 between radar and ALS sources, since the analysis requires paired plot-level metrics Compares Sentinel-1 radar-derived habitat-structure metrics against airborne laser scanning (ALS) metrics for the same 1-ha plots, using R-based canonical correlation analysis (CCoA) to quantify how strongly the two remote-sensing datasets capture the same structural gradient. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x
skills.summary: Compares Sentinel-1 radar-derived habitat-structure metrics against airborne laser scanning (ALS) metrics for the same 1-ha plots, using R-based canonical correlation analysis (CCoA) to quantify how strongly the two remote-sensing datasets capture the same structural gradient.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single feature table — no second metric set exists to correlate against, so CCoA is undefined Goal is biodiversity modelling of taxa (species composition/richness) rather than comparing remote-sensing structural datasets Plots cannot be spatially matched 1:1 between radar and ALS sources, since the analysis requires paired plot-level metrics

skills.description: Use when the input consists of multiple per-sample gene abundance/FPKM files (e.g., Cufflinks-style tabular gene output) that must be aligned by gene identifier and merged into one samples-and-genes matrix for downstream differential expression analysis.

skills.description: Use when building per-gene abundance tables from hit-filtered DIAMOND read-to-gene alignments ( e-value hits per read) and you need MetaLAFFA-compatible fractional counts for reads tied across multiple genes.
skills.name: fractional-gene-counting
skills.search_text: fractional-gene-counting Use when building per-gene abundance tables from hit-filtered DIAMOND read-to-gene alignments ( e-value hits per read) and you need MetaLAFFA-compatible fractional counts for reads tied across multiple genes. Input is already an aggregated abundance or feature table rather than raw read-to-gene alignment hits — recounting would double-apply normalization. You need per-ortholog or per-pathway abundances rather than per-gene abundances; MetaLAFFA handles those in separate ortholog counting and aggregation steps. Your alignment hits have not been filtered to best e-value matches, so ties across equally-good genes are not yet defined. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstructs MetaLAFFA's gene abundance calculation, in which per-gene abundances are obtained by summing retained DIAMOND read hits, and reads matching equally well to multiple genes contribute a fractional count (1/n) distributed evenly across those genes, followed by gene-length normalization. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Reconstructs MetaLAFFA's gene abundance calculation, in which per-gene abundances are obtained by summing retained DIAMOND read hits, and reads matching equally well to multiple genes contribute a fractional count (1/n) distributed evenly across those genes, followed by gene-length normalization.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aggregated abundance or feature table rather than raw read-to-gene alignment hits — recounting would double-apply normalization. You need per-ortholog or per-pathway abundances rather than per-gene abundances; MetaLAFFA handles those in separate ortholog counting and aggregation steps. Your alignment hits have not been filtered to best e-value matches, so ties across equally-good genes are not yet defined.

skills.description: Use when starting from a per-sample, gene-length-normalized gene abundance table plus a many-to-many gene-to-ortholog mapping, and the goal is a KO-level functional profile.
skills.name: fractional-ortholog-abundance-counting
skills.search_text: fractional-ortholog-abundance-counting Use when starting from a per-sample, gene-length-normalized gene abundance table plus a many-to-many gene-to-ortholog mapping, and the goal is a KO-level functional profile. Input is a raw read-to-gene hits table rather than a gene-length-normalized abundance table — the gene counting/normalization step must run first The ortholog grouping step has not yet been performed and only per-gene functions exist — gene-to-ortholog mapping must be generated before aggregating A read-level functional profile is needed rather than a gene-level KO abundance profile — this skill operates on aggregated gene abundances, not per-read alignments http://edamontology.org/topic_0176 MetaLAFFA's method for converting per-sample gene abundance tables into KEGG orthology group (KO) abundances by distributing each gene's abundance fractionally across all orthology groups it is mapped to, avoiding double-counting for many-to-many gene-to-ortholog assignments. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: MetaLAFFA's method for converting per-sample gene abundance tables into KEGG orthology group (KO) abundances by distributing each gene's abundance fractionally across all orthology groups it is mapped to, avoiding double-counting for many-to-many gene-to-ortholog assignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw read-to-gene hits table rather than a gene-length-normalized abundance table — the gene counting/normalization step must run first The ortholog grouping step has not yet been performed and only per-gene functions exist — gene-to-ortholog mapping must be generated before aggregating A read-level functional profile is needed rather than a gene-level KO abundance profile — this skill operates on aggregated gene abundances, not per-read alignments

skills.description: Use when estimating the fraction of adaptive substitutions (α) from DAF/polymorphism and divergence counts and slightly deleterious rare variants must be excluded to avoid biasing α downward.
skills.name: frequency-cutoff-filtering-of-polymorphisms
skills.search_text: frequency-cutoff-filtering-of-polymorphisms Use when estimating the fraction of adaptive substitutions (α) from DAF/polymorphism and divergence counts and slightly deleterious rare variants must be excluded to avoid biasing α downward. When performing the standard MKT, which uses all polymorphisms without any frequency cutoff When the input is raw variation data (FASTA alignments or VCF) that has not yet been converted into a DAF spectrum and divergence count table by the iMKTData pipelines When polarized derived-allele states are unavailable, since the unfolded DAF spectrum (as produced from 1000GP ancestral-state or DGN data) is required to define the low-frequency cutoff http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Excludes low-frequency (weakly deleterious) polymorphisms from a DAF spectrum table below a user-specified derived allele frequency cutoff before computing MK-derived statistics such as eMKT, FWWMKT, and aMKT, preventing downward bias in α estimates. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: Excludes low-frequency (weakly deleterious) polymorphisms from a DAF spectrum table below a user-specified derived allele frequency cutoff before computing MK-derived statistics such as eMKT, FWWMKT, and aMKT, preventing downward bias in α estimates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When performing the standard MKT, which uses all polymorphisms without any frequency cutoff When the input is raw variation data (FASTA alignments or VCF) that has not yet been converted into a DAF spectrum and divergence count table by the iMKTData pipelines When polarized derived-allele states are unavailable, since the unfolded DAF spectrum (as produced from 1000GP ancestral-state or DGN data) is required to define the low-frequency cutoff

skills.description: Use when aggregated functional-category summary files exist for multiple metatranscriptome samples in control vs. experimental groups and you need to identify significantly differing functions with adjusted p-values and fold changes.
skills.name: functional-category-differential-abundance-analysis
skills.search_text: functional-category-differential-abundance-analysis Use when aggregated functional-category summary files exist for multiple metatranscriptome samples in control vs. experimental groups and you need to identify significantly differing functions with adjusted p-values and fold changes. Input is raw FASTQ reads or per-read annotation output rather than aggregated functional summary tables — run aggregation first You need organism-level (taxonomic) rather than functional-category significance testing — use R_organism_script.Rmd instead Input features are already reduced to a short list (no long tail); thresholding and low-abundance filtering are unnecessary and could discard real signal http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Statistical comparison of functional annotation categories (e.g. SEED Subsystems or MG-RAST functional summaries) between control and experimental metatranscriptome groups using DESeq2 negative-binomial modeling, as implemented in the SAMSA pipeline's R_functional_script_w-md5s.Rmd. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1270-8
skills.summary: Statistical comparison of functional annotation categories (e.g. SEED Subsystems or MG-RAST functional summaries) between control and experimental metatranscriptome groups using DESeq2 negative-binomial modeling, as implemented in the SAMSA pipeline's R_functional_script_w-md5s.Rmd.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ reads or per-read annotation output rather than aggregated functional summary tables — run aggregation first You need organism-level (taxonomic) rather than functional-category significance testing — use R_organism_script.Rmd instead Input features are already reduced to a short list (no long tail); thresholding and low-abundance filtering are unnecessary and could discard real signal

skills.description: Use when you have a per-sample gene frequency table and KO assignments for the gene catalog, and need per-sample counts aggregated at KO, EC number, and reaction levels for downstream compositional analysis.
skills.name: functional-frequency-aggregation-across-samples
skills.search_text: functional-frequency-aggregation-across-samples Use when you have a per-sample gene frequency table and KO assignments for the gene catalog, and need per-sample counts aggregated at KO, EC number, and reaction levels for downstream compositional analysis. The input is already a KO/EC/reaction-level frequency table — re-aggregation would double-count gene-level counts. You need taxonomic (taxon-level) profiling, which CAMAMED handles separately via MetaPhlAn2 rather than through the KEGG annotation stage. No KEGG annotation exists for the gene catalog (e.g. genes from organisms outside KEGG coverage) — KO assignment would fail or be incomplete. http://edamontology.org/topic_0605 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 In CAMAMED, after KAAS/GhostKOALA assigns KEGG orthology (KO) groups to genes from the mapped gene catalog, per-sample gene frequencies are aggregated up the KO → EC number → reaction relation chains, yielding per-sample functional frequency tables at all annotation levels. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa107
skills.summary: In CAMAMED, after KAAS/GhostKOALA assigns KEGG orthology (KO) groups to genes from the mapped gene catalog, per-sample gene frequencies are aggregated up the KO → EC number → reaction relation chains, yielding per-sample functional frequency tables at all annotation levels.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a KO/EC/reaction-level frequency table — re-aggregation would double-count gene-level counts. You need taxonomic (taxon-level) profiling, which CAMAMED handles separately via MetaPhlAn2 rather than through the KEGG annotation stage. No KEGG annotation exists for the gene catalog (e.g. genes from organisms outside KEGG coverage) — KO assignment would fail or be incomplete.

skills.summary: Evaluate how many primer pairs are needed to capture the diversity of an environment-specific functional gene set (e.g., 78 nondegenerate amoA-AOB pairs covering 720 soil-abundant genes) by computing in silico PCR coverage curves of cumulative gene detection versus primer-set size.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo primer design from metagenome-ranked gene targets rather than evaluating coverage of an existing primer set Input is amplicon sequencing data or a qPCR readout rather than reference gene sequences and primer sequences Primers will be assessed by thermodynamic or experimental validation only, without an in silico reference gene set to match against

skills.description: Use when presence-absence species composition data are available for multiple plots and per-plot community-composition response variables (e.g. NMDS1/NMDS2 site scores) are needed for taxa or functional groups.
skills.name: functional-group-community-ordination
skills.search_text: functional-group-community-ordination Use when presence-absence species composition data are available for multiple plots and per-plot community-composition response variables (e.g. NMDS1/NMDS2 site scores) are needed for taxa or functional groups. When the target response variables are species richness or phylogenetic diversity (α-diversity measures) rather than assemblage composition (β-diversity). When abundance (count or cover) data are available and the analysis requires quantitative dissimilarity rather than presence-absence-based Bray-Curtis dissimilarity. Quantifies species assemblage composition (β-diversity) of the twelve functional groups as non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination scores computed from presence-absence ground-truth data, which then serve as response variables in the ALS- and radar-based biodiversity models. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x
skills.summary: Quantifies species assemblage composition (β-diversity) of the twelve functional groups as non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS) ordination scores computed from presence-absence ground-truth data, which then serve as response variables in the ALS- and radar-based biodiversity models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target response variables are species richness or phylogenetic diversity (α-diversity measures) rather than assemblage composition (β-diversity). When abundance (count or cover) data are available and the analysis requires quantitative dissimilarity rather than presence-absence-based Bray-Curtis dissimilarity.

skills.description: Use when evaluating or comparing annotation accuracy of metatranscriptome pipelines on simulated data with known ground-truth organism and function labels, e.g. reproducing SAMSA2's ~95% genus-level accuracy benchmark vs SAMSA 1.0.

skills.search_text: functional-hierarchy-annotation-benchmarking Use when evaluating or comparing annotation accuracy of metatranscriptome pipelines on simulated data with known ground-truth organism and function labels, e.g. reproducing SAMSA2's ~95% genus-level accuracy benchmark vs SAMSA 1.0. Input is raw FASTQ reads rather than a corrected ortholog abundance table — run upstream MetaLAFFA steps (host/duplicate filtering, quality trimming, read mapping, ortholog counting, MUSiCC correction) first The desired higher-level groupings are not KEGG modules or pathways (e.g. UniRef, eggNOG, or CARD-based functional categories), since the ko-to-module/ko-to-pathway mappings are KEGG-specific Aggregating taxonomic or abundance-normalized feature tables unrelated to functional orthologs http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0085 Aggregate MUSiCC-corrected KEGG ortholog (KO) abundances into KEGG module- and pathway-level functional profiles using EMPANADA, then emit KO-, module-, and pathway-level abundance tables as the pipeline's final outputs. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Aggregate MUSiCC-corrected KEGG ortholog (KO) abundances into KEGG module- and pathway-level functional profiles using EMPANADA, then emit KO-, module-, and pathway-level abundance tables as the pipeline's final outputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw FASTQ reads rather than a corrected ortholog abundance table — run upstream MetaLAFFA steps (host/duplicate filtering, quality trimming, read mapping, ortholog counting, MUSiCC correction) first The desired higher-level groupings are not KEGG modules or pathways (e.g. UniRef, eggNOG, or CARD-based functional categories), since the ko-to-module/ko-to-pathway mappings are KEGG-specific Aggregating taxonomic or abundance-normalized feature tables unrelated to functional orthologs

skills.description: Use when you have a fungal taxonomic or functional abundance feature table (e.g., FunOMIC-T/FunOMIC-P profiles) joined to sample metadata and need to find which species associate with variables like country, body site, or disease cohort.
skills.name: fungal-abundance-association-analysis
skills.search_text: fungal-abundance-association-analysis Use when you have a fungal taxonomic or functional abundance feature table (e.g., FunOMIC-T/FunOMIC-P profiles) joined to sample metadata and need to find which species associate with variables like country, body site, or disease cohort. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a processed abundance feature table — run the FunOMIC pipeline (bowtie2 mapping to FunOMIC-T, Diamond blastx to FunOMIC-P) first Question is inter-kingdom correlation structure rather than metadata association — use the correlation network approach (p < 0.001, |correlation| > 0.05) instead of MaAsLin2 Only a single metadata variable without covariates or repeated/age structure — a simple univariate test may suffice; MaAsLin2's multivariable model with age random effect is designed for multiple covariates http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Multivariable association testing between FunOMIC-derived fungal taxonomic/functional abundance tables and clinical-demographic metadata using MaAsLin2 in R, identifying species–metadata links (geography, body site, disease, extraction method) significant at FDR < 0.05. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: Multivariable association testing between FunOMIC-derived fungal taxonomic/functional abundance tables and clinical-demographic metadata using MaAsLin2 in R, identifying species–metadata links (geography, body site, disease, extraction method) significant at FDR < 0.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a processed abundance feature table — run the FunOMIC pipeline (bowtie2 mapping to FunOMIC-T, Diamond blastx to FunOMIC-P) first Question is inter-kingdom correlation structure rather than metadata association — use the correlation network approach (p < 0.001, |correlation| > 0.05) instead of MaAsLin2 Only a single metadata variable without covariates or repeated/age structure — a simple univariate test may suffice; MaAsLin2's multivariable model with age random effect is designed for multiple covariates

skills.description: Use when paired fungal and bacterial taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. FunOMIC-T output and MetaPhlAn profiles) from the same metagenomes must be subset to matched cohorts and combined for inter-kingdom correlation analysis.
skills.name: fungal-bacterial-taxonomic-profile-harmonization
skills.search_text: fungal-bacterial-taxonomic-profile-harmonization Use when paired fungal and bacterial taxonomic abundance tables (e.g. FunOMIC-T output and MetaPhlAn profiles) from the same metagenomes must be subset to matched cohorts and combined for inter-kingdom correlation analysis. Input is already a single joint feature table or edge list with per-cohort partitions applied The analysis goal is within-kingdom (fungus-fungus or bacterium-bacterium) association structure rather than inter-kingdom interactions Fungal profiles were generated with amplicon (ITS) methods rather than FunOMIC-T mapping, since database-specific filtering steps and abundance scales would not be comparable http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Harmonizes fungal taxonomic profiles generated with the FunOMIC pipeline (FunOMIC-T database, bowtie2 mapping) with bacterial taxonomic profiles from MetaPhlAn v3.0.9 so the two kingdom-level tables can be jointly analyzed, e.g. with SparCC correlation networks, on the same sample set. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: Harmonizes fungal taxonomic profiles generated with the FunOMIC pipeline (FunOMIC-T database, bowtie2 mapping) with bacterial taxonomic profiles from MetaPhlAn v3.0.9 so the two kingdom-level tables can be jointly analyzed, e.g. with SparCC correlation networks, on the same sample set.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a single joint feature table or edge list with per-cohort partitions applied The analysis goal is within-kingdom (fungus-fungus or bacterium-bacterium) association structure rather than inter-kingdom interactions Fungal profiles were generated with amplicon (ITS) methods rather than FunOMIC-T mapping, since database-specific filtering steps and abundance scales would not be comparable

skills.description: Use when validating that a fungal marker-gene database does not falsely map bacterial sequencing reads — i.e., you need a specificity metric for a taxonomic profiler before applying it to mixed metagenomic samples.

skills.search_text: fungal-database-specificity-assessment Use when validating that a fungal marker-gene database does not falsely map bacterial sequencing reads — i.e., you need a specificity metric for a taxonomic profiler before applying it to mixed metagenomic samples. Assessing functional profiling performance — that uses the FunOMIC-P protein database with Diamond blastx thresholds (coverage >95%, identity >99%, e-value < 10e-10), not the marker-gene mapping validated here Measuring sensitivity/recall of fungal detection — this skill only measures false-positive bacterial cross-mapping against a fungal database Profiling real (non-simulated) metagenomic samples, where true community composition is unknown and a specificity metric cannot be computed directly http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A mock-community validation procedure that quantifies how specific a fungal taxonomic database (FunOMIC-T, 1.69 million fungal single-copy marker genes) is by simulating bacterial Illumina reads with ART and measuring their false-mapping rate through the FunOMIC/bowtie2 pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010

skills.when_to_use_negative: Assessing functional profiling performance — that uses the FunOMIC-P protein database with Diamond blastx thresholds (coverage >95%, identity >99%, e-value < 10e-10), not the marker-gene mapping validated here Measuring sensitivity/recall of fungal detection — this skill only measures false-positive bacterial cross-mapping against a fungal database Profiling real (non-simulated) metagenomic samples, where true community composition is unknown and a specificity metric cannot be computed directly

skills.description: Use when profiling fungal taxonomic presence across a large cohort of human shotgun metagenomes and you need cohort-level detection rates and per-species prevalence tables (e.g. prevalence of S. cerevisiae across thousands of samples).
