skills.search_text: genome-catalog-metrics-extraction Use when a metagenomic binning study reports genome yields (e.g. complete vs draft counts) and you need to reproduce or extract the per-category, per-phylum breakdown from abstract text, tables, or supplementary tables. Input is raw metagenomic sequence data requiring assembly and binning rather than already-reported yield counts The goal is de novo genome binning (e.g. with abawaca using differential coverage and DNA signature) rather than extracting reported catalog metrics The study does not report both complete and draft genome categories or per-phylum distributions, so no breakdown table can be constructed http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Extract and tabulate genome reconstruction yield metrics from a metagenomic study — the number of complete (manually curated) versus draft-quality genomes, their phylum distribution, and characteristic genome size notes — into a structured CSV for reuse and validation. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486
skills.summary: Extract and tabulate genome reconstruction yield metrics from a metagenomic study — the number of complete (manually curated) versus draft-quality genomes, their phylum distribution, and characteristic genome size notes — into a structured CSV for reuse and validation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw metagenomic sequence data requiring assembly and binning rather than already-reported yield counts The goal is de novo genome binning (e.g. with abawaca using differential coverage and DNA signature) rather than extracting reported catalog metrics The study does not report both complete and draft genome categories or per-phylum distributions, so no breakdown table can be constructed

skills.description: Use when a paper reports a species-level genome bin count (e.g. 786 SGBs from 19,542 prokaryotic genomes at 95% ANI) and you must reproduce the clustering from the deposited genome FASTAs to verify it.
skills.name: genome-cluster-count-validation
skills.search_text: genome-cluster-count-validation Use when a paper reports a species-level genome bin count (e.g. 786 SGBs from 19,542 prokaryotic genomes at 95% ANI) and you must reproduce the clustering from the deposited genome FASTAs to verify it. Input genomes have not passed quality control — including unassembled or contaminated MAGs changes the cluster count; screen at >=50% completeness and <5% contamination first The goal is strain-level or genus-level dereplication rather than species-level 95% ANI clustering The genome set already contains only non-redundant representatives (e.g. VMGC_prokaryote_SGB.tar.gz, n=786) — dereplicating those again is circular http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Validates a reported count of species-level genome clusters (here, 786 SGBs in the VMGC) by independently dereplicating the quality-controlled prokaryotic genomes with dRep at the 95% nucleotide similarity threshold and comparing the resulting cluster count and membership to the published bins. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41564-024-01751-5
skills.summary: Validates a reported count of species-level genome clusters (here, 786 SGBs in the VMGC) by independently dereplicating the quality-controlled prokaryotic genomes with dRep at the 95% nucleotide similarity threshold and comparing the resulting cluster count and membership to the published bins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input genomes have not passed quality control — including unassembled or contaminated MAGs changes the cluster count; screen at >=50% completeness and <5% contamination first The goal is strain-level or genus-level dereplication rather than species-level 95% ANI clustering The genome set already contains only non-redundant representatives (e.g. VMGC_prokaryote_SGB.tar.gz, n=786) — dereplicating those again is circular

skills.name: genome-completeness-categorization-checkm-prokka
skills.search_text: genome-completeness-categorization-checkm-prokka Use when final cleaned scaffold FASTAs from hybrid metagenome assemblies (e.g. MetaPlatanus, metaFlye, MEGAHIT, OPERA-MS on 18 human gut samples with >1 Gbp ONT plus Illumina paired-end reads) must be categorized as over-half or near-complete bacterial genomes for assembler benchmarking. Input is raw ONT/Illumina FASTQ rather than cleaned, assembled scaffold FASTA — CheckM/Prokka categorization operates on finished assemblies, not reads The target elements are Swiss-Prot CDSs, biosynthetic gene clusters, or near-complete viral sequences rather than bacterial genome scaffold categories — these use separate evaluation criteria in the same benchmark A reference-based or strain-resolved completeness assessment is required — the study explicitly focuses on de novo methods and does not well examine reference information http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Categorizes scaffolds from de novo metagenome assemblies as over-half or near-complete bacterial genomes using CheckM completeness/contamination estimates and Prokka annotations, applied to benchmark assemblers such as MetaPlatanus on recovery of biologically important elements in the 18 human gut nanopore samples. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab831

skills.search_text: genome-completeness-contamination-estimation Use when you have a set of metagenome-assembled genomes (FASTA files) and need per-genome completeness/contamination estimates plus a defensible quality-tier classification (e.g. medium/high/near-complete) before downstream analyses. skills.when_to_use_negative: Genomes are viral — the VMGC used CheckV (e.g. >=50% completeness, 10.3% complete viral genomes) rather than CheckM2/MIMAG criteria Genomes are fungal — the study applied BUSCO fungi thresholds (C:>50%, D:<5%) instead of CheckM2-based prokaryotic quality classes You only need taxonomic or abundance profiling of the species-level genome bins rather than quality estimation of the underlying bins

skills.search_text: genome-completeness-marker-filtering Use when a COG presence/absence feature matrix (e.g. 97 genomes x 30,455 COGs) is being prepared for trait-prediction training and each genome must pass a marker-COG completeness screen before model fitting. Input is already a feature matrix whose genomes have all passed a 39/40 marker-COG completeness screen — re-filtering adds nothing. Input is raw sequencing reads or unannotated metagenomic contigs without COG annotation, so marker-COG presence cannot be tabulated. Goal is predicting traits on incomplete genome bins rather than building a training set — the article notes reliable prediction needs only 60-70% completeness, so a 39/40 hard filter for prediction-time bins is unnecessarily strict. Screens complete bacterial genomes for comparative-genomics phenotypic trait training by requiring near-full presence of a panel of marker COGs (39/40), so that only adequately complete genomes enter the PICA SVM training set. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1

skills.search_text: genome-completeness-prior-simulation Use when you need to benchmark or stress-test a core-genome estimator (e.g. mOTUpan) against simulated MAG/SAG incompleteness, or quantify how low-completeness genomes bias core-gene calls and bootstrap false-positive rates. The goal is a real core-genome estimate on empirical genomes (e.g. the 388-genome Prochlorococcus_A mOTU) — run mOTUpan directly on the faa/cog inputs instead of simulating Genomes are all high-quality (>95% complete, including closed genomes); incompleteness robustness is not the limiting factor and benchmarking against PPanGGOLiN/Roary is more informative Input is already a gene-cluster presence/absence table from another pangenome tool — use mOTUconvert.py rather than simulating new gene-trait sets http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Simulates idealized genome sets (one 'good' genome >45% completeness plus variable numbers of 'bad' genomes <45% completeness) as gene-trait presence/absence dictionaries in the mOTUpan --cog_file JSON format, to quantify how genome incompleteness and the number of low-quality genomes affect core-gene recovery and the false-positive rate of mOTUpan's Bayesian core-genome prediction. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac060

skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is a real core-genome estimate on empirical genomes (e.g. the 388-genome Prochlorococcus_A mOTU) — run mOTUpan directly on the faa/cog inputs instead of simulating Genomes are all high-quality (>95% complete, including closed genomes); incompleteness robustness is not the limiting factor and benchmarking against PPanGGOLiN/Roary is more informative Input is already a gene-cluster presence/absence table from another pangenome tool — use mOTUconvert.py rather than simulating new gene-trait sets

skills.description: Use when you need to validate a core-genome prediction made on genomes of heterogeneous completeness (e.g. MAGs with CheckM completeness priors) by simulating synthetic genomes degraded to match the incompleteness of the real input set.
skills.name: genome-completeness-rarefaction
skills.search_text: genome-completeness-rarefaction Use when you need to validate a core-genome prediction made on genomes of heterogeneous completeness (e.g. MAGs with CheckM completeness priors) by simulating synthetic genomes degraded to match the incompleteness of the real input set. When the genome set consists of complete, high-quality genomes only — the rarefaction models incompleteness that is not present, so bootstrap metrics would be uninformative When no completeness estimates (CheckM output or fixed values) are available for the input genomes, since the posterior completeness estimates used for rarefaction cannot be computed When you only need the core/accessory partitioning itself and do not need quality estimates (false discovery rate and sensitivity) for that prediction http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A bootstrap-quality step in mOTUpan where artificially generated genomes — built from all core gene clusters plus accessory clusters sampled from a frequency-conserving gene pool — are rarefied according to the posterior completeness estimates so that synthetic genomes are missing the same fraction of genes as the real (incomplete) MAGs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac060
skills.summary: A bootstrap-quality step in mOTUpan where artificially generated genomes — built from all core gene clusters plus accessory clusters sampled from a frequency-conserving gene pool — are rarefied according to the posterior completeness estimates so that synthetic genomes are missing the same fraction of genes as the real (incomplete) MAGs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the genome set consists of complete, high-quality genomes only — the rarefaction models incompleteness that is not present, so bootstrap metrics would be uninformative When no completeness estimates (CheckM output or fixed values) are available for the input genomes, since the posterior completeness estimates used for rarefaction cannot be computed When you only need the core/accessory partitioning itself and do not need quality estimates (false discovery rate and sensitivity) for that prediction

skills.description: Use when metagenomic bins or otherwise incomplete genomes must be scored with trait classifiers, and you need to quantify how much balanced accuracy degrades as genome completeness drops before trusting predictions on partial input.
skills.name: genome-completeness-simulation
skills.search_text: genome-completeness-simulation Use when metagenomic bins or otherwise incomplete genomes must be scored with trait classifiers, and you need to quantify how much balanced accuracy degrades as genome completeness drops before trusting predictions on partial input. The input genomes are already complete reference genomes and no assessment of robustness to incompleteness is needed — train and evaluate directly instead. No COG presence/absence feature matrix is available and traits must be inferred from sequences directly (use a sequence-based tool such as phenotrex predict on FASTA input instead of COG-profile thinning). http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Simulates incomplete genomes by randomly removing x% of the COGs (x = 10–90, in 10% steps, 3 replicates per level) from eggNOG 4.0 presence/absence profiles, so that SVM-based phenotypic trait models can be re-evaluated on fragmentary input mimicking metagenomic bins. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Simulates incomplete genomes by randomly removing x% of the COGs (x = 10–90, in 10% steps, 3 replicates per level) from eggNOG 4.0 presence/absence profiles, so that SVM-based phenotypic trait models can be re-evaluated on fragmentary input mimicking metagenomic bins.

skills.description: Use when sam alignments against the WoL reference database contain low-coverage hits that may be reference-overlap artifacts, and you need a model-predicted versus observed genome cover comparison to judge whether hits are true contaminants or spurious.
skills.name: genome-cover-recurrence-modeling
skills.search_text: genome-cover-recurrence-modeling Use when sam alignments against the WoL reference database contain low-coverage hits that may be reference-overlap artifacts, and you need a model-predicted versus observed genome cover comparison to judge whether hits are true contaminants or spurious. Input is already a filtered abundance table or biom table with no .sam alignments — the recurrence must be fit from per-genome coverage of raw alignments Alignments were generated against a database other than the Web of Life — calculate_coverages.py currently only works with the WoL database Only a single shallow sample is available with no like samples to aggregate, since genome cover may not saturate without 'artificially deep' composited sequencing http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Dynamically predict genome cover as a function of read count using the Zebra recurrence, evaluated on a Staphylococcus aureus monoculture, to separate true genomic hits from false reference-overlap artifacts produced by ambiguous reads mapping to overlapping reference genomes. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00758-22
skills.summary: Dynamically predict genome cover as a function of read count using the Zebra recurrence, evaluated on a Staphylococcus aureus monoculture, to separate true genomic hits from false reference-overlap artifacts produced by ambiguous reads mapping to overlapping reference genomes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a filtered abundance table or biom table with no .sam alignments — the recurrence must be fit from per-genome coverage of raw alignments Alignments were generated against a database other than the Web of Life — calculate_coverages.py currently only works with the WoL database Only a single shallow sample is available with no like samples to aggregate, since genome cover may not saturate without 'artificially deep' composited sequencing

skills.description: Use when short shotgun reads spuriously map to short common motifs or transposable elements against a large reference (e.g., Web of Life), creating ambiguous low-coverage false positives that per-sample coverage cannot resolve because shotgun sequencing is shallow.
skills.name: genome-cover-thresholding
skills.search_text: genome-cover-thresholding Use when short shotgun reads spuriously map to short common motifs or transposable elements against a large reference (e.g., Web of Life), creating ambiguous low-coverage false positives that per-sample coverage cannot resolve because shotgun sequencing is shallow. Input is already an abundance/biom table without alignments — filtering the table directly is explicitly 'not recommended' since it decreases apparent reads instead of redistributing them via Woltka Alignments were not generated by bowtie2 or SHOGUN (bowtie2 option), or the reference is not the Web of Life database, which calculate_coverages.py currently requires The dataset lacks multiple like samples from similar environments, so the aggregation assumption that true microbes recur across samples (making cover saturate) does not hold http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Zebra-style genome cover thresholding filters false-positive taxonomic hits from shotgun metagenomic alignments by aggregating unique genome coverage across like samples into 'artificially deep' sequencing, then dropping .sam alignments to genomes whose coverage_ratio falls below a user-set cutoff. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00758-22
skills.summary: Zebra-style genome cover thresholding filters false-positive taxonomic hits from shotgun metagenomic alignments by aggregating unique genome coverage across like samples into 'artificially deep' sequencing, then dropping .sam alignments to genomes whose coverage_ratio falls below a user-set cutoff.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an abundance/biom table without alignments — filtering the table directly is explicitly 'not recommended' since it decreases apparent reads instead of redistributing them via Woltka Alignments were not generated by bowtie2 or SHOGUN (bowtie2 option), or the reference is not the Web of Life database, which calculate_coverages.py currently requires The dataset lacks multiple like samples from similar environments, so the aggregation assumption that true microbes recur across samples (making cover saturate) does not hold

skills.description: Use when metagenomic reads (e.g., paired-end FASTQ such as KLyo_C) have been classified against a reference database and you need per-genome window coverage profiles to identify false-positive candidate genomes before final taxonomic assignment.
skills.name: genome-coverage-profile-computation-from-assigned-reads
skills.search_text: genome-coverage-profile-computation-from-assigned-reads Use when metagenomic reads (e.g., paired-end FASTQ such as KLyo_C) have been classified against a reference database and you need per-genome window coverage profiles to identify false-positive candidate genomes before final taxonomic assignment. Input is a raw read file with no prior classification — coverage profiles require query output assigning reads to candidate genomes first The classification task has no suspected false-positive candidates from shared DNA regions and no target-reference filtering step is desired (the filter step is optional in the AFS pipeline) You need alignment-level base-pair coverage (e.g., BWA/Bowtie2 pileups); this skill uses MetaCache's window-level minhashing hits, not per-base alignment coverage http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Groups MetaCache/MetaCacheSpark query-assigned reads by candidate reference genome and computes, for each genome, the fraction of reference windows covered by reads — the per-genome coverage profile used downstream by the coverage-based false-positive filter in AFS-MetaCache. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-3429-6
skills.summary: Groups MetaCache/MetaCacheSpark query-assigned reads by candidate reference genome and computes, for each genome, the fraction of reference windows covered by reads — the per-genome coverage profile used downstream by the coverage-based false-positive filter in AFS-MetaCache.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw read file with no prior classification — coverage profiles require query output assigning reads to candidate genomes first The classification task has no suspected false-positive candidates from shared DNA regions and no target-reference filtering step is desired (the filter step is optional in the AFS pipeline) You need alignment-level base-pair coverage (e.g., BWA/Bowtie2 pileups); this skill uses MetaCache's window-level minhashing hits, not per-base alignment coverage

skills.description: Use when you have FASTA genome files (public references plus MAGs) with a table of source associations (e.g., cow, pig, dog, sewage) and need a formatted database to run sourceapp.py for metagenomic fecal source tracking.
skills.name: genome-database-construction
skills.search_text: genome-database-construction Use when you have FASTA genome files (public references plus MAGs) with a table of source associations (e.g., cow, pig, dog, sewage) and need a formatted database to run sourceapp.py for metagenomic fecal source tracking. Input is raw metagenomic reads rather than assembled genomes/MAGs — reads must first be assembled and binned into MAGs before database construction The prebuilt default SourceApp database (available on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.12795076, browsable on MiGA at disc-genomics.uibk.ac.at) already covers your sources and supplementary genomes are not needed The goal is running source attribution on water metagenomes — that is the sourceapp.py analysis step, which consumes the database this skill produces http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Builds a de novo SourceApp source-associated genome database by quality-filtering (CheckM2, aggregate quality ≥ 50), dereplicating (95% ANI), and cross-reactivity-flagging input reference genomes and MAGs assigned to fecal source categories, enabling metagenomic fecal source tracking without sequencing the sources. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Builds a de novo SourceApp source-associated genome database by quality-filtering (CheckM2, aggregate quality ≥ 50), dereplicating (95% ANI), and cross-reactivity-flagging input reference genomes and MAGs assigned to fecal source categories, enabling metagenomic fecal source tracking without sequencing the sources.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw metagenomic reads rather than assembled genomes/MAGs — reads must first be assembled and binned into MAGs before database construction The prebuilt default SourceApp database (available on Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.12795076, browsable on MiGA at disc-genomics.uibk.ac.at) already covers your sources and supplementary genomes are not needed The goal is running source attribution on water metagenomes — that is the sourceapp.py analysis step, which consumes the database this skill produces

skills.description: Use when you have Illumina short reads (FASTA/FASTQ/BAM, paired-end or mate-pair) from a genome project and need a draft assembly (contigs and scaffold sequences) evaluated by N50 and error rates.
skills.name: genome-de-novo-assembly
skills.search_text: genome-de-novo-assembly Use when you have Illumina short reads (FASTA/FASTQ/BAM, paired-end or mate-pair) from a genome project and need a draft assembly (contigs and scaffold sequences) evaluated by N50 and error rates. Input is single-cell or metagenomics data — the README points to MEGAHIT, which generates longer contigs with less memory for such data Only long reads or a hybrid strategy is available — SOAPdenovo2 is specially designed for Illumina short reads The machine is 32-bit or has under ~5 GB physical memory for small genomes (150 GB needed for human-sized projects) http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 De novo assembly of short-read (Illumina GA) sequencing data into contigs and scaffolds using SOAPdenovo2, a memory-efficient de Bruijn graph assembler with multi-k-mer graph construction, improved scaffolding and GapCloser-based gap closure. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/2047-217x-1-18
skills.summary: De novo assembly of short-read (Illumina GA) sequencing data into contigs and scaffolds using SOAPdenovo2, a memory-efficient de Bruijn graph assembler with multi-k-mer graph construction, improved scaffolding and GapCloser-based gap closure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is single-cell or metagenomics data — the README points to MEGAHIT, which generates longer contigs with less memory for such data Only long reads or a hybrid strategy is available — SOAPdenovo2 is specially designed for Illumina short reads The machine is 32-bit or has under ~5 GB physical memory for small genomes (150 GB needed for human-sized projects)

skills.description: Use when per-genome mapped read counts/sequence depths (e.g. CoverM genome-mode output against source-associated genome databases) must be converted into genome-equivalent cell fractions for metagenomic fecal source tracking or apportionment.
skills.name: genome-equivalent-abundance-normalization
skills.search_text: genome-equivalent-abundance-normalization Use when per-genome mapped read counts/sequence depths (e.g. CoverM genome-mode output against source-associated genome databases) must be converted into genome-equivalent cell fractions for metagenomic fecal source tracking or apportionment. You need true mass-balance apportionment of inputs — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of cells based on genome equivalents, not a mass balance Your input is already a normalized feature/abundance table rather than raw per-genome mapped read counts and sequence depths You need to infer contamination age or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations, which the framework cannot do http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Normalizes mapped-read counts from metagenomes against source-associated genome databases into genome equivalents (GEQ), yielding per-source cell fractions comparable to prokaryotic cell proportions for fecal source attribution and apportionment. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Normalizes mapped-read counts from metagenomes against source-associated genome databases into genome equivalents (GEQ), yielding per-source cell fractions comparable to prokaryotic cell proportions for fecal source attribution and apportionment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need true mass-balance apportionment of inputs — SourceApp portions estimate proportions of cells based on genome equivalents, not a mass balance Your input is already a normalized feature/abundance table rather than raw per-genome mapped read counts and sequence depths You need to infer contamination age or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations, which the framework cannot do

skills.description: Use when shotgun metagenomic reads from water samples must be converted into per-source cell-fraction estimates for fecal source attribution and apportionment, and genome-equivalent normalization is needed to compare summed sequence depth across source categories.
skills.name: genome-equivalent-cell-fraction-estimation
skills.search_text: genome-equivalent-cell-fraction-estimation Use when shotgun metagenomic reads from water samples must be converted into per-source cell-fraction estimates for fecal source attribution and apportionment, and genome-equivalent normalization is needed to compare summed sequence depth across source categories. When the goal is a mass-balance of source contributions — the portions reported by SourceApp do not represent a mass balance but proportions of cells based on genome equivalents. When contamination sources lack representative genomes in the database (e.g., cow feces was underestimated due to undersampling of cow fecal microbiomes) — cell-fraction estimates will be biased. When the input is targeted amplicon data or a pre-computed taxonomy feature table rather than shotgun FASTQ reads mapped to genome databases. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Estimate per-source prokaryotic cell fractions from shotgun metagenomes by mapping reads (bwa mem via CoverM) to source-associated genome databases, summing per-genome sequence depth per source category, and normalizing summed depth to genome equivalents with MicrobeCensus. This is the quantitative core of SourceApp's metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: Estimate per-source prokaryotic cell fractions from shotgun metagenomes by mapping reads (bwa mem via CoverM) to source-associated genome databases, summing per-genome sequence depth per source category, and normalizing summed depth to genome equivalents with MicrobeCensus. This is the quantitative core of SourceApp's metagenomic fecal source tracking (FST) framework.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a mass-balance of source contributions — the portions reported by SourceApp do not represent a mass balance but proportions of cells based on genome equivalents. When contamination sources lack representative genomes in the database (e.g., cow feces was underestimated due to undersampling of cow fecal microbiomes) — cell-fraction estimates will be biased. When the input is targeted amplicon data or a pre-computed taxonomy feature table rather than shotgun FASTQ reads mapped to genome databases.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking taxonomic classifiers on genera underrepresented in reference databases via leave-one-genome-out protein/k-mer databases and simulated reads (Illumina/Roche-454).
skills.name: genome-exclusion-benchmark-database-construction
skills.search_text: genome-exclusion-benchmark-database-construction Use when benchmarking taxonomic classifiers on genera underrepresented in reference databases via leave-one-genome-out protein/k-mer databases and simulated reads (Illumina/Roche-454). When the sequenced strain is itself in the reference database — nucleotide-level classifiers will be more sensitive and the exclusion design does not apply When reads originate from non-protein-coding genomic regions — Kaiju's protein-level classification cannot assign them When target genera have no available reference genomes — genus-level classification (and thus this benchmark stratification) is impossible http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reproduces the Kaiju genome-exclusion benchmark: for each of 882 complete bacterial/archaeal genomes (242 genera with 2–10 genomes), a Kaiju protein reference database excluding the source genome is built with kaiju-mkbwt/kaiju-mkfmi, ART-simulated reads are classified, and genus/phylum sensitivity and precision are computed against Kraken and Clark. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms11257
skills.summary: Reproduces the Kaiju genome-exclusion benchmark: for each of 882 complete bacterial/archaeal genomes (242 genera with 2–10 genomes), a Kaiju protein reference database excluding the source genome is built with kaiju-mkbwt/kaiju-mkfmi, ART-simulated reads are classified, and genus/phylum sensitivity and precision are computed against Kraken and Clark.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the sequenced strain is itself in the reference database — nucleotide-level classifiers will be more sensitive and the exclusion design does not apply When reads originate from non-protein-coding genomic regions — Kaiju's protein-level classification cannot assign them When target genera have no available reference genomes — genus-level classification (and thus this benchmark stratification) is impossible

skills.description: Use when one or more genome assemblies (FASTA contigs) must be scored against a known reference genome to quantify how much of the reference is covered and whether contigs redundantly cover the same regions.
skills.name: genome-fraction-and-duplication-ratio-computation
skills.search_text: genome-fraction-and-duplication-ratio-computation Use when one or more genome assemblies (FASTA contigs) must be scored against a known reference genome to quantify how much of the reference is covered and whether contigs redundantly cover the same regions. No reference genome (even a close one) is available — QUAST is 'much more informative if at least a close reference genome is provided'; reference-free mode will not yield genome fraction or duplication ratio Large genomes (e.g., mammalian) better suited to the QUAST-LG extension rather than the standard E. coli-scale workflow Goal is functional completeness assessment via conserved genes — BUSCO/CEGMA-style gene-based evaluation is a different skill http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Compute reference-based completeness and redundancy metrics — genome fraction %, duplication ratio, and NGA50 — by aligning contigs to a reference genome with QUAST/WebQUAST, as demonstrated on four E. coli K-12 MG1655 assemblies. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad406
skills.summary: Compute reference-based completeness and redundancy metrics — genome fraction %, duplication ratio, and NGA50 — by aligning contigs to a reference genome with QUAST/WebQUAST, as demonstrated on four E. coli K-12 MG1655 assemblies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genome (even a close one) is available — QUAST is 'much more informative if at least a close reference genome is provided'; reference-free mode will not yield genome fraction or duplication ratio Large genomes (e.g., mammalian) better suited to the QUAST-LG extension rather than the standard E. coli-scale workflow Goal is functional completeness assessment via conserved genes — BUSCO/CEGMA-style gene-based evaluation is a different skill

skills.description: Use when a Quast/metaQuast genome-fraction table comparing StrainXpress against IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3 and MEGAHIT across benchmark metagenome data sets must be turned into per-dataset and aggregate gain statistics.
skills.name: genome-fraction-benchmark-analysis
skills.search_text: genome-fraction-benchmark-analysis Use when a Quast/metaQuast genome-fraction table comparing StrainXpress against IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3 and MEGAHIT across benchmark metagenome data sets must be turned into per-dataset and aggregate gain statistics. Input is raw reads or assemblies rather than an existing Quast/metaQuast genome-fraction table — run the assemblies and Quast evaluation first (gain cannot be computed directly). The comparison does not include a StrainXpress column, since the gain is defined relative to StrainXpress's genome fraction. Only a single assembler's output is available, so no best-competitor baseline across IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3 and MEGAHIT can be established. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Reproduce the headline benchmark result of StrainXpress by computing per-dataset genome-fraction gains over the best state-of-the-art assembler (IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3, MEGAHIT) from Quast/metaQuast tables, yielding a mean gain of 26.75% with quartiles 18.51/26.60/35.05. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac543
skills.summary: Reproduce the headline benchmark result of StrainXpress by computing per-dataset genome-fraction gains over the best state-of-the-art assembler (IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3, MEGAHIT) from Quast/metaQuast tables, yielding a mean gain of 26.75% with quartiles 18.51/26.60/35.05.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw reads or assemblies rather than an existing Quast/metaQuast genome-fraction table — run the assemblies and Quast evaluation first (gain cannot be computed directly). The comparison does not include a StrainXpress column, since the gain is defined relative to StrainXpress's genome fraction. Only a single assembler's output is available, so no best-competitor baseline across IDBA-UD, SPAdes, Minia3 and MEGAHIT can be established.

skills.description: Use when comparing metagenomic assembler outputs (FASTA contigs from tools like MetaCortex, MEGAHIT, metaSPAdes, Ray Meta) and you need per-reference genome fraction and misassembly counts to rank assemblers quantitatively.

skills.search_text: genome-fraction-misassembly-quantification Use when comparing metagenomic assembler outputs (FASTA contigs from tools like MetaCortex, MEGAHIT, metaSPAdes, Ray Meta) and you need per-reference genome fraction and misassembly counts to rank assemblers quantitatively. Input is a raw read set rather than assembled contigs — assembly must happen before genome fraction/misassembly evaluation No reference genomes are available for the community, so genome fraction cannot be computed against references The goal is diversity capture (sequence graph variants) rather than assembly accuracy benchmarking against a consensus reference http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Benchmark metagenomic assemblies by computing genome fraction and misassembly counts against reference genomes, as done to show MetaCortex reached 98.78% overall genome fraction with no misassemblies on a CAMISIM-simulated viral community versus MEGAHIT, metaSPAdes and Ray Meta. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad020
skills.summary: Benchmark metagenomic assemblies by computing genome fraction and misassembly counts against reference genomes, as done to show MetaCortex reached 98.78% overall genome fraction with no misassemblies on a CAMISIM-simulated viral community versus MEGAHIT, metaSPAdes and Ray Meta.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a raw read set rather than assembled contigs — assembly must happen before genome fraction/misassembly evaluation No reference genomes are available for the community, so genome fraction cannot be computed against references The goal is diversity capture (sequence graph variants) rather than assembly accuracy benchmarking against a consensus reference

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how a graph-based pangenome pipeline scales with panel size, e.g. testing whether graph construction and traversal tools remain tractable at 5,000–20,000 genome scale.
skills.name: genome-graph-scalability-benchmarking
skills.search_text: genome-graph-scalability-benchmarking Use when you need to quantify how a graph-based pangenome pipeline scales with panel size, e.g. testing whether graph construction and traversal tools remain tractable at 5,000–20,000 genome scale. The goal is variant-detection accuracy rather than runtime/memory scaling — use the accuracy benchmarking workflow on Datasets 1/2 instead Panels contain highly dissimilar sequences or complex variant types (large indels, inversions, reverse tandem duplications), where the cSupB variant model degrades and the scalability numbers would not be meaningful Sequences are highly repetitive (e.g. tandem repeats), since the cutting method fragments sequences and inflates computational difficulty, confounding the scaling measurement http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Benchmark the computational scalability of a colored de Bruijn graph pangenome pipeline (VARI-merge graph construction plus cSupB analysis) on simulated panels of 5,000 and 20,000 human mitochondrial genomes, measuring wall-clock time and peak memory to characterize runtime growth with sample count. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Benchmark the computational scalability of a colored de Bruijn graph pangenome pipeline (VARI-merge graph construction plus cSupB analysis) on simulated panels of 5,000 and 20,000 human mitochondrial genomes, measuring wall-clock time and peak memory to characterize runtime growth with sample count.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is variant-detection accuracy rather than runtime/memory scaling — use the accuracy benchmarking workflow on Datasets 1/2 instead Panels contain highly dissimilar sequences or complex variant types (large indels, inversions, reverse tandem duplications), where the cSupB variant model degrades and the scalability numbers would not be meaningful Sequences are highly repetitive (e.g. tandem repeats), since the cutting method fragments sequences and inflates computational difficulty, confounding the scaling measurement

skills.description: Use when genome bins (draft or complete, e.g., CPR/TM6) must be assigned to lineages via 16S rRNA gene or rp16 concatenated ribosomal protein phylogeny, especially before building lineage-level presence/absence matrices.

skills.search_text: genome-lineage-phylogenetic-assignment Use when genome bins (draft or complete, e.g., CPR/TM6) must be assigned to lineages via 16S rRNA gene or rp16 concatenated ribosomal protein phylogeny, especially before building lineage-level presence/absence matrices. The genomes already have trusted lineage/taxonomic labels and the goal is only ribosomal protein profiling 16S rRNA genes cannot be recovered or are too short/divergent for alignment (<800 bp aligned bases) and no rp16 data are available The analysis targets functional annotation rather than lineage-level phylogenetic placement http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 Assigns metagenome-assembled genome bins (e.g., CPR and TM6 bacteria) to lineages using 16S rRNA gene phylogeny or concatenated ribosomal protein (rp16) phylogeny, with intron removal and strict quality filtering so that presence/absence analyses (such as ribosomal protein L30 loss) can be reported per lineage. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486
skills.summary: Assigns metagenome-assembled genome bins (e.g., CPR and TM6 bacteria) to lineages using 16S rRNA gene phylogeny or concatenated ribosomal protein (rp16) phylogeny, with intron removal and strict quality filtering so that presence/absence analyses (such as ribosomal protein L30 loss) can be reported per lineage.

skills.description: Use when benchmarking ANI/strain-comparison tools (inStrain popANI, dRep, MIDAS, StrainPhlAn) on synthetic data where the ground-truth ANI between genomes is known by construction.
skills.name: genome-mutation-simulation-with-known-ani
skills.search_text: genome-mutation-simulation-with-known-ani Use when benchmarking ANI/strain-comparison tools (inStrain popANI, dRep, MIDAS, StrainPhlAn) on synthetic data where the ground-truth ANI between genomes is known by construction. Input is real metagenomic data rather than simulated reads — this skill's validation depends on known true ANI from controlled mutation counts The goal is ANI estimation between genuinely divergent genomes (>~95-99% ANI) where read-mapping-based popANI is expected to deviate from true ANI rather than match it http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark protocol for strain-comparison accuracy: introduce a known number of mutations into a reference genome with SNP Mutator, simulate Illumina reads with pIRS at 20x coverage, map them with Bowtie2, and compare calculated popANI from inStrain against the true ANI. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Benchmark protocol for strain-comparison accuracy: introduce a known number of mutations into a reference genome with SNP Mutator, simulate Illumina reads with pIRS at 20x coverage, map them with Bowtie2, and compare calculated popANI from inStrain against the true ANI.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is real metagenomic data rather than simulated reads — this skill's validation depends on known true ANI from controlled mutation counts The goal is ANI estimation between genuinely divergent genomes (>~95-99% ANI) where read-mapping-based popANI is expected to deviate from true ANI rather than match it

skills.description: Use when curating a set of reference genomes (e.g., NCBI/JGI assemblies) prior to extracting marker genes, to discard assemblies that are too fragmented or too incomplete to yield reliable single-copy markers.
skills.name: genome-quality-filtering
skills.search_text: genome-quality-filtering Use when curating a set of reference genomes (e.g., NCBI/JGI assemblies) prior to extracting marker genes, to discard assemblies that are too fragmented or too incomplete to yield reliable single-copy markers. Input is already a curated, de-redundant reference database (e.g., an existing marker-gene catalog like the FunOMIC-T FASTA) — re-filtering at the genome level is redundant Analysis targets short-read metagenomic samples for taxonomic/functional profiling rather than reference genome curation The goal is functional protein database construction, which uses a separate 95% CD-HIT clustering workflow rather than genome contiguity cutoffs http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Quality-control filtering of reference fungal genomes before marker-gene database construction, using assembly contiguity cutoffs (>500 contigs, N50 < 10 kbp) and downstream BUSCO single-copy marker gene counts (<30 marker genes) to remove low-quality or fragmented assemblies. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: Quality-control filtering of reference fungal genomes before marker-gene database construction, using assembly contiguity cutoffs (>500 contigs, N50 < 10 kbp) and downstream BUSCO single-copy marker gene counts (<30 marker genes) to remove low-quality or fragmented assemblies.

skills.description: Use when a pipeline needs homologous genomic regions extracted per sample from metagenomic assemblies relative to a reference genome, prior to pairwise synteny or strain-comparison scoring.

skills.search_text: genome-region-binning-and-indexing Use when a pipeline needs homologous genomic regions extracted per sample from metagenomic assemblies relative to a reference genome, prior to pairwise synteny or strain-comparison scoring. skills.summary: Generates and organizes homologous genomic regions from a reference genome and per-sample metagenomic assemblies by BLASTn-searching 1-kbp reference central regions, retrieving each hit with 2-kbp flanks, and writing hit-plus-flank sequences into region-specific bins with a TSV sample/region index.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than assembled metagenomic contigs/genomes — SynTracker requires per-sample assembly files The analysis goal is SNP-based strain tracking on a fixed reference (e.g. MIDAS, StrainPhlAn, inStrain popANI) rather than synteny-based structural comparison Target sequences are expected to diverge beyond 97% identity to the reference — the BLASTn step will drop such homologs entirely

The input is already a complete-genome isolate with a high-quality reference GSMM, so no MAG gapfilling is needed The goal is only KEGG Module completeness summarization with no genome-scale model — use --skip_gsmm / KEGG Module evaluation alone instead Existing gap-filled draft models are already trusted and no genomic-evidence-based refinement of added reactions is required http://edamontology.org/topic_2259 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstruct and expand genome-scale metabolic models (GSMM/GEM) from MAGs or complete genomes by gapfilling with HMM-recovered KEGG orthologs, then quantify metabolic capability via flux variability analysis (FVA). KEMET-driven annotation expansion closes ~10% of the accuracy gap between MAG-derived and complete-genome models. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.03.015
skills.summary: Reconstruct and expand genome-scale metabolic models (GSMM/GEM) from MAGs or complete genomes by gapfilling with HMM-recovered KEGG orthologs, then quantify metabolic capability via flux variability analysis (FVA). KEMET-driven annotation expansion closes ~10% of the accuracy gap between MAG-derived and complete-genome models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a complete-genome isolate with a high-quality reference GSMM, so no MAG gapfilling is needed The goal is only KEGG Module completeness summarization with no genome-scale model — use --skip_gsmm / KEGG Module evaluation alone instead Existing gap-filled draft models are already trusted and no genomic-evidence-based refinement of added reactions is required

skills.description: Use when you must detect and type Dsr-dependent dissimilatory sulphur metabolism proteins across thousands of complete genomes or (meta)genomic protein records on a personal computer, without reconstructing phylogenies or running blast-based marker searches.
skills.name: genome-scale-sequence-screening
skills.search_text: genome-scale-sequence-screening Use when you must detect and type Dsr-dependent dissimilatory sulphur metabolism proteins across thousands of complete genomes or (meta)genomic protein records on a personal computer, without reconstructing phylogenies or running blast-based marker searches. The input is nucleotide sequence rather than protein FASTA — DiSCo.pl expects protein sequences ('takes user-supplied protein sequences'). The goal is a phylogenetic classification of DsrAB sequences or manual distinction of paralogous families where small marker proteins (~100 aa, e.g. DsrEFH) are involved — DiSCo's HMM best-hit assignment is not a phylogeny replacement in those cases. The records are already classified: re-running the screen adds no information if a validated DiSCo hitlist already exists. http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Screens large collections of protein FASTA records (thousands of genomes or metagenomes) for Dsr-dependent dissimilatory sulphur metabolism proteins by running them against the curated DiSCo HMM library with HMMER3 hmmsearch, then classifies each hit by predicted enzyme type. It replaces slow phylogeny-based or blast-based marker screening with a fast, laptop-scale HMM workflow. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000603
skills.summary: Screens large collections of protein FASTA records (thousands of genomes or metagenomes) for Dsr-dependent dissimilatory sulphur metabolism proteins by running them against the curated DiSCo HMM library with HMMER3 hmmsearch, then classifies each hit by predicted enzyme type. It replaces slow phylogeny-based or blast-based marker screening with a fast, laptop-scale HMM workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is nucleotide sequence rather than protein FASTA — DiSCo.pl expects protein sequences ('takes user-supplied protein sequences'). The goal is a phylogenetic classification of DsrAB sequences or manual distinction of paralogous families where small marker proteins (~100 aa, e.g. DsrEFH) are involved — DiSCo's HMM best-hit assignment is not a phylogeny replacement in those cases. The records are already classified: re-running the screen adds no information if a validated DiSCo hitlist already exists.

skills.description: Use when characterizing plasmid vs. chromosome sequence sets by %G+C content and length (e.g. reproducing PlasFlow's RefSeq training-set statistics) or checking whether a nucleotide FASTA dataset matches reported composition properties.
skills.name: genome-signature-characterization
skills.search_text: genome-signature-characterization Use when characterizing plasmid vs. chromosome sequence sets by %G+C content and length (e.g. reproducing PlasFlow's RefSeq training-set statistics) or checking whether a nucleotide FASTA dataset matches reported composition properties. Classifying metagenomic contigs as plasmid/chromosome — that is PlasFlow's prediction task (neural network on k-mer counts with a 0.7 probability threshold), not signature characterization Input is already a k-mer count table (e.g. kmern_split_raw_counts_tax_classes_numeric_annotated_filtered_tax.tsv) rather than nucleotide FASTA sequences Sequences shorter than ~1000 bp — k-mer/genome-signature approaches do not perform well on short contigs, so their composition statistics are not informative for this purpose http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes nucleotide-composition genome signatures — %G+C content and sequence length — across FASTA sequence collections (e.g. 1961 RefSeq chromosomes and 7604 plasmids) and aggregates them by molecule type or phylum, providing the descriptive statistics that underpin PlasFlow's genome-signature approach and validate its training dataset. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321
skills.summary: Computes nucleotide-composition genome signatures — %G+C content and sequence length — across FASTA sequence collections (e.g. 1961 RefSeq chromosomes and 7604 plasmids) and aggregates them by molecule type or phylum, providing the descriptive statistics that underpin PlasFlow's genome-signature approach and validate its training dataset.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Classifying metagenomic contigs as plasmid/chromosome — that is PlasFlow's prediction task (neural network on k-mer counts with a 0.7 probability threshold), not signature characterization Input is already a k-mer count table (e.g. kmern_split_raw_counts_tax_classes_numeric_annotated_filtered_tax.tsv) rather than nucleotide FASTA sequences Sequences shorter than ~1000 bp — k-mer/genome-signature approaches do not perform well on short contigs, so their composition statistics are not informative for this purpose

skills.description: Use when metagenomic or genome assembly contigs (ideally >1000 bp, FASTA) must be labelled plasmid vs chromosome without prior knowledge of sample taxonomic composition, e.g. plasmidome profiling of environmental assemblies.
skills.name: genome-signature-plasmid-prediction
skills.search_text: genome-signature-plasmid-prediction Use when metagenomic or genome assembly contigs (ideally >1000 bp, FASTA) must be labelled plasmid vs chromosome without prior knowledge of sample taxonomic composition, e.g. plasmidome profiling of environmental assemblies. Input sequences are shorter than 1000 bp — kmer-based prediction does not perform well on short sequences and results are unreliable The goal is recovering circular plasmids from a de Bruijn assembly graph with paired reads (use PlasmidSpades or Recycler instead, which require the assembly graph) Plasmid replicon identification in complete bacterial genome assemblies via known replicon sequences (PlasmidFinder's web-based approach) is the target http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Classify metagenomic contigs as plasmid or chromosome using kmer-frequency genome signatures scored by an averaged ensemble of TensorFlow neural network models (PlasFlow), applying a probability threshold (default 0.7) to exclude uncertain predictions. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321
skills.summary: Classify metagenomic contigs as plasmid or chromosome using kmer-frequency genome signatures scored by an averaged ensemble of TensorFlow neural network models (PlasFlow), applying a probability threshold (default 0.7) to exclude uncertain predictions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are shorter than 1000 bp — kmer-based prediction does not perform well on short sequences and results are unreliable The goal is recovering circular plasmids from a de Bruijn assembly graph with paired reads (use PlasmidSpades or Recycler instead, which require the assembly graph) Plasmid replicon identification in complete bacterial genome assemblies via known replicon sequences (PlasmidFinder's web-based approach) is the target

skills.description: Use when reproducing or reporting genome yield tables (complete vs draft bin counts) and per-phylum distributions of curated genomes from metagenomic binning results.

skills.search_text: genome-size-metric-recording Use when reproducing or reporting genome yield tables (complete vs draft bin counts) and per-phylum distributions of curated genomes from metagenomic binning results. Input is already a completed genome-count or phylum-distribution table with validated totals The task requires re-binning scaffolds or recomputing SCG copy numbers rather than recording reported yield metrics Genome counts come from a study with different completion criteria (e.g. no scaffold curation step) so the 8/789 framing does not apply Extracts and tabulates genome reconstruction yields (manually curated complete vs draft bins) and their phylum-level distribution from a metagenomic binning study, e.g. the CPR study's 8 complete and 789 draft genomes from >35 phyla, into a structured CSV for downstream validation. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nature14486

skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a completed genome-count or phylum-distribution table with validated totals The task requires re-binning scaffolds or recomputing SCG copy numbers rather than recording reported yield metrics Genome counts come from a study with different completion criteria (e.g. no scaffold curation step) so the 8/789 framing does not apply

skills.description: Use when you need to mine single-copy nuclear markers (e.g., OrthoDB USCOs) for phylogenomics from genome-skimming (LC-WGS) data provided as Illumina short reads or de novo contigs, especially at coverages of 1x–40x.
skills.name: genome-skimming-marker-retrieval
skills.search_text: genome-skimming-marker-retrieval Use when you need to mine single-copy nuclear markers (e.g., OrthoDB USCOs) for phylogenomics from genome-skimming (LC-WGS) data provided as Illumina short reads or de novo contigs, especially at coverages of 1x–40x. Your query data is already high-quality, unfragmented annotated genomic sequence with full-length genes — assembly-free marker mining of skimming data is unnecessary You need trees inferred directly from unassembled reads without marker retrieval — a tool like Read2Tree targets that workflow instead Your references are not universal single-copy orthologs; the authors recommend limiting references to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Retrieval and concatenation of phylogenetic markers (universal single-copy orthologs, USCOs) from low-coverage whole-genome sequencing data — either fragmented SPAdes short-read assemblies or raw reads — using the Julia/DIAMOND alignment-based tool Patchwork, which stitches overlapping DIAMOND hits, trims noncoding regions via a sliding window, and concatenates remaining regions per reference sequence. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Retrieval and concatenation of phylogenetic markers (universal single-copy orthologs, USCOs) from low-coverage whole-genome sequencing data — either fragmented SPAdes short-read assemblies or raw reads — using the Julia/DIAMOND alignment-based tool Patchwork, which stitches overlapping DIAMOND hits, trims noncoding regions via a sliding window, and concatenates remaining regions per reference sequence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your query data is already high-quality, unfragmented annotated genomic sequence with full-length genes — assembly-free marker mining of skimming data is unnecessary You need trees inferred directly from unassembled reads without marker retrieval — a tool like Read2Tree targets that workflow instead Your references are not universal single-copy orthologs; the authors recommend limiting references to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences

skills.description: Use when you need to test whether a biologically defined subset of protein-coding genes (e.g. by recombination rate bin or chromosome localization) shows a different alpha than the genome-wide gene set, using DAF and divergence tables.
skills.name: genome-wide-alpha-distribution-comparison
skills.search_text: genome-wide-alpha-distribution-comparison Use when you need to test whether a biologically defined subset of protein-coding genes (e.g. by recombination rate bin or chromosome localization) shows a different alpha than the genome-wide gene set, using DAF and divergence tables. Your input is raw variant calls or VCF/FASTA alignments rather than pre-computed DAF/divergence tables — first run the iMKTData pipelines (dmelProteins notebook) to generate the SFS and divergence files You need to test a single gene or genomic region in isolation without a genome-wide comparison distribution Your data are human rather than D. melanogaster — use the humanProteins pipeline and PopHuman/1000GP-derived tables instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Runs the eMKT (via iMKT web service or R package) on a user-selected gene set using the 'Compare against whole-genome distribution' option, and compares the resulting adaptive substitution fraction (alpha) distribution against the genome-wide alpha distribution to test hypotheses such as whether genes in high-recombination regions undergo higher rates of adaptation. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: Runs the eMKT (via iMKT web service or R package) on a user-selected gene set using the 'Compare against whole-genome distribution' option, and compares the resulting adaptive substitution fraction (alpha) distribution against the genome-wide alpha distribution to test hypotheses such as whether genes in high-recombination regions undergo higher rates of adaptation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is raw variant calls or VCF/FASTA alignments rather than pre-computed DAF/divergence tables — first run the iMKTData pipelines (dmelProteins notebook) to generate the SFS and divergence files You need to test a single gene or genomic region in isolation without a genome-wide comparison distribution Your data are human rather than D. melanogaster — use the humanProteins pipeline and PopHuman/1000GP-derived tables instead

skills.description: Use when benchmarking genome-mining candidate generation on a genome set (e.g., 36 ACTI RefSeq FASTA assemblies) where you need per-genome BGC and RiPP counts from antiSMASH plus short-ORF candidate counts under both motif-ORF and all-ORF modes.
skills.name: genome-wide-orf-counting-acquisition-modes
skills.search_text: genome-wide-orf-counting-acquisition-modes Use when benchmarking genome-mining candidate generation on a genome set (e.g., 36 ACTI RefSeq FASTA assemblies) where you need per-genome BGC and RiPP counts from antiSMASH plus short-ORF candidate counts under both motif-ORF and all-ORF modes. The motifs of the RiPP class of interest show no sequence similarity to known RiPPs — the motif-ORF strategy is explicitly not sensitive and will miss such peptides; all-ORF mode is the fallback despite the huge candidate count The analysis goal is NRPS/non-ribosomal peptide discovery, where short-ORF precursor databases are irrelevant (many spectral families belong to non-ribosomal peptides, per Dereplicator+ annotation) No paired genomics/metagenomics data exist for the spectra to be searched — MetaMiner cannot run at all (99% of GNPS spectra lack paired genomic data) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Counts short ORF precursor candidates across whole genomes using MetaMiner's two acquisition strategies — motif-ORF (10 kbp windows around HMMer-detected modification enzymes) and all-ORF (6-frame translation with a 200-aa cutoff) — to quantify how sharply the motif-guided mode trims the candidate space versus exhaustive 6-frame scanning. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2019.09.004
skills.summary: Counts short ORF precursor candidates across whole genomes using MetaMiner's two acquisition strategies — motif-ORF (10 kbp windows around HMMer-detected modification enzymes) and all-ORF (6-frame translation with a 200-aa cutoff) — to quantify how sharply the motif-guided mode trims the candidate space versus exhaustive 6-frame scanning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The motifs of the RiPP class of interest show no sequence similarity to known RiPPs — the motif-ORF strategy is explicitly not sensitive and will miss such peptides; all-ORF mode is the fallback despite the huge candidate count The analysis goal is NRPS/non-ribosomal peptide discovery, where short-ORF precursor databases are irrelevant (many spectral families belong to non-ribosomal peptides, per Dereplicator+ annotation) No paired genomics/metagenomics data exist for the spectra to be searched — MetaMiner cannot run at all (99% of GNPS spectra lack paired genomic data)

skills.description: Use when you have inStrain profile output per sample (computed against concatenated representative sub-species .fasta references) and need per-sub-species genome-level microdiversity metrics (e.g. nucleotide diversity of Klebsiella) for group-level comparison such as birth mode.
skills.name: genome-wide-scaffold-aggregation
skills.search_text: genome-wide-scaffold-aggregation Use when you have inStrain profile output per sample (computed against concatenated representative sub-species .fasta references) and need per-sub-species genome-level microdiversity metrics (e.g. nucleotide diversity of Klebsiella) for group-level comparison such as birth mode. You only need strain-to-strain relatedness between samples (ConANI/popANI) — use inStrain compare on two profile objects instead of genome_wide aggregation No inStrain profile output exists yet for the .bam/.fasta pair — aggregation requires per-scaffold profile results from `inStrain profile` as input You only need raw per-scaffold or per-gene coverage — a fast coverage tool like CoverM computes this without the SNV/diversity aggregation step http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Aggregate scaffold-level inStrain profile results (coverage, clonality, SNV-based nucleotide diversity) into genome-level (sub-species-level) microdiversity metrics using the inStrain genome_wide module, so that individual sub-species populations can be detected, filtered, and statistically compared across sample groups. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Aggregate scaffold-level inStrain profile results (coverage, clonality, SNV-based nucleotide diversity) into genome-level (sub-species-level) microdiversity metrics using the inStrain genome_wide module, so that individual sub-species populations can be detected, filtered, and statistically compared across sample groups.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need strain-to-strain relatedness between samples (ConANI/popANI) — use inStrain compare on two profile objects instead of genome_wide aggregation No inStrain profile output exists yet for the .bam/.fasta pair — aggregation requires per-scaffold profile results from `inStrain profile` as input You only need raw per-scaffold or per-gene coverage — a fast coverage tool like CoverM computes this without the SNV/diversity aggregation step

skills.description: Use when in-silico virulence/typing gene calls from sequencing reads must be validated against PCR or another phenotypic reference across a clinical isolate cohort, with per-isolate concordance reported.
skills.name: genomic-epidemiology-reporting
skills.search_text: genomic-epidemiology-reporting Use when in-silico virulence/typing gene calls from sequencing reads must be validated against PCR or another phenotypic reference across a clinical isolate cohort, with per-isolate concordance reported. Parsing M. tuberculosis resistance results with phac-nml/mykrobe-parser — the parser is written for Mykrobe's MTB-specific 201901/202010 panels, not S. aureus PVL probes Only text/CSV Mykrobe output is available — per the README, CSV 'does not fit easily in tabular/csv format' and some per-probe information is lost Samples are suspected mixed cultures — the article removed samples exceeding 40 confident heterozygous SNPs as contaminated by an unrelated strain http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3303 Generates per-isolate in-silico gene-presence genotypes (e.g. PVL lukPV-S/lukPV-K) from bacterial outbreak-isolate read sets using Mykrobe predictor, then joins them to a PCR reference phenotype table to report typing concordance across the outbreak cohort. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms10063
skills.summary: Generates per-isolate in-silico gene-presence genotypes (e.g. PVL lukPV-S/lukPV-K) from bacterial outbreak-isolate read sets using Mykrobe predictor, then joins them to a PCR reference phenotype table to report typing concordance across the outbreak cohort.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Parsing M. tuberculosis resistance results with phac-nml/mykrobe-parser — the parser is written for Mykrobe's MTB-specific 201901/202010 panels, not S. aureus PVL probes Only text/CSV Mykrobe output is available — per the README, CSV 'does not fit easily in tabular/csv format' and some per-probe information is lost Samples are suspected mixed cultures — the article removed samples exceeding 40 confident heterozygous SNPs as contaminated by an unrelated strain

skills.description: Use when a viral scaffold FASTA may contain redundant/overlapping sequences from fragmented genome assemblies and a dereplicated representative set is required before binning.
skills.name: genomic-overlap-merging
skills.search_text: genomic-overlap-merging Use when a viral scaffold FASTA may contain redundant/overlapping sequences from fragmented genome assemblies and a dereplicated representative set is required before binning. The goal is binning whole metagenomes or microbes — vRhyme is built for viral sequences/scaffolds and 'is not meant to bin microbes'. Preservation of each original scaffold sequence is required — the composite method produces chimeric merged representatives rather than selecting existing sequences. Scaffolds are already dereplicated or come from complete circular genomes flagged for removal pre-binning. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 vRhyme's scaffold dereplication module (Mash + Nucmer) that collapses duplicate viral scaffolds either by keeping the longest representative or by merging overlapping duplicates into a single composite sequence, writing dereplicated_scaffolds.fasta. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac341
skills.summary: vRhyme's scaffold dereplication module (Mash + Nucmer) that collapses duplicate viral scaffolds either by keeping the longest representative or by merging overlapping duplicates into a single composite sequence, writing dereplicated_scaffolds.fasta.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is binning whole metagenomes or microbes — vRhyme is built for viral sequences/scaffolds and 'is not meant to bin microbes'. Preservation of each original scaffold sequence is required — the composite method produces chimeric merged representatives rather than selecting existing sequences. Scaffolds are already dereplicated or come from complete circular genomes flagged for removal pre-binning.

skills.description: Use when building a Kraken-compatible taxonomy database from NCBI RefSeq complete microbial genomes so that exact k-mer lookups resolve to specific taxon IDs for metagenomic classification.
skills.name: genomic-reference-library-processing
skills.search_text: genomic-reference-library-processing Use when building a Kraken-compatible taxonomy database from NCBI RefSeq complete microbial genomes so that exact k-mer lookups resolve to specific taxon IDs for metagenomic classification. The goal is abundance estimation of metagenomes (programs like MetaPhlAn classify only a small percentage of sequences and do not build k-mer-to-LCA databases) The classification strategy requires inexact alignment of sequences rather than exact-match database queries of k-mers Draft GenBank microbial genomes contain contaminating sequences and cannot be used directly without removing adapter-derived k-mers and terminal k-mers of draft contigs http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Constructs a Kraken k-mer-to-LCA database from a user-specified library of complete genomes: count all 31-mers with Jellyfish, then overwrite the 4-byte count spaces with the NCBI taxonomic ID of each k-mer's lowest common ancestor (LCA). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/gb-2014-15-3-r46
skills.summary: Constructs a Kraken k-mer-to-LCA database from a user-specified library of complete genomes: count all 31-mers with Jellyfish, then overwrite the 4-byte count spaces with the NCBI taxonomic ID of each k-mer's lowest common ancestor (LCA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is abundance estimation of metagenomes (programs like MetaPhlAn classify only a small percentage of sequences and do not build k-mer-to-LCA databases) The classification strategy requires inexact alignment of sequences rather than exact-match database queries of k-mers Draft GenBank microbial genomes contain contaminating sequences and cannot be used directly without removing adapter-derived k-mers and terminal k-mers of draft contigs

skills.description: Use when you need per-region pairwise comparisons of homologous sequences (e.g., BLAST-derived region bins from metagenomic assemblies) quantified as synteny scores rather than SNP distances.
skills.name: genomic-region-sequence-handling
skills.search_text: genomic-region-sequence-handling Use when you need per-region pairwise comparisons of homologous sequences (e.g., BLAST-derived region bins from metagenomic assemblies) quantified as synteny scores rather than SNP distances. Comparing sequences with extensive divergence below the BLAST detection thresholds (identity <97% or query coverage <70%), since no homologous region bins will exist to align Quantifying SNP-based strain differences — SynTracker is deliberately insensitive to SNPs and designed to detect structural changes; use an SNP-based tool such as inStrain or MIDAS instead Pairs of sequences whose cumulative aligned overlap is below 4,800 bp, which are excluded from downstream analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Handles homologous genomic region bins from SynTracker: within each bin (1-kbp central regions with 2-kbp flanks per BLAST hit), performs all-versus-all pairwise alignment with DECIPHER's FindSynteny to compute region-specific pairwise synteny scores used downstream for APSS calculation. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-024-02276-2
skills.summary: Handles homologous genomic region bins from SynTracker: within each bin (1-kbp central regions with 2-kbp flanks per BLAST hit), performs all-versus-all pairwise alignment with DECIPHER's FindSynteny to compute region-specific pairwise synteny scores used downstream for APSS calculation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Comparing sequences with extensive divergence below the BLAST detection thresholds (identity <97% or query coverage <70%), since no homologous region bins will exist to align Quantifying SNP-based strain differences — SynTracker is deliberately insensitive to SNPs and designed to detect structural changes; use an SNP-based tool such as inStrain or MIDAS instead Pairs of sequences whose cumulative aligned overlap is below 4,800 bp, which are excluded from downstream analysis

skills.description: Use when designing k-mer-based sequence detectors and you need to choose the k-mer length k: sweep k over a candidate range and compute the analytical false-positive rate of spurious k-mer occurrence for given target/non-target sequence lengths.
skills.name: genomic-sequence-composition-analysis
skills.search_text: genomic-sequence-composition-analysis Use when designing k-mer-based sequence detectors and you need to choose the k-mer length k: sweep k over a candidate range and compute the analytical false-positive rate of spurious k-mer occurrence for given target/non-target sequence lengths. You already have a trained baseLess model or pre-generated 16S k-mer networks — no k-size sweep is needed Input is raw MinION fast5 signal data for inference (use baseLess run_inference, not composition analysis) The goal is abundance estimation against whole genomes rather than read-level salient k-mer selection http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Analyzes k-mer composition of target and non-target sequences via an analytical Poisson occurrence model to select the k-mer lengths (k) whose salient k-mers minimize false-positive detection, as done in baseLess Section 4.2 to select k=8 and k=9. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad017
skills.summary: Analyzes k-mer composition of target and non-target sequences via an analytical Poisson occurrence model to select the k-mer lengths (k) whose salient k-mers minimize false-positive detection, as done in baseLess Section 4.2 to select k=8 and k=9.

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample predicted resistance calls in JSON from Mykrobe predictor plus phenotypic DST labels and need sensitivity/specificity per antibiotic, or when reproducing error tables like St_B1's 99.1%/99.6% or minor-allele sensitivity deltas.

skills.search_text: genotype-phenotype-concordance-analysis Use when you have per-sample predicted resistance calls in JSON from Mykrobe predictor plus phenotypic DST labels and need sensitivity/specificity per antibiotic, or when reproducing error tables like St_B1's 99.1%/99.6% or minor-allele sensitivity deltas. When only one method (prediction or phenotype) is available — concordance metrics need both per-sample calls and DST labels When per-drug error rates are requested for a drug with fewer than ~10 phenotypically resistant validation samples — false-negative rates were only estimated where >10 resistant samples existed When the goal is pyrazinamide prediction from known mutations — the article states known mutations are poorly predictive and the drug is excluded Computes per-drug sensitivity (false-negative rate) and specificity (false-positive rate) by comparing sequence-based resistance predictions (Mykrobe predictor JSON calls) against gold-standard phenotypic DST labels (BSAC disc test, Phoenix, MGIT), as done for S. aureus across 12 antibiotics and for M. tuberculosis second-line drugs. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms10063

skills.when_to_use_negative: When only one method (prediction or phenotype) is available — concordance metrics need both per-sample calls and DST labels When per-drug error rates are requested for a drug with fewer than ~10 phenotypically resistant validation samples — false-negative rates were only estimated where >10 resistant samples existed When the goal is pyrazinamide prediction from known mutations — the article states known mutations are poorly predictive and the drug is excluded
