skills.summary: Reconstructs inStrain's four-stage read filtering of a sorted .bam file: un-paired reads are removed by default and the orientation/insert-size, mapQ, and nucleotide-identity filters are applied to read pairs in combination rather than to individual reads, reducing erroneous mappings before coverage, SNV, and linkage analysis.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are single-end/un-paired and you intend to retain them — inStrain removes all un-paired reads by default You only need raw coverage/breadth estimates without filtering — a faster tool like CoverM may be more appropriate than pair-level filtering You need per-read filtering statistics rather than pair-level decisions — inStrain applies filters to pairs of reads in combination, not individual reads

skills.description: Use when you must quantify how much of a newly built sequence database cross-maps to an independent reference catalog (e.g. checking a fungal marker database for bacterial contamination), or when computing a defensible mapping-rate summary for a large sequence set.
skills.name: mapping-rate-quantification
skills.search_text: mapping-rate-quantification Use when you must quantify how much of a newly built sequence database cross-maps to an independent reference catalog (e.g. checking a fungal marker database for bacterial contamination), or when computing a defensible mapping-rate summary for a large sequence set. You need genuine biological read alignment rather than a contamination/specificity bound — this skill quantifies cross-mapping of simulated reads, not real sample profiling The database is small enough to align query sequences directly without read simulation — ART simulation exists specifically to work around memory limits on 1.69 M sequences You are doing functional protein annotation — that uses Diamond blastx with coverage >95%, identity >99%, e-value <10e-10 thresholds, not this read-mapping rate check http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 A cross-mapping contamination check that simulates paired-end Illumina reads covering a large marker-gene database (e.g. the 1.69 million FunOMIC-T fungal single-copy marker genes), aligns them to a reference catalog (UHGG, 204,938 non-redundant gut prokaryote genomes) with bowtie2, applies a strict samtools mapping filter, and reports the fraction of reads mapping — here validating that <0.01% of fungal markers cross-map to bacteria. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.07.010
skills.summary: A cross-mapping contamination check that simulates paired-end Illumina reads covering a large marker-gene database (e.g. the 1.69 million FunOMIC-T fungal single-copy marker genes), aligns them to a reference catalog (UHGG, 204,938 non-redundant gut prokaryote genomes) with bowtie2, applies a strict samtools mapping filter, and reports the fraction of reads mapping — here validating that <0.01% of fungal markers cross-map to bacteria.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need genuine biological read alignment rather than a contamination/specificity bound — this skill quantifies cross-mapping of simulated reads, not real sample profiling The database is small enough to align query sequences directly without read simulation — ART simulation exists specifically to work around memory limits on 1.69 M sequences You are doing functional protein annotation — that uses Diamond blastx with coverage >95%, identity >99%, e-value <10e-10 thresholds, not this read-mapping rate check

skills.description: Use when comparing raw nanopore signal mappers for adaptive-sampling benefits: PAF mappings from multiple tools (e.g., RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) are available on the same FAST5 datasets and you need per-tool averages of read prefix length or chunks consumed per mapped read.
skills.name: mapping-tool-benchmark-comparison
skills.search_text: mapping-tool-benchmark-comparison Use when comparing raw nanopore signal mappers for adaptive-sampling benefits: PAF mappings from multiple tools (e.g., RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) are available on the same FAST5 datasets and you need per-tool averages of read prefix length or chunks consumed per mapped read. The tool comparison involves read accuracy or throughput rather than sequencing time/cost proxies (read prefix length / chunks per read) — use the accuracy/throughput evaluation workflow instead. Input data is r10.4.1; UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data, so this three-tool comparison is invalid for newer chemistries. Only one mapper's PAF output is available — the prefix-length and chunk-consumption comparisons require matched mappings from RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap on the same datasets. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 A benchmarking skill for comparing real-time nanopore raw-signal mapping tools (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) on sequencing time/cost proxies, measured as average sequenced read prefix length (bases) and average number of sequenced signal chunks per read from modified PAF outputs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for comparing real-time nanopore raw-signal mapping tools (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) on sequencing time/cost proxies, measured as average sequenced read prefix length (bases) and average number of sequenced signal chunks per read from modified PAF outputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The tool comparison involves read accuracy or throughput rather than sequencing time/cost proxies (read prefix length / chunks per read) — use the accuracy/throughput evaluation workflow instead. Input data is r10.4.1; UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data, so this three-tool comparison is invalid for newer chemistries. Only one mapper's PAF output is available — the prefix-length and chunk-consumption comparisons require matched mappings from RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap on the same datasets.

skills.description: Use when you need an all-vs-all distance matrix between many (FASTA/FASTQ) metagenomic samples at scale, and a per-pair loop is infeasible; a k-mer index directory already exists or can be built.
skills.name: mapreduce-distributed-pairwise-scoring
skills.search_text: mapreduce-distributed-pairwise-scoring Use when you need an all-vs-all distance matrix between many (FASTA/FASTQ) metagenomic samples at scale, and a per-pair loop is infeasible; a k-mer index directory already exists or can be built. Input data has already been reduced, normalized by read count, or binarized to presence/absence — the paper shows such data reduction and presence/absence distance metrics greatly diminish the resolution of large-scale comparative analyses You only need a small number of pairwise comparisons (n << all-vs-all); a direct pairwise scan is simpler than a MapReduce sweep-line over an inverted index http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Implements Libra's Hadoop MapReduce scoring stage, which computes the all-vs-all pairwise distance matrix between metagenomic samples using a sweep-line over a k-mer inverted index with the COSINESIMILARITY scoring algorithm, avoiding quadratic scans of individual vector pairs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Implements Libra's Hadoop MapReduce scoring stage, which computes the all-vs-all pairwise distance matrix between metagenomic samples using a sweep-line over a k-mer inverted index with the COSINESIMILARITY scoring algorithm, avoiding quadratic scans of individual vector pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has already been reduced, normalized by read count, or binarized to presence/absence — the paper shows such data reduction and presence/absence distance metrics greatly diminish the resolution of large-scale comparative analyses You only need a small number of pairwise comparisons (n << all-vs-all); a direct pairwise scan is simpler than a MapReduce sweep-line over an inverted index

skills.description: Use when you have binned contigs (e.g. MetaBAT2 bins from a HiFi metagenome assembly) and need to grade MAG recovery into quality categories from marker-gene completeness/contamination estimates.
skills.name: marker-gene-based-genome-recovery-assessment
skills.search_text: marker-gene-based-genome-recovery-assessment Use when you have binned contigs (e.g. MetaBAT2 bins from a HiFi metagenome assembly) and need to grade MAG recovery into quality categories from marker-gene completeness/contamination estimates. You need assembly-level contiguity/read-mapping metrics rather than per-bin marker-gene quality — use Mapler's read_contig_mapping evaluation instead Bins have not been produced yet (no FASTA bins) — run binning (e.g. MetaBAT2) first You need to classify the whole assembly quality, not the individual MAGs it contains http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Assesses the quality of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) by predicting completeness and contamination with CheckM2 and classifying each bin into GSC-style quality categories (near complete, high, medium, low) as implemented in the Mapler pipeline for HiFi metagenome assemblies. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btaf334
skills.summary: Assesses the quality of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) by predicting completeness and contamination with CheckM2 and classifying each bin into GSC-style quality categories (near complete, high, medium, low) as implemented in the Mapler pipeline for HiFi metagenome assemblies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need assembly-level contiguity/read-mapping metrics rather than per-bin marker-gene quality — use Mapler's read_contig_mapping evaluation instead Bins have not been produced yet (no FASTA bins) — run binning (e.g. MetaBAT2) first You need to classify the whole assembly quality, not the individual MAGs it contains

skills.description: Use when binned contig FASTA files (MAGs) have been produced by a binning step and you need per-bin completeness/contamination estimates plus assembly statistics to judge bin quality.
skills.name: marker-gene-completeness-contamination-estimation
skills.search_text: marker-gene-completeness-contamination-estimation Use when binned contig FASTA files (MAGs) have been produced by a binning step and you need per-bin completeness/contamination estimates plus assembly statistics to judge bin quality. Input is raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) rather than already-binned contig FASTA files — this skill operates downstream of assembly and binning. A machine-learning alternative is preferred when bins represent lineages with few high-quality genomic representatives, e.g. CheckM2's universally trained models instead of marker-gene lineage lookup. The goal is taxonomic classification of MAGs rather than quantitative completeness/contamination assessment of bin quality. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quality-controls metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) by estimating completeness and contamination from near-universal single-copy marker genes with BUSCO, complemented by QUAST assembly statistics (contig count, total length, N50) for each binned contig set produced by nf-core/mag. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Quality-controls metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) by estimating completeness and contamination from near-universal single-copy marker genes with BUSCO, complemented by QUAST assembly statistics (contig count, total length, N50) for each binned contig set produced by nf-core/mag.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) rather than already-binned contig FASTA files — this skill operates downstream of assembly and binning. A machine-learning alternative is preferred when bins represent lineages with few high-quality genomic representatives, e.g. CheckM2's universally trained models instead of marker-gene lineage lookup. The goal is taxonomic classification of MAGs rather than quantitative completeness/contamination assessment of bin quality.

skills.description: Use when building a PICRUSt-style reference pipeline: a marker gene phylogeny (e.g. Greengenes 16S tree) must be aligned with a gene-by-genome KO/COG table before ancestral state reconstruction or tip gene content prediction.
skills.name: marker-gene-tree-formatting-and-pruning
skills.search_text: marker-gene-tree-formatting-and-pruning Use when building a PICRUSt-style reference pipeline: a marker gene phylogeny (e.g. Greengenes 16S tree) must be aligned with a gene-by-genome KO/COG table before ancestral state reconstruction or tip gene content prediction. The input is a 16S OTU table of sample data rather than a reference genome set — downstream PICRUSt steps (copy-number normalization, metagenome prediction) expect an already-built, trait-annotated reference tree. The community or genomes of interest are viral or eukaryotic — PICRUSt only includes bacterial and archaeal marker gene sequences. A reference genome already exists for the organism's gene content, making prediction via the pruned tree unnecessary. Formats and prunes the 16S marker gene reference tree (tax2tree Greengenes) so that every tip with a sequenced reference genome carries its gene family content vector of KEGG Ortholog (KO) and COG annotations, preparing the tree for ancestral state reconstruction in PICRUSt. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nbt.2676
skills.summary: Formats and prunes the 16S marker gene reference tree (tax2tree Greengenes) so that every tip with a sequenced reference genome carries its gene family content vector of KEGG Ortholog (KO) and COG annotations, preparing the tree for ancestral state reconstruction in PICRUSt.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a 16S OTU table of sample data rather than a reference genome set — downstream PICRUSt steps (copy-number normalization, metagenome prediction) expect an already-built, trait-annotated reference tree. The community or genomes of interest are viral or eukaryotic — PICRUSt only includes bacterial and archaeal marker gene sequences. A reference genome already exists for the organism's gene content, making prediction via the pruned tree unnecessary.

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify marker-retrieval accuracy of a phylogenomic mining tool (e.g. Patchwork) against a divergent reference species, using recovery counts, unique reciprocal alignments, percent identity, and query coverage as validation metrics.
skills.name: marker-recovery-accuracy-evaluation
skills.search_text: marker-recovery-accuracy-evaluation Use when you need to quantify marker-retrieval accuracy of a phylogenomic mining tool (e.g. Patchwork) against a divergent reference species, using recovery counts, unique reciprocal alignments, percent identity, and query coverage as validation metrics. The reference set contains non-near-USCO sequences — the article recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences. Query and reference are the same species and high quality — for that scenario the article's own-species benchmark (815 same-species USCOs, 95.9% identity, 92.2% coverage) is the appropriate comparison, not the divergent-reference benchmark. You want to compare against other tools on low-coverage read data rather than evaluate a single assembly-based retrieval accuracy profile. http://edamontology.org/topic_0157 http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 Benchmarking skill that quantifies how well a marker-retrieval tool recovers phylogenetic markers when query and reference species are divergent, by searching a de novo query assembly against distant near-USCO references and scoring retrieval, uniqueness, identity, and coverage metrics. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Benchmarking skill that quantifies how well a marker-retrieval tool recovers phylogenetic markers when query and reference species are divergent, by searching a de novo query assembly against distant near-USCO references and scoring retrieval, uniqueness, identity, and coverage metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reference set contains non-near-USCO sequences — the article recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences. Query and reference are the same species and high quality — for that scenario the article's own-species benchmark (815 same-species USCOs, 95.9% identity, 92.2% coverage) is the appropriate comparison, not the divergent-reference benchmark. You want to compare against other tools on low-coverage read data rather than evaluate a single assembly-based retrieval accuracy profile.

skills.description: Use when computing background-adjusted alignment-free distances (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp) in CAFE and the sequence's Markov order is unknown — the default '-1' triggers automatic BIC-based inference.
skills.name: markov-background-model-estimation
skills.search_text: markov-background-model-estimation Use when computing background-adjusted alignment-free distances (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp) in CAFE and the sequence's Markov order is unknown — the default '-1' triggers automatic BIC-based inference. Running conventional k-mer count measures (Ma, Eu, Ch, etc.) or presence/absence measures (Jaccard, Dice, etc.) — these do not require a Markov background model Using -M -1 automatic inference with the JS (Jensen-Shannon) measure — the README states the '-1' BIC inference is 'not suitable for JS' When a reliable Markov order is already known for all sequences and BIC estimation would add unnecessary runtime http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Estimate the appropriate Markov order (background sequence model) used by CAFE's background-adjusted k-mer dissimilarity measures (D2star, D2shepp, CVtree), either per-sequence via the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) or with user-specified order values. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx351
skills.summary: Estimate the appropriate Markov order (background sequence model) used by CAFE's background-adjusted k-mer dissimilarity measures (D2star, D2shepp, CVtree), either per-sequence via the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) or with user-specified order values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Running conventional k-mer count measures (Ma, Eu, Ch, etc.) or presence/absence measures (Jaccard, Dice, etc.) — these do not require a Markov background model Using -M -1 automatic inference with the JS (Jensen-Shannon) measure — the README states the '-1' BIC inference is 'not suitable for JS' When a reliable Markov order is already known for all sequences and BIC estimation would add unnecessary runtime

skills.description: Use when computing background-adjusted k-mer dissimilarities (D2star, D2shepp, CVtree) in CAFE and the Markov background order must be chosen or auto-inferred per sequence set.
skills.name: markov-order-background-adjusted-kmer-statistics
skills.search_text: markov-order-background-adjusted-kmer-statistics Use when computing background-adjusted k-mer dissimilarities (D2star, D2shepp, CVtree) in CAFE and the Markov background order must be chosen or auto-inferred per sequence set. Input analysis uses only conventional k-mer count measures (Ma, Eu, Ch, JS, etc.) that do not require a background Markov model Using the JS divergence measure with -M -1: BIC-based automatic order inference is explicitly not suitable for JS Sequences are being compared via alignment-based methods where full alignments are appropriate and available http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Configure the Markov order (-M) that defines the background sequence model for CAFE's background-adjusted alignment-free dissimilarity measures (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp), either with a fixed order or automatic inference via BIC. This order corrects raw k-mer counts for expected occurrences under a Markov model, which is essential for these statistics. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx351
skills.summary: Configure the Markov order (-M) that defines the background sequence model for CAFE's background-adjusted alignment-free dissimilarity measures (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp), either with a fixed order or automatic inference via BIC. This order corrects raw k-mer counts for expected occurrences under a Markov model, which is essential for these statistics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input analysis uses only conventional k-mer count measures (Ma, Eu, Ch, JS, etc.) that do not require a background Markov model Using the JS divergence measure with -M -1: BIC-based automatic order inference is explicitly not suitable for JS Sequences are being compared via alignment-based methods where full alignments are appropriate and available

skills.description: Use when running CAFE background-adjusted measures (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp) on genomes or NGS shotgun reads and the appropriate Markov order is unclear to the user.
skills.name: markov-order-model-selection
skills.search_text: markov-order-model-selection Use when running CAFE background-adjusted measures (CVtree, D2star, D2shepp) on genomes or NGS shotgun reads and the appropriate Markov order is unclear to the user. Using the JS (Jensen-Shannon) distance in CAFE — BIC-based automatic order inference is explicitly 'not suitable for JS' The user already knows the appropriate Markov order (e.g. order 0 for the gut metagenome d2S analysis) — fixing -M directly is faster than the time-consuming BIC search http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Automatic inference of the Markov model order required by CAFE's background-adjusted alignment-free measures (CVtree, D2star/D2*, D2shepp/d2S) by setting the -M parameter to -1, which selects the order minimizing the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) from the sequence data itself. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx351
skills.summary: Automatic inference of the Markov model order required by CAFE's background-adjusted alignment-free measures (CVtree, D2star/D2*, D2shepp/d2S) by setting the -M parameter to -1, which selects the order minimizing the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC) from the sequence data itself.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Using the JS (Jensen-Shannon) distance in CAFE — BIC-based automatic order inference is explicitly 'not suitable for JS' The user already knows the appropriate Markov order (e.g. order 0 for the gut metagenome d2S analysis) — fixing -M directly is faster than the time-consuming BIC search

skills.description: Use when you have assembled plasmid contigs (e.g. from Unicycler within Plassembler) and need to annotate each contig with its closest PLSDB plasmid match using Mash distance.
skills.name: mash-distance-screening
skills.search_text: mash-distance-screening Use when you have assembled plasmid contigs (e.g. from Unicycler within Plassembler) and need to annotate each contig with its closest PLSDB plasmid match using Mash distance. Input is raw long/short reads rather than assembled plasmid contigs — mash screening here operates on Unicycler-assembled contigs after read extraction and hybrid assembly. You need full functional annotation or alignment-level comparison of plasmids rather than a fast MinHash similarity lookup — mash dist gives approximate distances, not alignments. Plasmid contigs are linear or from non-bacterial assemblies where PLSDB (a bacterial plasmid database) is not an appropriate reference space. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Screens assembled plasmid contigs against the PLSDB sketch database with Mash MinHash distances to determine whether each contig matches a known plasmid, keeping the lowest-distance top hit under the Plassembler threshold of 0.1. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad409
skills.summary: Screens assembled plasmid contigs against the PLSDB sketch database with Mash MinHash distances to determine whether each contig matches a known plasmid, keeping the lowest-distance top hit under the Plassembler threshold of 0.1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw long/short reads rather than assembled plasmid contigs — mash screening here operates on Unicycler-assembled contigs after read extraction and hybrid assembly. You need full functional annotation or alignment-level comparison of plasmids rather than a fast MinHash similarity lookup — mash dist gives approximate distances, not alignments. Plasmid contigs are linear or from non-bacterial assemblies where PLSDB (a bacterial plasmid database) is not an appropriate reference space.

skills.description: Use when you have a large published phylogenetic tree (e.g., a Mash distance tree over >10,000 genomes supplied as a newick file) and a smaller subset of analyzed genomes, and need a pruned reference tree to quantify agreement with trees built from your own distance matrix.
skills.name: mash-distance-tree-pruning
skills.search_text: mash-distance-tree-pruning Use when you have a large published phylogenetic tree (e.g., a Mash distance tree over >10,000 genomes supplied as a newick file) and a smaller subset of analyzed genomes, and need a pruned reference tree to quantify agreement with trees built from your own distance matrix. The comparison tree is already restricted to the analyzed genomes and needs no tip pruning You need to compare against a tree built de novo from your own distances rather than a published reference topology The published tree lacks external nodes corresponding to the genomes being analyzed (tips cannot be matched) http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 Prune a published Mash distance-based phylogenetic tree (newick format) so that only the external nodes of the genomes under analysis are retained, yielding a reference tree for comparing against de novo synteny-based phylogenies. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-024-02276-2
skills.summary: Prune a published Mash distance-based phylogenetic tree (newick format) so that only the external nodes of the genomes under analysis are retained, yielding a reference tree for comparing against de novo synteny-based phylogenies.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The comparison tree is already restricted to the analyzed genomes and needs no tip pruning You need to compare against a tree built de novo from your own distances rather than a published reference topology The published tree lacks external nodes corresponding to the genomes being analyzed (tips cannot be matched)

skills.description: Use when computing fast all-vs-all pairwise distances between many metagenomic FASTA/FASTQ samples where sketching unique k-mers is acceptable, or when benchmarking abundance-aware k-mer metrics against Mash.
skills.name: mash-minhash-distance-computation
skills.search_text: mash-minhash-distance-computation Use when computing fast all-vs-all pairwise distances between many metagenomic FASTA/FASTQ samples where sketching unique k-mers is acceptable, or when benchmarking abundance-aware k-mer metrics against Mash. The analysis goal requires abundance-resolved distances — the paper shows that data reduction approaches like unique-k-mer sketching 'greatly diminish the resolution' of large-scale comparative analyses (Mash distances compress across mock 1–4). Input is already a pairwise distance matrix or feature table rather than raw metagenomic reads. No sketching approximation is acceptable and exact k-mer abundance distances are required (use Libra scoring instead). http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Generates MinHash-based pairwise distances between metagenomes by indexing samples with sketches of unique k-mers, used in the Libra paper as a fast comparison baseline against Libra's k-mer abundance distances on simulated 454 mock-community data. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Generates MinHash-based pairwise distances between metagenomes by indexing samples with sketches of unique k-mers, used in the Libra paper as a fast comparison baseline against Libra's k-mer abundance distances on simulated 454 mock-community data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal requires abundance-resolved distances — the paper shows that data reduction approaches like unique-k-mer sketching 'greatly diminish the resolution' of large-scale comparative analyses (Mash distances compress across mock 1–4). Input is already a pairwise distance matrix or feature table rather than raw metagenomic reads. No sketching approximation is acceptable and exact k-mer abundance distances are required (use Libra scoring instead).

skills.description: Use when auditing which overlap mismatches PANDAseq corrected probabilistically, to quantify whether uncertain corrections are driven by low-quality (masked) bases flagged by upstream Illumina processing.
skills.name: masked-base-probability-scoring
skills.search_text: masked-base-probability-scoring Use when auditing which overlap mismatches PANDAseq corrected probabilistically, to quantify whether uncertain corrections are driven by low-quality (masked) bases flagged by upstream Illumina processing. Data were not processed by CASAVA-style upstream quality masking (end-of-read lowest-quality masking convention), so the mask annotation is undefined. The input is raw paired-end FASTQ before assembly — corrections do not exist yet; run PANDAseq first. Sequences lack known truth (mixed-template data), so mismatched bases cannot be confidently identified as correction events. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Classifies PANDAseq's uncertain overlap-mismatch corrections by whether the conflicting bases were quality-masked (CASAVA end-of-read low-quality positions) in the forward read, reverse read, both, or neither, to test the claim that uncertain corrections come from reads with many low-quality bases. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-13-31
skills.summary: Classifies PANDAseq's uncertain overlap-mismatch corrections by whether the conflicting bases were quality-masked (CASAVA end-of-read low-quality positions) in the forward read, reverse read, both, or neither, to test the claim that uncertain corrections come from reads with many low-quality bases.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data were not processed by CASAVA-style upstream quality masking (end-of-read lowest-quality masking convention), so the mask annotation is undefined. The input is raw paired-end FASTQ before assembly — corrections do not exist yet; run PANDAseq first. Sequences lack known truth (mixed-template data), so mismatched bases cannot be confidently identified as correction events.

skills.description: Use when cleaning microbial FASTQ reads against a human host reference and microbial retention (not just host removal) is a priority, e.g. bacterial Illumina or ONT metagenomic reads that are being over-removed by the unmasked human-t2t-hla index.
skills.name: masked-reference-index-selection
skills.search_text: masked-reference-index-selection Use when cleaning microbial FASTQ reads against a human host reference and microbial retention (not just host removal) is a priority, e.g. bacterial Illumina or ONT metagenomic reads that are being over-removed by the unmasked human-t2t-hla index. When the target organism is viral or phage and retention of viral sequences is the priority — use the index masked against RefSeq viral and Millard Lab phage genomes (human-t2t-hla.argos-bacteria-985_rs-viral-202401_ml-phage-202401) instead When maximal human read removal matters more than microbial retention — the default unmasked human-t2t-hla index is precise by default but masked indexes slightly relax depletion (≤0.001% reduction) When input data contains no microbial host-organism overlap concern, e.g. pure host sequencing, where masking provides no benefit http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Select and apply Hostile's masked human reference indexes (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140, masked with 150mers from 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial and 140 mycobacterial genomes) to maximize bacterial read retention during host depletion while keeping human read removal essentially unchanged. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Select and apply Hostile's masked human reference indexes (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140, masked with 150mers from 985 FDA-ARGOS bacterial and 140 mycobacterial genomes) to maximize bacterial read retention during host depletion while keeping human read removal essentially unchanged.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the target organism is viral or phage and retention of viral sequences is the priority — use the index masked against RefSeq viral and Millard Lab phage genomes (human-t2t-hla.argos-bacteria-985_rs-viral-202401_ml-phage-202401) instead When maximal human read removal matters more than microbial retention — the default unmasked human-t2t-hla index is precise by default but masked indexes slightly relax depletion (≤0.001% reduction) When input data contains no microbial host-organism overlap concern, e.g. pure host sequencing, where masking provides no benefit

skills.description: Use when thousands-to-millions of tandem MS/MS spectra from LC-MS/MS datasets (e.g. GNPS MSV datasets) must be grouped by fragmentation-pattern similarity, either to propagate peptide/spectrum identifications across related spectra or to estimate true chemical diversity.
skills.name: mass-spectra-similarity-network-construction
skills.search_text: mass-spectra-similarity-network-construction Use when thousands-to-millions of tandem MS/MS spectra from LC-MS/MS datasets (e.g. GNPS MSV datasets) must be grouped by fragmentation-pattern similarity, either to propagate peptide/spectrum identifications across related spectra or to estimate true chemical diversity. The goal is de novo identification of individual spectra rather than grouping related spectra — use MetaMiner/RiPPquest peptidogenomics search (1% FDR) instead of networking alone Spectra are known to be highly heterogeneous in precursor type/charge such that pairwise spectral similarity is not meaningful; networking assumes comparable fragmentation behavior within families Input spectra lack paired MS/MS fragmentation information (e.g. MS1-only features) — spectral networking requires tandem spectra http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0121 Clusters large collections of tandem mass spectra into spectral families via GNPS molecular networking / spectral networks (Bandeira et al., 2007; Watrous et al., 2012), collapsing raw spectrum counts into effective chemical diversity. In MetaMiner it both enlarges RiPP identifications and quantifies dataset redundancy (~10 million spectra resolving into only 8,071 families). metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2019.09.004
skills.summary: Clusters large collections of tandem mass spectra into spectral families via GNPS molecular networking / spectral networks (Bandeira et al., 2007; Watrous et al., 2012), collapsing raw spectrum counts into effective chemical diversity. In MetaMiner it both enlarges RiPP identifications and quantifies dataset redundancy (~10 million spectra resolving into only 8,071 families).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo identification of individual spectra rather than grouping related spectra — use MetaMiner/RiPPquest peptidogenomics search (1% FDR) instead of networking alone Spectra are known to be highly heterogeneous in precursor type/charge such that pairwise spectral similarity is not meaningful; networking assumes comparable fragmentation behavior within families Input spectra lack paired MS/MS fragmentation information (e.g. MS1-only features) — spectral networking requires tandem spectra

skills.description: Use when choosing or validating a minimum match length (or similar alignment-length) cutoff for a classifier by comparing match-length distributions on real versus shuffled reference databases.
skills.name: match-length-distribution-analysis
skills.search_text: match-length-distribution-analysis Use when choosing or validating a minimum match length (or similar alignment-length) cutoff for a classifier by comparing match-length distributions on real versus shuffled reference databases. When a nucleotide-level classifier is appropriate because the sequenced strains are present in the reference database — Kaiju's protein-level matching is then less sensitive since non-protein-coding regions cannot be classified When the goal is classification accuracy benchmarking (genome exclusion) rather than calibrating a match-length parameter — use the 882-genome/242-genus exclusion benchmark workflow instead When reads are already protein sequences and only need scoring parameter tuning (Greedy mode score s=65), since this skill targets MEM-mode match length http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Empirically calibrates a protein-level metagenome classifier's minimum match length cutoff by classifying simulated reads against both an original and a composition-preserving shuffled reference database, then comparing match-length distributions to pick a cutoff (Kaiju MEM mode: m=11) that excludes random spurious matches while preserving sensitivity. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms11257
skills.summary: Empirically calibrates a protein-level metagenome classifier's minimum match length cutoff by classifying simulated reads against both an original and a composition-preserving shuffled reference database, then comparing match-length distributions to pick a cutoff (Kaiju MEM mode: m=11) that excludes random spurious matches while preserving sensitivity.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a nucleotide-level classifier is appropriate because the sequenced strains are present in the reference database — Kaiju's protein-level matching is then less sensitive since non-protein-coding regions cannot be classified When the goal is classification accuracy benchmarking (genome exclusion) rather than calibrating a match-length parameter — use the 882-genome/242-genus exclusion benchmark workflow instead When reads are already protein sequences and only need scoring parameter tuning (Greedy mode score s=65), since this skill targets MEM-mode match length

skills.description: Use when classifying basecalled nanopore reads as target vs non-target against a repetitive pan-genomic reference for targeted sequencing/depletion, especially when alignment tools like minimap2 are too slow or memory-heavy.
skills.name: matching-statistics-hypothesis-testing
skills.search_text: matching-statistics-hypothesis-testing Use when classifying basecalled nanopore reads as target vs non-target against a repetitive pan-genomic reference for targeted sequencing/depletion, especially when alignment tools like minimap2 are too slow or memory-heavy. When working directly with raw nanopore electrical signal via the Read Until API — SPUMONI operates on sequences of bases, so a separate base caller must run upstream When the depletion target and non-targets share substantial sequence similarity (e.g. conserved genes between species), where the reverse-sequence null index may be insufficient When indexing a single, non-repetitive genome where alignment-based classifiers are already fast enough and the pan-genome matching-statistics advantage does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 A read-classification method (SPUMONI) that uses compressed pan-genome indexes to compute matching statistics (MS) or pseudo-matching lengths (PML), then applies a null-index KS-statistic hypothesis test to decide whether a read is a target for nanopore read-until depletion, achieving minimap2-comparable accuracy with far less index size and memory. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.isci.2021.102696
skills.summary: A read-classification method (SPUMONI) that uses compressed pan-genome indexes to compute matching statistics (MS) or pseudo-matching lengths (PML), then applies a null-index KS-statistic hypothesis test to decide whether a read is a target for nanopore read-until depletion, achieving minimap2-comparable accuracy with far less index size and memory.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When working directly with raw nanopore electrical signal via the Read Until API — SPUMONI operates on sequences of bases, so a separate base caller must run upstream When the depletion target and non-targets share substantial sequence similarity (e.g. conserved genes between species), where the reverse-sequence null index may be insufficient When indexing a single, non-repetitive genome where alignment-based classifiers are already fast enough and the pan-genome matching-statistics advantage does not apply

skills.description: Use when assembling metagenome mock or real communities from Illumina paired-end reads plus mate-pair libraries (e.g. 4 kbp/8 kbp jumping libraries), and NGA50 contiguity versus short-read-only assemblers must be quantified.
skills.name: mate-pair-scaffolding
skills.search_text: mate-pair-scaffolding Use when assembling metagenome mock or real communities from Illumina paired-end reads plus mate-pair libraries (e.g. 4 kbp/8 kbp jumping libraries), and NGA50 contiguity versus short-read-only assemblers must be quantified. Only short paired-end reads are available and no mate-pair/jumping library or other long-range information exists — mate-pair scaffolding links cannot be exploited The analysis is reference-based; the study focuses on de novo methods and reference information has not been well examined Aiming to assess assembly of biologically important elements (genes, viral sequences, near-complete genomes) on nanopore long-read data rather than mate-pair benchmarks http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Scaffold metagenome contigs using Illumina mate-pair (jumping library) long-range links while suppressing interspecies misjoins, as implemented in MetaPlatanus by iteratively combining long-range links, coverage depth, k-mer/species-specific composition and binning. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab831
skills.summary: Scaffold metagenome contigs using Illumina mate-pair (jumping library) long-range links while suppressing interspecies misjoins, as implemented in MetaPlatanus by iteratively combining long-range links, coverage depth, k-mer/species-specific composition and binning.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only short paired-end reads are available and no mate-pair/jumping library or other long-range information exists — mate-pair scaffolding links cannot be exploited The analysis is reference-based; the study focuses on de novo methods and reference information has not been well examined Aiming to assess assembly of biologically important elements (genes, viral sequences, near-complete genomes) on nanopore long-read data rather than mate-pair benchmarks

skills.description: Use when per-taxon natural-language extraction records (character and character-state values from prokaryotic taxonomic descriptions) must be pivoted into a standard taxon-by-character matrix usable by phylogenetic analysis software.
skills.name: matrix-pivot-transformation
skills.search_text: matrix-pivot-transformation Use when per-taxon natural-language extraction records (character and character-state values from prokaryotic taxonomic descriptions) must be pivoted into a standard taxon-by-character matrix usable by phylogenetic analysis software. The input is already a structured taxon-by-character matrix and no text extraction is needed The source text is semi-structured morphological descriptions better suited to CharaParser, rather than prokaryotic descriptions rich in physiological and ecological traits The task requires extracting character types outside MicroPIE's designated 42-character set without extending the Term Lists http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3068 http://edamontology.org/topic_3299 Assembles per-taxon character and character-state values extracted by MicroPIE's extractor components into a structured taxon-by-character matrix, the standard table format (rows = taxa, columns = characters) required by phylogenetic comparative analysis software such as Mesquite and MacClade. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1396-8
skills.summary: Assembles per-taxon character and character-state values extracted by MicroPIE's extractor components into a structured taxon-by-character matrix, the standard table format (rows = taxa, columns = characters) required by phylogenetic comparative analysis software such as Mesquite and MacClade.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already a structured taxon-by-character matrix and no text extraction is needed The source text is semi-structured morphological descriptions better suited to CharaParser, rather than prokaryotic descriptions rich in physiological and ecological traits The task requires extracting character types outside MicroPIE's designated 42-character set without extending the Term Lists

skills.description: Use when a continuous trait measured across taxa (e.g., 16S rRNA gene copy number estimates from CopyRighter's Greengenes files) must be tested for phylogenetic signal on a tree, and the strength of that signal needs to be compared between a phylogeny and a taxonomic tree.
skills.name: maximum-likelihood-model-comparison
skills.search_text: maximum-likelihood-model-comparison Use when a continuous trait measured across taxa (e.g., 16S rRNA gene copy number estimates from CopyRighter's Greengenes files) must be tested for phylogenetic signal on a tree, and the strength of that signal needs to be compared between a phylogeny and a taxonomic tree. Input is an amplicon OTU table needing GCN abundance correction — use the copyrighter correction step instead; lambda estimation only quantifies trait signal, it does not correct profiles The trait data are not mapped to the Greengenes taxonomy/phylogeny — CopyRighter GCN estimates currently cover Greengenes only and are not yet extended to other taxonomies such as Silva The trait of interest is binary or discrete rather than a continuous quantitative estimate like GCN, for which the continuous-trait lambda model is inappropriate http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Estimates Pagel's lambda by maximum likelihood to quantify the strength of phylogenetic signal in a continuously valued trait (here, empirically determined 16S rRNA gene copy numbers) on both a phylogenetic tree and a taxonomic tree, testing lambda against zero with a likelihood-ratio P value. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/2049-2618-2-11
skills.summary: Estimates Pagel's lambda by maximum likelihood to quantify the strength of phylogenetic signal in a continuously valued trait (here, empirically determined 16S rRNA gene copy numbers) on both a phylogenetic tree and a taxonomic tree, testing lambda against zero with a likelihood-ratio P value.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an amplicon OTU table needing GCN abundance correction — use the copyrighter correction step instead; lambda estimation only quantifies trait signal, it does not correct profiles The trait data are not mapped to the Greengenes taxonomy/phylogeny — CopyRighter GCN estimates currently cover Greengenes only and are not yet extended to other taxonomies such as Silva The trait of interest is binary or discrete rather than a continuous quantitative estimate like GCN, for which the continuous-trait lambda model is inappropriate

skills.description: Use when you already have per-locus marker sequences (e.g. Patchwork-recovered near-USCOs) and need a well-supported phylogenomic tree via alignment, trimming, concatenation, and ML tree inference.
skills.name: maximum-likelihood-phylogenetic-inference
skills.search_text: maximum-likelihood-phylogenetic-inference Use when you already have per-locus marker sequences (e.g. Patchwork-recovered near-USCOs) and need a well-supported phylogenomic tree via alignment, trimming, concatenation, and ML tree inference. When marker sequences have not yet been retrieved/homology-screened (e.g. raw WGS reads or contigs lacking Patchwork DIAMOND search, hit stitching, and sliding-window trimming) — this skill starts from recovered per-locus sequences. When the question calls for the marker-retrieval benchmark itself rather than phylogeny construction from recovered markers. Infer a maximum-likelihood phylogeny from a concatenated supermatrix of trimmed multiple sequence alignments using IQ-TREE 2 with extended model selection (-m MFP) and 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, as applied downstream of Patchwork-recovered USCO markers. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Infer a maximum-likelihood phylogeny from a concatenated supermatrix of trimmed multiple sequence alignments using IQ-TREE 2 with extended model selection (-m MFP) and 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates, as applied downstream of Patchwork-recovered USCO markers.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When marker sequences have not yet been retrieved/homology-screened (e.g. raw WGS reads or contigs lacking Patchwork DIAMOND search, hit stitching, and sliding-window trimming) — this skill starts from recovered per-locus sequences. When the question calls for the marker-retrieval benchmark itself rather than phylogeny construction from recovered markers.

skills.description: Use when error-corrected local haplotypes from ShoRAH windows must be stitched into full-genome haplotypes and their frequencies estimated from deep sequencing of a mixed sample.
skills.name: maximum-weight-matching-optimization
skills.search_text: maximum-weight-matching-optimization Use when error-corrected local haplotypes from ShoRAH windows must be stitched into full-genome haplotypes and their frequencies estimated from deep sequencing of a mixed sample. ShoRAH2 is installed and only SNV calling or local (window-level) analysis is needed — global haplotype reconstruction is disabled there The goal is single nucleotide variant detection with strand-bias correction — use shorah snv instead of global reconstruction Coverage is low: the article detects haplotypes as rare as 0.1% only at coverage 5000, so low-coverage data will not support reliable global assembly http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Reconstruct global (full-length) haplotypes from ShoRAH's error-corrected local window haplotypes by computing a minimal set of haplotypes that explain all unique reads via maximum weight matching, then estimating their population frequencies with an Expectation Maximization algorithm (freqEst). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-12-119
skills.summary: Reconstruct global (full-length) haplotypes from ShoRAH's error-corrected local window haplotypes by computing a minimal set of haplotypes that explain all unique reads via maximum weight matching, then estimating their population frequencies with an Expectation Maximization algorithm (freqEst).
skills.when_to_use_negative: ShoRAH2 is installed and only SNV calling or local (window-level) analysis is needed — global haplotype reconstruction is disabled there The goal is single nucleotide variant detection with strand-bias correction — use shorah snv instead of global reconstruction Coverage is low: the article detects haplotypes as rare as 0.1% only at coverage 5000, so low-coverage data will not support reliable global assembly

skills.description: Use when quality-controlled paired/singleton FASTQs (e.g. host-filtered <sample_id>.<type_id>.fastq.gz files) still contain low-quality read ends and short reads that must be trimmed before read-to-gene mapping.
skills.name: maxinfo-criterion-trim-calculation
skills.search_text: maxinfo-criterion-trim-calculation Use when quality-controlled paired/singleton FASTQs (e.g. host-filtered <sample_id>.<type_id>.fastq.gz files) still contain low-quality read ends and short reads that must be trimmed before read-to-gene mapping. Input FASTQs are already post-HMP quality control — in the article's HMP stool samples, minimal reads were discarded during this phase, so heavy trimming is unnecessary The goal is host read removal or duplicate removal — MetaLAFFA performs those before this step using Bowtie 2/hs37d5 and PICARD MarkDuplicates, respectively You need adapter removal — MetaLAFFA expects raw FASTQs with sequencing adapters already removed as pipeline input http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quality trimming and filtering of shotgun metagenomic FASTQs as implemented in MetaLAFFA: Trimmomatic with the MAXINFO criterion trims low-quality bases from read ends, and reads shorter than the 60bp length threshold are discarded, with per-sample summary statistics generated afterward. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03815-9
skills.summary: Quality trimming and filtering of shotgun metagenomic FASTQs as implemented in MetaLAFFA: Trimmomatic with the MAXINFO criterion trims low-quality bases from read ends, and reads shorter than the 60bp length threshold are discarded, with per-sample summary statistics generated afterward.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input FASTQs are already post-HMP quality control — in the article's HMP stool samples, minimal reads were discarded during this phase, so heavy trimming is unnecessary The goal is host read removal or duplicate removal — MetaLAFFA performs those before this step using Bowtie 2/hs37d5 and PICARD MarkDuplicates, respectively You need adapter removal — MetaLAFFA expects raw FASTQs with sequencing adapters already removed as pipeline input

skills.description: Use when estimating adaptive evolution (alpha) from DAF and divergence tables for coding genes, or when comparing selective regimes of a user-selected gene set (e.g. recombination-rate bins) against a genome-wide distribution.
skills.name: mcdonald-kreitman-adaptation-estimation
skills.search_text: mcdonald-kreitman-adaptation-estimation Use when estimating adaptive evolution (alpha) from DAF and divergence tables for coding genes, or when comparing selective regimes of a user-selected gene set (e.g. recombination-rate bins) against a genome-wide distribution. Input is raw variant data (FASTA/VCF) rather than pre-computed DAF/divergence tables — run the iMKTData pipeline first to extract the unfolded site frequency spectrum Analyzing non-coding or non-protein-coding sequence — the data model is built on 0-fold (selected) vs 4-fold (neutral) coding classes Human data lacking ancestral-state information or accessible-genome masking (e.g. the 1000GP pilot mask for low-quality variants) needed for correct polarisation and quality filtering http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 http://edamontology.org/topic_0102 Estimate the fraction of adaptive substitutions (alpha) from polymorphism and divergence data using MK-derived tests (standard MKT, eMKT, aMKT, FWWMKT) implemented in the iMKT R package/web service, applied to D. melanogaster (DGN/PopFly) or human (1000GP/PopHuman) protein-coding genes. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: Estimate the fraction of adaptive substitutions (alpha) from polymorphism and divergence data using MK-derived tests (standard MKT, eMKT, aMKT, FWWMKT) implemented in the iMKT R package/web service, applied to D. melanogaster (DGN/PopFly) or human (1000GP/PopHuman) protein-coding genes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw variant data (FASTA/VCF) rather than pre-computed DAF/divergence tables — run the iMKTData pipeline first to extract the unfolded site frequency spectrum Analyzing non-coding or non-protein-coding sequence — the data model is built on 0-fold (selected) vs 4-fold (neutral) coding classes Human data lacking ancestral-state information or accessible-genome masking (e.g. the 1000GP pilot mask for low-quality variants) needed for correct polarisation and quality filtering

skills.description: Use when you have gene cluster assignments plus per-contig ORF ordering (all_genes_cluster.tsv + all_genes.fna) and want to group co-localized genes into synteny clusters for pathway-level functional insight.
skills.name: mcl-weighted-graph-clustering
skills.search_text: mcl-weighted-graph-clustering Use when you have gene cluster assignments plus per-contig ORF ordering (all_genes_cluster.tsv + all_genes.fna) and want to group co-localized genes into synteny clusters for pathway-level functional insight. You need operon-aware synteny detection — MAGinator currently lacks operon awareness, limiting synteny cluster accuracy You only have gene sequence similarity (no contig-level positional information), since adjacency on contigs is the sole grouping signal Your input is raw reads or unclustered ORFs — gene clusters must already exist (e.g. from MAGinator's VAMB-based gene clustering step) http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Clusters gene clusters into synteny clusters by building a weighted adjacency graph over gene clusters — edge weights encode how often genes from each pair of clusters occur adjacent on contigs — and partitioning it with Markov clustering (MCL) at the default inflation, as implemented in MAGinator's Snakemake workflow. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-024-49958-8
skills.summary: Clusters gene clusters into synteny clusters by building a weighted adjacency graph over gene clusters — edge weights encode how often genes from each pair of clusters occur adjacent on contigs — and partitioning it with Markov clustering (MCL) at the default inflation, as implemented in MAGinator's Snakemake workflow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need operon-aware synteny detection — MAGinator currently lacks operon awareness, limiting synteny cluster accuracy You only have gene sequence similarity (no contig-level positional information), since adjacency on contigs is the sole grouping signal Your input is raw reads or unclustered ORFs — gene clusters must already exist (e.g. from MAGinator's VAMB-based gene clustering step)

skills.description: Use when fitting a Bayesian DTM regression on compositional microbiome data (e.g. genus-level OTU counts) and you must choose inclusion-prior hyperparameters, MCMC run length/burn-in, and association-selection cutoffs before comparing variable-selection counts across methods.
skills.name: mcmc-hyperparameter-and-burnin-tuning
skills.search_text: mcmc-hyperparameter-and-burnin-tuning Use when fitting a Bayesian DTM regression on compositional microbiome data (e.g. genus-level OTU counts) and you must choose inclusion-prior hyperparameters, MCMC run length/burn-in, and association-selection cutoffs before comparing variable-selection counts across methods. The data are not compositional counts with (or without) a tree structure to which a DTM model applies — e.g. they are already a feature table of normalized abundances rather than OTU counts. A deterministic penalized fit (e.g. sparse grouped-lasso DTM with lambda selected by AIC) is sufficient and MCMC sampling overhead is unnecessary. Convergence cannot be assessed because covariate correlation structure or model sparsity prevents the sampler from mixing within the feasible iteration budget. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Configure and tune the MCMC sampler of the MicroBVS Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression with Bayesian variable selection, including the Beta-Binomial inclusion prior (a=1, b=1), iteration count (150,000 with 75,000 burn-in), and downstream Bayesian FDR/MPPI thresholds, so that posterior inclusion probabilities and association counts are stable and comparable. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03640-0
skills.summary: Configure and tune the MCMC sampler of the MicroBVS Dirichlet-tree multinomial (DTM) regression with Bayesian variable selection, including the Beta-Binomial inclusion prior (a=1, b=1), iteration count (150,000 with 75,000 burn-in), and downstream Bayesian FDR/MPPI thresholds, so that posterior inclusion probabilities and association counts are stable and comparable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not compositional counts with (or without) a tree structure to which a DTM model applies — e.g. they are already a feature table of normalized abundances rather than OTU counts. A deterministic penalized fit (e.g. sparse grouped-lasso DTM with lambda selected by AIC) is sufficient and MCMC sampling overhead is unnecessary. Convergence cannot be assessed because covariate correlation structure or model sparsity prevents the sampler from mixing within the feasible iteration budget.

skills.description: Use when posterior samples of covariate-taxon or mediation-effect inclusion are needed from compositional count data via MicroBVS MCMC (DMbvs_R, MCMC_Med) before applying selected_DM or Selection_Med1/Med2.
skills.name: mcmc-posterior-inference
skills.search_text: mcmc-posterior-inference Use when posterior samples of covariate-taxon or mediation-effect inclusion are needed from compositional count data via MicroBVS MCMC (DMbvs_R, MCMC_Med) before applying selected_DM or Selection_Med1/Med2. Input is non-compositional (e.g. raw feature tables without a compositional/DM or DTM structure) or lacks covariates whose association with taxa/mediation is the target You need per-covariate frequentist testing rather than Bayesian posterior inclusion probabilities — this skill is specific to MicroBVS's MCMC + MPPI framework Data has a known phylogenetic tree structure and you need graph-based inclusion priors with branch-level inference (232 dietary factor-branch associations case study), which goes beyond the plain MCMC posterior-inference workflow here Run MCMC posterior sampling for Bayesian variable selection on compositional microbiome data using MicroBVS — Dirichlet-multinomial (DMbvs_R) and Dirichlet-tree multinomial (MCMC_Med) samplers whose posterior samples feed MPPI-based selection at a 0.5 threshold. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03640-0
skills.summary: Run MCMC posterior sampling for Bayesian variable selection on compositional microbiome data using MicroBVS — Dirichlet-multinomial (DMbvs_R) and Dirichlet-tree multinomial (MCMC_Med) samplers whose posterior samples feed MPPI-based selection at a 0.5 threshold.

skills.description: Use when you have per-iteration error rates (e.g. proportion of taxa with p < 0.05 under 1000 artificial case/control splits) and need a compact median (IQR) summary table per method and taxonomic level (phylum l2, family l5).
skills.name: median-iqr-summary-tabulation
skills.search_text: median-iqr-summary-tabulation Use when you have per-iteration error rates (e.g. proportion of taxa with p < 0.05 under 1000 artificial case/control splits) and need a compact median (IQR) summary table per method and taxonomic level (phylum l2, family l5). skills.when_to_use_negative: You need per-taxa differential abundance effect estimates or FDR-adjusted p-values, not a global type I error summary (use taxcomtab.show / metatab.show instead).
