skills.search_text: microbial-phenotype-prediction-from-genome Use when you have bacterial nucleotide FASTA assemblies or predicted genes (e.g. population genomes such as unClos_1/unFirm_1) and need phenotype calls for 67 traits to verify or complement a metabolic reconstruction. The task requires integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, or other omics data — Traitar only takes presence/absence of protein families into account You need trait prediction for features outside the 67 supported phenotypes (e.g. the plant biomass predictor prototype is not included in the release) You require confident phenotype absence calls from highly incomplete genomes, since absence may simply reflect missing protein families in the input http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Predict up to 67 bacterial phenotypes (present/absent) directly from genome sequences using Traitar, which trains phenotype classifiers on Pfam protein family profiles. Useful for phenotyping draft/incomplete genomes (e.g. metagenome-assembled genomes) and cross-checking manual metabolic reconstructions. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00101-16
skills.summary: Predict up to 67 bacterial phenotypes (present/absent) directly from genome sequences using Traitar, which trains phenotype classifiers on Pfam protein family profiles. Useful for phenotyping draft/incomplete genomes (e.g. metagenome-assembled genomes) and cross-checking manual metabolic reconstructions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires integrating transcriptomic, proteomic, or other omics data — Traitar only takes presence/absence of protein families into account You need trait prediction for features outside the 67 supported phenotypes (e.g. the plant biomass predictor prototype is not included in the release) You require confident phenotype absence calls from highly incomplete genomes, since absence may simply reflect missing protein families in the input

skills.description: Use when sentences from natural-language microbial taxonomic descriptions must be assigned to phenotypic characters (e.g., Gram stain, motility, NaCl optimum) prior to rule-based character-state extraction, or when reproducing MicroPIE's reported SVM cross-validation metrics.
skills.name: microbial-phenotypic-character-prediction
skills.search_text: microbial-phenotypic-character-prediction Use when sentences from natural-language microbial taxonomic descriptions must be assigned to phenotypic characters (e.g., Gram stain, motility, NaCl optimum) prior to rule-based character-state extraction, or when reproducing MicroPIE's reported SVM cross-validation metrics. The input text is not natural-language taxonomic description sentences but already structured data (e.g., a filled taxon-by-character matrix) — no character prediction is needed. A domain-independent extraction setting without labelled training sentences is required; the paper shows OIE/DeepDive alternatives were inadequate, and MicroPIE's SVM requires the labelled 17,147-instance corpus and domain Term Lists. The target characters are outside MicroPIE's scope (0.1.0 supports 42 characters; characters like antibiotic production or biofilm formation require version 0.2.0). http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Train and apply 42 per-character LibSVM sentence classifiers (the MicroPIE Character Predictor) to assign sentences from prokaryotic taxonomic descriptions to one of 42 microbial phenotypic characters before rule-based character-state extraction. The SVM component filters out sentences unlikely to describe a character, which notably improves extraction precision. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1396-8
skills.summary: Train and apply 42 per-character LibSVM sentence classifiers (the MicroPIE Character Predictor) to assign sentences from prokaryotic taxonomic descriptions to one of 42 microbial phenotypic characters before rule-based character-state extraction. The SVM component filters out sentences unlikely to describe a character, which notably improves extraction precision.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input text is not natural-language taxonomic description sentences but already structured data (e.g., a filled taxon-by-character matrix) — no character prediction is needed. A domain-independent extraction setting without labelled training sentences is required; the paper shows OIE/DeepDive alternatives were inadequate, and MicroPIE's SVM requires the labelled 17,147-instance corpus and domain Term Lists. The target characters are outside MicroPIE's scope (0.1.0 supports 42 characters; characters like antibiotic production or biofilm formation require version 0.2.0).

skills.description: Use when host genotype (SNP/SNV matrix) and 16S rRNA microbial abundance data are available and the goal is to find taxa-SNP associations and flag LD SNV blocks via rho estimation.
skills.name: microbial-qtl-association-analysis
skills.search_text: microbial-qtl-association-analysis Use when host genotype (SNP/SNV matrix) and 16S rRNA microbial abundance data are available and the goal is to find taxa-SNP associations and flag LD SNV blocks via rho estimation. The analysis goal is linear-regression mbQTL estimation via the core MatrixEQTL model (Approach A) rather than correlation/LD-aware rho estimation Taxa are presence/absence (categorical) and the aim is logistic regression of one SNP against one taxa Input is raw 16S reads rather than a normalized abundance table or metagenomeSeq object http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Estimate rho correlations between SNPs/SNVs and microbial taxa with mbQTL's Approach B, which first estimates taxa-taxa R values and then adjusts taxa-SNP associations by them, jointly enabling identification of taxa-SNP associations and linkage disequilibrium (LD) SNP regions. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad565
skills.summary: Estimate rho correlations between SNPs/SNVs and microbial taxa with mbQTL's Approach B, which first estimates taxa-taxa R values and then adjusts taxa-SNP associations by them, jointly enabling identification of taxa-SNP associations and linkage disequilibrium (LD) SNP regions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is linear-regression mbQTL estimation via the core MatrixEQTL model (Approach A) rather than correlation/LD-aware rho estimation Taxa are presence/absence (categorical) and the aim is logistic regression of one SNP against one taxa Input is raw 16S reads rather than a normalized abundance table or metagenomeSeq object

skills.description: Use when benchmarking host-depletion tools for precision on non-human reads: you need to measure microbial read retention (reads_out/reads_in) from DWGSIM/PBSIM2-simulated Illumina and ONT reads against Hostile, HRRT, or masked Hostile indexes.
skills.name: microbial-read-retention-quantification
skills.search_text: microbial-read-retention-quantification Use when benchmarking host-depletion tools for precision on non-human reads: you need to measure microbial read retention (reads_out/reads_in) from DWGSIM/PBSIM2-simulated Illumina and ONT reads against Hostile, HRRT, or masked Hostile indexes. The goal is measuring human read depletion (host removal sensitivity) rather than microbial read retention/precision The input reads are real clinical metagenomic samples rather than simulated reads with known ground truth, since retention percentages require reads_in/reads_out accounting on known microbial content The sample is dominated by viral reads and only the bacterial-masked index (human-t2t-hla-argos985) is used — the virus/phage-masked index is required when retention of viral sequences is a priority http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Quantifies what fraction of simulated microbial reads survive host-read decontamination with Hostile versus the NCBI Human Read Removal Tool (HRRT), on Illumina and ONT data, and evaluates masked indexes (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140) for improving retention. Grounded in the Hostile paper's guarantee of ≥99.989% retention of simulated bacterial reads. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Quantifies what fraction of simulated microbial reads survive host-read decontamination with Hostile versus the NCBI Human Read Removal Tool (HRRT), on Illumina and ONT data, and evaluates masked indexes (e.g. human-t2t-hla-argos985-mycob140) for improving retention. Grounded in the Hostile paper's guarantee of ≥99.989% retention of simulated bacterial reads.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is measuring human read depletion (host removal sensitivity) rather than microbial read retention/precision The input reads are real clinical metagenomic samples rather than simulated reads with known ground truth, since retention percentages require reads_in/reads_out accounting on known microbial content The sample is dominated by viral reads and only the bacterial-masked index (human-t2t-hla-argos985) is used — the virus/phage-masked index is required when retention of viral sequences is a priority

skills.description: Use when host-filtered paired-end FASTQ files from RNA-seq data must be assigned taxonomically to detect microbial (bacterial, archaeal, viral) content, e.g. in metagenomic analysis of SSc skin RNA-seq samples like SRR5074528.
skills.name: microbial-sequence-characterization
skills.search_text: microbial-sequence-characterization Use when host-filtered paired-end FASTQ files from RNA-seq data must be assigned taxonomically to detect microbial (bacterial, archaeal, viral) content, e.g. in metagenomic analysis of SSc skin RNA-seq samples like SRR5074528. When raw RNA-seq reads have not yet been host-filtered — the classification stage expects exogenous reads only; run the filtering/classification step (run.FilterClassify) pipeline instead of kraken2 alone on unfiltered input When the goal is differential gene expression or host transcriptome analysis rather than microbial taxonomic characterization When the sample content is expected to include non-bacterial/archaeal/viral taxa (e.g. fungal or parasitic genomes), since the K2DB database used here is constructed only from bacterial, archaeal, and viral genomes http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Taxonomically characterize exogenous (non-host) RNA-seq reads remaining after host filtering by running kraken2 against a database built from bacterial, archaeal, and viral genomes within the nf-rnaSeqMetagen Nextflow pipeline, producing per-read classification files and per-sample taxon reports. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.medmic.2020.100011
skills.summary: Taxonomically characterize exogenous (non-host) RNA-seq reads remaining after host filtering by running kraken2 against a database built from bacterial, archaeal, and viral genomes within the nf-rnaSeqMetagen Nextflow pipeline, producing per-read classification files and per-sample taxon reports.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When raw RNA-seq reads have not yet been host-filtered — the classification stage expects exogenous reads only; run the filtering/classification step (run.FilterClassify) pipeline instead of kraken2 alone on unfiltered input When the goal is differential gene expression or host transcriptome analysis rather than microbial taxonomic characterization When the sample content is expected to include non-bacterial/archaeal/viral taxa (e.g. fungal or parasitic genomes), since the K2DB database used here is constructed only from bacterial, archaeal, and viral genomes

skills.description: Use when comparing fecal source tracking tools on shotgun metagenomes with ground-truth source compositions (e.g., spike-in mesocosms), or when deciding which FST tool and tuning parameters to adopt.
skills.name: microbial-source-tracking-benchmarking
skills.search_text: microbial-source-tracking-benchmarking Use when comparing fecal source tracking tools on shotgun metagenomes with ground-truth source compositions (e.g., spike-in mesocosms), or when deciding which FST tool and tuning parameters to adopt. Input data are 16S amplicon reads or otherwise not short-read shotgun metagenomes in FASTQ format, since SourceApp and this benchmark are built on shotgun data The goal is taxonomic profiling, strain-level outbreak tracking, or dating contamination rather than fecal source attribution/apportionment — SourceApp cannot infer contamination age or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations Expected sources include categories with poorly represented reference genomes (e.g., cow feces), where apportionment estimates are known to be unreliable (cows were underestimated and showed false negatives) http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 A benchmarking skill for comparing metagenomic fecal source tracking and apportionment tools (SourceApp, FEAST, metaSourceTracker, decOM) on spike-in mesocosm metagenomes with known ground-truth cell fractions, using sensitivity/specificity and correlation with true source proportions as the metrics. metagenomics/v1 10.1021/acs.est.5c03603
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for comparing metagenomic fecal source tracking and apportionment tools (SourceApp, FEAST, metaSourceTracker, decOM) on spike-in mesocosm metagenomes with known ground-truth cell fractions, using sensitivity/specificity and correlation with true source proportions as the metrics.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data are 16S amplicon reads or otherwise not short-read shotgun metagenomes in FASTQ format, since SourceApp and this benchmark are built on shotgun data The goal is taxonomic profiling, strain-level outbreak tracking, or dating contamination rather than fecal source attribution/apportionment — SourceApp cannot infer contamination age or identify nonconservative (growth-capable) populations Expected sources include categories with poorly represented reference genomes (e.g., cow feces), where apportionment estimates are known to be unreliable (cows were underestimated and showed false negatives)

skills.description: Use when you have a microbial abundance table (OTU or species table) plus sample disease/status labels and need to train and benchmark a phylogeny-aware deep-learning classifier for microbiome status or disease detection.
skills.name: microbiome-abundance-table-model-evaluation
skills.search_text: microbiome-abundance-table-model-evaluation Use when you have a microbial abundance table (OTU or species table) plus sample disease/status labels and need to train and benchmark a phylogeny-aware deep-learning classifier for microbiome status or disease detection. Input is not a microbial feature table (OTU or species table) in the README's expected format — the README states the input 'should exclusively adhere to the microbial feature table structure' You need a purely supervised tabular classifier without phylogenetic ordering — PM-CNN requires a NEWICK phylogenetic tree or clustered feature order derived from cophenetic distances Only raw sequences are available with no abundance table or status metadata — build the abundance table and labels first before invoking this skill http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Train PM-CNN, a phylogeny-ordered four-path convolutional neural network with ensemble fusion, on a microbial abundance table (OTU or species table) with sample status metadata, and evaluate per-category classification performance with Kappa, Recall, Accuracy, Precision, and F1. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae013
skills.summary: Train PM-CNN, a phylogeny-ordered four-path convolutional neural network with ensemble fusion, on a microbial abundance table (OTU or species table) with sample status metadata, and evaluate per-category classification performance with Kappa, Recall, Accuracy, Precision, and F1.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a microbial feature table (OTU or species table) in the README's expected format — the README states the input 'should exclusively adhere to the microbial feature table structure' You need a purely supervised tabular classifier without phylogenetic ordering — PM-CNN requires a NEWICK phylogenetic tree or clustered feature order derived from cophenetic distances Only raw sequences are available with no abundance table or status metadata — build the abundance table and labels first before invoking this skill

skills.description: Use when you have effect estimates and standard errors per study and marker (≥10 studies), want a global conclusion on 'α-diversity' across multiple related markers, and have no prior marker-by-marker correlation estimates.
skills.name: microbiome-alpha-diversity-marker-combination
skills.search_text: microbiome-alpha-diversity-marker-combination Use when you have effect estimates and standard errors per study and marker (≥10 studies), want a global conclusion on 'α-diversity' across multiple related markers, and have no prior marker-by-marker correlation estimates. You have fewer than 10 studies (the README requires the number of studies ≥ 10 for est and std.err) You need pooled effect estimation per marker only and already have a priori marker-by-marker correlation results — a standard multivariate meta-analysis approach applies instead Raw 16S rRNA read data or OTU tables are all you have — mMeta/aMeta require already-computed effect estimates and standard errors per study and marker (hard to obtain in practice when studies report only graphs or stratified summaries) http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Combine multiple microbiome studies across multiple related α-diversity markers (e.g., Richness, Shannon, Simpson, PD, PE, PQE) using only summary statistics (effect estimates and standard errors) with no a priori marker-by-marker correlations, via the mMeta and aMeta methods implemented in the R package mMeta. metagenomics/v1 10.1002/sim.8940
skills.summary: Combine multiple microbiome studies across multiple related α-diversity markers (e.g., Richness, Shannon, Simpson, PD, PE, PQE) using only summary statistics (effect estimates and standard errors) with no a priori marker-by-marker correlations, via the mMeta and aMeta methods implemented in the R package mMeta.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You have fewer than 10 studies (the README requires the number of studies ≥ 10 for est and std.err) You need pooled effect estimation per marker only and already have a priori marker-by-marker correlation results — a standard multivariate meta-analysis approach applies instead Raw 16S rRNA read data or OTU tables are all you have — mMeta/aMeta require already-computed effect estimates and standard errors per study and marker (hard to obtain in practice when studies report only graphs or stratified summaries)

skills.description: Use when a processed microbiome OTU table (e.g., otu.tab.txt or a phyloseq object such as biom.Rdata) must be converted into a Jaccard dissimilarity matrix for beta-diversity analysis or survival association testing in the MiSurv/MiRKAT workflow.
skills.name: microbiome-beta-diversity-jaccard-computation
skills.search_text: microbiome-beta-diversity-jaccard-computation Use when a processed microbiome OTU table (e.g., otu.tab.txt or a phyloseq object such as biom.Rdata) must be converted into a Jaccard dissimilarity matrix for beta-diversity analysis or survival association testing in the MiSurv/MiRKAT workflow. When a phylogenetically informed beta-diversity metric (e.g., weighted/unweighted UniFrac) is required — Jaccard uses only presence/absence, not the 'tree.tre' phylogeny or abundances When the input is raw sequence data rather than a processed OTU/feature table — run the QIIME 2.0 processing (97% open-reference picking against Greengenes, chimera removal) first http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Computes pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity (presence/absence-based beta-diversity) from a processed OTU/feature table using the phyloseq 'distance' function with method='jaccard', producing the distance matrix that MiSurv Module 3 (MiRKAT-S) consumes for microbiome–survival association testing. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Computes pairwise Jaccard dissimilarity (presence/absence-based beta-diversity) from a processed OTU/feature table using the phyloseq 'distance' function with method='jaccard', producing the distance matrix that MiSurv Module 3 (MiRKAT-S) consumes for microbiome–survival association testing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a phylogenetically informed beta-diversity metric (e.g., weighted/unweighted UniFrac) is required — Jaccard uses only presence/absence, not the 'tree.tre' phylogeny or abundances When the input is raw sequence data rather than a processed OTU/feature table — run the QIIME 2.0 processing (97% open-reference picking against Greengenes, chimera removal) first

skills.description: Use when you have paired-end WGS or simulated long-read metagenome samples with known body-site labels and need to compare how k-mer-based tools cluster them by origin.
skills.name: microbiome-body-site-clustering
skills.search_text: microbiome-body-site-clustering Use when you have paired-end WGS or simulated long-read metagenome samples with known body-site labels and need to compare how k-mer-based tools cluster them by origin. Your goal is single-pair sample comparison rather than all-vs-all clustering across many samples — Libra/Mash/Simka matrices are designed for all-vs-all comparison Samples lack known body-site or origin labels, so clustering outcomes cannot be validated against expected groupings You need strain- or variant-level resolution rather than metagenome-level community composition/abundance comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Clusters human microbiome samples by body site using all-vs-all k-mer distance matrices from Mash, Libra, and Simka, then compares how each tool's metric (MinHash distance, Libra's log-weighted cosine similarity, Simka's Jaccard-ab and Bray-Curtis) resolves body-site structure. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Clusters human microbiome samples by body site using all-vs-all k-mer distance matrices from Mash, Libra, and Simka, then compares how each tool's metric (MinHash distance, Libra's log-weighted cosine similarity, Simka's Jaccard-ab and Bray-Curtis) resolves body-site structure.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is single-pair sample comparison rather than all-vs-all clustering across many samples — Libra/Mash/Simka matrices are designed for all-vs-all comparison Samples lack known body-site or origin labels, so clustering outcomes cannot be validated against expected groupings You need strain- or variant-level resolution rather than metagenome-level community composition/abundance comparison

skills.description: Use when a merged MetaPhlAn or QIIME OTU/BIOM taxonomy table needs rescaling across samples before GLM, Random Forest, or SVM model building, or when comparing how normalization choices affect classifier accuracy.
skills.name: microbiome-count-normalization-css-tmm-quantile
skills.search_text: microbiome-count-normalization-css-tmm-quantile Use when a merged MetaPhlAn or QIIME OTU/BIOM taxonomy table needs rescaling across samples before GLM, Random Forest, or SVM model building, or when comparing how normalization choices affect classifier accuracy. Input is not a merged OTU/BIOM taxonomy table from MetaPhlAn or QIIME (e.g. raw sequencing reads or metadata files). The data have already been normalized upstream and re-scaling would distort the counts before model building. The goal is differential-abundance testing rather than preparing a feature matrix for machine learning classification. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Normalize aggregated metagenomic count tables in MegaR using one of four scaling choices — Cumulative Sum Scaling (CSS), Quantile, Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM), or NO normalization — after taxonomic-level extraction and low-abundance filtering, to prepare comparable feature matrices for machine learning models. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03933-4
skills.summary: Normalize aggregated metagenomic count tables in MegaR using one of four scaling choices — Cumulative Sum Scaling (CSS), Quantile, Trimmed Mean of M-values (TMM), or NO normalization — after taxonomic-level extraction and low-abundance filtering, to prepare comparable feature matrices for machine learning models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is not a merged OTU/BIOM taxonomy table from MetaPhlAn or QIIME (e.g. raw sequencing reads or metadata files). The data have already been normalized upstream and re-scaling would distort the counts before model building. The goal is differential-abundance testing rather than preparing a feature matrix for machine learning classification.

skills.search_text: microbiome-count-normalization-undersampling-correction Use when calling differentially abundant features (OTUs, species, or other taxa) across two or more sample groups from sparse, undersampled microbial count matrices where library-size normalization biases dominate. skills.summary: Applies metagenomeSeq's novel normalization technique and zero-inflated under-sampling statistical model to identify differentially abundant OTUs/taxa in sparse high-throughput marker-gene survey data, where standard RNA-seq tools (DESeq, edgeR) and Metastats/LEfSe underperform.

skills.description: Use when a binary or continuous grouping factor and a microbiome feature table are available and you need to test differential abundance while quantifying robustness of individual features and the overall microbiome-group association.
skills.name: microbiome-differential-abundance-testing
skills.search_text: microbiome-differential-abundance-testing Use when a binary or continuous grouping factor and a microbiome feature table are available and you need to test differential abundance while quantifying robustness of individual features and the overall microbiome-group association. The goal requires formal inference, FDR control, or adjusted p-values — the article states the method 'does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values' and AOI/AUMC are descriptive only The task is unsupervised ordination or community-structure comparison (NMDS/PCoA/PERMANOVA) rather than per-feature differential testing with robustness assessment top_pm exceeds the number of microbial features — the README notes top_pm must be less than the number of features http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A progressive permutation workflow (ProgPerm/ProgPermute) for testing microbiome differential abundance that assesses the robustness of discoveries by permuting grouping factor labels across mixing scenarios and comparing observed p-values against fully permuted (noise) p-values. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: A progressive permutation workflow (ProgPerm/ProgPermute) for testing microbiome differential abundance that assesses the robustness of discoveries by permuting grouping factor labels across mixing scenarios and comparing observed p-values against fully permuted (noise) p-values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal requires formal inference, FDR control, or adjusted p-values — the article states the method 'does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values' and AOI/AUMC are descriptive only The task is unsupervised ordination or community-structure comparison (NMDS/PCoA/PERMANOVA) rather than per-feature differential testing with robustness assessment top_pm exceeds the number of microbial features — the README notes top_pm must be less than the number of features
