skills.description: Use when you have a cophenetic distance matrix from a phylogenetic tree (e.g., from the R ape package) of OTU features and need to reorder/group them phylogenetically before training a CNN-based microbiome classifier.
skills.name: microbiome-feature-ordering-for-cnn-input
skills.search_text: microbiome-feature-ordering-for-cnn-input Use when you have a cophenetic distance matrix from a phylogenetic tree (e.g., from the R ape package) of OTU features and need to reorder/group them phylogenetically before training a CNN-based microbiome classifier. No phylogenetic tree or cophenetic distance matrix exists for the features (e.g., feature table lacks OTU representative sequences or a NEWICK tree was not built/provided) The feature table is already ordered by a prior clustering run and only model training is needed (proceed directly to PMCNN.py --train) http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Transforms a cophenetic distance matrix into a Gaussian-kernel-normalized correlation matrix, then performs hierarchical clustering with silhouette-based layer selection to produce phylogeny-sorted cluster feature orderings (large/medium/small layers at 1/20, 1/100, 1/500 features per cluster) for PM-CNN input. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae013
skills.summary: Transforms a cophenetic distance matrix into a Gaussian-kernel-normalized correlation matrix, then performs hierarchical clustering with silhouette-based layer selection to produce phylogeny-sorted cluster feature orderings (large/medium/small layers at 1/20, 1/100, 1/500 features per cluster) for PM-CNN input.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No phylogenetic tree or cophenetic distance matrix exists for the features (e.g., feature table lacks OTU representative sequences or a NEWICK tree was not built/provided) The feature table is already ordered by a prior clustering run and only model training is needed (proceed directly to PMCNN.py --train)

skills.description: Use when binary-grouped microbiome count data has yielded significant differential features and you need to rank how robust each discovery is to progressive permutation of grouping labels.
skills.name: microbiome-feature-robustness-ranking
skills.search_text: microbiome-feature-robustness-ranking Use when binary-grouped microbiome count data has yielded significant differential features and you need to rank how robust each discovery is to progressive permutation of grouping labels. You need formal statistical inference, FDR control, or adjusted p-values — the paper states the method does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values The grouping factor is continuous or multi-class rather than binary — bin_permute_all and bin_fragility operate on a binary outcome variable Input has no initially significant features to assess — bin_fragility requires lowindx of initially significant features from bin_true_initial http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Computes a fragility index for each discovered microbiome feature via progressive permutation: the minimum number of label-exchange permutation steps needed to render a significant feature nonsignificant, then ranks discoveries by robustness using the ProgPermute R package. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Computes a fragility index for each discovered microbiome feature via progressive permutation: the minimum number of label-exchange permutation steps needed to render a significant feature nonsignificant, then ranks discoveries by robustness using the ProgPermute R package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need formal statistical inference, FDR control, or adjusted p-values — the paper states the method does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values The grouping factor is continuous or multi-class rather than binary — bin_permute_all and bin_fragility operate on a binary outcome variable Input has no initially significant features to assess — bin_fragility requires lowindx of initially significant features from bin_true_initial

skills.description: Use when a high-dimensional OTU/taxa count matrix (e.g. 856 OTUs x 60 samples) and an adjusted response vector must be reduced to a non-empty subset S of taxa likely associated with the outcome, prior to a data-adaptive multivariate association test under a generalized linear model.
skills.name: microbiome-feature-screening
skills.search_text: microbiome-feature-screening Use when a high-dimensional OTU/taxa count matrix (e.g. 856 OTUs x 60 samples) and an adjusted response vector must be reduced to a non-empty subset S of taxa likely associated with the outcome, prior to a data-adaptive multivariate association test under a generalized linear model. The taxa set is already small and pre-specified — the paper restricts association analysis to taxa-sets containing at least five taxa, where screening adds no value The response has not been covariate-adjusted; screening is defined on the adjusted response, and an unadjusted outcome would confound the distance correlations The goal is per-taxon (univariate) testing rather than multivariate clade/community association analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_0610 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 A distance-correlation-based, data-adaptive feature screening stage (Algorithm 1 of AMAT) that shrinks noise taxa to exactly zero before multivariate microbiome association testing, selecting a data-driven testing subset S of outcome-associated taxa from an OTU matrix and adjusted response. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab120
skills.summary: A distance-correlation-based, data-adaptive feature screening stage (Algorithm 1 of AMAT) that shrinks noise taxa to exactly zero before multivariate microbiome association testing, selecting a data-driven testing subset S of outcome-associated taxa from an OTU matrix and adjusted response.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The taxa set is already small and pre-specified — the paper restricts association analysis to taxa-sets containing at least five taxa, where screening adds no value The response has not been covariate-adjusted; screening is defined on the adjusted response, and an unadjusted outcome would confound the distance correlations The goal is per-taxon (univariate) testing rather than multivariate clade/community association analysis

skills.description: Use when a set of differentially abundant microbiome features from a binary-group comparison must be ranked by robustness, by counting how many progressive label-permutation steps flip each feature to nonsignificance.
skills.name: microbiome-fragility-index-computation
skills.search_text: microbiome-fragility-index-computation Use when a set of differentially abundant microbiome features from a binary-group comparison must be ranked by robustness, by counting how many progressive label-permutation steps flip each feature to nonsignificance. The method does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values — do not use fragility indices as a substitute for FDR-corrected significance testing Do not apply when the grouping factor is not a binary variable, since bin_permute_all/bin_true_initial/bin_fragility assume a binary outcome (e.g. 'variable') AOI/AUMC and fragility measures are descriptive, not inferential — do not cite them as formal statistical inference of association http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Computes the ProgPermute fragility index — the minimum number of progressive permutation steps k at which a discovered microbiome feature's median Wilcoxon p-value crosses the 0.05 significance cutoff — to rank discovered taxa from most to least robust against label mixing. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Computes the ProgPermute fragility index — the minimum number of progressive permutation steps k at which a discovered microbiome feature's median Wilcoxon p-value crosses the 0.05 significance cutoff — to rank discovered taxa from most to least robust against label mixing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The method does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values — do not use fragility indices as a substitute for FDR-corrected significance testing Do not apply when the grouping factor is not a binary variable, since bin_permute_all/bin_true_initial/bin_fragility assume a binary outcome (e.g. 'variable') AOI/AUMC and fragility measures are descriptive, not inferential — do not cite them as formal statistical inference of association

skills.description: Use when input is PICRUSt2 predicted functional output (e.g., KO abundance tables and sample metadata) and the goal is differential pathway abundance, pathway annotation, or GSEA between comparison groups.
skills.name: microbiome-functional-data-interpretation
skills.search_text: microbiome-functional-data-interpretation Use when input is PICRUSt2 predicted functional output (e.g., KO abundance tables and sample metadata) and the goal is differential pathway abundance, pathway annotation, or GSEA between comparison groups. Input is already pathway-level or a non-PICRUSt2 feature table requiring no KO-to-KEGG conversion or functional prediction interpretation Single-feature differential testing is preferred and pathway-set (GSEA) framing is not appropriate for the question No comparison-group design exists (no metadata grouping or contrasts), so differential abundance or enrichment testing is not applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Interprets PICRUSt2-predicted functional profiles from 16S rRNA sequencing data using the ggpicrust2 R package, covering KO-to-KEGG pathway conversion, differential abundance analysis, pathway annotation, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad470
skills.summary: Interprets PICRUSt2-predicted functional profiles from 16S rRNA sequencing data using the ggpicrust2 R package, covering KO-to-KEGG pathway conversion, differential abundance analysis, pathway annotation, and gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already pathway-level or a non-PICRUSt2 feature table requiring no KO-to-KEGG conversion or functional prediction interpretation Single-feature differential testing is preferred and pathway-set (GSEA) framing is not appropriate for the question No comparison-group design exists (no metadata grouping or contrasts), so differential abundance or enrichment testing is not applicable

skills.description: Use when you have a DA results table from pathway_daa() applied to PICRUSt2 KEGG pathway abundances and need a publication-quality figure showing which pathways differ between groups and by how much.
skills.name: microbiome-functional-profile-visualization
skills.search_text: microbiome-functional-profile-visualization Use when you have a DA results table from pathway_daa() applied to PICRUSt2 KEGG pathway abundances and need a publication-quality figure showing which pathways differ between groups and by how much. When the goal is single-feature pathway significance testing rather than visualization of existing DA results — use pathway_daa() first When pathway-set-level enrichment (GSEA) is more appropriate than per-pathway error-bar plots of DA results — use pathway_gsea()/visualize_gsea() instead When the input is still raw KO-level abundance that has not been converted to pathway-level abundance (use ko2kegg_abundance() first) http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Visualize differential abundance (DA) results for PICRUSt2-predicted functional profiles using ggpicrust2's ggplot2-based plotting functions, chiefly pathway_errorbar(), which renders group mean relative abundances with error bars annotated with log2 fold change and P-values for differential KEGG pathways. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad470
skills.summary: Visualize differential abundance (DA) results for PICRUSt2-predicted functional profiles using ggpicrust2's ggplot2-based plotting functions, chiefly pathway_errorbar(), which renders group mean relative abundances with error bars annotated with log2 fold change and P-values for differential KEGG pathways.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is single-feature pathway significance testing rather than visualization of existing DA results — use pathway_daa() first When pathway-set-level enrichment (GSEA) is more appropriate than per-pathway error-bar plots of DA results — use pathway_gsea()/visualize_gsea() instead When the input is still raw KO-level abundance that has not been converted to pathway-level abundance (use ko2kegg_abundance() first)

skills.description: Use when you have a SNP genotype matrix and a microbial taxa abundance matrix over the same sample cohort and need to identify significant taxa-SNP (mbQTL) relationships, including all-to-all R² estimates or a single specified rsID.
skills.name: microbiome-genotype-association-analysis
skills.search_text: microbiome-genotype-association-analysis Use when you have a SNP genotype matrix and a microbial taxa abundance matrix over the same sample cohort and need to identify significant taxa-SNP (mbQTL) relationships, including all-to-all R² estimates or a single specified rsID. Your taxa are presence/absence (categorical) and you need the one-SNP-one-taxa logistic regression workflow instead of the linear-regression allToAllProduct correlation Your microbiome data is not yet in taxa-by-sample data frame format (e.g. raw phyloseq/metagenomeSeq objects) and must first be normalized or converted with metagenomeSeqToMbqtl / phyloseq_to_metagenomeSeq() http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 http://edamontology.org/topic_3305 Estimate SNP–taxa associations (mbQTLs) with the mbQTL R/Bioconductor package, which computes R²/rho correlation values between host SNP genotypes and microbial taxa abundances using allToAllProduct and the core MatrixEQTL linear regression model. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad565
skills.summary: Estimate SNP–taxa associations (mbQTLs) with the mbQTL R/Bioconductor package, which computes R²/rho correlation values between host SNP genotypes and microbial taxa abundances using allToAllProduct and the core MatrixEQTL linear regression model.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your taxa are presence/absence (categorical) and you need the one-SNP-one-taxa logistic regression workflow instead of the linear-regression allToAllProduct correlation Your microbiome data is not yet in taxa-by-sample data frame format (e.g. raw phyloseq/metagenomeSeq objects) and must first be normalized or converted with metagenomeSeqToMbqtl / phyloseq_to_metagenomeSeq()

skills.description: Use when you have a PICRUSt2-predicted pathway-level abundance table (KO converted to KEGG pathway abundance) plus sample metadata with a grouping variable, and you must test which pathways differ significantly between groups.
skills.name: microbiome-group-comparison-design
skills.search_text: microbiome-group-comparison-design Use when you have a PICRUSt2-predicted pathway-level abundance table (KO converted to KEGG pathway abundance) plus sample metadata with a grouping variable, and you must test which pathways differ significantly between groups. Input is raw 16S rRNA reads not yet processed by PICRUSt2 — functional prediction must come first. The goal is pathway-set-level enrichment rather than single-feature differential abundance — use the GSEA workflow (pathway_gsea()) instead. The goal is to compare agreement between DA methods on the same dataset rather than test group differences — use compare_daa_results()/compare_metagenome_results() instead. Designs group-comparison differential abundance analysis of PICRUSt2-predicted pathway profiles (e.g., KEGG pathways from 16S rRNA-derived metagenomes) using ggpicrust2's pathway_daa(), which integrates advanced DA methods such as LinDA and ALDEx2 so that significant pathways between comparison groups can be identified and compared for robustness. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad470
skills.summary: Designs group-comparison differential abundance analysis of PICRUSt2-predicted pathway profiles (e.g., KEGG pathways from 16S rRNA-derived metagenomes) using ggpicrust2's pathway_daa(), which integrates advanced DA methods such as LinDA and ALDEx2 so that significant pathways between comparison groups can be identified and compared for robustness.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw 16S rRNA reads not yet processed by PICRUSt2 — functional prediction must come first. The goal is pathway-set-level enrichment rather than single-feature differential abundance — use the GSEA workflow (pathway_gsea()) instead. The goal is to compare agreement between DA methods on the same dataset rather than test group differences — use compare_daa_results()/compare_metagenome_results() instead.

skills.description: Use when a microbiome OTU/feature count table has a binary grouping factor and you need to characterize overall association strength and the robustness of significant features across progressive label permutations.
skills.name: microbiome-group-difference-analysis
skills.search_text: microbiome-group-difference-analysis Use when a microbiome OTU/feature count table has a binary grouping factor and you need to characterize overall association strength and the robustness of significant features across progressive label permutations. The goal is formal inference: the method is 'mainly designed for the general exploration and visualization of microbiome data, and does not come with a formal inference method' and does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values. The grouping factor is not a binary variable — bin_permute_all is documented for a binary outcome ('"variable" denotes the name of binary outcome'). top_pm is not smaller than the number of microbial features (README: '"top_pm" must be less than the number of microbial features'). http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Applies progressive permutation of a binary grouping factor in the ProgPermute R package: sample labels are progressively mixed between groups, differential abundance tests (default Wilcoxon rank sum, alpha=0.05) are rerun at each scenario, and the number of significant features is plotted against the proportion of mixing to yield a U-curve that conveys the strength of the overall microbiome–grouping association. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Applies progressive permutation of a binary grouping factor in the ProgPermute R package: sample labels are progressively mixed between groups, differential abundance tests (default Wilcoxon rank sum, alpha=0.05) are rerun at each scenario, and the number of significant features is plotted against the proportion of mixing to yield a U-curve that conveys the strength of the overall microbiome–grouping association.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is formal inference: the method is 'mainly designed for the general exploration and visualization of microbiome data, and does not come with a formal inference method' and does not control the false discovery rate or calculate adjusted p-values. The grouping factor is not a binary variable — bin_permute_all is documented for a binary outcome ('"variable" denotes the name of binary outcome'). top_pm is not smaller than the number of microbial features (README: '"top_pm" must be less than the number of microbial features').

skills.description: Use when the input is a sparse high-throughput microbiome OTU/taxa count matrix with two or more sample groups and the goal is to identify features that are differentially abundant across populations.
skills.name: microbiome-marker-gene-survey-analysis
skills.search_text: microbiome-marker-gene-survey-analysis Use when the input is a sparse high-throughput microbiome OTU/taxa count matrix with two or more sample groups and the goal is to identify features that are differentially abundant across populations. The data are not sparse marker-gene count data — metagenomeSeq is designed for sparse high-throughput sequencing from marker-gene surveys, not for continuous or non-count measurements. The analysis goal is not differential abundance between two or more groups of samples (e.g., unsupervised ordination or clustering without group labels). A dense, well-sampled count matrix with no under-sampling concern is already available — other DA tools may suffice since metagenomeSeq's advantage comes from addressing normalization and undersampling. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Differential abundance analysis of OTU/taxa count matrices from microbial marker-gene surveys using metagenomeSeq, which combines a novel normalization technique with a statistical model (zero-inflated Gaussian fit by expectation-maximization) that accounts for under-sampling of microbial communities. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nmeth.2658
skills.summary: Differential abundance analysis of OTU/taxa count matrices from microbial marker-gene surveys using metagenomeSeq, which combines a novel normalization technique with a statistical model (zero-inflated Gaussian fit by expectation-maximization) that accounts for under-sampling of microbial communities.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are not sparse marker-gene count data — metagenomeSeq is designed for sparse high-throughput sequencing from marker-gene surveys, not for continuous or non-count measurements. The analysis goal is not differential abundance between two or more groups of samples (e.g., unsupervised ordination or clustering without group labels). A dense, well-sampled count matrix with no under-sampling concern is already available — other DA tools may suffice since metagenomeSeq's advantage comes from addressing normalization and undersampling.

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample inStrain profile objects (or equivalent strain calls) plus per-infant metadata (sibling/twin relationships, birth day, birth weight, gestational age) and need to test whether strain sharing correlates with these host properties.
skills.name: microbiome-metadata-association-analysis
skills.search_text: microbiome-metadata-association-analysis Use when you have per-sample inStrain profile objects (or equivalent strain calls) plus per-infant metadata (sibling/twin relationships, birth day, birth weight, gestational age) and need to test whether strain sharing correlates with these host properties. You only need species-level abundance association (e.g. differential abundance of taxa vs metadata) rather than sub-species strain-sharing inference — inStrain popANI/strain clustering is unnecessary. Your samples lack paired metadata such as kinship (siblings/MZ vs DZ), birth day, birth weight, or gestational age, so the Fisher's exact and rank-sum tests cannot be framed. Strains are called from reference genomes at species-level ANI thresholds rather than 99.999% ANI strain clusters, making the two-infant strain-sharing design inapplicable. http://edamontology.org/topic_0610 http://edamontology.org/topic_0203 Tests whether strain-level microbial sharing among NICU infants (detected with inStrain popANI comparisons and 99.999% ANI strain clustering) is associated with host metadata — sibling relationship, twin zygosity (MZ vs DZ), birth-day distance, birth weight, and gestational age — using SciPy statistical tests and Figure 3-style visualizations. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Tests whether strain-level microbial sharing among NICU infants (detected with inStrain popANI comparisons and 99.999% ANI strain clustering) is associated with host metadata — sibling relationship, twin zygosity (MZ vs DZ), birth-day distance, birth weight, and gestational age — using SciPy statistical tests and Figure 3-style visualizations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need species-level abundance association (e.g. differential abundance of taxa vs metadata) rather than sub-species strain-sharing inference — inStrain popANI/strain clustering is unnecessary. Your samples lack paired metadata such as kinship (siblings/MZ vs DZ), birth day, birth weight, or gestational age, so the Fisher's exact and rank-sum tests cannot be framed. Strains are called from reference genomes at species-level ANI thresholds rather than 99.999% ANI strain clusters, making the two-infant strain-sharing design inapplicable.

skills.description: Use when comparing whether two sequence variant callers yield comparable microbiome-biological-variable association performance, or when building supervised classification models from a variant count table (e.g., SvTable.txt) merged with sample metadata.
skills.name: microbiome-metadata-association-modeling
skills.search_text: microbiome-metadata-association-modeling Use when comparing whether two sequence variant callers yield comparable microbiome-biological-variable association performance, or when building supervised classification models from a variant count table (e.g., SvTable.txt) merged with sample metadata. The goal is detecting true low-abundance variants: HashSeq is not sensitive for low-abundance sequences and DADA2 is recommended there (association-parity modeling does not solve sensitivity limits). Input is raw FASTQ rather than a variant count table — variant calling (e.g., inferTrueSequences) must be run first before metadata association modeling. Studying indel variation relative to a parent sequence — HashSeq does not model indels; Deblur or alignment-based methods are suggested instead. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Train random forest classifiers (100 trees, scikit-learn) on 16S rRNA sequence variant count tables (e.g., from HashSeq and DADA2) merged with sample metadata, evaluating association performance via RepeatedKFold cross-validation (4 splits x 10 repeats). Used in the HashSeq paper to show HashSeq variants behave almost identically to DADA2 in supervised classification of gut microbiota data. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Train random forest classifiers (100 trees, scikit-learn) on 16S rRNA sequence variant count tables (e.g., from HashSeq and DADA2) merged with sample metadata, evaluating association performance via RepeatedKFold cross-validation (4 splits x 10 repeats). Used in the HashSeq paper to show HashSeq variants behave almost identically to DADA2 in supervised classification of gut microbiota data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is detecting true low-abundance variants: HashSeq is not sensitive for low-abundance sequences and DADA2 is recommended there (association-parity modeling does not solve sensitivity limits). Input is raw FASTQ rather than a variant count table — variant calling (e.g., inferTrueSequences) must be run first before metadata association modeling. Studying indel variation relative to a parent sequence — HashSeq does not model indels; Deblur or alignment-based methods are suggested instead.

skills.description: Use when a merged MetaPhlAn or QIIME OTU/BIOM profile table must be paired with a tab-separated metadata file whose class column (e.g. column 7, T1D_Diagnosed with t/f labels) and sample ID column (e.g. column 2, Gid_shotgun) must be identified before MegaR model building.
skills.name: microbiome-metadata-matching
skills.search_text: microbiome-metadata-matching Use when a merged MetaPhlAn or QIIME OTU/BIOM profile table must be paired with a tab-separated metadata file whose class column (e.g. column 7, T1D_Diagnosed with t/f labels) and sample ID column (e.g. column 2, Gid_shotgun) must be identified before MegaR model building. Input is already a merged feature table with class labels embedded — re-matching metadata would be redundant Only exploratory visualization of abundance profiles is needed without phenotype prediction, since no metadata linkage is required Sample IDs between the profile table and metadata cannot be reconciled (formatting or renaming differences) — matching must be fixed upstream first http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Prepares and aligns tab-separated phenotype metadata (class labels and sample IDs) with MetaPhlAn2/QIIME taxonomic profile tables in MegaR so that every sample in the profile table has a matching phenotype class for machine learning model training and benchmarking. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03933-4
skills.summary: Prepares and aligns tab-separated phenotype metadata (class labels and sample IDs) with MetaPhlAn2/QIIME taxonomic profile tables in MegaR so that every sample in the profile table has a matching phenotype class for machine learning model training and benchmarking.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a merged feature table with class labels embedded — re-matching metadata would be redundant Only exploratory visualization of abundance profiles is needed without phenotype prediction, since no metadata linkage is required Sample IDs between the profile table and metadata cannot be reconciled (formatting or renaming differences) — matching must be fixed upstream first

skills.description: Use when benchmarking differential-abundance methods for zero-inflated microbiome relative abundance data, e.g. to quantify empirical power of GAMLSS-BEZI vs. transformed linear models across effect sizes.
skills.name: microbiome-method-comparison-benchmarking
skills.search_text: microbiome-method-comparison-benchmarking Use when benchmarking differential-abundance methods for zero-inflated microbiome relative abundance data, e.g. to quantify empirical power of GAMLSS-BEZI vs. transformed linear models across effect sizes. Input is a real taxon relative-abundance table for a substantive comparison rather than simulated BEZI data — use the standard taxa.compare / meta.taxa analysis workflow instead The target method addresses zero inflation through a non-beta model (e.g. zero-inflated Gaussian or compositional methods like ALDEx2/ANCOM) not implemented in metamicrobiomeR — this benchmark harness only covers GAMLSS-BEZI vs. LMAS The goal is meta-analysis pooling across studies (meta.taxa) rather than within-study differential-abundance power comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Simulation-based benchmarking skill that compares statistical power of GAMLSS-BEZI (via the metamicrobiomeR R package) against transformation-based linear modeling (MaAsLin-style arcsin square root, LMAS) for detecting differential relative abundances, replicating the paper's Fig 1b power curves across effect sizes. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: Simulation-based benchmarking skill that compares statistical power of GAMLSS-BEZI (via the metamicrobiomeR R package) against transformation-based linear modeling (MaAsLin-style arcsin square root, LMAS) for detecting differential relative abundances, replicating the paper's Fig 1b power curves across effect sizes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a real taxon relative-abundance table for a substantive comparison rather than simulated BEZI data — use the standard taxa.compare / meta.taxa analysis workflow instead The target method addresses zero inflation through a non-beta model (e.g. zero-inflated Gaussian or compositional methods like ALDEx2/ANCOM) not implemented in metamicrobiomeR — this benchmark harness only covers GAMLSS-BEZI vs. LMAS The goal is meta-analysis pooling across studies (meta.taxa) rather than within-study differential-abundance power comparison

skills.description: Use when the input is a raw OTU abundance count matrix (e.g. 16S V1-V2 OTUs from QIIME) that must be compositional-normalized and OTU-wise standardized before feature screening or multivariate association testing in the AMAT framework.
skills.name: microbiome-otu-compositional-normalization
skills.search_text: microbiome-otu-compositional-normalization Use when the input is a raw OTU abundance count matrix (e.g. 16S V1-V2 OTUs from QIIME) that must be compositional-normalized and OTU-wise standardized before feature screening or multivariate association testing in the AMAT framework. Input is already a compositional or standardized feature matrix (e.g. previously relabeled relative abundances on the same scale) — re-normalization would distort the intended scale Downstream analysis is not multivariate association testing in the AMAT/aSPU framework and requires untransformed counts (e.g. some differential-abundance or phylogenetic kernel methods that operate on counts or other transforms) http://edamontology.org/topic_0610 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Prepares a raw OTU count table for AMAT-style multivariate association testing by converting counts to compositional (relative-abundance) form and then standardizing each OTU column to produce the transformed matrix Z* used downstream for feature screening and the aSPU/AMAT test. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab120
skills.summary: Prepares a raw OTU count table for AMAT-style multivariate association testing by converting counts to compositional (relative-abundance) form and then standardizing each OTU column to produce the transformed matrix Z* used downstream for feature screening and the aSPU/AMAT test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a compositional or standardized feature matrix (e.g. previously relabeled relative abundances on the same scale) — re-normalization would distort the intended scale Downstream analysis is not multivariate association testing in the AMAT/aSPU framework and requires untransformed counts (e.g. some differential-abundance or phylogenetic kernel methods that operate on counts or other transforms)

skills.description: Use when you must benchmark type I error calibration or statistical power of a microbiome multivariate association test against synthetic OTU count data generated to mimic a real community.
skills.name: microbiome-otu-data-simulation
skills.search_text: microbiome-otu-data-simulation Use when you must benchmark type I error calibration or statistical power of a microbiome multivariate association test against synthetic OTU count data generated to mimic a real community. The goal is testing association on the real OTU data itself (run AMAT with 10,000 permutations on the actual table instead of simulating). The input is a real, already-filtered OTU table needing only QC and taxonomic classification (this skill generates synthetic data, not downstream annotations). http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A simulation workflow that generates synthetic OTU count tables mimicking a real microbiome (e.g., the 856-OTU throat community) via multinomial/Dirichlet-multinomial sampling, then evaluates empirical type I error (null, beta = 0) and power of microbiome association tests such as AMAT under continuous (linear) and binary (logistic) outcome models. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab120
skills.summary: A simulation workflow that generates synthetic OTU count tables mimicking a real microbiome (e.g., the 856-OTU throat community) via multinomial/Dirichlet-multinomial sampling, then evaluates empirical type I error (null, beta = 0) and power of microbiome association tests such as AMAT under continuous (linear) and binary (logistic) outcome models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is testing association on the real OTU data itself (run AMAT with 10,000 permutations on the actual table instead of simulating). The input is a real, already-filtered OTU table needing only QC and taxonomic classification (this skill generates synthetic data, not downstream annotations).

skills.description: Use when you have feature/OTU tables from multiple denoising or clustering methods (e.g. vsearch open/closed-reference, de novo, DADA2, Deblur) and need to assess how similarly they resolve community composition using phylogeny-aware beta-diversity metrics.
skills.name: microbiome-phylogeny-aware-abundance-profiling
skills.search_text: microbiome-phylogeny-aware-abundance-profiling Use when you have feature/OTU tables from multiple denoising or clustering methods (e.g. vsearch open/closed-reference, de novo, DADA2, Deblur) and need to assess how similarly they resolve community composition using phylogeny-aware beta-diversity metrics. You only have a single OTU/feature table from one method and no comparison across DC methods — UniFrac cross-method comparison requires the same samples processed by multiple methods Your sequences lack a phylogeny (e.g. non-16S amplicons without reference-tree placement) — weighted/unweighted UniFrac requires phylogenetic relationships between observations The goal is network inference (correlation/direct association steps like sparcc or spieceasi) rather than comparing abundance profiles themselves http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0194 Converts OTU tables produced by alternative denoising/clustering (DC) methods into sample-by-observation abundance profiles that retain phylogenetic information, then quantifies similarity between methods using weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances, as done in the MiCoNE pipeline evaluation on the FMT (Qiita study 10532) 16S data. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00961-22
skills.summary: Converts OTU tables produced by alternative denoising/clustering (DC) methods into sample-by-observation abundance profiles that retain phylogenetic information, then quantifies similarity between methods using weighted and unweighted UniFrac distances, as done in the MiCoNE pipeline evaluation on the FMT (Qiita study 10532) 16S data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have a single OTU/feature table from one method and no comparison across DC methods — UniFrac cross-method comparison requires the same samples processed by multiple methods Your sequences lack a phylogeny (e.g. non-16S amplicons without reference-tree placement) — weighted/unweighted UniFrac requires phylogenetic relationships between observations The goal is network inference (correlation/direct association steps like sparcc or spieceasi) rather than comparing abundance profiles themselves

skills.description: Use when a progressive permutation run (bin_permute_all output on a binary grouping outcome) needs interpretation via U-curves and p-value traces to assess overall microbiome association strength.
skills.name: microbiome-pvalue-trace-interpretation
skills.search_text: microbiome-pvalue-trace-interpretation Use when a progressive permutation run (bin_permute_all output on a binary grouping outcome) needs interpretation via U-curves and p-value traces to assess overall microbiome association strength. The grouping outcome is continuous or multi-class rather than binary — the bin_* functions of ProgPermute expect a binary outcome ('variable' denotes the name of binary outcome) The user needs formal inference or FDR-adjusted p-values — the paper states the method 'does not come with a formal inference method' and does not control the false discovery rate The question is an omnibus group-comparison test (e.g. PERMANOVA/PCoA ordination) rather than interpretation of progressive-permutation robustness curves http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Interprets ProgPermute progressive-permutation outputs by reading the U-curve of the number of significant features versus proportion of mixing and the per-feature p-value traces to judge the strength of the microbiome–grouping-factor association and the robustness of individual hits. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04061-3
skills.summary: Interprets ProgPermute progressive-permutation outputs by reading the U-curve of the number of significant features versus proportion of mixing and the per-feature p-value traces to judge the strength of the microbiome–grouping-factor association and the robustness of individual hits.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The grouping outcome is continuous or multi-class rather than binary — the bin_* functions of ProgPermute expect a binary outcome ('variable' denotes the name of binary outcome) The user needs formal inference or FDR-adjusted p-values — the paper states the method 'does not come with a formal inference method' and does not control the false discovery rate The question is an omnibus group-comparison test (e.g. PERMANOVA/PCoA ordination) rather than interpretation of progressive-permutation robustness curves

skills.description: Use when a taxa-by-sample 16S abundance table (plus an optional SNP/covariate file) must be prepared for mbQTL rho estimation, and taxa–taxa R values need to be estimated as inputs to taxa–SNP association analysis.
skills.name: microbiome-qtl-preprocessing
skills.search_text: microbiome-qtl-preprocessing Use when a taxa-by-sample 16S abundance table (plus an optional SNP/covariate file) must be prepared for mbQTL rho estimation, and taxa–taxa R values need to be estimated as inputs to taxa–SNP association analysis. The analysis goal is mbQTL's Approach A linear regression (MatrixEQTL model) or the logistic regression for presence/absence (categorical) taxa, which do not require the coringTaxa taxa–taxa R matrix as preprocessing. The input is already a taxa–taxa correlation matrix or a pre-estimated R² goodness-of-fit table, in which case you can proceed directly to rho estimation/taxaSnpCor. The data are not 16S rRNA abundance plus SNP/SNV data — mbQTL is designed for integrating 16S rRNA sequencing with SNV/SNP data. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Preprocess microbiome and genotype inputs for mbQTL mbQTL estimation: load the taxa-by-sample abundance data (microbeAbund) and compute the taxa–taxa correlation matrix (R values) and R² goodness-of-fit measures with coringTaxa, which are required before the Approach B rho estimation of taxa–SNP correlations. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad565
skills.summary: Preprocess microbiome and genotype inputs for mbQTL mbQTL estimation: load the taxa-by-sample abundance data (microbeAbund) and compute the taxa–taxa correlation matrix (R values) and R² goodness-of-fit measures with coringTaxa, which are required before the Approach B rho estimation of taxa–SNP correlations.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is mbQTL's Approach A linear regression (MatrixEQTL model) or the logistic regression for presence/absence (categorical) taxa, which do not require the coringTaxa taxa–taxa R matrix as preprocessing. The input is already a taxa–taxa correlation matrix or a pre-estimated R² goodness-of-fit table, in which case you can proceed directly to rho estimation/taxaSnpCor. The data are not 16S rRNA abundance plus SNP/SNV data — mbQTL is designed for integrating 16S rRNA sequencing with SNV/SNP data.

skills.description: Use when raw OTU count tables and taxonomy tables (e.g., otu.tab.txt / tax.tab.txt from phyloseq) must be quality-controlled before survival-microbiome analysis and you need MiSurv's default filtering criteria reproduced.
skills.name: microbiome-quality-control-filtering
skills.search_text: microbiome-quality-control-filtering Use when raw OTU count tables and taxonomy tables (e.g., otu.tab.txt / tax.tab.txt from phyloseq) must be quality-controlled before survival-microbiome analysis and you need MiSurv's default filtering criteria reproduced. Input is already a post-QC feature table — the deposited post-QC data (biom.Rdata / otu.tab.txt / tax.tab.txt) already reflect these filters Input is raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) — this skill operates on OTU count and taxonomy tables, not on read-level QC such as the >75% length / <3 consecutive low-quality-base (Phred <20) trimming done upstream in QIIME 2.0 The analysis target is continuous or binary responses — use MiCloud rather than MiSurv's survival-oriented processing module http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Reproduces MiSurv's default microbiome quality control pipeline — kingdom annotation, library-size, mean-proportion, and taxonomic-name filters — which, applied to the example Zhang et al. T1D gut microbiome dataset, retains 294 features across 172 subjects. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Reproduces MiSurv's default microbiome quality control pipeline — kingdom annotation, library-size, mean-proportion, and taxonomic-name filters — which, applied to the example Zhang et al. T1D gut microbiome dataset, retains 294 features across 172 subjects.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a post-QC feature table — the deposited post-QC data (biom.Rdata / otu.tab.txt / tax.tab.txt) already reflect these filters Input is raw sequencing reads (FASTQ) — this skill operates on OTU count and taxonomy tables, not on read-level QC such as the >75% length / <3 consecutive low-quality-base (Phred <20) trimming done upstream in QIIME 2.0 The analysis target is continuous or binary responses — use MiCloud rather than MiSurv's survival-oriented processing module

skills.description: Use when evaluating the false positive control of a differential abundance test on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data — e.g. simulating null data with mu1=mu2=0.5, alpha1=alpha2=0.5, phi=5 to reproduce Table 1 type I error rates at alpha=0.01/0.05/0.1.
skills.name: microbiome-relabundance-null-data-generation
skills.search_text: microbiome-relabundance-null-data-generation Use when evaluating the false positive control of a differential abundance test on zero-inflated beta relative abundance data — e.g. simulating null data with mu1=mu2=0.5, alpha1=alpha2=0.5, phi=5 to reproduce Table 1 type I error rates at alpha=0.01/0.05/0.1. The goal is estimating statistical power or differential abundance effects — this skill simulates strictly under the null (mu1=mu2), so rejections are false positives, not true discoveries The data are real observed microbiome relative abundances rather than simulated BEZI data — use the package's taxa.compare/meta.taxa analysis workflow instead The abundance distribution of interest is not zero-inflated beta (e.g. count data) — BEZI simulation parameters would not be applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Generates simulated microbiome relative abundance data drawn from a zero-inflated beta (BEZI) distribution under the null hypothesis (no between-group difference) so that empirical type I error rates of GAMLSS-BEZI tests can be estimated via Monte Carlo replication. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: Generates simulated microbiome relative abundance data drawn from a zero-inflated beta (BEZI) distribution under the null hypothesis (no between-group difference) so that empirical type I error rates of GAMLSS-BEZI tests can be estimated via Monte Carlo replication.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is estimating statistical power or differential abundance effects — this skill simulates strictly under the null (mu1=mu2), so rejections are false positives, not true discoveries The data are real observed microbiome relative abundances rather than simulated BEZI data — use the package's taxa.compare/meta.taxa analysis workflow instead The abundance distribution of interest is not zero-inflated beta (e.g. count data) — BEZI simulation parameters would not be applicable

skills.description: Use when testing differential relative abundance of microbial taxa (phylum to genus, e.g. levels l2/l4/l5/l6) between groups in compositional, zero-inflated 16S microbiome data, especially longitudinal designs with covariate adjustment.
skills.name: microbiome-relative-abundance-modeling
skills.search_text: microbiome-relative-abundance-modeling Use when testing differential relative abundance of microbial taxa (phylum to genus, e.g. levels l2/l4/l5/l6) between groups in compositional, zero-inflated 16S microbiome data, especially longitudinal designs with covariate adjustment. Data are not relative abundances (e.g. already a feature/count table without compositional normalization) — the BEZI family models zero-inflated beta relative abundance data specifically The goal is alpha diversity comparison — use alpha.compare with standardized diversity indexes and linear/linear mixed models instead Input is metagenomic functional profiles or non-taxon omics data — the workflow targets bacterial taxon relative abundance tables from 16S-style pipelines (e.g. QIIME L6 taxonomy tables) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Model microbiome taxon relative abundances with GAMLSS using a zero-inflated beta (BEZI) family via metamicrobiomeR's taxa.compare, directly addressing the zero-inflated beta distribution of relative abundance data where linear/linear mixed models and arcsin-square-root transformations (e.g., MaAsLin/LMAS) fail. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: Model microbiome taxon relative abundances with GAMLSS using a zero-inflated beta (BEZI) family via metamicrobiomeR's taxa.compare, directly addressing the zero-inflated beta distribution of relative abundance data where linear/linear mixed models and arcsin-square-root transformations (e.g., MaAsLin/LMAS) fail.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data are not relative abundances (e.g. already a feature/count table without compositional normalization) — the BEZI family models zero-inflated beta relative abundance data specifically The goal is alpha diversity comparison — use alpha.compare with standardized diversity indexes and linear/linear mixed models instead Input is metagenomic functional profiles or non-taxon omics data — the workflow targets bacterial taxon relative abundance tables from 16S-style pipelines (e.g. QIIME L6 taxonomy tables)

skills.description: Use when a microbiome survival analysis needs clinical/design variables (survival time, event indicator, treatment group, covariates) pulled from a sample-data table such as MiSurv's sam.dat.txt or the phyloseq object biom.Rdata.
skills.name: microbiome-sample-metadata-extraction
skills.search_text: microbiome-sample-metadata-extraction Use when a microbiome survival analysis needs clinical/design variables (survival time, event indicator, treatment group, covariates) pulled from a sample-data table such as MiSurv's sam.dat.txt or the phyloseq object biom.Rdata. The goal is microbial composition or diversity analysis (MiSurv Modules 2–4), which additionally requires otu.tab.txt, tax.tab.txt, and tree.tre rather than metadata alone. The input is raw 16S reads or a QIIME 2.0 feature table that still requires the data-processing module (quality control, rarefaction via rarefy_even_depth) before metadata extraction is meaningful. The metadata lacks survival columns (survival time and censoring indicator), so no Surv() object can be constructed for comparative survival analysis. http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Extracts the survival-relevant columns (T1Dweek, T1D, Antibiotics, Sex) from the MiSurv sample metadata file (sam.dat.txt) of the Zhang et al. T1D NOD-mouse study (QIITA 10508) so they can feed a covariate-adjusted Cox model in R's survival package. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/spectrum.05059-22
skills.summary: Extracts the survival-relevant columns (T1Dweek, T1D, Antibiotics, Sex) from the MiSurv sample metadata file (sam.dat.txt) of the Zhang et al. T1D NOD-mouse study (QIITA 10508) so they can feed a covariate-adjusted Cox model in R's survival package.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is microbial composition or diversity analysis (MiSurv Modules 2–4), which additionally requires otu.tab.txt, tax.tab.txt, and tree.tre rather than metadata alone. The input is raw 16S reads or a QIIME 2.0 feature table that still requires the data-processing module (quality control, rarefaction via rarefy_even_depth) before metadata extraction is meaningful. The metadata lacks survival columns (survival time and censoring indicator), so no Surv() object can be constructed for comparative survival analysis.

skills.description: Use when comparing power/type I error of multivariate microbiome association tests on simulated OTU count data with continuous or binary outcomes, e.g. Dirichlet-multinomial scenarios varying signal density.
skills.name: microbiome-simulation-benchmarking
skills.search_text: microbiome-simulation-benchmarking Use when comparing power/type I error of multivariate microbiome association tests on simulated OTU count data with continuous or binary outcomes, e.g. Dirichlet-multinomial scenarios varying signal density. The goal is real-data taxon-level association testing with FWER control via Bonferroni correction, not simulation-based power benchmarking Only one method is of interest — benchmarking requires running all six competing tests on identical scenarios to make power comparisons meaningful The association signal density is extremely sparse, where AMAT is known to lose its power advantage http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Benchmark AMAT against existing multivariate microbiome association tests (aMiSPU, OMiRKAT, OMiAT, LDM, MiHC) using Dirichlet-multinomial OTU simulations mimicking the real throat microbiome, estimating empirical power and type I error at the 0.05 level. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab120
skills.summary: Benchmark AMAT against existing multivariate microbiome association tests (aMiSPU, OMiRKAT, OMiAT, LDM, MiHC) using Dirichlet-multinomial OTU simulations mimicking the real throat microbiome, estimating empirical power and type I error at the 0.05 level.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is real-data taxon-level association testing with FWER control via Bonferroni correction, not simulation-based power benchmarking Only one method is of interest — benchmarking requires running all six competing tests on identical scenarios to make power comparisons meaningful The association signal density is extremely sparse, where AMAT is known to lose its power advantage

skills.description: Use when evaluating or comparing source-tracking algorithms on compositional data with many candidate sources (e.g., M=50 environments, K=10 true contributors) and substantial unknown-source mixing (0–90%), or when validating that a new MST method actually reduces noise from noncontributing sources.
skills.name: microbiome-source-tracking-simulation
skills.search_text: microbiome-source-tracking-simulation Use when evaluating or comparing source-tracking algorithms on compositional data with many candidate sources (e.g., M=50 environments, K=10 true contributors) and substantial unknown-source mixing (0–90%), or when validating that a new MST method actually reduces noise from noncontributing sources. The candidate-source pool is small and fully enumerated with no unknown source — the sparsity/nuisance-source advantage of STENSL is irrelevant and standard FEAST suffices. The goal is running source tracking on real (not simulated) sinks; this skill is a benchmarking protocol, not a production estimation pipeline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0621 Benchmark microbial source tracking methods (STENSL, SourceTracker2, FEAST, RAD) on synthetic sinks built from real Earth Microbiome Project samples, scoring mean-squared error of mixing proportions, false-positive source rate, and unknown-contribution absolute error. Rationale: existing MST methods accumulate error as the pool of candidate sources grows, so controlled simulations with nuisance sources and large unknown fractions are needed to expose that failure mode. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00995-21
skills.summary: Benchmark microbial source tracking methods (STENSL, SourceTracker2, FEAST, RAD) on synthetic sinks built from real Earth Microbiome Project samples, scoring mean-squared error of mixing proportions, false-positive source rate, and unknown-contribution absolute error. Rationale: existing MST methods accumulate error as the pool of candidate sources grows, so controlled simulations with nuisance sources and large unknown fractions are needed to expose that failure mode.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The candidate-source pool is small and fully enumerated with no unknown source — the sparsity/nuisance-source advantage of STENSL is irrelevant and standard FEAST suffices. The goal is running source tracking on real (not simulated) sinks; this skill is a benchmarking protocol, not a production estimation pipeline.

skills.description: Use when longitudinal OTU count tables (taxa x samples with sequence IDs and sample times) have been denoised by LUMINATE 'estimate', and the goal is to infer cLV parameters (A, g, B) and predict future community trajectories under external perturbations.
skills.name: microbiome-time-series-trajectory-prediction
skills.search_text: microbiome-time-series-trajectory-prediction Use when longitudinal OTU count tables (taxa x samples with sequence IDs and sample times) have been denoised by LUMINATE 'estimate', and the goal is to infer cLV parameters (A, g, B) and predict future community trajectories under external perturbations. The data are a single cross-sectional sample with no longitudinal replicates, so no time-series dynamics or one-step-ahead prediction can be learned Raw count data have not been through LUMINATE 'estimate' and the goal is only denoised relative abundance or biological-zero detection rather than cLV parameter inference and trajectory prediction The OTU table contains ultra-sparse taxa (>90% missing entries) that have not been filtered; the authors note such taxa carry too little temporal information for trajectory reconstruction http://edamontology.org/topic_3173 Train a compositional Lotka-Volterra (cLV) model on LUMINATE's denoised relative abundance estimates and use it to predict longitudinal community trajectories one step at a time, producing more accurate trajectory predictions than models trained on raw pseudo-counts. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2020.05.006
skills.summary: Train a compositional Lotka-Volterra (cLV) model on LUMINATE's denoised relative abundance estimates and use it to predict longitudinal community trajectories one step at a time, producing more accurate trajectory predictions than models trained on raw pseudo-counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are a single cross-sectional sample with no longitudinal replicates, so no time-series dynamics or one-step-ahead prediction can be learned Raw count data have not been through LUMINATE 'estimate' and the goal is only denoised relative abundance or biological-zero detection rather than cLV parameter inference and trajectory prediction The OTU table contains ultra-sparse taxa (>90% missing entries) that have not been filtered; the authors note such taxa carry too little temporal information for trajectory reconstruction

skills.description: Use when you have coReads .bam files mapped to representative sub-species .fasta references and need per-genome SNV calling, nucleotide diversity, clonality, and breadth for population-genome comparisons across sample groups.
skills.name: microdiversity-profiling-of-mapped-reads
skills.search_text: microdiversity-profiling-of-mapped-reads Use when you have coReads .bam files mapped to representative sub-species .fasta references and need per-genome SNV calling, nucleotide diversity, clonality, and breadth for population-genome comparisons across sample groups. You only need read coverage/relative abundance without microdiversity — CoverM (coverm genome/contig) is a faster coverage-only alternative Your goal is dereplication of a genome set rather than profiling mapped-read microdiversity — use dRep dereplicate instead Reads are mapped to many highly similar (>98% ANI) references without dereplication, risking multi-mapped reads inflating diversity estimates http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Profile strain-level microdiversity (SNVs, nucleotide diversity, clonality, coverage breadth) from metagenomic read mappings to reference genomes using inStrain, then aggregate scaffold-level metrics to genome level and test group differences (e.g., Klebsiella nucleotide diversity by birth mode). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Profile strain-level microdiversity (SNVs, nucleotide diversity, clonality, coverage breadth) from metagenomic read mappings to reference genomes using inStrain, then aggregate scaffold-level metrics to genome level and test group differences (e.g., Klebsiella nucleotide diversity by birth mode).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need read coverage/relative abundance without microdiversity — CoverM (coverm genome/contig) is a faster coverage-only alternative Your goal is dereplication of a genome set rather than profiling mapped-read microdiversity — use dRep dereplicate instead Reads are mapped to many highly similar (>98% ANI) references without dereplication, risking multi-mapped reads inflating diversity estimates

skills.description: Use when TreeMix has been run across multiple user-defined migration-edge values (optionally with bootstrapping) and you must choose the optimal number of migration edges for the inferred population tree from biallelic SNP data.
skills.name: migration-edge-optimization-optm
skills.search_text: migration-edge-optimization-optm Use when TreeMix has been run across multiple user-defined migration-edge values (optionally with bootstrapping) and you must choose the optimal number of migration edges for the inferred population tree from biallelic SNP data. The analysis goal is genome-wide population structure (PCA/admixture with optimal K) rather than tree-based relationships with migration — use the 'explore genetic structure' sub-workflow instead. The input is unfiltered or multi-allelic variant data — TreeMix input must come from the filtered biallelic SNP set produced upstream in scalepopgen. Only a single TreeMix run at one fixed migration-edge count was performed — OptM needs runs across multiple edge counts to compute Δm. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3299 Summarize replicate TreeMix runs with the OptM package to identify the optimal number of migration edges on a population tree, using the second-order rate of change in likelihood (Δm) across models with different edge counts. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/molbev/msae057
skills.summary: Summarize replicate TreeMix runs with the OptM package to identify the optimal number of migration edges on a population tree, using the second-order rate of change in likelihood (Δm) across models with different edge counts.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The analysis goal is genome-wide population structure (PCA/admixture with optimal K) rather than tree-based relationships with migration — use the 'explore genetic structure' sub-workflow instead. The input is unfiltered or multi-allelic variant data — TreeMix input must come from the filtered biallelic SNP set produced upstream in scalepopgen. Only a single TreeMix run at one fixed migration-edge count was performed — OptM needs runs across multiple edge counts to compute Δm.

skills.search_text: mimag-quality-class-thresholding Use when a set of MAG FASTA files needs completeness/contamination estimation and assignment to revised-MIMAG quality tiers (e.g. retaining genomes with >=50% completeness and <5% contamination). skills.description: Use when training iDeLUCS (or a DeLUCS-style contrastive network) on unlabeled DNA sequences in FASTA format and per-sequence augmented training pairs are needed to stabilize unsupervised clustering.
skills.name: mimic-sequence-data-augmentation
skills.search_text: mimic-sequence-data-augmentation Use when training iDeLUCS (or a DeLUCS-style contrastive network) on unlabeled DNA sequences in FASTA format and per-sequence augmented training pairs are needed to stabilize unsupervised clustering. Input sequences already carry taxonomic labels to be used during training — the mimic pipeline is unsupervised; ground-truth labels (GT_file) are only for post hoc analysis The task requires alignment-based comparison — iDeLUCS clusters via genomic signatures without sequence alignment batch_sz cannot be set to a multiple of n_mimics on the available machine (batch limits may restrict viable mimic counts) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Generates 'mimic' augmented copies of each DNA sequence in a FASTA file so that the iDeLUCS contrastive deep learning network can be trained on original–mimic pairs that share the same genomic k-mer signature. The number of mimics per sequence (n_mimics) directly shapes training pairs, batch composition, and final cluster variance. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad508
skills.summary: Generates 'mimic' augmented copies of each DNA sequence in a FASTA file so that the iDeLUCS contrastive deep learning network can be trained on original–mimic pairs that share the same genomic k-mer signature. The number of mimics per sequence (n_mimics) directly shapes training pairs, batch composition, and final cluster variance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences already carry taxonomic labels to be used during training — the mimic pipeline is unsupervised; ground-truth labels (GT_file) are only for post hoc analysis The task requires alignment-based comparison — iDeLUCS clusters via genomic signatures without sequence alignment batch_sz cannot be set to a multiple of n_mimics on the available machine (batch limits may restrict viable mimic counts)
