skills.search_text: noun-phrase-term-matching Use when extracting phenotypic character values (e.g., cell shape, Gram stain type, NaCl/pH/temperature optima, aerophilicity) from natural-language taxonomic description sentences of prokaryotes without training data for supervised classification. The task requires morphology-focused extraction from semi-structured descriptions better handled by CharaParser, since prokaryotic descriptions contain little morphological data and focus on physiological and ecological traits You need domain-independent open extraction without domain knowledge; OIE was shown inadequate because this task required substantial domain knowledge A trained SVM character model is available and character prediction is desired to improve precision — use MicroPIE's full pipeline rather than pure term matching http://edamontology.org/topic_0218 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A term-matching character extraction mechanism from MicroPIE that segments prokaryotic taxonomic description sentences into noun phrases and matches them against curated per-character Term Lists (models\CharacterValueExtractors0.1.0) to populate a taxon-by-character matrix, using coordinated noun-phrase expansion to compensate for insufficient term-list coverage. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1396-8
skills.summary: A term-matching character extraction mechanism from MicroPIE that segments prokaryotic taxonomic description sentences into noun phrases and matches them against curated per-character Term Lists (models\CharacterValueExtractors0.1.0) to populate a taxon-by-character matrix, using coordinated noun-phrase expansion to compensate for insufficient term-list coverage.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task requires morphology-focused extraction from semi-structured descriptions better handled by CharaParser, since prokaryotic descriptions contain little morphological data and focus on physiological and ecological traits You need domain-independent open extraction without domain knowledge; OIE was shown inadequate because this task required substantial domain knowledge A trained SVM character model is available and character prediction is desired to improve precision — use MicroPIE's full pipeline rather than pure term matching

skills.description: Use when building an absent-species false-positive benchmark: you have a genome set (e.g. PRJNA348753 human gut MAGs) and need to pick genomes whose closest RefSeq/training relative fails novelty cutoffs (AQ<60%, ANI<95%).
skills.name: novel-species-genome-selection-by-ani-aq-thresholds
skills.search_text: novel-species-genome-selection-by-ani-aq-thresholds Use when building an absent-species false-positive benchmark: you have a genome set (e.g. PRJNA348753 human gut MAGs) and need to pick genomes whose closest RefSeq/training relative fails novelty cutoffs (AQ<60%, ANI<95%). Your goal is to benchmark precision/recall on species that ARE present in reference databases — this filter deliberately excludes any genome with a close relative (ANI>=95% or AQ>=60%) You need all genomes regardless of novelty; this skill discards genomes whose species are already represented in RefSeq or training data http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Identifies genomes whose species are absent from all reference databases by screening each candidate genome's closest database relative with Mash/dnadiff and keeping only those with alignment query coverage (AQ) below 60% and ANI below 95%, yielding a truly novel-species benchmark set (121 genomes in the DeepMicrobes study). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa009
skills.summary: Identifies genomes whose species are absent from all reference databases by screening each candidate genome's closest database relative with Mash/dnadiff and keeping only those with alignment query coverage (AQ) below 60% and ANI below 95%, yielding a truly novel-species benchmark set (121 genomes in the DeepMicrobes study).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is to benchmark precision/recall on species that ARE present in reference databases — this filter deliberately excludes any genome with a close relative (ANI>=95% or AQ>=60%) You need all genomes regardless of novelty; this skill discards genomes whose species are already represented in RefSeq or training data

skills.description: Use when predicting metagenomes from 16S rRNA OTU tables with PICRUSt and you must quantify per-sample prediction reliability from reference-genome coverage, especially for host-associated or environmental communities with sparse reference genomes.
skills.name: nsti-accuracy-assessment
skills.search_text: nsti-accuracy-assessment Use when predicting metagenomes from 16S rRNA OTU tables with PICRUSt and you must quantify per-sample prediction reliability from reference-genome coverage, especially for host-associated or environmental communities with sparse reference genomes. Input is already shotgun WGS metagenome data (annotated with HUMAnN) — functional potential can be measured directly rather than predicted and its uncertainty estimated via NSTI The community is dominated by viral or eukaryotic members — PICRUSt only includes bacterial and archaeal 16S marker gene sequences and does not infer viral or eukaryotic metagenome components Strain-level functional resolution is required — PICRUSt cannot distinguish variation at the strain level if the marker gene sequence is identical among strains, so NSTI does not capture within-species functional divergence http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Quantify the expected accuracy of PICRUSt 16S-to-metagenome predictions by computing a per-sample weighted Nearest Sequenced Taxon Index (NSTI), which reflects the phylogenetic proximity of community members to reference genomes in IMG/Greengenes. It is the article's recommended gate for judging whether predicted functional shifts (e.g. secretion-system genes correlated with coral mucus algal cover) are trustworthy. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nbt.2676
skills.summary: Quantify the expected accuracy of PICRUSt 16S-to-metagenome predictions by computing a per-sample weighted Nearest Sequenced Taxon Index (NSTI), which reflects the phylogenetic proximity of community members to reference genomes in IMG/Greengenes. It is the article's recommended gate for judging whether predicted functional shifts (e.g. secretion-system genes correlated with coral mucus algal cover) are trustworthy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already shotgun WGS metagenome data (annotated with HUMAnN) — functional potential can be measured directly rather than predicted and its uncertainty estimated via NSTI The community is dominated by viral or eukaryotic members — PICRUSt only includes bacterial and archaeal 16S marker gene sequences and does not infer viral or eukaryotic metagenome components Strain-level functional resolution is required — PICRUSt cannot distinguish variation at the strain level if the marker gene sequence is identical among strains, so NSTI does not capture within-species functional divergence

skills.description: Use when predicting metagenomes from 16S data with PICRUSt and you need a per-sample confidence metric, or when testing whether prediction accuracy decays with phylogenetic distance to reference genomes.
skills.name: nsti-phylogenetic-distance-calculation
skills.search_text: nsti-phylogenetic-distance-calculation Use when predicting metagenomes from 16S data with PICRUSt and you need a per-sample confidence metric, or when testing whether prediction accuracy decays with phylogenetic distance to reference genomes. Input is shotgun metagenome data rather than 16S marker gene sequences — NSTI/PICRUSt confidence scoring presumes marker-gene-only samples needing predicted metagenomes The community includes viral or eukaryotic components — only bacterial and archaeal 16S marker gene sequences are included, so NSTI will not characterize those fractions Samples' marker gene sequences are identical among strains — the metric cannot resolve strain-level variation, so NSTI-based confidence will not capture intra-strain functional differences http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Computes the Nearest Sequenced Taxon Index (NSTI): the abundance-weighted phylogenetic distance, on the 16S marker gene tree, between each community OTU and its nearest sequenced reference genome, summed to one NSTI value per sample. This quantifies the expected PICRUSt metagenome-prediction accuracy for that sample. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nbt.2676
skills.summary: Computes the Nearest Sequenced Taxon Index (NSTI): the abundance-weighted phylogenetic distance, on the 16S marker gene tree, between each community OTU and its nearest sequenced reference genome, summed to one NSTI value per sample. This quantifies the expected PICRUSt metagenome-prediction accuracy for that sample.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is shotgun metagenome data rather than 16S marker gene sequences — NSTI/PICRUSt confidence scoring presumes marker-gene-only samples needing predicted metagenomes The community includes viral or eukaryotic components — only bacterial and archaeal 16S marker gene sequences are included, so NSTI will not characterize those fractions Samples' marker gene sequences are identical among strains — the metric cannot resolve strain-level variation, so NSTI-based confidence will not capture intra-strain functional differences

skills.description: Use when you need to compute nucleotide composition features (tetranucleotide/k-mer frequencies, GC, CpG, GC skew, codon usage) for viral scaffolds and build a length-7 pairwise scaffold-by-scaffold distance table for downstream binning or machine learning.
skills.name: nucleotide-composition-feature-extraction
skills.search_text: nucleotide-composition-feature-extraction Use when you need to compute nucleotide composition features (tetranucleotide/k-mer frequencies, GC, CpG, GC skew, codon usage) for viral scaffolds and build a length-7 pairwise scaffold-by-scaffold distance table for downstream binning or machine learning. Input is an entire (unfiltered) metagenome rather than predicted viral scaffolds — vRhyme is built to run on viral sequences and 'is not meant to bin microbes' You need sequence-similarity-based distances (e.g. Mash/Nucmer dereplication) rather than composition-feature distances Scaffolds are shorter than the 2000bp minimum length cutoff and would be filtered out anyway http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reconstructs vRhyme's per-scaffold nucleotide feature extraction and pairwise distance module, computing seven composition features (k-mer/tetranucleotide frequencies, GC content, CpG content, GC skew, codon usage from Prodigal ORFs) and comparing scaffold pairs via cosine distances for frequency vectors and absolute differences for scalars, written to vRhyme_machine_distances.tsv as input to the supervised machine learning models. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac341
skills.summary: Reconstructs vRhyme's per-scaffold nucleotide feature extraction and pairwise distance module, computing seven composition features (k-mer/tetranucleotide frequencies, GC content, CpG content, GC skew, codon usage from Prodigal ORFs) and comparing scaffold pairs via cosine distances for frequency vectors and absolute differences for scalars, written to vRhyme_machine_distances.tsv as input to the supervised machine learning models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an entire (unfiltered) metagenome rather than predicted viral scaffolds — vRhyme is built to run on viral sequences and 'is not meant to bin microbes' You need sequence-similarity-based distances (e.g. Mash/Nucmer dereplication) rather than composition-feature distances Scaffolds are shorter than the 2000bp minimum length cutoff and would be filtered out anyway

skills.description: Use when you have coReads .bam files mapped to representative sub-species reference genomes and need to compare per-genome nucleotide diversity (microdiversity) across metadata groups such as birth mode.
skills.name: nucleotide-diversity-birth-mode-comparison
skills.search_text: nucleotide-diversity-birth-mode-comparison Use when you have coReads .bam files mapped to representative sub-species reference genomes and need to compare per-genome nucleotide diversity (microdiversity) across metadata groups such as birth mode. Reads are not yet mapped to sub-species reference genomes — no .bam input exists for inStrain profile A sub-species falls below the >= 0.5 unmaskedBreadth detection threshold or is flagged 'likely contaminant' (negative control or campaign-enriched), so its diversity estimate is not trustworthy The question is strain sharing between samples rather than within-sample microdiversity — use inStrain compare (ConANI/popANI) instead http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Profiles SNV-based nucleotide diversity of sub-species populations (e.g., Klebsiella) from metagenomic read mappings with inStrain, then tests whether microdiversity differs by metadata group — here, birth mode (cesarean vs. vaginal) in premature infants. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-020-00797-0
skills.summary: Profiles SNV-based nucleotide diversity of sub-species populations (e.g., Klebsiella) from metagenomic read mappings with inStrain, then tests whether microdiversity differs by metadata group — here, birth mode (cesarean vs. vaginal) in premature infants.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are not yet mapped to sub-species reference genomes — no .bam input exists for inStrain profile A sub-species falls below the >= 0.5 unmaskedBreadth detection threshold or is flagged 'likely contaminant' (negative control or campaign-enriched), so its diversity estimate is not trustworthy The question is strain sharing between samples rather than within-sample microdiversity — use inStrain compare (ConANI/popANI) instead

skills.description: Use when you have a cellsnp-lite VCF pile-up (e.g., cellSNP.cells_ARG.vcf.gz) plus MetaQuad BIC_params.csv and need per-gene, per-sample nucleotide diversity to detect polymorphism shifts such as ARG diversity changes after antibiotic treatment.
skills.name: nucleotide-diversity-calculation
skills.search_text: nucleotide-diversity-calculation Use when you have a cellsnp-lite VCF pile-up (e.g., cellSNP.cells_ARG.vcf.gz) plus MetaQuad BIC_params.csv and need per-gene, per-sample nucleotide diversity to detect polymorphism shifts such as ARG diversity changes after antibiotic treatment. You only need raw variant calling/clustering — MetaQuad's BIC_params.csv already provides shared informative variants without diversity estimates. No per-gene normalization is available (neither genome lengths nor covbases), since raw pile-up counts cannot be fairly compared across genes of different lengths. Input is single-cell mitochondrial data intended for clonal substructure inference (MQuad/vireoSNP use case), not shotgun metagenomic diversity analysis. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Computes nucleotide diversity per gene and sample from cellsnp-lite variant pile-ups and MetaQuad cluster parameters, normalized by genome length or covbases, to quantify polymorphism within metagenomic populations (e.g., ARGs after antibiotic treatment). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae030
skills.summary: Computes nucleotide diversity per gene and sample from cellsnp-lite variant pile-ups and MetaQuad cluster parameters, normalized by genome length or covbases, to quantify polymorphism within metagenomic populations (e.g., ARGs after antibiotic treatment).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need raw variant calling/clustering — MetaQuad's BIC_params.csv already provides shared informative variants without diversity estimates. No per-gene normalization is available (neither genome lengths nor covbases), since raw pile-up counts cannot be fairly compared across genes of different lengths. Input is single-cell mitochondrial data intended for clonal substructure inference (MQuad/vireoSNP use case), not shotgun metagenomic diversity analysis.

skills.description: Use when assembled contigs and multi-sample short-read data are available and contigs must be clustered into MAGs using sequence composition plus per-sample depth/co-abundance signals.
skills.name: nucleotide-frequency-composition-analysis
skills.search_text: nucleotide-frequency-composition-analysis Use when assembled contigs and multi-sample short-read data are available and contigs must be clustered into MAGs using sequence composition plus per-sample depth/co-abundance signals. Only a single sample is available and no group of samples exists, so group-wise co-abundance cannot inform binning The contigs are already binned or the input is a MAG FASTA set rather than raw contigs Bin refinement/refinement of existing bins is the goal — nf-core/mag 2.1.0 does not include a bin refinement step http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Binning of assembled metagenomic contigs into MAGs using nucleotide (tetranucleotide) frequencies combined with group-wise co-abundance patterns, as implemented for MetaBAT2 in the nf-core/mag pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Binning of assembled metagenomic contigs into MAGs using nucleotide (tetranucleotide) frequencies combined with group-wise co-abundance patterns, as implemented for MetaBAT2 in the nf-core/mag pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only a single sample is available and no group of samples exists, so group-wise co-abundance cannot inform binning The contigs are already binned or the input is a MAG FASTA set rather than raw contigs Bin refinement/refinement of existing bins is the goal — nf-core/mag 2.1.0 does not include a bin refinement step

skills.description: Use when metagenomic contigs (e.g. VirMAP improved dual assembly) must be taxonomically classified using both nucleotide and protein alignment evidence, independent of genome coverage or read overlap.
skills.name: nucleotide-protein-alignment-integration
skills.search_text: nucleotide-protein-alignment-integration Use when metagenomic contigs (e.g. VirMAP improved dual assembly) must be taxonomically classified using both nucleotide and protein alignment evidence, independent of genome coverage or read overlap. Input is raw metagenomic reads rather than assembled/improved contigs — VirMAP's classification stage operates on the improved dual assembly Reference database coverage of the target viral clade is insufficient; the paper notes insufficient database coverage of the viral tree of life limits existing approaches Goal is per-read (not per-contig) classification; current methods classify individual reads and/or contigs through alignments or kmer analyses, but this skill targets contig-level LCA assignment http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Taxonomically classify reconstructed viral contigs by merging nucleotide alignments (BBMap) and translated/protein alignments (DIAMOND) into a two-pass bits-per-base scoring system, followed by superkingdom-Virus filtering and a rank-wise LCA assignment. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-05658-8
skills.summary: Taxonomically classify reconstructed viral contigs by merging nucleotide alignments (BBMap) and translated/protein alignments (DIAMOND) into a two-pass bits-per-base scoring system, followed by superkingdom-Virus filtering and a rank-wise LCA assignment.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw metagenomic reads rather than assembled/improved contigs — VirMAP's classification stage operates on the improved dual assembly Reference database coverage of the target viral clade is insufficient; the paper notes insufficient database coverage of the viral tree of life limits existing approaches Goal is per-read (not per-contig) classification; current methods classify individual reads and/or contigs through alignments or kmer analyses, but this skill targets contig-level LCA assignment

skills.description: Use when metagenomic paired-end reads must be reconstructed into virus-like super-scaffolds by combining nucleotide (BBMap) and translated-protein (DIAMOND) alignments against Genbank viral/phage references, especially for low-coverage or divergent viruses.
skills.name: nucleotide-protein-super-scaffold-merging
skills.search_text: nucleotide-protein-super-scaffold-merging Use when metagenomic paired-end reads must be reconstructed into virus-like super-scaffolds by combining nucleotide (BBMap) and translated-protein (DIAMOND) alignments against Genbank viral/phage references, especially for low-coverage or divergent viruses. The goal is purely de-novo assembly of novel genomes absent from gbvrl/gbphage references rather than mapping-assembly reconstruction against Genbank viral/phage divisions. Only taxonomic classification (bits-per-base scoring / LCA) of already-assembled contigs is needed, not per-genome read-set reconstruction and super-scaffold building. Input is a single non-viral genome sample where alignment to viral/phage reference databases would mostly produce filtered or empty genomic read sets. http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 VirMAP's mapping-assembly stage merges nucleotide and amino-acid alignment information in a tiered manner: reads are assigned to viral genomes from clustered BBMap/DIAMOND alignments to Genbank gbvrl and gbphage, each genome entry is naive-pileup reconstructed, and CDS-derived protein calls are tiled onto the nucleotide scaffold to produce one virus-like super-scaffold per genome. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-05658-8
skills.summary: VirMAP's mapping-assembly stage merges nucleotide and amino-acid alignment information in a tiered manner: reads are assigned to viral genomes from clustered BBMap/DIAMOND alignments to Genbank gbvrl and gbphage, each genome entry is naive-pileup reconstructed, and CDS-derived protein calls are tiled onto the nucleotide scaffold to produce one virus-like super-scaffold per genome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is purely de-novo assembly of novel genomes absent from gbvrl/gbphage references rather than mapping-assembly reconstruction against Genbank viral/phage divisions. Only taxonomic classification (bits-per-base scoring / LCA) of already-assembled contigs is needed, not per-genome read-set reconstruction and super-scaffold building. Input is a single non-viral genome sample where alignment to viral/phage reference databases would mostly produce filtered or empty genomic read sets.

skills.description: Use when you have raw paired-end Illumina reads from isolate genomes or metagenomes and need to recover CRISPR arrays or a repeat-defined locus without complete genome assembly, especially when the target repeat sequence is known.
skills.name: nucleotide-seed-read-expansion
skills.search_text: nucleotide-seed-read-expansion Use when you have raw paired-end Illumina reads from isolate genomes or metagenomes and need to recover CRISPR arrays or a repeat-defined locus without complete genome assembly, especially when the target repeat sequence is known. When a complete genome assembly is required for other downstream analyses — targeted assembly only recovers repeat-adjacent and cas gene regions, not the whole genome When no CRISPR repeat or cas gene reference (HMMs or nucleotide seeds) is available for the organism of interest, since DNA-mode seeding depends on a user-defined repeat FASTA For long-read (e.g., PacBio/ONT) datasets — the pipeline is built for short paired-end Illumina reads http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 CasCollect's DNA-mode strategy for recovering a targeted genomic locus (e.g., cas operons and CRISPR arrays) from unassembled FASTQ reads: seed reads are matched against user-provided CRISPR repeat sequences via VSEARCH identity search, then the read subset is iteratively expanded over multiple cycles before targeted SPAdes assembly. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: CasCollect's DNA-mode strategy for recovering a targeted genomic locus (e.g., cas operons and CRISPR arrays) from unassembled FASTQ reads: seed reads are matched against user-provided CRISPR repeat sequences via VSEARCH identity search, then the read subset is iteratively expanded over multiple cycles before targeted SPAdes assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When a complete genome assembly is required for other downstream analyses — targeted assembly only recovers repeat-adjacent and cas gene regions, not the whole genome When no CRISPR repeat or cas gene reference (HMMs or nucleotide seeds) is available for the organism of interest, since DNA-mode seeding depends on a user-defined repeat FASTA For long-read (e.g., PacBio/ONT) datasets — the pipeline is built for short paired-end Illumina reads

skills.description: Use when a nucleotide FASTA of predicted coding sequences (e.g. ~5.5M CDSs from assembled vaginal metagenomes) must be de-replicated into a non-redundant gene catalog at ≥95% identity over ≥90% of the shorter gene length.
skills.name: nucleotide-sequence-clustering
skills.search_text: nucleotide-sequence-clustering Use when a nucleotide FASTA of predicted coding sequences (e.g. ~5.5M CDSs from assembled vaginal metagenomes) must be de-replicated into a non-redundant gene catalog at ≥95% identity over ≥90% of the shorter gene length. Input sequences are proteins/amino acids — CD-HIT-EST is nucleotide-only; for protein families use the paper's VOG Jaccard-clustering workflow (Module 7, --linkscore=0.6, 80% identity, 60% coverage) The VIRGO catalog already exists and the goal is per-sample abundance/annotation — map reads with VIRGO's runMapping.step1.sh against the existing non-redundant database instead of re-clustering You need orthologous-group or taxonomy-aware structure rather than nucleotide redundancy removal — the 95%/90% rule collapses any sufficiently similar nucleotide pair regardless of function or annotation http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Greedy nucleotide-level de-redundancy of predicted CDSs using CD-HIT-EST v4.6 (-c 0.95 identity, -aS 0.90 coverage of the shorter gene), which collapsed ~5.5 million predicted vaginal metagenomic CDSs into the 948,158-gene VIRGO non-redundant gene catalog, retaining the longest sequence per cluster as representative. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-14677-3
skills.summary: Greedy nucleotide-level de-redundancy of predicted CDSs using CD-HIT-EST v4.6 (-c 0.95 identity, -aS 0.90 coverage of the shorter gene), which collapsed ~5.5 million predicted vaginal metagenomic CDSs into the 948,158-gene VIRGO non-redundant gene catalog, retaining the longest sequence per cluster as representative.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are proteins/amino acids — CD-HIT-EST is nucleotide-only; for protein families use the paper's VOG Jaccard-clustering workflow (Module 7, --linkscore=0.6, 80% identity, 60% coverage) The VIRGO catalog already exists and the goal is per-sample abundance/annotation — map reads with VIRGO's runMapping.step1.sh against the existing non-redundant database instead of re-clustering You need orthologous-group or taxonomy-aware structure rather than nucleotide redundancy removal — the 95%/90% rule collapses any sufficiently similar nucleotide pair regardless of function or annotation

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample FASTA sequences of putative elements (e.g. insertion sequences from many metagenomes) and need a non-redundant catalogue by clustering at ~95% nucleotide identity.
skills.name: nucleotide-sequence-clustering-redundancy-removal
skills.search_text: nucleotide-sequence-clustering-redundancy-removal Use when you have per-sample FASTA sequences of putative elements (e.g. insertion sequences from many metagenomes) and need a non-redundant catalogue by clustering at ~95% nucleotide identity. Input sequences are proteins or need clustering at identities far from nucleotide level (use CD-HIT protein mode instead of CD-HIT-EST). The target insertion sequences lack inverted terminal repeats (>=25 nt), since upstream Palidis detection — and hence the pooled input — cannot recover ITR-less ISs. You need to annotate against the released ISC v1.0.0 rather than build a catalogue: use it as a reference database instead of re-clustering. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Pool nucleotide sequences identified per-sample (e.g. insertion sequences detected by Palidis in 264 HMP metagenomes) and cluster them with CD-HIT-EST at a 0.95 sequence identity threshold to emit a non-redundant catalogue (ISC v1.0.0: 879 unique ISs, 87 unique transposases). metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000917
skills.summary: Pool nucleotide sequences identified per-sample (e.g. insertion sequences detected by Palidis in 264 HMP metagenomes) and cluster them with CD-HIT-EST at a 0.95 sequence identity threshold to emit a non-redundant catalogue (ISC v1.0.0: 879 unique ISs, 87 unique transposases).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are proteins or need clustering at identities far from nucleotide level (use CD-HIT protein mode instead of CD-HIT-EST). The target insertion sequences lack inverted terminal repeats (>=25 nt), since upstream Palidis detection — and hence the pooled input — cannot recover ITR-less ISs. You need to annotate against the released ISC v1.0.0 rather than build a catalogue: use it as a reference database instead of re-clustering.

skills.description: Use when annotating metagenomic contigs that are too short for self-training gene finding, and sequenced genomes of close relatives (species-level pan-genomes) are available to supply protein-coding region parameters via nucleotide similarity assignment.
skills.name: nucleotide-similarity-search
skills.search_text: nucleotide-similarity-search Use when annotating metagenomic contigs that are too short for self-training gene finding, and sequenced genomes of close relatives (species-level pan-genomes) are available to supply protein-coding region parameters via nucleotide similarity assignment. Contigs are long enough for reliable self-training with GeneMarkS-2, or belong to taxa with no available reference genomes (no pan-genome assignment possible) Input is raw reads rather than assembled contigs; the pipeline expects metagenome assemblies The goal is de novo model estimation on complete genomes, which GeneMarkS-2 self-training handles directly http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 A similarity-search step at the core of the GeneMark-HM pipeline: genes initially predicted in each metagenomic contig are used as queries against a pan-genome nucleotide database (indexed with NCBI makeblastdb) to assign the contig to a species-level pan-genome and select a near-optimal gene prediction model. It is also used to validate that pan-genome-selected models reproduce native GeneMarkS-2 annotations across rGenomes of 1849 SGBs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab047
skills.summary: A similarity-search step at the core of the GeneMark-HM pipeline: genes initially predicted in each metagenomic contig are used as queries against a pan-genome nucleotide database (indexed with NCBI makeblastdb) to assign the contig to a species-level pan-genome and select a near-optimal gene prediction model. It is also used to validate that pan-genome-selected models reproduce native GeneMarkS-2 annotations across rGenomes of 1849 SGBs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Contigs are long enough for reliable self-training with GeneMarkS-2, or belong to taxa with no available reference genomes (no pan-genome assignment possible) Input is raw reads rather than assembled contigs; the pipeline expects metagenome assemblies The goal is de novo model estimation on complete genomes, which GeneMarkS-2 self-training handles directly

skills.description: Use when a set of candidate duplicate viral scaffolds (already rough-grouped, e.g. by Mash dist) needs exact pairwise nucleotide alignment to compute percent identity and percent coverage before dereplication (longest or composite mode).
skills.name: nucmer-whole-genome-alignment
skills.search_text: nucmer-whole-genome-alignment Use when a set of candidate duplicate viral scaffolds (already rough-grouped, e.g. by Mash dist) needs exact pairwise nucleotide alignment to compute percent identity and percent coverage before dereplication (longest or composite mode). The goal is binning scaffolds into vMAGs rather than dereplicating them — vRhyme's main binning mode, not its Mash/Nucmer dereplication function, is the right tool Input scaffolds are already dereplicated or derive from distinct taxa with no expected near-identical pairs, so alignment-based duplicate detection adds cost without benefit Comparison should be at the protein level (e.g., redundancy checking with Mmseqs2) rather than nucleotide sequence similarity http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Nucleotide-level whole-genome pairwise alignment with Nucmer as used inside vRhyme's scaffold dereplication module, where Mash-sketching forms rough duplicate groups and Nucmer alignments quantify exact sequence similarity and overlap to decide which scaffolds to merge or discard. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac341
skills.summary: Nucleotide-level whole-genome pairwise alignment with Nucmer as used inside vRhyme's scaffold dereplication module, where Mash-sketching forms rough duplicate groups and Nucmer alignments quantify exact sequence similarity and overlap to decide which scaffolds to merge or discard.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is binning scaffolds into vMAGs rather than dereplicating them — vRhyme's main binning mode, not its Mash/Nucmer dereplication function, is the right tool Input scaffolds are already dereplicated or derive from distinct taxa with no expected near-identical pairs, so alignment-based duplicate detection adds cost without benefit Comparison should be at the protein level (e.g., redundancy checking with Mmseqs2) rather than nucleotide sequence similarity

skills.description: Use when a Bayesian compositional time-series model (e.g. TGP-CODA or MALLARD) must be fit by MCMC to longitudinal 16S count data to obtain posterior estimates of latent relative abundances for accuracy/runtime benchmarking.
skills.name: nuts-mcmc-posterior-inference
skills.search_text: nuts-mcmc-posterior-inference Use when a Bayesian compositional time-series model (e.g. TGP-CODA or MALLARD) must be fit by MCMC to longitudinal 16S count data to obtain posterior estimates of latent relative abundances for accuracy/runtime benchmarking. When the goal is fast inference from large numbers of samples or many taxa — TGP-CODA and MALLARD have difficulty scaling with sample size and taxa, and the paper shows they are orders of magnitude slower than LUMINATE When the input is already denoised relative abundances rather than raw sequencing counts When a non-Bayesian point-estimate method (e.g. LUMINATE's variational inference) suffices for the analysis http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Run No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) posterior inference for latent relative abundances in Bayesian compositional state-space models (TGP-CODA via PyStan 2.17.1.0, MALLARD via RStan 2.19.2) on longitudinal 16S count data, taking the posterior mean as the denoised trajectory estimate. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2020.05.006
skills.summary: Run No-U-Turn Sampler (NUTS) posterior inference for latent relative abundances in Bayesian compositional state-space models (TGP-CODA via PyStan 2.17.1.0, MALLARD via RStan 2.19.2) on longitudinal 16S count data, taking the posterior mean as the denoised trajectory estimate.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is fast inference from large numbers of samples or many taxa — TGP-CODA and MALLARD have difficulty scaling with sample size and taxa, and the paper shows they are orders of magnitude slower than LUMINATE When the input is already denoised relative abundances rather than raw sequencing counts When a non-Bayesian point-estimate method (e.g. LUMINATE's variational inference) suffices for the analysis

skills.description: Use when the goal is all-vs-all comparison or clustering of many large metagenomes/viromes (billions of reads) by k-mer content at full read depth, e.g. reproducing Tara Ocean Virome temperature-structured clustering (Fig. 5).
skills.name: ocean-virome-community-analysis
skills.search_text: ocean-virome-community-analysis Use when the goal is all-vs-all comparison or clustering of many large metagenomes/viromes (billions of reads) by k-mer content at full read depth, e.g. reproducing Tara Ocean Virome temperature-structured clustering (Fig. 5). The dataset is small or the analysis tolerates sketch-based approximations — the article notes faster MinHash tools like Mash/Sourmash, but Libra's value is full-depth comparison, so it is the wrong choice if speed at reduced resolution is acceptable. Input is already a reduced feature table or presence/absence matrix — the article warns that 'presence/absence distance metrics greatly diminish the resolution of large-scale comparative analyses', so this k-mer-based full-read workflow should not be applied to pre-summarized data. The goal is taxonomic or functional profiling of individual viromes rather than all-vs-all similarity and clustering across samples. http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Reproduce Libra's all-vs-all k-mer comparison of the 43 Tara Ocean Viromes (~4.2 billion reads, 2009–2011 Expedition) on a Hadoop cluster to cluster global ocean viral populations and recover the four temperature-gradient groupings reported in Fig. 5. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Reproduce Libra's all-vs-all k-mer comparison of the 43 Tara Ocean Viromes (~4.2 billion reads, 2009–2011 Expedition) on a Hadoop cluster to cluster global ocean viral populations and recover the four temperature-gradient groupings reported in Fig. 5.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The dataset is small or the analysis tolerates sketch-based approximations — the article notes faster MinHash tools like Mash/Sourmash, but Libra's value is full-depth comparison, so it is the wrong choice if speed at reduced resolution is acceptable. Input is already a reduced feature table or presence/absence matrix — the article warns that 'presence/absence distance metrics greatly diminish the resolution of large-scale comparative analyses', so this k-mer-based full-read workflow should not be applied to pre-summarized data. The goal is taxonomic or functional profiling of individual viromes rather than all-vs-all similarity and clustering across samples.

skills.description: Use when traversing a colored de Bruijn graph built from multiple sample haplotypes (e.g., 5000–20,000 simulated mitochondrial genomes) to assign positional coordinates to nodes and colored superbubbles (cSupBs), or to detect cycles during the traversal.
skills.name: offset-value-computation
skills.search_text: offset-value-computation Use when traversing a colored de Bruijn graph built from multiple sample haplotypes (e.g., 5000–20,000 simulated mitochondrial genomes) to assign positional coordinates to nodes and colored superbubbles (cSupBs), or to detect cycles during the traversal. Sequences with insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number), where the variant detection model built on this coordinate system is not applicable Graphs with degeneracy or gene elements shorter than k, which map to multiple nodes and complicate offset/coordinate analysis Detection of large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications, which the offset-based variant method does not address Computation of offset values for each node of a colored de Bruijn graph (a VARI-merge-constructed graph) during the postorder-like cSupB traversal, where a node's offset is the maximum offset among its incoming parents plus one. The offset value is one component of the paper's tri-tuple coordinate system (offset value, topological structure, sample information) and also powers the cycle-identification step. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Computation of offset values for each node of a colored de Bruijn graph (a VARI-merge-constructed graph) during the postorder-like cSupB traversal, where a node's offset is the maximum offset among its incoming parents plus one. The offset value is one component of the paper's tri-tuple coordinate system (offset value, topological structure, sample information) and also powers the cycle-identification step.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Sequences with insufficient similarity (source number far less than variant number), where the variant detection model built on this coordinate system is not applicable Graphs with degeneracy or gene elements shorter than k, which map to multiple nodes and complicate offset/coordinate analysis Detection of large indels, inversions, or reverse tandem duplications, which the offset-based variant method does not address

skills.description: Use when you need per-node or per-base coordinates on a VARI-merge colored de Bruijn graph pangenome — e.g., for offset-based cycle detection, reference position determination (RPD), or projecting GTF gene annotations onto the graph as (position, bubid, basecolor) triples.
skills.name: offset-value-coordinate-assignment
skills.search_text: offset-value-coordinate-assignment Use when you need per-node or per-base coordinates on a VARI-merge colored de Bruijn graph pangenome — e.g., for offset-based cycle detection, reference position determination (RPD), or projecting GTF gene annotations onto the graph as (position, bubid, basecolor) triples. Gene or feature elements shorter than k (e.g., < 22 bp): they may correspond to multiple graph nodes, making the assigned coordinates complicated and ambiguous Graphs containing degenerate positions — the method cannot handle degeneracy efficiently Highly repetitive sequences such as tandem repeats, where sequence cutting fragments the sequence too much and increases computational difficulty and error http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0654 Assigns each node and base of a VARI-merge colored de Bruijn graph an offset value computed from source/sink node positions, completing the tri-tuple (position, bubid, basecolor) that uniquely locates any graph element. This coordinate layer is what allows existing linear references (e.g., GTF gene coordinates on the 12 human mitogenomes) to be projected onto the graph pangenome. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: Assigns each node and base of a VARI-merge colored de Bruijn graph an offset value computed from source/sink node positions, completing the tri-tuple (position, bubid, basecolor) that uniquely locates any graph element. This coordinate layer is what allows existing linear references (e.g., GTF gene coordinates on the 12 human mitogenomes) to be projected onto the graph pangenome.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Gene or feature elements shorter than k (e.g., < 22 bp): they may correspond to multiple graph nodes, making the assigned coordinates complicated and ambiguous Graphs containing degenerate positions — the method cannot handle degeneracy efficiently Highly repetitive sequences such as tandem repeats, where sequence cutting fragments the sequence too much and increases computational difficulty and error

skills.description: Use when building a colored de Bruijn graph over highly similar haplotypes (e.g., mitochondrial genomes) and the postorder-like traversal finishes with unvisited nodes, signaling cycles that block cSupB decomposition.
skills.name: offset-value-cycle-identification
skills.search_text: offset-value-cycle-identification Use when building a colored de Bruijn graph over highly similar haplotypes (e.g., mitochondrial genomes) and the postorder-like traversal finishes with unvisited nodes, signaling cycles that block cSupB decomposition. The graph is already acyclic (traversal completes with all nodes visited) — cycle handling is unnecessary and sequence cutting would fragment repeats unnecessarily Sequences are highly repetitive (especially tandem repeats), where the cutting method 'will make the sequence too fragmented, thereby increasing the computational difficulty and error' Sequence similarity is insufficient (source number far less than variant number), where the variant detection model this cycle handling feeds into is not applicable http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A method from the cSupB/VARI-cSupB pipeline that detects cycles in the colored de Bruijn graph during postorder-like traversal using offset values, then localizes the cycle interval and reconstructs an acyclic graph by cutting the underlying sequences at a selected point. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04149-w
skills.summary: A method from the cSupB/VARI-cSupB pipeline that detects cycles in the colored de Bruijn graph during postorder-like traversal using offset values, then localizes the cycle interval and reconstructs an acyclic graph by cutting the underlying sequences at a selected point.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The graph is already acyclic (traversal completes with all nodes visited) — cycle handling is unnecessary and sequence cutting would fragment repeats unnecessarily Sequences are highly repetitive (especially tandem repeats), where the cutting method 'will make the sequence too fragmented, thereby increasing the computational difficulty and error' Sequence similarity is insufficient (source number far less than variant number), where the variant detection model this cycle handling feeds into is not applicable

skills.description: Use when the input is interleaved FASTQ metagenomic short-read data (e.g. all_reads.fq from an Illumina MiSeq run) and the goal is de novo, strain-resolved assembly without a reference genome.
skills.name: olc-assembly-pipeline-handling
skills.search_text: olc-assembly-pipeline-handling Use when the input is interleaved FASTQ metagenomic short-read data (e.g. all_reads.fq from an Illumina MiSeq run) and the goal is de novo, strain-resolved assembly without a reference genome. Input is long third-generation reads — the paper notes the high error rate of third-generation sequencing reads introduces unresolved issues, and the method targets short Illumina-type reads A high-quality reference genome is available and reference-assisted assembly is acceptable — StrainXpress is a de novo method designed to avoid reference bias Only a single isolate genome needs assembly without strain mixture — general assemblers like SPAdes or MEGAHIT may suffice http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Runs the StrainXpress divide-and-conquer strain-aware metagenome assembly pipeline, whose OLC paradigm passes through three stages — 'Clustering Reads', 'Local Assembly' and 'Global Assembly' — to reconstruct strain-specific genomes from short Illumina-style reads at strain resolution. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac543
skills.summary: Runs the StrainXpress divide-and-conquer strain-aware metagenome assembly pipeline, whose OLC paradigm passes through three stages — 'Clustering Reads', 'Local Assembly' and 'Global Assembly' — to reconstruct strain-specific genomes from short Illumina-style reads at strain resolution.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is long third-generation reads — the paper notes the high error rate of third-generation sequencing reads introduces unresolved issues, and the method targets short Illumina-type reads A high-quality reference genome is available and reference-assisted assembly is acceptable — StrainXpress is a de novo method designed to avoid reference bias Only a single isolate genome needs assembly without strain mixture — general assemblers like SPAdes or MEGAHIT may suffice

skills.description: Use when whole-genome FASTA sequences of viruses or host organisms are available and you need an alignment-free, k-mer-frequency-based pairwise dissimilarity/similarity matrix to seed a network-based prediction method.
skills.name: oligonucleotide-frequency-dissimilarity-computation
skills.search_text: oligonucleotide-frequency-dissimilarity-computation Use when whole-genome FASTA sequences of viruses or host organisms are available and you need an alignment-free, k-mer-frequency-based pairwise dissimilarity/similarity matrix to seed a network-based prediction method. When host genomes of the query virus are absent from the genome database — sequence-composition signals cannot recover associations that lack reference genomes (unlike homology limits, composition-based dissimilarity needs genomic context in the network) When the goal is genus-level rather than species-level host prediction only — ONF-based methods achieved less than 40% species-level accuracy on their own, so fused methods like ILMF-VH are preferred When a similarity matrix is already available (e.g. datasets/onf pre-computed values) — do not recompute dissimilarity from scratch http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Computes alignment-free d2* oligonucleotide frequency dissimilarity between genomes (k=6) to quantify pairwise sequence composition distances, which are then transformed into similarity matrices for the virus-virus and host-host networks in ILMF-VH. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3082-0
skills.summary: Computes alignment-free d2* oligonucleotide frequency dissimilarity between genomes (k=6) to quantify pairwise sequence composition distances, which are then transformed into similarity matrices for the virus-virus and host-host networks in ILMF-VH.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When host genomes of the query virus are absent from the genome database — sequence-composition signals cannot recover associations that lack reference genomes (unlike homology limits, composition-based dissimilarity needs genomic context in the network) When the goal is genus-level rather than species-level host prediction only — ONF-based methods achieved less than 40% species-level accuracy on their own, so fused methods like ILMF-VH are preferred When a similarity matrix is already available (e.g. datasets/onf pre-computed values) — do not recompute dissimilarity from scratch

skills.description: Use when designing degenerate or nondegenerate primers from aligned nucleotide sequences and candidate oligos must be filtered by hairpin/homodimer Tm, GC content bounds, and per-primer degeneracy limits before amplification testing.
skills.name: oligonucleotide-thermodynamic-stability-assessment
skills.search_text: oligonucleotide-thermodynamic-stability-assessment Use when designing degenerate or nondegenerate primers from aligned nucleotide sequences and candidate oligos must be filtered by hairpin/homodimer Tm, GC content bounds, and per-primer degeneracy limits before amplification testing. Input sequences are unaligned or in a non-FASTA format — EcoFunPrimer's select subcommand requires aligned FASTA input and cannot enumerate stable oligos from raw reads or protein sequences alone. The goal is ranking or prioritizing which genes to target (the upstream R-score/cumulative R-score threshold step) rather than assessing stability of already-designed candidate oligos. Experimental (wet-lab) validation of primer thermodynamics is required; this skill covers only computational/in silico assessment, and the authors note further experimental validation is required. http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 Assess candidate PCR/qPCR primers for thermodynamic stability — hairpin and homodimer melting temperatures, G+C content, and degeneracy — so that only thermodynamically stable oligos proceed to in silico PCR screening, as done by EcoFunPrimer within MetaFunPrimer. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00201-21
skills.summary: Assess candidate PCR/qPCR primers for thermodynamic stability — hairpin and homodimer melting temperatures, G+C content, and degeneracy — so that only thermodynamically stable oligos proceed to in silico PCR screening, as done by EcoFunPrimer within MetaFunPrimer.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are unaligned or in a non-FASTA format — EcoFunPrimer's select subcommand requires aligned FASTA input and cannot enumerate stable oligos from raw reads or protein sequences alone. The goal is ranking or prioritizing which genes to target (the upstream R-score/cumulative R-score threshold step) rather than assessing stability of already-designed candidate oligos. Experimental (wet-lab) validation of primer thermodynamics is required; this skill covers only computational/in silico assessment, and the authors note further experimental validation is required.

skills.description: Use when you must design targeted-capture baits across many related genomes (e.g., 56 RefSeq coronaviruses) and need to compare tiling-only, hybridization-modeled (CATCH), and homology-hierarchy (HUBDesign) strategies by efficiency metric.
skills.name: oligonucleotide-tiling-probe-design
skills.search_text: oligonucleotide-tiling-probe-design Use when you must design targeted-capture baits across many related genomes (e.g., 56 RefSeq coronaviruses) and need to compare tiling-only, hybridization-modeled (CATCH), and homology-hierarchy (HUBDesign) strategies by efficiency metric. Target genomes are unknown or unannotatable — HUBDesign relies on annotated genomes to cluster sequences and cannot design probes for them You need validated wet-lab capture performance, not in silico benchmarking — the article notes enrichment is target-sequence dependent and validation used only artificial pooled samples A single-genome or single-locus assay is needed — efficiency gains come from multi-genome/multi-taxonomic-level design, not single-target capture http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_0797 Designs and benchmarks hybridization-capture oligonucleotide probe sets (75-mers tiled at 15 bp spacing, CATCH strict/permissive, HUBDesign) against a multi-genome target set, scoring each set by probe count and capture efficiency (average number of distinct genomes each probe maps to). metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.crmeth.2021.100069
skills.summary: Designs and benchmarks hybridization-capture oligonucleotide probe sets (75-mers tiled at 15 bp spacing, CATCH strict/permissive, HUBDesign) against a multi-genome target set, scoring each set by probe count and capture efficiency (average number of distinct genomes each probe maps to).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Target genomes are unknown or unannotatable — HUBDesign relies on annotated genomes to cluster sequences and cannot design probes for them You need validated wet-lab capture performance, not in silico benchmarking — the article notes enrichment is target-sequence dependent and validation used only artificial pooled samples A single-genome or single-locus assay is needed — efficiency gains come from multi-genome/multi-taxonomic-level design, not single-target capture

The data has not been preprocessed — the analysis core presupposes that the data is quality controlled and filtered before use The input is raw microarray-based data, which cannot be used directly as input The input is a raw (non-tabular) FASTA archive that still needs importing and embedding into a tabular structure first http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3172 Applies optional clustering (KMeans or OPTICS) and low-dimensional projection (PCA, MDS, or t-SNE) to filtered time-series multi-omics tabular data within MOVIS's analyzing step, so that temporal omics structure (e.g., physico-chemical properties sampled at a 2-h rate from the BWWTP dataset) can be explored as cluster-colored, publication-ready visualizations. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.02.012

skills.when_to_use_negative: The data has not been preprocessed — the analysis core presupposes that the data is quality controlled and filtered before use The input is raw microarray-based data, which cannot be used directly as input The input is a raw (non-tabular) FASTA archive that still needs importing and embedding into a tabular structure first

skills.description: Use when the input is only the eBWT file of a raw-read collection (e.g. reads.fasta.bwt from BCR) and you need positional-clustering variant detection without the memory cost of explicit LCP/GSA arrays.
skills.name: on-the-fly-lcp-extraction-from-bwt
skills.search_text: on-the-fly-lcp-extraction-from-bwt Use when the input is only the eBWT file of a raw-read collection (e.g. reads.fasta.bwt from BCR) and you need positional-clustering variant detection without the memory cost of explicit LCP/GSA arrays. You only have short k-mer/de Bruijn graph machinery or already possess a reference genome to map reads against — the paper's method is explicitly reference-free and alignment-free You need the parallel pipeline for INDEL detection — as a limitation, the parallel version works for SNPs only The input BWT was not produced by a tool compatible with ebwt2InDel's expected format (e.g. reads.fasta.bwt from BCR_LCP_GSA) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_3316 Simulates suffix-tree traversal on the extended Burrows-Wheeler Transform of a read collection, computing local LCP minima on-the-fly (Kmin, Kright, localMin bitvectors) without materializing the full LCP array or generalized suffix array, reducing working space by about one order of magnitude. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03586-3
skills.summary: Simulates suffix-tree traversal on the extended Burrows-Wheeler Transform of a read collection, computing local LCP minima on-the-fly (Kmin, Kright, localMin bitvectors) without materializing the full LCP array or generalized suffix array, reducing working space by about one order of magnitude.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only have short k-mer/de Bruijn graph machinery or already possess a reference genome to map reads against — the paper's method is explicitly reference-free and alignment-free You need the parallel pipeline for INDEL detection — as a limitation, the parallel version works for SNPs only The input BWT was not produced by a tool compatible with ebwt2InDel's expected format (e.g. reads.fasta.bwt from BCR_LCP_GSA)

skills.description: Use when processing 16S rRNA amplicon FASTQ data to form parent/one-mismatch-child clusters with HashSeq and you need a verified cluster table before LOESS-based error inference.
skills.name: one-mismatch-child-variant-assignment
skills.search_text: one-mismatch-child-variant-assignment Use when processing 16S rRNA amplicon FASTQ data to form parent/one-mismatch-child clusters with HashSeq and you need a verified cluster table before LOESS-based error inference. When the input is already a variant count table or when the analysis only needs taxonomic assignment — this step is a de novo clustering of raw preprocessed FASTQ variants. When true low-abundance sequence variants are the target: HashSeq is not sensitive for low-abundance sequences and more sensitive algorithms such as DADA2 are recommended in that case. When variants with two or more mismatches, indels relative to a parent, or long-read (e.g. PacBio) data are in scope — HashSeq considers only one-mismatch children and treats indel events as separate parent sequences. Assign each one-mismatch sequence variant (child) to its most abundant parent using HashSeq's fast HashMap-based clustering, then filter clusters by a parent-abundance threshold (default 1,000 reads) to build the parent/child cluster table used for downstream variant inference. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Assign each one-mismatch sequence variant (child) to its most abundant parent using HashSeq's fast HashMap-based clustering, then filter clusters by a parent-abundance threshold (default 1,000 reads) to build the parent/child cluster table used for downstream variant inference.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the input is already a variant count table or when the analysis only needs taxonomic assignment — this step is a de novo clustering of raw preprocessed FASTQ variants. When true low-abundance sequence variants are the target: HashSeq is not sensitive for low-abundance sequences and more sensitive algorithms such as DADA2 are recommended in that case. When variants with two or more mismatches, indels relative to a parent, or long-read (e.g. PacBio) data are in scope — HashSeq considers only one-mismatch children and treats indel events as separate parent sequences.

skills.description: Use when running HashSeq on Illumina 16S rRNA amplicon data and you need to check that the LOESS regression of one-mismatch children's mean/SD versus parent abundance fits well above the filtering threshold before trusting inferred variants.
skills.name: one-mismatch-children-statistics
skills.search_text: one-mismatch-children-statistics Use when running HashSeq on Illumina 16S rRNA amplicon data and you need to check that the LOESS regression of one-mismatch children's mean/SD versus parent abundance fits well above the filtering threshold before trusting inferred variants. Your input is already a feature/count table (e.g. SvTable.txt) rather than childrenProperties.txt from a HashSeq inferTrueSequences run — no parent-child cluster statistics exist to fit You need to detect true low-abundance sequence variants or indel variation — HashSeq's threshold-based approach and one-mismatch-only model are inappropriate; DADA2 or Deblur are recommended instead Sequences come from long-read technologies such as PacBio, where the assumption that multiple-mismatch sequences are rare may not hold http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Model the mean and standard deviation of one-mismatch child variant abundances as a smooth LOESS function of parent sequence abundance, providing the depth-dependent background error model (normal + LOESS) that underlies HashSeq's variant inference for 16S rRNA gene data. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Model the mean and standard deviation of one-mismatch child variant abundances as a smooth LOESS function of parent sequence abundance, providing the depth-dependent background error model (normal + LOESS) that underlies HashSeq's variant inference for 16S rRNA gene data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your input is already a feature/count table (e.g. SvTable.txt) rather than childrenProperties.txt from a HashSeq inferTrueSequences run — no parent-child cluster statistics exist to fit You need to detect true low-abundance sequence variants or indel variation — HashSeq's threshold-based approach and one-mismatch-only model are inappropriate; DADA2 or Deblur are recommended instead Sequences come from long-read technologies such as PacBio, where the assumption that multiple-mismatch sequences are rare may not hold

skills.description: Use when you have pre-processed 16S rRNA gene fastq reads (primers removed, paired, trimmed to 250 bases) and need to enumerate one-mismatch children per parent and model their observation rate versus parent abundance.
skills.name: one-mismatch-variant-enumeration
skills.search_text: one-mismatch-variant-enumeration Use when you have pre-processed 16S rRNA gene fastq reads (primers removed, paired, trimmed to 250 bases) and need to enumerate one-mismatch children per parent and model their observation rate versus parent abundance. You need to detect true low-abundance variants — HashSeq with a 1,000-read threshold is deliberately conservative and insensitive; the article recommends DADA2 for low-abundance sequences Your data contain indel variation or multi-mismatch variants relative to a parent — HashSeq only considers exactly one-mismatch children and treats indels as separate parent sequences; Deblur or alignment-based methods are suggested instead Long-read data (e.g. PacBio), where the assumption that multiple-mismatch sequences are rare may not hold http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Clusters 16S rRNA amplicon sequences into parent sequences and their one-nucleotide-difference children with HashSeq, then models the fraction of all possible one-mismatch children observed per parent as a single-parameter Poisson process with fitted per-nucleotide error rate P (P = 10^-4 in the paper's mock communities). metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Clusters 16S rRNA amplicon sequences into parent sequences and their one-nucleotide-difference children with HashSeq, then models the fraction of all possible one-mismatch children observed per parent as a single-parameter Poisson process with fitted per-nucleotide error rate P (P = 10^-4 in the paper's mock communities).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to detect true low-abundance variants — HashSeq with a 1,000-read threshold is deliberately conservative and insensitive; the article recommends DADA2 for low-abundance sequences Your data contain indel variation or multi-mismatch variants relative to a parent — HashSeq only considers exactly one-mismatch children and treats indels as separate parent sequences; Deblur or alignment-based methods are suggested instead Long-read data (e.g. PacBio), where the assumption that multiple-mismatch sequences are rare may not hold

skills.description: Use when a metagenome sample has both Illumina paired-end reads and ONT long reads (e.g. 28-75 Gbp PromethION) and the goal is highly contiguous scaffolds or near-complete genomes for high-abundance species.
skills.name: ont-long-read-scaffolding
skills.search_text: ont-long-read-scaffolding Use when a metagenome sample has both Illumina paired-end reads and ONT long reads (e.g. 28-75 Gbp PromethION) and the goal is highly contiguous scaffolds or near-complete genomes for high-abundance species. Only short-read data are available — MetaPlatanus requires at least one short-read paired-end library and this skill depends on long-range ONT links Reference-based reassembly or strain-typing against known genomes is the goal — the study focuses on de novo methods and reference information was not well examined Extremely low-coverage long-read data where hybrid assemblers are reported advantageous and ONT links are too sparse to scaffold reliably http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Scaffold short-read metagenomic contigs into near-complete scaffolds using Oxford Nanopore PromethION long reads as long-range links via MetaPlatanus, which combines contig-assembly, scaffolding, gap-closing and binning with species-specific composition and coverage-depth checks to suppress interspecies misjoins. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkab831
skills.summary: Scaffold short-read metagenomic contigs into near-complete scaffolds using Oxford Nanopore PromethION long reads as long-range links via MetaPlatanus, which combines contig-assembly, scaffolding, gap-closing and binning with species-specific composition and coverage-depth checks to suppress interspecies misjoins.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only short-read data are available — MetaPlatanus requires at least one short-read paired-end library and this skill depends on long-range ONT links Reference-based reassembly or strain-typing against known genomes is the goal — the study focuses on de novo methods and reference information was not well examined Extremely low-coverage long-read data where hybrid assemblers are reported advantageous and ONT links are too sparse to scaffold reliably

skills.description: Use when benchmarking host-read-removal precision on Nanopore data: reference-grade bacterial or mycobacterial assemblies must be turned into simulated ONT FASTQ reads so read retention (reads_out/reads_in) can be measured against tools like Hostile and HRRT.
skills.name: ont-read-simulation
skills.search_text: ont-read-simulation Use when benchmarking host-read-removal precision on Nanopore data: reference-grade bacterial or mycobacterial assemblies must be turned into simulated ONT FASTQ reads so read retention (reads_out/reads_in) can be measured against tools like Hostile and HRRT. You need to benchmark real human read removal on genuine human data (e.g. 1000 Genomes Project samples) — this skill covers simulated microbial reads only. Short-read (Illumina) benchmarking is the goal — that workflow uses DWGSIM simulation and Hostile's Bowtie2 mode, not the Minimap2/map-ont long-read path. Input reads are already decontaminated or you only need to inspect an existing index (e.g. via `hostile index list`); there is nothing to simulate or benchmark. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Simulates Oxford Nanopore long reads from reference-grade bacterial assemblies (PBSIM2) to benchmark how many microbial reads survive host-read decontamination with Hostile versus the NCBI Human Read Removal Tool (HRRT). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad728
skills.summary: Simulates Oxford Nanopore long reads from reference-grade bacterial assemblies (PBSIM2) to benchmark how many microbial reads survive host-read decontamination with Hostile versus the NCBI Human Read Removal Tool (HRRT).
skills.when_to_use_negative: You need to benchmark real human read removal on genuine human data (e.g. 1000 Genomes Project samples) — this skill covers simulated microbial reads only. Short-read (Illumina) benchmarking is the goal — that workflow uses DWGSIM simulation and Hostile's Bowtie2 mode, not the Minimap2/map-ont long-read path. Input reads are already decontaminated or you only need to inspect an existing index (e.g. via `hostile index list`); there is nothing to simulate or benchmark.

skills.description: Decision support for comparing metagenomic taxonomic profilers (KMA variants, MetaPhlAn, mOTUs, Bracken) on benchmark data with known ground truth, when per-level Purity/Completeness/F1 must be recomputed from profiler output files rather than trusted from published figures.
skills.name: opal-output-metric-recomputation
skills.search_text: opal-output-metric-recomputation Decision support for comparing metagenomic taxonomic profilers (KMA variants, MetaPhlAn, mOTUs, Bracken) on benchmark data with known ground truth, when per-level Purity/Completeness/F1 must be recomputed from profiler output files rather than trusted from published figures. The data are real metagenomic samples without ground-truth profiles — the paper's own caveat is that 'Our choice was based on the in silico datasets, and while real data might contain many more unknowns', so these binary metrics are not meaningful without CAMI-style truth labels. The profiler outputs are already in non-CAMI native formats and the goal is only qualitative inspection rather than uniform metric recomputation against a gold standard. Abundance estimation (not profiling accuracy) is the target metric — Purity/Completeness/F1 measure taxon classification, not quantitative abundance accuracy. http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Recompute OPAL-style binary classification metrics (Purity, Completeness, F1) from microbial profiler outputs on the CAMI in silico datasets, applying a low-abundance filter before scoring. This reproduces the benchmark that justified selecting KMA-mOTUs as the taxonomic profiler for ARGprofiler. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae086
skills.summary: Recompute OPAL-style binary classification metrics (Purity, Completeness, F1) from microbial profiler outputs on the CAMI in silico datasets, applying a low-abundance filter before scoring. This reproduces the benchmark that justified selecting KMA-mOTUs as the taxonomic profiler for ARGprofiler.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The data are real metagenomic samples without ground-truth profiles — the paper's own caveat is that 'Our choice was based on the in silico datasets, and while real data might contain many more unknowns', so these binary metrics are not meaningful without CAMI-style truth labels. The profiler outputs are already in non-CAMI native formats and the goal is only qualitative inspection rather than uniform metric recomputation against a gold standard. Abundance estimation (not profiling accuracy) is the target metric — Purity/Completeness/F1 measure taxon classification, not quantitative abundance accuracy.
