skills.name: read-subset-expansion-parameter-tuning
skills.search_text: read-subset-expansion-parameter-tuning Use when running CasCollect on raw paired-end FASTQ data and you need to decide how many expansion cycles or what identity threshold will yield sufficient read coverage of a target CRISPR/Cas locus without redundant searching. The input is already assembled contigs or an annotated genome rather than raw unassembled sequencing reads — CasCollect's seed-and-expansion design targets raw FASTQ data You need whole-metagenome or whole-genome assembly rather than targeted recovery of CRISPR/Cas regions The target gene set has no suitable profile HMMs or repeat references, since seed generation depends on HMM profiles (protein mode) or CRISPR array repeats (DNA mode via VSEARCH) http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Tuning CasCollect's vsearch-driven read subset expansion (default 95% identity, five cycles via -match/-cycle) to control how seed read subsets grow around cas-gene seeds, and assessing whether added cycles close coverage gaps on a target operon. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa063
skills.summary: Tuning CasCollect's vsearch-driven read subset expansion (default 95% identity, five cycles via -match/-cycle) to control how seed read subsets grow around cas-gene seeds, and assessing whether added cycles close coverage gaps on a target operon.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already assembled contigs or an annotated genome rather than raw unassembled sequencing reads — CasCollect's seed-and-expansion design targets raw FASTQ data You need whole-metagenome or whole-genome assembly rather than targeted recovery of CRISPR/Cas regions The target gene set has no suitable profile HMMs or repeat references, since seed generation depends on HMM profiles (protein mode) or CRISPR array repeats (DNA mode via VSEARCH)

skills.description: Use when building or modifying an nf-core/mag (Nextflow DSL2) workflow that mixes short-read, long-read, and hybrid metagenomic data and each module must be routed only to the read types it supports.
skills.name: read-type-aware-tool-gating
skills.search_text: read-type-aware-tool-gating Use when building or modifying an nf-core/mag (Nextflow DSL2) workflow that mixes short-read, long-read, and hybrid metagenomic data and each module must be routed only to the read types it supports. The workflow handles a single uniform read type with tools that are already valid for it, so no gating logic is needed Input is not metagenomic sequencing data routed through nf-core/mag modules (e.g. already-assembled contigs without associated reads) You need tool selection based on data content (e.g. quality thresholds) rather than read type — gating by read type alone will not enforce quality cut-offs http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Gates each nf-core/mag analysis tool to the sequencing read type it supports (short, long, or hybrid), because not every tool is valid for every read type. Ensures e.g. Bowtie2/Porechop/fastp handle short or Nanopore reads while minimap2/Filtlong handle long reads, and that downstream stages (binning, taxonomic classification) only receive eligible inputs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac007
skills.summary: Gates each nf-core/mag analysis tool to the sequencing read type it supports (short, long, or hybrid), because not every tool is valid for every read type. Ensures e.g. Bowtie2/Porechop/fastp handle short or Nanopore reads while minimap2/Filtlong handle long reads, and that downstream stages (binning, taxonomic classification) only receive eligible inputs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The workflow handles a single uniform read type with tools that are already valid for it, so no gating logic is needed Input is not metagenomic sequencing data routed through nf-core/mag modules (e.g. already-assembled contigs without associated reads) You need tool selection based on data content (e.g. quality thresholds) rather than read type — gating by read type alone will not enforce quality cut-offs

skills.description: Use when comparing how early competing real-time raw-signal mappers stop sequencing a read (bases sequenced per read) or how many signal chunks they consume per read, to estimate adaptive-sampling time/cost benefits.
skills.name: real-time-mapping-behavior-analysis
skills.search_text: real-time-mapping-behavior-analysis Use when comparing how early competing real-time raw-signal mappers stop sequencing a read (bases sequenced per read) or how many signal chunks they consume per read, to estimate adaptive-sampling time/cost benefits. Input reads are already basecalled FASTQ/FASTA — this skill measures signal-prefix and chunk consumption from raw signal mapping, not sequence-level alignment statistics Data is r10.4.1 — UNCALLED (one of the comparison baselines) only supports legacy r9.4.1 data, so the time/cost comparison cannot be run The goal is mapping accuracy or throughput rather than sequencing time/cost proxies — use the accuracy/throughput evaluation workflow instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Quantifies the real-time sequencing behavior of raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) by measuring the sequenced read prefix length and number of signal chunks consumed per mapped read, which proxy sequencing time and cost under adaptive sampling. This reproduces the paper's Table 4 comparison showing RawHash stops earlier than UNCALLED on large genomes but consumes ~1.58x more chunks than Sigmap. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Quantifies the real-time sequencing behavior of raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap) by measuring the sequenced read prefix length and number of signal chunks consumed per mapped read, which proxy sequencing time and cost under adaptive sampling. This reproduces the paper's Table 4 comparison showing RawHash stops earlier than UNCALLED on large genomes but consumes ~1.58x more chunks than Sigmap.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are already basecalled FASTQ/FASTA — this skill measures signal-prefix and chunk consumption from raw signal mapping, not sequence-level alignment statistics Data is r10.4.1 — UNCALLED (one of the comparison baselines) only supports legacy r9.4.1 data, so the time/cost comparison cannot be run The goal is mapping accuracy or throughput rather than sequencing time/cost proxies — use the accuracy/throughput evaluation workflow instead

skills.description: Use when a task asks to quantify estimation accuracy of relative abundance from truncated or subsampled nanopore signal read sets, or to measure the fraction of reads a real-time mapper consumes before safe early run termination (Sequence Until).
skills.name: real-time-mapping-stopping-evaluation
skills.search_text: real-time-mapping-stopping-evaluation Use when a task asks to quantify estimation accuracy of relative abundance from truncated or subsampled nanopore signal read sets, or to measure the fraction of reads a real-time mapper consumes before safe early run termination (Sequence Until). Input is basecalled sequence reads (FASTQ/FASTA) rather than raw nanopore signal files (FAST5/POD5/SLOW5/BLOW5) — RawHash operates on raw signals Data is r10.4.1 rather than legacy r9.4 data, since the UNCALLED baseline used here can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data The goal is de novo assembly or all-vs-all overlapping without a reference genome — Rawsamble, not this relative-abundance/stopping evaluation, is the appropriate workflow http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 A protocol for evaluating how accurately raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED) estimate relative abundance from small randomly shuffled read fractions (0.01%–25%) and for measuring how early RawHash's real-time Sequence Until mechanism can safely stop sequencing while preserving accuracy. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: A protocol for evaluating how accurately raw nanopore signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED) estimate relative abundance from small randomly shuffled read fractions (0.01%–25%) and for measuring how early RawHash's real-time Sequence Until mechanism can safely stop sequencing while preserving accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is basecalled sequence reads (FASTQ/FASTA) rather than raw nanopore signal files (FAST5/POD5/SLOW5/BLOW5) — RawHash operates on raw signals Data is r10.4.1 rather than legacy r9.4 data, since the UNCALLED baseline used here can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data The goal is de novo assembly or all-vs-all overlapping without a reference genome — Rawsamble, not this relative-abundance/stopping evaluation, is the appropriate workflow

skills.description: Use when a non-redundant gene/protein catalog needs to be grouped into orthologous families using Jaccard similarity clustering followed by reciprocal--hit merging of clusters.
skills.name: reciprocal-best-hit-ortholog-merging
skills.search_text: reciprocal-best-hit-ortholog-merging Use when a non-redundant gene/protein catalog needs to be grouped into orthologous families using Jaccard similarity clustering followed by reciprocal--hit merging of clusters. Input is raw nucleotide reads or unfiltered FASTQ rather than a non-redundant polypeptide set — BLASTP clustering requires translated proteins The ortholog families already exist (e.g. eggNOG/COG/KOfam annotation is sufficient) and no vaginal-specific protein family catalog is needed Sequences are primarily viral or fungal — the VIRGO/VOG database has limited inclusion of viral and fungal gene sequences http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Constructs Vaginal Orthologous Groups (VOGs) by merging modified-Jaccard protein clusters (JACs) into JOCs via bidirectional best hit analysis of Wu-blastp all-vs-all hits. Used in VIRGO (0.95M non-redundant vaginal genes) to yield 617,127 JACs and 552,679 JOCs, of which 177,684 contain ≥2 genes and 374,995 are singletons. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-020-14677-3
skills.summary: Constructs Vaginal Orthologous Groups (VOGs) by merging modified-Jaccard protein clusters (JACs) into JOCs via bidirectional best hit analysis of Wu-blastp all-vs-all hits. Used in VIRGO (0.95M non-redundant vaginal genes) to yield 617,127 JACs and 552,679 JOCs, of which 177,684 contain ≥2 genes and 374,995 are singletons.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw nucleotide reads or unfiltered FASTQ rather than a non-redundant polypeptide set — BLASTP clustering requires translated proteins The ortholog families already exist (e.g. eggNOG/COG/KOfam annotation is sufficient) and no vaginal-specific protein family catalog is needed Sequences are primarily viral or fungal — the VIRGO/VOG database has limited inclusion of viral and fungal gene sequences

skills.description: Use when testing complex hypotheses that require comparing selective regimes (α, adaptive/neutral/deleterious fractions) of a user-selected gene set — e.g. defined by recombination rate bins or chromosome localization — against the whole-genome distribution.
skills.name: recombination-rate-stratified-gene-comparison
skills.search_text: recombination-rate-stratified-gene-comparison Use when testing complex hypotheses that require comparing selective regimes (α, adaptive/neutral/deleterious fractions) of a user-selected gene set — e.g. defined by recombination rate bins or chromosome localization — against the whole-genome distribution. Input is raw sequencing data (e.g. unprocessed VCF/FASTA) rather than per-gene MKT count tables — the data-retrieval/preprocessing pipeline skill should run first The question concerns a single gene or a non-genic region without a defined gene set to contrast against the genome-wide distribution The organism or population has no compatible pre-loaded PopFly/PopHuman data or user-supplied count tables in iMKT's expected daf/divergence format http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Stratifies protein-coding genes into a high-recombination set versus a genome-wide set using published recombination maps (Bhèrer et al. 2017 for human, Comeron et al. 2012 for Drosophila), then runs MK-derived tests (e.g. eMKT) per stratum via iMKT to test whether genes in high-recombination regions show different rates of adaptation (α). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: Stratifies protein-coding genes into a high-recombination set versus a genome-wide set using published recombination maps (Bhèrer et al. 2017 for human, Comeron et al. 2012 for Drosophila), then runs MK-derived tests (e.g. eMKT) per stratum via iMKT to test whether genes in high-recombination regions show different rates of adaptation (α).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing data (e.g. unprocessed VCF/FASTA) rather than per-gene MKT count tables — the data-retrieval/preprocessing pipeline skill should run first The question concerns a single gene or a non-genic region without a defined gene set to contrast against the genome-wide distribution The organism or population has no compatible pre-loaded PopFly/PopHuman data or user-supplied count tables in iMKT's expected daf/divergence format

skills.description: Use when comparing HGT local-strain reconstruction methods (LEMON vs LUMPY) on simulated metagenomic reads at multiple coverage levels to verify that graph-based reconstruction outperforms split-read-only methods.
skills.name: reconstruction-accuracy-delta-computation
skills.search_text: reconstruction-accuracy-delta-computation Use when comparing HGT local-strain reconstruction methods (LEMON vs LUMPY) on simulated metagenomic reads at multiple coverage levels to verify that graph-based reconstruction outperforms split-read-only methods. Evaluation is on real (non-simulated) metagenomic data where ground-truth donor/receptor strains and true breakpoints are unknown, so RA cannot be computed against reference segments The goal is HGT breakpoint detection accuracy rather than transferred-segment reconstruction quality Input is a single coverage condition — the delta-RA trend criterion (ΔRA decreasing with coverage) requires at least 5X and 30X conditions to compare http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Quantifies how well LEMON reconstructs transferred genome segments versus LUMPY by computing Reconstruction Accuracy (RA) from Smith-Waterman alignment scores and evaluating ΔRA = RA_LEMON − RA_LUMPY across WGSIM-simulated 5X and 30X coverage, reproducing the Fig. 5a trend. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3301-8
skills.summary: Quantifies how well LEMON reconstructs transferred genome segments versus LUMPY by computing Reconstruction Accuracy (RA) from Smith-Waterman alignment scores and evaluating ΔRA = RA_LEMON − RA_LUMPY across WGSIM-simulated 5X and 30X coverage, reproducing the Fig. 5a trend.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Evaluation is on real (non-simulated) metagenomic data where ground-truth donor/receptor strains and true breakpoints are unknown, so RA cannot be computed against reference segments The goal is HGT breakpoint detection accuracy rather than transferred-segment reconstruction quality Input is a single coverage condition — the delta-RA trend criterion (ΔRA decreasing with coverage) requires at least 5X and 30X conditions to compare

skills.description: Use when de novo metagenomic assembly (e.g., MetaSPAdes) yields seed contigs of only a few kb that need extension using raw sequencing reads, and contig accuracy must be preserved (e.g., >98% BLAST alignment to a reference viral genome).
skills.name: recursive-overlap-layout-candidate-assembly
skills.search_text: recursive-overlap-layout-candidate-assembly Use when de novo metagenomic assembly (e.g., MetaSPAdes) yields seed contigs of only a few kb that need extension using raw sequencing reads, and contig accuracy must be preserved (e.g., >98% BLAST alignment to a reference viral genome). Input contigs are already complete genomes or longer than the target stop-length, so extension would only trigger circular-genome repeat termination Reads have not had adaptors removed — the README warns extension results will be suboptimal without this preprocessing The goal is general de novo assembly of reads rather than extension of existing seed contigs; use a DBG assembler like MetaSPAdes, MEGAHIT, or IDBA-UD instead http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_0781 Extends fragmented MetaSPAdes seed contigs from viral metagenomics data using ContigExtender's recursive Overlap Layout Candidates (r-OLC) strategy, which iteratively appends overlapping reads while exploring alternative branches to produce longer, highly accurate contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-021-04038-2
skills.summary: Extends fragmented MetaSPAdes seed contigs from viral metagenomics data using ContigExtender's recursive Overlap Layout Candidates (r-OLC) strategy, which iteratively appends overlapping reads while exploring alternative branches to produce longer, highly accurate contigs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input contigs are already complete genomes or longer than the target stop-length, so extension would only trigger circular-genome repeat termination Reads have not had adaptors removed — the README warns extension results will be suboptimal without this preprocessing The goal is general de novo assembly of reads rather than extension of existing seed contigs; use a DBG assembler like MetaSPAdes, MEGAHIT, or IDBA-UD instead

skills.description: Use when building a k-mer prefilter for protein sequence clustering or search where alphabet reduction plus lowest-hash k-mer selection must keep the index linear in input size N.
skills.name: reduced-amino-acid-alphabet-encoding
skills.search_text: reduced-amino-acid-alphabet-encoding Use when building a k-mer prefilter for protein sequence clustering or search where alphabet reduction plus lowest-hash k-mer selection must keep the index linear in input size N. Input sequences are nucleotide rather than protein, since the 13-letter reduced amino acid alphabet and Blosum62 scoring are protein-specific Exact all-against-all pairwise similarity is required rather than an approximate k-mer-based prefilter, as k-mer matching can miss sequence pairs sharing no selected k-mer http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Reduces protein sequences to a 13-letter alphabet and selects m=20 representative k-mers per sequence via a 16-bit rolling hash, as done in Linclust's step 1 to build a linear-size k-mer table for clustering huge protein sequence sets. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Reduces protein sequences to a 13-letter alphabet and selects m=20 representative k-mers per sequence via a 16-bit rolling hash, as done in Linclust's step 1 to build a linear-size k-mer table for clustering huge protein sequence sets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are nucleotide rather than protein, since the 13-letter reduced amino acid alphabet and Blosum62 scoring are protein-specific Exact all-against-all pairwise similarity is required rather than an approximate k-mer-based prefilter, as k-mer matching can miss sequence pairs sharing no selected k-mer

skills.description: Use when a downloaded or rebuilt Plass protein catalog (SRC or MERC FASTA) must be checked against published sequence counts, source-sample counts, and the 90%/90% redundancy-reduction parameters.
skills.name: redundancy-filtering-parameter-verification
skills.search_text: redundancy-filtering-parameter-verification Use when a downloaded or rebuilt Plass protein catalog (SRC or MERC FASTA) must be checked against published sequence counts, source-sample counts, and the 90%/90% redundancy-reduction parameters. Input is raw metagenomic/metatranscriptomic FASTQ reads needing assembly itself — use 'plass assemble' to build the catalog first rather than verifying an existing one The catalog under inspection was clustered at different thresholds (not 90% identity / 90% coverage), so published SRC/MERC size figures are not valid comparison targets The goal is nucleotide contig assembly — that is PenguiN's scope, not protein catalog verification http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Verifies that large de novo protein reference catalogs (SRC from 640 soil metagenomes, MERC from TARA ocean metatranscriptomes) match their reported redundancy-filtered sizes (2 billion and 292 million sequences) and the stated 90% sequence identity / 90% coverage clustering parameters. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41592-019-0437-4
skills.summary: Verifies that large de novo protein reference catalogs (SRC from 640 soil metagenomes, MERC from TARA ocean metatranscriptomes) match their reported redundancy-filtered sizes (2 billion and 292 million sequences) and the stated 90% sequence identity / 90% coverage clustering parameters.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw metagenomic/metatranscriptomic FASTQ reads needing assembly itself — use 'plass assemble' to build the catalog first rather than verifying an existing one The catalog under inspection was clustered at different thresholds (not 90% identity / 90% coverage), so published SRC/MERC size figures are not valid comparison targets The goal is nucleotide contig assembly — that is PenguiN's scope, not protein catalog verification

skills.description: Use when benchmarking de novo metagenomic assembly performance on a defined mock community where complete reference genomes/replicons are known and per-reference accuracy, contiguity, and completeness metrics are required.
skills.name: reference-based-assembly-evaluation
skills.search_text: reference-based-assembly-evaluation Use when benchmarking de novo metagenomic assembly performance on a defined mock community where complete reference genomes/replicons are known and per-reference accuracy, contiguity, and completeness metrics are required. The community is not a defined mock community and no complete reference genomes/replicons are available — reference-based metrics (Contiguity, Validity, Identity, Breadth of coverage) cannot be computed The goal is assembling a eukaryotic genome or a bacterial isolate rather than benchmarking metagenomic short-read de novo assemblers SNP-level strain resolution is the target — the article found meaningful strain resolution at the single-nucleotide polymorphism level was not achieved, even by the best assemblers tested http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Evaluates de novo metagenomic assemblies against known reference replicons using LMAS, which aligns assembler contigs to a concatenated multi-fasta reference and reports global and per-reference metrics (Contiguity, Multiplicity, Validity, Identity, Breadth of coverage, Lx, NAx, NGx) for benchmarking assemblers on defined mock communities such as BMock12. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giac122
skills.summary: Evaluates de novo metagenomic assemblies against known reference replicons using LMAS, which aligns assembler contigs to a concatenated multi-fasta reference and reports global and per-reference metrics (Contiguity, Multiplicity, Validity, Identity, Breadth of coverage, Lx, NAx, NGx) for benchmarking assemblers on defined mock communities such as BMock12.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The community is not a defined mock community and no complete reference genomes/replicons are available — reference-based metrics (Contiguity, Validity, Identity, Breadth of coverage) cannot be computed The goal is assembling a eukaryotic genome or a bacterial isolate rather than benchmarking metagenomic short-read de novo assemblers SNP-level strain resolution is the target — the article found meaningful strain resolution at the single-nucleotide polymorphism level was not achieved, even by the best assemblers tested

skills.description: Use when benchmarking metagenomic de novo assemblies against a known mock community and you need a per-replicon measure of contig contiguity (single-alignment coverage of a reference, not NGA50/total coverage).
skills.name: reference-based-contiguity-assessment
skills.search_text: reference-based-contiguity-assessment Use when benchmarking metagenomic de novo assemblies against a known mock community and you need a per-replicon measure of contig contiguity (single-alignment coverage of a reference, not NGA50/total coverage). No reference replicon sequences are available (reference-free metrics such as contig-length distributions or N50 should be used instead). You need total reference coverage combining multiple disjoint alignments — LSA only measures the single longest contiguous alignment, so it will underestimate multi-contig coverage. Evaluating assembly accuracy (misassembly classes such as chimera, inversion, translocation) rather than contiguity — those are separate LMAS metrics. http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Computes the LSA (longest single alignment) contiguity metric per reference replicon: the length of the single longest contig-to-reference alignment (from minimap2 PAF records of filtered-set contigs) divided by the reference replicon length. This captures how much of each replicon a single contig spans, without merging disjoint alignments. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giac122
skills.summary: Computes the LSA (longest single alignment) contiguity metric per reference replicon: the length of the single longest contig-to-reference alignment (from minimap2 PAF records of filtered-set contigs) divided by the reference replicon length. This captures how much of each replicon a single contig spans, without merging disjoint alignments.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference replicon sequences are available (reference-free metrics such as contig-length distributions or N50 should be used instead). You need total reference coverage combining multiple disjoint alignments — LSA only measures the single longest contiguous alignment, so it will underestimate multi-contig coverage. Evaluating assembly accuracy (misassembly classes such as chimera, inversion, translocation) rather than contiguity — those are separate LMAS metrics.

skills.description: Use when a gold-standard or close reference genome (e.g., E. coli K-12 MG1655, NC_000913.3) is available and multiple assemblies must be compared on structural errors and per-base accuracy.
skills.name: reference-based-genome-assembly-alignment
skills.search_text: reference-based-genome-assembly-alignment Use when a gold-standard or close reference genome (e.g., E. coli K-12 MG1655, NC_000913.3) is available and multiple assemblies must be compared on structural errors and per-base accuracy. No reference genome (true or close) is available for the organism — use reference-free evaluation instead, which computes 30 quality metrics Assemblies are of a large (e.g., mammalian) genome where standard QUAST is inappropriate — QUAST-LG is the intended extension The dataset is metagenomic — MetaQUAST, not plain reference-based QUAST, is the appropriate extension http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Evaluate genome assemblies by aligning contigs to a known reference genome with QUAST (via WebQUAST or the command line), yielding >60 reference-based metrics such as extensive misassemblies, genome fraction %, duplication ratio, NGA50, and mismatches/indels per 100 kb. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad406
skills.summary: Evaluate genome assemblies by aligning contigs to a known reference genome with QUAST (via WebQUAST or the command line), yielding >60 reference-based metrics such as extensive misassemblies, genome fraction %, duplication ratio, NGA50, and mismatches/indels per 100 kb.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genome (true or close) is available for the organism — use reference-free evaluation instead, which computes 30 quality metrics Assemblies are of a large (e.g., mammalian) genome where standard QUAST is inappropriate — QUAST-LG is the intended extension The dataset is metagenomic — MetaQUAST, not plain reference-based QUAST, is the appropriate extension

skills.description: Use when assembled contig FASTA files and a reference genome (true or close, e.g. W3110 for E. coli K-12) are available and you need misassembly counts, NGA50, genome fraction or duplication ratio to compare assemblies.
skills.name: reference-based-misassembly-detection
skills.search_text: reference-based-misassembly-detection Use when assembled contig FASTA files and a reference genome (true or close, e.g. W3110 for E. coli K-12) are available and you need misassembly counts, NGA50, genome fraction or duplication ratio to compare assemblies. No reference genome is available or relevant — use WebQUAST/QUAST in reference-free mode, which computes 30 contiguity/completeness metrics instead of >60 reference-based ones Input is raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs — QUAST evaluates assemblies, not reads Comparing against a very distant or wrong reference where misassembly counts reflect true structural differences rather than assembly errors http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Detects and characterizes structural assembly errors (inversions, relocations, translocations, local misassemblies) by aligning contigs to a provided reference genome with QUAST/WebQUAST, yielding misassembly counts, NGA50, genome fraction and duplication ratio in report.tsv and per-assembly contigs_reports/misassemblies_report files. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad406
skills.summary: Detects and characterizes structural assembly errors (inversions, relocations, translocations, local misassemblies) by aligning contigs to a provided reference genome with QUAST/WebQUAST, yielding misassembly counts, NGA50, genome fraction and duplication ratio in report.tsv and per-assembly contigs_reports/misassemblies_report files.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genome is available or relevant — use WebQUAST/QUAST in reference-free mode, which computes 30 contiguity/completeness metrics instead of >60 reference-based ones Input is raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs — QUAST evaluates assemblies, not reads Comparing against a very distant or wrong reference where misassembly counts reflect true structural differences rather than assembly errors

skills.description: Use when reference-free variant calls exist as .snp files (ebwt2InDel output) and a reference genome assembly (e.g. hg38) is available, so variants must be converted to .vcf with reference coordinates.
skills.name: reference-based-vcf-generation
skills.search_text: reference-based-vcf-generation Use when reference-free variant calls exist as .snp files (ebwt2InDel output) and a reference genome assembly (e.g. hg38) is available, so variants must be converted to .vcf with reference coordinates. No reference genome is available — the ebwt2InDel suite itself is reference-free, and this conversion pipeline requires aligning against an assembly such as hg38 The variant calls already come as .vcf (e.g. validated with hap.py) — no snp2vcf conversion is needed The parallel pipeline is being used for INDELs — the article notes the parallel pipeline 'at the moment works for SNPs only' http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Converts reference-free variant calls (the KisSNP2-format .snp output of ebwt2InDel) into standard .vcf entries by anchoring variant fragments onto a reference genome. It uses the snp2vcf pipeline: filter_snp -> seqtk -> bwa-mem -> sam2vcf. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03586-3
skills.summary: Converts reference-free variant calls (the KisSNP2-format .snp output of ebwt2InDel) into standard .vcf entries by anchoring variant fragments onto a reference genome. It uses the snp2vcf pipeline: filter_snp -> seqtk -> bwa-mem -> sam2vcf.
skills.when_to_use_negative: No reference genome is available — the ebwt2InDel suite itself is reference-free, and this conversion pipeline requires aligning against an assembly such as hg38 The variant calls already come as .vcf (e.g. validated with hap.py) — no snp2vcf conversion is needed The parallel pipeline is being used for INDELs — the article notes the parallel pipeline 'at the moment works for SNPs only'

skills.description: Use when a new reference gene/genome catalogue (e.g. VMGC-90) must be quantitatively compared against a prior catalogue (e.g. VIRGO) using read-mapping rates over a shared, publicly available metagenomic sample set.
skills.name: reference-catalogue-benchmarking
skills.search_text: reference-catalogue-benchmarking Use when a new reference gene/genome catalogue (e.g. VMGC-90) must be quantitatively compared against a prior catalogue (e.g. VIRGO) using read-mapping rates over a shared, publicly available metagenomic sample set. Samples are not vaginal metagenomes or are not present in the paper's Supplementary Table 2 sample list — the reported 74.5% vs 71.7% rates apply to that 4,472-sample vaginal set The goal is taxonomic profiling rather than gene-catalogue read capture — use the paper's customized Kraken2/Bracken SGB database workflow instead A reference catalogue of genomes (not a non-redundant gene catalogue) is being benchmarked — mapping to full genome collections (e.g. VMGC MAGs, median mapping rate 91.7%) is a different comparison http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Benchmarks a newly built reference gene catalogue against an established one by mapping the same set of metagenomic samples to both catalogues and comparing average per-sample mapping rates. Used here to show VMGC-90 captures vaginal metagenome reads more efficiently (~74.5%) than VIRGO (~71.7%). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41564-024-01751-5

skills.description: Use when a 16S reference database FASTA (Greengenes or SILVA) must be prepared for CD-HIT-OTU-Miseq / CDSnake OTU assignment, or when cluster representatives must be matched to the most specific available taxonomy lineages.
skills.name: reference-database-preprocessing-for-otu-annotation
skills.search_text: reference-database-preprocessing-for-otu-annotation Use when a 16S reference database FASTA (Greengenes or SILVA) must be prepared for CD-HIT-OTU-Miseq / CDSnake OTU assignment, or when cluster representatives must be matched to the most specific available taxonomy lineages. The database is already in CD-HIT-OTU-Miseq format — use the authors' pre-reformatted Greengenes/SILVA downloads instead of re-splicing. The downstream pipeline does not match cluster representatives against an ordered annotated database (e.g., QIIME2-DADA2 or deblur), where record ordering provides no benefit. The task is read-level preprocessing (quality cropping with Trimmomatic, chimeric read removal), which operates on FASTQ reads, not on the reference database. http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 Reformats annotated 16S reference FASTA databases (e.g., Greengenes gg_13_8, SILVA SSU) by reordering records so that sequences carrying more specific taxonomic annotations appear at the beginning of the file, as required by CD-HIT-OTU-Miseq's cluster-annotation stage in the CDSnake pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-020-03591-6

A reference genome is available — reference-based QUAST reports >60 metrics, eight assessment plots and two Icarus viewers, so use reference-based evaluation instead The input is already a QUAST report or quality metrics table rather than raw assembly contigs The dataset is metagenomic or very large (mammalian-scale), where MetaQUAST or QUAST-LG extensions are the appropriate tools http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Evaluates and compares genome assemblies without a reference genome using QUAST/WebQUAST, which computes 30 reference-free quality metrics (contig counts, total length, largest contig, N50/N90/auN, G+C content, # N's per 100 kbp) and three assessment plots focused on contiguity and completeness. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkad406

No reference genome is available and only contiguity/completeness metrics are needed — use reference-free QUAST evaluation instead (30 metrics, three plots). The dataset is metagenomic — MetaQUAST with interspecies translocation handling is the appropriate extension, not plain reference-based QUAST. skills.search_text: reference-genome-fragmentation Use when comparing conspecific microbial strains across metagenomic assemblies or genomes with SynTracker and you need homologous genomic regions binned per sample from a single reference genome. The goal is to detect strain differences driven mainly by point mutations — SynTracker has low sensitivity to SNPs, so an SNP-based tool (e.g., MIDAS, StrainPhlAn, inStrain) is preferable Input is raw sequencing reads rather than per-sample metagenomic assemblies or assembled genomes Only short homologous stretches exist — hits without at least 2 kbp both upstream and downstream are excluded and yield no bins http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Fragment a per-species reference genome into 1-kbp central regions (spaced 4 kbp apart) and use BLASTn to retrieve homologous hit-plus-2-kbp-flank regions (~5 kbp) from per-sample metagenomic assemblies, organizing them into region-specific bins that feed SynTracker's synteny-based strain tracking. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-024-02276-2

skills.search_text: reference-genome-selection Use when building a reduced, non-redundant species-level reference gene database (pan-genomes) from thousands of complete genomes to support gene prediction model selection on metagenomic contigs. Input is already a non-redundant gene/pan-genome database rather than a genome collection needing redundancy filtering The target taxa lack complete genome representations in public repositories, so species-specific parameters cannot be estimated The goal is de novo gene prediction without a similarity-based model selection step (contigs not assignable to a pan-genome should instead fall back to MetaGeneMark or GeneMarkS-2 based on contig length) http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Selects a non-redundant, species-level pan-genome reference set from >310,000 prokaryotic rGenomes by seeding each pan-genome with its representative genome's genes and admitting additional genes only when no MegaBLAST/blastn target reaches ANI >95% with >90% query coverage, capped at the 150 longest rGenomes per SGB. This yields a reduced reference database (~20 Gb pan.fasta) for model selection in GeneMark-HM. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqab047

This yields a reduced reference database (~20 Gb pan.fasta) for model selection in GeneMark-HM.

skills.name: relative-abundance-computation-metagenomics
skills.search_text: relative-abundance-computation-metagenomics Use when you need relative abundances for reconstructed full-length SSU rRNA sequences from metagenomics data: map reads with BBMap, sum counts within 97% VSEARCH clusters, and report percent abundances. When the goal is to assign taxonomy directly to short-length Illumina reads without reconstruction — the article shows this yields a high rate of false positives When abundances must be corrected for 16S rRNA gene copy number — RiboTaxa explicitly chose not to use gene copy number correction When the input is already a taxonomic abundance table rather than FASTQ reads plus reconstructed SSU FASTA http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Compute per-sequence and per-cluster relative abundances of reconstructed SSU rRNA sequences by mapping short metagenomic reads with BBMap, summing abundances of VSEARCH 97% clusters, and reporting percentages without 16S rRNA gene copy-number correction, as done in the RiboTaxa pipeline. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac070
skills.summary: Compute per-sequence and per-cluster relative abundances of reconstructed SSU rRNA sequences by mapping short metagenomic reads with BBMap, summing abundances of VSEARCH 97% clusters, and reporting percentages without 16S rRNA gene copy-number correction, as done in the RiboTaxa pipeline.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to assign taxonomy directly to short-length Illumina reads without reconstruction — the article shows this yields a high rate of false positives When abundances must be corrected for 16S rRNA gene copy number — RiboTaxa explicitly chose not to use gene copy number correction When the input is already a taxonomic abundance table rather than FASTQ reads plus reconstructed SSU FASTA

skills.description: Use when a mock community is pooled from FAST5 read sets and raw signals must be mapped to a combined multi-genome reference to obtain per-genome relative abundance estimates and compare their accuracy to ground truth.
skills.name: relative-abundance-estimation-from-read-mappings
skills.search_text: relative-abundance-estimation-from-read-mappings Use when a mock community is pooled from FAST5 read sets and raw signals must be mapped to a combined multi-genome reference to obtain per-genome relative abundance estimates and compare their accuracy to ground truth. Input is basecalled FASTQ/FASTA reads rather than raw nanopore signals — use a base-level mapper (e.g., minimap2) instead, since RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap map raw electrical signal Data is not legacy r9.4.1 chemistry — UNCALLED explicitly supports only legacy r9.4.1 data, and the 6-mer pore models used here are R9.4-specific The goal is reference-free comparison or de novo assembly — use Rawsamble for all-vs-all raw-signal overlap finding instead of reference-based abundance estimation http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Estimate per-genome relative abundances of a mock community by mapping raw nanopore signals (FAST5) against a concatenated multi-species reference with raw-signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap), tallying mapped reads per reference genome, and computing Euclidean distance of the abundance vector to the ground-truth mixing proportions. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Estimate per-genome relative abundances of a mock community by mapping raw nanopore signals (FAST5) against a concatenated multi-species reference with raw-signal mappers (RawHash, UNCALLED, Sigmap), tallying mapped reads per reference genome, and computing Euclidean distance of the abundance vector to the ground-truth mixing proportions.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is basecalled FASTQ/FASTA reads rather than raw nanopore signals — use a base-level mapper (e.g., minimap2) instead, since RawHash, UNCALLED, and Sigmap map raw electrical signal Data is not legacy r9.4.1 chemistry — UNCALLED explicitly supports only legacy r9.4.1 data, and the 6-mer pore models used here are R9.4-specific The goal is reference-free comparison or de novo assembly — use Rawsamble for all-vs-all raw-signal overlap finding instead of reference-based abundance estimation

skills.description: Use when you have reconstructed full-length SSU rRNA sequences (e.g. metagenome_SSU_sequences.fasta from EMIRGE/MetaRib) plus the original quality-controlled reads and need per-sequence relative abundances for taxonomic profiling.
skills.name: relative-abundance-normalization
skills.search_text: relative-abundance-normalization Use when you have reconstructed full-length SSU rRNA sequences (e.g. metagenome_SSU_sequences.fasta from EMIRGE/MetaRib) plus the original quality-controlled reads and need per-sequence relative abundances for taxonomic profiling. Input is a short-read amplicon classification task where taxa should be assigned directly to reads — direct classification of short Illumina reads yields a high rate of false positives in this pipeline's benchmarking Reads have not been adapter-trimmed and quality-filtered with BBTOOLS first, since the mapper expects the pipeline's quality-controlled trimmed reads You need copy-number-corrected absolute abundances — RiboTaxa intentionally does not use 16S rRNA gene copy number correction http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Quantifies the relative abundance of reconstructed full-length SSU rRNA sequences in the RiboTaxa pipeline by mapping unfiltered high-quality reads onto the reconstructed sequences with BBMap (BBTools) and normalizing per-sequence read counts to percentages before 97% clustering and taxonomic affiliation. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac070
skills.summary: Quantifies the relative abundance of reconstructed full-length SSU rRNA sequences in the RiboTaxa pipeline by mapping unfiltered high-quality reads onto the reconstructed sequences with BBMap (BBTools) and normalizing per-sequence read counts to percentages before 97% clustering and taxonomic affiliation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is a short-read amplicon classification task where taxa should be assigned directly to reads — direct classification of short Illumina reads yields a high rate of false positives in this pipeline's benchmarking Reads have not been adapter-trimmed and quality-filtered with BBTOOLS first, since the mapper expects the pipeline's quality-controlled trimmed reads You need copy-number-corrected absolute abundances — RiboTaxa intentionally does not use 16S rRNA gene copy number correction

skills.description: Use when a relative abundance table (taxonomy levels l2–l6, e.g. Bangladesh taxtab.rm[[5]]) contains rare taxa that would destabilize downstream GAMLSS-BEZI differential abundance testing or clutter phylum-level mean plots.
skills.name: relative-abundance-table-filtering
skills.search_text: relative-abundance-table-filtering Use when a relative abundance table (taxonomy levels l2–l6, e.g. Bangladesh taxtab.rm[[5]]) contains rare taxa that would destabilize downstream GAMLSS-BEZI differential abundance testing or clutter phylum-level mean plots. Input is an absolute-count (OTU/feature) table rather than a relative abundance table — normalize to relative abundances first Downstream analysis is meta-analysis pooling (meta.taxa) of already-computed taxa.compare estimates — filtering should have been applied upstream per study The table has already been filtered with the same percent.filter/relabund.filter thresholds and no new rare taxa were introduced http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 A pre-analysis filtering skill from metamicrobiomeR that removes rare bacterial taxa from taxonomy-level relative abundance tables (e.g., taxtab.rm7 level 5 = genus) using prevalence and abundance thresholds, plus optional mean-abundance filtering for plotting and selecting taxa to display downstream. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: A pre-analysis filtering skill from metamicrobiomeR that removes rare bacterial taxa from taxonomy-level relative abundance tables (e.g., taxtab.rm7 level 5 = genus) using prevalence and abundance thresholds, plus optional mean-abundance filtering for plotting and selecting taxa to display downstream.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is an absolute-count (OTU/feature) table rather than a relative abundance table — normalize to relative abundances first Downstream analysis is meta-analysis pooling (meta.taxa) of already-computed taxa.compare estimates — filtering should have been applied upstream per study The table has already been filtered with the same percent.filter/relabund.filter thresholds and no new rare taxa were introduced

skills.description: Use when a benchmark table reports a per-dataset quality metric (e.g., genome fraction) for a new method and several baselines, and the goal is to quantify how much the new method exceeds the baseline per dataset and across all datasets.
skills.name: relative-percentage-gain-computation
skills.search_text: relative-percentage-gain-computation Use when a benchmark table reports a per-dataset quality metric (e.g., genome fraction) for a new method and several baselines, and the goal is to quantify how much the new method exceeds the baseline per dataset and across all datasets. The input does not contain per-dataset metric values for both the proposed method and at least one competitor baseline, so a relative gain cannot be formed. The claim to verify is an absolute metric (e.g., Genome Fraction 93.45% vs 74.74% for SPAdes) rather than a relative improvement over the best competitor. The metric distribution is better summarized by per-dataset pairwise rankings than by relative differences from the best baseline. http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Computes per-dataset relative percentage gains of a proposed method (StrainXpress) over the best state-of-the-art competitor on a quality metric (genome fraction from Quast/metaQuast), then aggregates gains into mean, first quartile, median, and third quartile summary statistics to reproduce headline claims such as an average 26.75% excess in reconstructed strain-specific sequence. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkac543
skills.summary: Computes per-dataset relative percentage gains of a proposed method (StrainXpress) over the best state-of-the-art competitor on a quality metric (genome fraction from Quast/metaQuast), then aggregates gains into mean, first quartile, median, and third quartile summary statistics to reproduce headline claims such as an average 26.75% excess in reconstructed strain-specific sequence.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input does not contain per-dataset metric values for both the proposed method and at least one competitor baseline, so a relative gain cannot be formed. The claim to verify is an absolute metric (e.g., Genome Fraction 93.45% vs 74.74% for SPAdes) rather than a relative improvement over the best competitor. The metric distribution is better summarized by per-dataset pairwise rankings than by relative differences from the best baseline.

skills.description: Use when a text-mining or information-extraction pipeline produces a character matrix (or equivalent structured extractions) that must be scored against a hand-curated gold standard, especially when per-character precision/recall/F1 and component ablations are needed.
skills.name: relaxed-precision-recall-f1-evaluation
skills.search_text: relaxed-precision-recall-f1-evaluation Use when a text-mining or information-extraction pipeline produces a character matrix (or equivalent structured extractions) that must be scored against a hand-curated gold standard, especially when per-character precision/recall/F1 and component ablations are needed. When extractions must match gold standard values verbatim and no partial/relaxed match criterion is defensible — the relaxed scoring tolerates approximate state matches When no hand-generated gold standard matrix exists for the designated characters, since all metrics are computed against expert-curated ground truth When the target text is morphological or semi-structured descriptions better suited to tools like CharaParser rather than prokaryotic physiological/ecological trait descriptions http://edamontology.org/topic_3071 http://edamontology.org/topic_0219 Evaluates an automatically generated taxon-by-character matrix against a hand-generated gold standard by computing Relaxed_Precision, Relaxed_Recall, and Relaxed_F1 per character (42 phenotypic characters), plus an overall accuracy, enabling ablation comparisons such as MicroPIE with vs. without its SVM Character Predictor. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1396-8
skills.summary: Evaluates an automatically generated taxon-by-character matrix against a hand-generated gold standard by computing Relaxed_Precision, Relaxed_Recall, and Relaxed_F1 per character (42 phenotypic characters), plus an overall accuracy, enabling ablation comparisons such as MicroPIE with vs. without its SVM Character Predictor.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When extractions must match gold standard values verbatim and no partial/relaxed match criterion is defensible — the relaxed scoring tolerates approximate state matches When no hand-generated gold standard matrix exists for the designated characters, since all metrics are computed against expert-curated ground truth When the target text is morphological or semi-structured descriptions better suited to tools like CharaParser rather than prokaryotic physiological/ecological trait descriptions

skills.description: Use when a binary phenotypic trait model (e.g. obligate intracellular vs free-living) trained on COG presence/absence vectors must be validated with a robust, replicate-averaged accuracy estimate rather than a single train/test split.
skills.name: repeated-cross-validation-accuracy-estimation
skills.search_text: repeated-cross-validation-accuracy-estimation Use when a binary phenotypic trait model (e.g. obligate intracellular vs free-living) trained on COG presence/absence vectors must be validated with a robust, replicate-averaged accuracy estimate rather than a single train/test split. The goal is prediction on new metagenomic bins with an already-trained model — use phenotrex predict rather than re-running cross-validation Genomes fail the marker-COG completeness screen (fewer than 39/40 marker COGs); the paper's traits are only reliably predictable in ~60-70% complete genomes, so incomplete inputs should not enter training/evaluation The analysis needs method comparison across different ML algorithms rather than replicate accuracy estimation for one classifier http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Estimates generalization accuracy of an SVM-based phenotypic trait classifier by aggregating balanced accuracy over 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times (e.g. PICA/libSVM on COG presence/absence matrices), reporting mean ± standard deviation and the per-fold misclassification pattern. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-16-s14-s1
skills.summary: Estimates generalization accuracy of an SVM-based phenotypic trait classifier by aggregating balanced accuracy over 5-fold cross-validation repeated 10 times (e.g. PICA/libSVM on COG presence/absence matrices), reporting mean ± standard deviation and the per-fold misclassification pattern.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is prediction on new metagenomic bins with an already-trained model — use phenotrex predict rather than re-running cross-validation Genomes fail the marker-COG completeness screen (fewer than 39/40 marker COGs); the paper's traits are only reliably predictable in ~60-70% complete genomes, so incomplete inputs should not enter training/evaluation The analysis needs method comparison across different ML algorithms rather than replicate accuracy estimation for one classifier

skills.description: Use when two or more sequence variant calling methods (e.g., HashSeq vs. DADA2) must be compared for downstream association performance on the same microbiota data set, requiring cross-validated classifier metrics per caller per metadata variable.
skills.name: repeated-kfold-cross-validation-evaluation
skills.search_text: repeated-kfold-cross-validation-evaluation Use when two or more sequence variant calling methods (e.g., HashSeq vs. DADA2) must be compared for downstream association performance on the same microbiota data set, requiring cross-validated classifier metrics per caller per metadata variable. The goal is detecting true low-abundance sequence variants — HashSeq is conservative and not sensitive for low-abundance sequences; DADA2 is recommended instead Input data have not been variant-called yet (raw FASTQ) — this skill evaluates already-generated variant count tables, not the calling itself Only one variant caller's features are of interest and no caller-vs-caller comparison is intended http://edamontology.org/topic_3474 Trains random forest classifiers (100 trees in scikit-learn) on 16S rRNA gene sequence variant count tables from competing variant callers (HashSeq vs. DADA2) and evaluates their association performance against sample metadata variables using RepeatedKFold cross-validation (4 splits x 10 repeats), so caller-derived variant sets can be compared on equal footing. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Trains random forest classifiers (100 trees in scikit-learn) on 16S rRNA gene sequence variant count tables from competing variant callers (HashSeq vs. DADA2) and evaluates their association performance against sample metadata variables using RepeatedKFold cross-validation (4 splits x 10 repeats), so caller-derived variant sets can be compared on equal footing.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is detecting true low-abundance sequence variants — HashSeq is conservative and not sensitive for low-abundance sequences; DADA2 is recommended instead Input data have not been variant-called yet (raw FASTQ) — this skill evaluates already-generated variant count tables, not the calling itself Only one variant caller's features are of interest and no caller-vs-caller comparison is intended

skills.description: Use when quantifying the runtime scaling of CATHAI's graph-generation/plotting pipeline against sample count (n), e.g. to reproduce the timing-versus-sample-count benchmark table or to decide the maximum sample size for usable operation.
skills.name: repeated-timing-measurement-averaging
skills.search_text: repeated-timing-measurement-averaging Use when quantifying the runtime scaling of CATHAI's graph-generation/plotting pipeline against sample count (n), e.g. to reproduce the timing-versus-sample-count benchmark table or to decide the maximum sample size for usable operation. The goal is user-facing clustering accuracy or visualization quality rather than runtime scaling of graph generation and plotting Input distances are not pairwise genomic-cluster distances loadable into CATHAI's shiny/data directory, so the Docker process step cannot be exercised Only a single timing run per configuration is feasible and the averaging protocol (10 repetitions) cannot be applied, making the benchmark table non-comparable Benchmark method for characterizing how CATHAI's precomputed network graph generation and local plotting scale with sample count, using 10 averaged wall-clock repetitions per sample count across iteration thresholds to establish the usable operating envelope. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbac040
skills.summary: Benchmark method for characterizing how CATHAI's precomputed network graph generation and local plotting scale with sample count, using 10 averaged wall-clock repetitions per sample count across iteration thresholds to establish the usable operating envelope.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is user-facing clustering accuracy or visualization quality rather than runtime scaling of graph generation and plotting Input distances are not pairwise genomic-cluster distances loadable into CATHAI's shiny/data directory, so the Docker process step cannot be exercised Only a single timing run per configuration is feasible and the averaging protocol (10 repetitions) cannot be applied, making the benchmark table non-comparable

skills.description: Use when a paper reports summary statistics (counts of items above thresholds) over a per-item results table — such as the Traitar Table S2 macroaccuracy table for 67 GIDEON phenotypes — and you must verify the reported numbers against the raw data.
skills.name: reported-count-verification
skills.search_text: reported-count-verification Use when a paper reports summary statistics (counts of items above thresholds) over a per-item results table — such as the Traitar Table S2 macroaccuracy table for 67 GIDEON phenotypes — and you must verify the reported numbers against the raw data. Input is already an aggregated summary (e.g., overall accuracies like phypat 82.6% / phypat+PGL 85.5%) rather than a per-item table — nothing to recount The claim concerns prediction outputs on new genomes (use the traitar phenotype workflow) rather than verifying counts over existing cross-validation results The reported statistic is not a count over per-item rows (e.g., a mean, AUC, or effect size) — a different verification approach is needed http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_3297 A reproducibility skill for recomputing aggregate counts reported in a publication (e.g., '53 of 67 phenotypes >80% macroaccuracy, 26 >=90%') from the underlying per-item data, using pandas to re-derive the numbers and flag agreement or mismatch. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00101-16
skills.summary: A reproducibility skill for recomputing aggregate counts reported in a publication (e.g., '53 of 67 phenotypes >80% macroaccuracy, 26 >=90%') from the underlying per-item data, using pandas to re-derive the numbers and flag agreement or mismatch.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already an aggregated summary (e.g., overall accuracies like phypat 82.6% / phypat+PGL 85.5%) rather than a per-item table — nothing to recount The claim concerns prediction outputs on new genomes (use the traitar phenotype workflow) rather than verifying counts over existing cross-validation results The reported statistic is not a count over per-item rows (e.g., a mean, AUC, or effect size) — a different verification approach is needed

skills.description: Use when a source card reports specific numeric findings (e.g. alpha mean 0.633 ± SD 0.028 for 475 high-recombination genes) that must be independently reproduced from pre-calculated polymorphism/divergence tables using a named tool.
skills.name: reported-result-reproducibility-check
skills.search_text: reported-result-reproducibility-check Use when a source card reports specific numeric findings (e.g. alpha mean 0.633 ± SD 0.028 for 475 high-recombination genes) that must be independently reproduced from pre-calculated polymorphism/divergence tables using a named tool. Input is raw population genomic data (FASTA/VCF alignments) rather than the pre-calculated polymorphism/divergence tables expected by iMKT — use the iMKTData pipelines first The target population or divergence species differs from D. melanogaster ZI vs D. simulans, since the reported alpha values being validated are specific to that comparison The goal is to test a novel hypothesis rather than verify already-reported numeric findings http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 Reproduces a published quantitative result — here, the eMKT alpha estimate for D. melanogaster genes in high-recombination regions vs the whole genome in the Zambia (ZI) population — by re-running the iMKT pipeline and comparing computed summary statistics against reported values before acceptance. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkz372
skills.summary: Reproduces a published quantitative result — here, the eMKT alpha estimate for D. melanogaster genes in high-recombination regions vs the whole genome in the Zambia (ZI) population — by re-running the iMKT pipeline and comparing computed summary statistics against reported values before acceptance.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw population genomic data (FASTA/VCF alignments) rather than the pre-calculated polymorphism/divergence tables expected by iMKT — use the iMKTData pipelines first The target population or divergence species differs from D. melanogaster ZI vs D. simulans, since the reported alpha values being validated are specific to that comparison The goal is to test a novel hypothesis rather than verify already-reported numeric findings

skills.description: Use when a paper reports a concrete quantitative outcome (cluster count, runtime, input size) and the underlying dataset or pipeline is re-accessible, so the reported figure can be independently recomputed and compared.
skills.name: reported-vs-computed-statistics-comparison
skills.search_text: reported-vs-computed-statistics-comparison Use when a paper reports a concrete quantitative outcome (cluster count, runtime, input size) and the underlying dataset or pipeline is re-accessible, so the reported figure can be independently recomputed and compared. The reported statistic cannot be traced to a re-accessible artifact (dataset unavailable, no parameters given), leaving nothing to recompute The input is a full-scale benchmark claim (e.g., >1000x speedup) that depends on dedicated 2 x 14-core server hardware not available to the practitioner — verify only configuration, not runtime equivalence The claim is qualitative (e.g., 'clusters of comparable quality as other tools') rather than a countable figure http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Recompute a published statistic from the underlying data or a feasible re-run and compare it numerically against the paper's reported value, stating relative deviation as the acceptance check. Applied here to the Metaclust clustering result (424 million clusters from 1,595,926,152 metagenomic proteins clustered in 10 h at ≥50% sequence identity). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Recompute a published statistic from the underlying data or a feasible re-run and compare it numerically against the paper's reported value, stating relative deviation as the acceptance check. Applied here to the Metaclust clustering result (424 million clusters from 1,595,926,152 metagenomic proteins clustered in 10 h at ≥50% sequence identity).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The reported statistic cannot be traced to a re-accessible artifact (dataset unavailable, no parameters given), leaving nothing to recompute The input is a full-scale benchmark claim (e.g., >1000x speedup) that depends on dedicated 2 x 14-core server hardware not available to the practitioner — verify only configuration, not runtime equivalence The claim is qualitative (e.g., 'clusters of comparable quality as other tools') rather than a countable figure

skills.description: Use when comparing 16S DC methods (DADA2, Deblur, de novo, closed/open-reference) by measuring how accurately each predicted feature table recapitulates a known mock-community composition via weighted UniFrac.
skills.name: representative-sequence-distribution-comparison
skills.search_text: representative-sequence-distribution-comparison Use when comparing 16S DC methods (DADA2, Deblur, de novo, closed/open-reference) by measuring how accurately each predicted feature table recapitulates a known mock-community composition via weighted UniFrac. Input is already a co-occurrence network or interaction matrix — this skill operates on feature/representative-sequence tables, not network objects The true (expected) community composition is unknown — weighted UniFrac comparison to a ground truth cannot be computed Comparing methods on natural environmental samples where no expected distribution exists http://edamontology.org/topic_0637 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Benchmark denoising/clustering (DC) methods by computing the weighted UniFrac distance between predicted representative-sequence (feature) distributions and the expected mockrobiota distributions on the Greengenes phylogeny, to identify which DC method best recapitulates true mock-community sequences. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00961-22
skills.summary: Benchmark denoising/clustering (DC) methods by computing the weighted UniFrac distance between predicted representative-sequence (feature) distributions and the expected mockrobiota distributions on the Greengenes phylogeny, to identify which DC method best recapitulates true mock-community sequences.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a co-occurrence network or interaction matrix — this skill operates on feature/representative-sequence tables, not network objects The true (expected) community composition is unknown — weighted UniFrac comparison to a ground truth cannot be computed Comparing methods on natural environmental samples where no expected distribution exists

skills.description: Use when you need to estimate how many clusterable sequence pairs a clustering tool misses (false-negative rate) on a protein set too large (e.g. 123M UniProt sequences) for exhaustive pairwise verification.
skills.name: representative-sequence-sampling
skills.search_text: representative-sequence-sampling Use when you need to estimate how many clusterable sequence pairs a clustering tool misses (false-negative rate) on a protein set too large (e.g. 123M UniProt sequences) for exhaustive pairwise verification. The sequence set is small enough that exhaustive all-against-all pairwise comparison is feasible — then compute true cluster quality directly instead of sampling representatives. You need sensitivity/recall of a search tool against a curated ground truth (e.g. Swiss-Prot) rather than an estimate of pairs missed by a clustering prefilter. The clustering threshold differs from the BLAST filtering criteria — mismatched identity/coverage settings (e.g. 90% identity with -n 5 for CD-HIT vs 50% with -n 3) make the reference set invalid for the comparison. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 Randomly sample ~1000 representative sequences from each clustering tool's output and run BLAST all-against-all among them to build a trusted reference set of homologous pairs, enabling estimation of false-negative rates (missed clusterable pairs) for huge-scale sequence clustering tools such as Linclust, MMseqs2, CD-HIT, and UCLUST. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Randomly sample ~1000 representative sequences from each clustering tool's output and run BLAST all-against-all among them to build a trusted reference set of homologous pairs, enabling estimation of false-negative rates (missed clusterable pairs) for huge-scale sequence clustering tools such as Linclust, MMseqs2, CD-HIT, and UCLUST.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sequence set is small enough that exhaustive all-against-all pairwise comparison is feasible — then compute true cluster quality directly instead of sampling representatives. You need sensitivity/recall of a search tool against a curated ground truth (e.g. Swiss-Prot) rather than an estimate of pairs missed by a clustering prefilter. The clustering threshold differs from the BLAST filtering criteria — mismatched identity/coverage settings (e.g. 90% identity with -n 5 for CD-HIT vs 50% with -n 3) make the reference set invalid for the comparison.

skills.description: Use when averaging per-region pairwise synteny scores into APSS matrices over all sample pairs and runs must be reproducible despite random subsampling of regions.
skills.name: reproducible-random-seed-sampling
skills.search_text: reproducible-random-seed-sampling Use when averaging per-region pairwise synteny scores into APSS matrices over all sample pairs and runs must be reproducible despite random subsampling of regions. A sample pair has fewer than n homologous regions detected — such pairs are excluded from downstream analysis rather than subsampled The goal is to compare sequences without homologous genomic regions or when SNP-based resolution of point mutations is the target (SynTracker is insensitive to SNPs; combine with an SNP-based tool instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Randomly subsample n homologous genomic regions per pairwise comparison (default n = 40, 60, 80, 100, 200) and average the per-region synteny scores into an APSS, using a fixed seed=1 so repeated SynTracker runs are reproducible. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41587-024-02276-2
skills.summary: Randomly subsample n homologous genomic regions per pairwise comparison (default n = 40, 60, 80, 100, 200) and average the per-region synteny scores into an APSS, using a fixed seed=1 so repeated SynTracker runs are reproducible.
skills.when_to_use_negative: A sample pair has fewer than n homologous regions detected — such pairs are excluded from downstream analysis rather than subsampled The goal is to compare sequences without homologous genomic regions or when SNP-based resolution of point mutations is the target (SynTracker is insensitive to SNPs; combine with an SNP-based tool instead)

skills.description: Use when you need to train (or retrain) an end-to-end DNN contact predictor from an MSA, e.g. reproducing the DeepECA Baseline Model rows of the CASP11/CASP12 precision tables.
skills.name: residual-dnn-contact-prediction-training
skills.search_text: residual-dnn-contact-prediction-training Use when you need to train (or retrain) an end-to-end DNN contact predictor from an MSA, e.g. reproducing the DeepECA Baseline Model rows of the CASP11/CASP12 precision tables. You only need to run inference with the released pre-trained model — use pipeline.py directly rather than retraining. The target proteins exceed 700 residues or are shorter than 25 residues, or lack DSSP-assignable secondary structure for ≥80% of residues, since such proteins were excluded from the training dataset. A local, non-DNN ECA method (e.g. PSICOV, CCMpred) suffices — this skill is for end-to-end DNN training, not graphical-lasso/pseudolikelihood estimation. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0130 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 Trains a 60-layer residual network with the ADAM optimizer (learning rate 0.0005) and batch normalization to predict protein contacts end-to-end from covariance matrices computed on HHblits-generated MSAs, so that even this baseline outperforms existing ECA methods on CASP11/CASP12. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-3190-x
skills.summary: Trains a 60-layer residual network with the ADAM optimizer (learning rate 0.0005) and batch normalization to predict protein contacts end-to-end from covariance matrices computed on HHblits-generated MSAs, so that even this baseline outperforms existing ECA methods on CASP11/CASP12.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You only need to run inference with the released pre-trained model — use pipeline.py directly rather than retraining. The target proteins exceed 700 residues or are shorter than 25 residues, or lack DSSP-assignable secondary structure for ≥80% of residues, since such proteins were excluded from the training dataset. skills.description: Use when a synthetic dataset with known OTU composition is available and you need to score how faithfully different amplicon pipelines (MICCA, QIIME, UPARSE, mothur) reproduce true relative abundances.

skills.description: Decision support for choosing a MetaMiner database-construction mode when RiPPs must be identified from spectra with paired genomic data and the analyst must weigh sensitivity for novel RiPPs (motif-ORF) against broader ORF enumeration (all-ORF) at strict FDR.

skills.search_text: ripp-identification-mode-comparison Decision support for choosing a MetaMiner database-construction mode when RiPPs must be identified from spectra with paired genomic data and the analyst must weigh sensitivity for novel RiPPs (motif-ORF) against broader ORF enumeration (all-ORF) at strict FDR. The spectra lack paired genomics/metagenomics data — per the article, ~99% of GNPS spectra cannot be searched against genomes, making peptidogenomic mode comparison inapplicable. The goal is discovery of non-ribosomal peptides — Dereplicator+ analysis showed many spectral families belong to non-ribosomal peptide classes outside MetaMiner's RiPP scope. The candidate RiPPs have no sequence similarity to known RiPPs and the analysis depends solely on motif-ORF mode, which the article states misses such peptides. http://edamontology.org/topic_3520 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 Compares MetaMiner's motif-ORF versus all-ORF precursor-peptide database construction modes for RiPP identification from spectra paired with genomes/metagenomes, evaluated at target-decoy FDR thresholds of 0% and 1%. It quantifies how genome-mining mode sensitivity trades off against known/unknown RiPP discovery yield. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2019.09.004
skills.summary: Compares MetaMiner's motif-ORF versus all-ORF precursor-peptide database construction modes for RiPP identification from spectra paired with genomes/metagenomes, evaluated at target-decoy FDR thresholds of 0% and 1%. skills.search_text: rmse-trajectory-accuracy-evaluation Use when comparing two dynamical-system parameterizations (e.g., trained on denoised vs raw/pseudo-count abundances) by measuring RMSE of predicted versus observed community trajectories over time. The model output is not a time-series trajectory prediction (e.g., static cross-sectional abundance estimates) — RMSE over trajectories is meaningless without a temporal dimension Evaluating zero-detection performance (biological vs technical zeros), where posterior probabilities from LUMINATE's `estimate` step are the relevant output instead Trajectories contain ultra-sparse taxa (>90% missing entries) that were not filtered, since these have little information and can distort RMSE comparisons http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Evaluates dynamical-system (cLV/gLV) trajectory prediction accuracy by computing root-mean-square-error (RMSE) between one-step-ahead predicted and observed taxa trajectories, here to show that cLV trained on LUMINATE-estimated relative abundances outperforms pseudo-count-trained baselines on the C. diff and Diet datasets. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.cels.2020.05.006
skills.summary: Evaluates dynamical-system (cLV/gLV) trajectory prediction accuracy by computing root-mean-square-error (RMSE) between one-step-ahead predicted and observed taxa trajectories, here to show that cLV trained on LUMINATE-estimated relative abundances outperforms pseudo-count-trained baselines on the C. diff and Diet datasets.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The model output is not a time-series trajectory prediction (e.g., static cross-sectional abundance estimates) — RMSE over trajectories is meaningless without a temporal dimension Evaluating zero-detection performance (biological vs technical zeros), where posterior probabilities from LUMINATE's `estimate` step are the relevant output instead Trajectories contain ultra-sparse taxa (>90% missing entries) that were not filtered, since these have little information and can distort RMSE comparisons

skills.description: Use when you need to benchmark a differential abundance method's classification performance against a comparator on simulated taxa with known null/differential status, requiring ROC curves, AUC with 95% CI, and a DeLong test for correlated ROC curves.
skills.name: roc-auc-evaluation
skills.search_text: roc-auc-evaluation Use when you need to benchmark a differential abundance method's classification performance against a comparator on simulated taxa with known null/differential status, requiring ROC curves, AUC with 95% CI, and a DeLong test for correlated ROC curves. Analyzing real microbiome data without known ground-truth null/differential labels — ROC/AUC classification metrics are not computable Comparing methods on independently simulated datasets (DeLong's test requires correlated ROC curves from the same paired data) The goal is meta-analysis pooling of effect estimates across studies (use random-effects meta-analysis via meta.taxa instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Benchmark differential abundance methods (e.g., GAMLSS-BEZI vs LMAS) on simulated zero-inflated beta relative abundance data with known ground truth by computing ROC curves, AUC estimates with 95% CIs, and comparing paired AUCs via DeLong's test. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2744-2
skills.summary: Benchmark differential abundance methods (e.g., GAMLSS-BEZI vs LMAS) on simulated zero-inflated beta relative abundance data with known ground truth by computing ROC curves, AUC estimates with 95% CIs, and comparing paired AUCs via DeLong's test.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Analyzing real microbiome data without known ground-truth null/differential labels — ROC/AUC classification metrics are not computable Comparing methods on independently simulated datasets (DeLong's test requires correlated ROC curves from the same paired data) The goal is meta-analysis pooling of effect estimates across studies (use random-effects meta-analysis via meta.taxa instead)
