skills.description: Use when scoring gene-finder output (e.g. Glimmer-MG, FragGeneScan, MetaGeneMark predictions) on simulated metagenomic reads where true gene coordinates are known and per-condition sensitivity/precision must be tabulated by read technology and error rate.
skills.name: sensitivity-precision-computation
skills.search_text: sensitivity-precision-computation Use when scoring gene-finder output (e.g. Glimmer-MG, FragGeneScan, MetaGeneMark predictions) on simulated metagenomic reads where true gene coordinates are known and per-condition sensitivity/precision must be tabulated by read technology and error rate. Real metagenomic reads with no reference annotation — sensitivity cannot be computed without ground truth gene coordinates Comparing against whole-genome gene finders on complete genomes — Glimmer3 already identifies >99% of genes there; fragmented-gene scoring specific to metagenomic reads is the relevant regime Evaluating phylogenetic classification or clustering quality itself rather than gene-prediction accuracy http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 Computes nucleotide-level (and gene-level) sensitivity and precision of metagenomic gene predictions by aligning predicted coordinates against simulated reference annotations, as used to benchmark Glimmer-MG against FragGeneScan and MetaGeneMark across Sanger, 454, and Illumina reads at 0–2% error rates. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkr1067
skills.summary: Computes nucleotide-level (and gene-level) sensitivity and precision of metagenomic gene predictions by aligning predicted coordinates against simulated reference annotations, as used to benchmark Glimmer-MG against FragGeneScan and MetaGeneMark across Sanger, 454, and Illumina reads at 0–2% error rates.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Real metagenomic reads with no reference annotation — sensitivity cannot be computed without ground truth gene coordinates Comparing against whole-genome gene finders on complete genomes — Glimmer3 already identifies >99% of genes there; fragmented-gene scoring specific to metagenomic reads is the relevant regime Evaluating phylogenetic classification or clustering quality itself rather than gene-prediction accuracy

skills.description: Use when you have per-isolate resistant/susceptible predictions plus phenotypic DST labels on an independent validation set and need overall and per-drug sensitivity/specificity, e.g. reproducing Mykrobe's 82.6%/98.5% MTBC_B result.
skills.name: sensitivity-specificity-benchmark-evaluation
skills.search_text: sensitivity-specificity-benchmark-evaluation Use when you have per-isolate resistant/susceptible predictions plus phenotypic DST labels on an independent validation set and need overall and per-drug sensitivity/specificity, e.g. reproducing Mykrobe's 82.6%/98.5% MTBC_B result. You lack phenotypic DST ground truth for the isolates, so no confusion matrix against a reference can be built A drug has ≤10 resistant samples in the validation set — the paper only estimated false-negative rates where there were sufficiently many (>10) resistant samples Pyrazinamide evaluation: the paper completely excluded pyrazinamide since known mutations are poorly predictive, so benchmarks should not include it http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 http://edamontology.org/topic_2815 Benchmark a genotype-based resistance predictor by tabulating per-drug predictions against phenotypic DST labels in confusion matrices and computing overall and per-drug sensitivity/specificity, as done for Mykrobe predictor on the 1,609-sample MTBC_B M. tuberculosis validation set (82.6%/98.5%) with a side-by-side KvarQ comparison. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms10063
skills.summary: Benchmark a genotype-based resistance predictor by tabulating per-drug predictions against phenotypic DST labels in confusion matrices and computing overall and per-drug sensitivity/specificity, as done for Mykrobe predictor on the 1,609-sample MTBC_B M. tuberculosis validation set (82.6%/98.5%) with a side-by-side KvarQ comparison.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You lack phenotypic DST ground truth for the isolates, so no confusion matrix against a reference can be built A drug has ≤10 resistant samples in the validation set — the paper only estimated false-negative rates where there were sufficiently many (>10) resistant samples Pyrazinamide evaluation: the paper completely excluded pyrazinamide since known mutations are poorly predictive, so benchmarks should not include it

skills.description: Use when you have per-sample resistance predictions (e.g. Mykrobe JSON calls) plus phenotype labels and must quantify false negatives/positives as sensitivity and specificity, per drug and overall.
skills.name: sensitivity-specificity-calculation
skills.search_text: sensitivity-specificity-calculation Use when you have per-sample resistance predictions (e.g. Mykrobe JSON calls) plus phenotype labels and must quantify false negatives/positives as sensitivity and specificity, per drug and overall. The predictions have not yet been parsed from Mykrobe JSON into a tabular report (run Mykrobe Parser first) No phenotypic reference labels exist for the samples — sensitivity/specificity cannot be defined without gold-standard calls A drug has fewer than ~10 resistant samples in the validation set, making false-negative rate estimates unreliable per the article's own criterion http://edamontology.org/topic_3303 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Compute per-drug and overall sensitivity/specificity of Mykrobe predictor's resistance calls by comparing parsed JSON predictions against phenotypic references (BSAC disc test, Phoenix), as done for S. aureus (99.1%/99.6% across 12 antibiotics) and M. tuberculosis (82.6%/98.5%). metagenomics/v1 10.1038/ncomms10063
skills.summary: Compute per-drug and overall sensitivity/specificity of Mykrobe predictor's resistance calls by comparing parsed JSON predictions against phenotypic references (BSAC disc test, Phoenix), as done for S. aureus (99.1%/99.6% across 12 antibiotics) and M. tuberculosis (82.6%/98.5%).
skills.when_to_use_negative: The predictions have not yet been parsed from Mykrobe JSON into a tabular report (run Mykrobe Parser first) No phenotypic reference labels exist for the samples — sensitivity/specificity cannot be defined without gold-standard calls A drug has fewer than ~10 resistant samples in the validation set, making false-negative rate estimates unreliable per the article's own criterion

skills.description: Use when a heuristic HMM score filter (e.g. KEMET --threshold_value) must be calibrated so candidate missing-KO calls agree with an independently verified reference set such as translated BLASTp hits against NCBI nr.
skills.name: sensitivity-specificity-threshold-optimization
skills.search_text: sensitivity-specificity-threshold-optimization Use when a heuristic HMM score filter (e.g. KEMET --threshold_value) must be calibrated so candidate missing-KO calls agree with an independently verified reference set such as translated BLASTp hits against NCBI nr. Input hits are already experimentally or manually verified — no threshold calibration against ground truth is needed The annotation tool used does not expose a tunable score filter (e.g. eggNOG-mapper or KAAS KO annotation used only for KEGG MODULES recap tables) The task is KEGG Module completeness evaluation only, run with --skip_hmm, since no HMM hit filtering occurs http://edamontology.org/topic_0154 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Empirical tuning of a profile-HMM hit quality threshold (KEMET's nhmmer score-per-length --threshold_value, default 0.43) against a manually curated BLASTp/NCBI nr ground truth, to maximize recovery of genuine missing KEGG orthologs while minimizing false positives. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.csbj.2022.03.015
skills.summary: Empirical tuning of a profile-HMM hit quality threshold (KEMET's nhmmer score-per-length --threshold_value, default 0.43) against a manually curated BLASTp/NCBI nr ground truth, to maximize recovery of genuine missing KEGG orthologs while minimizing false positives.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input hits are already experimentally or manually verified — no threshold calibration against ground truth is needed The annotation tool used does not expose a tunable score filter (e.g. eggNOG-mapper or KAAS KO annotation used only for KEGG MODULES recap tables) The task is KEGG Module completeness evaluation only, run with --skip_hmm, since no HMM hit filtering occurs

skills.description: Use when raw Sentinel-1 GRDH IW products (uncalibrated digital numbers in slant-range coordinates) must be converted to calibrated, terrain-flattened, orthorectified gamma_0 backscatter at 10 m pixel spacing.
skills.name: sentinel-1-sar-preprocessing
skills.search_text: sentinel-1-sar-preprocessing Use when raw Sentinel-1 GRDH IW products (uncalibrated digital numbers in slant-range coordinates) must be converted to calibrated, terrain-flattened, orthorectified gamma_0 backscatter at 10 m pixel spacing. Input is Single Look Complex (SLC) data — the study used only backscatter coefficients, so deriving GRDH from SLC was deemed unnecessary and this chain targets GRDH only The analysis requires spatial speckle filtering or per-scene spatial smoothing — this chain deliberately skips speckle filtering and relies on temporal median compositing instead The task needs preprocessed data before precise orbits become available (~2 weeks after data take), since the workflow depends on precise orbit state vectors Reproduce the Sentinel-1 GRDH-to-gamma_0 preprocessing chain of Bae et al. (2019) using ESA's open-source SNAP toolbox via its Graph Processing Tools (GPT) command-line interface and the provided Sentinel1_GRDH_to_gamma0.xml batch file. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-019-12737-x
skills.summary: Reproduce the Sentinel-1 GRDH-to-gamma_0 preprocessing chain of Bae et al. (2019) using ESA's open-source SNAP toolbox via its Graph Processing Tools (GPT) command-line interface and the provided Sentinel1_GRDH_to_gamma0.xml batch file.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is Single Look Complex (SLC) data — the study used only backscatter coefficients, so deriving GRDH from SLC was deemed unnecessary and this chain targets GRDH only The analysis requires spatial speckle filtering or per-scene spatial smoothing — this chain deliberately skips speckle filtering and relies on temporal median compositing instead The task needs preprocessed data before precise orbits become available (~2 weeks after data take), since the workflow depends on precise orbit state vectors

skills.description: Use when auditing probe coverage of an existing HUBDesign probe set (e.g., probes/Sepsis FASTA) against annotated bacterial genomes to quantify per-species and per-genus targeting fractions.
skills.name: sepsis-pathogen-probe-set-reanalysis
skills.search_text: sepsis-pathogen-probe-set-reanalysis Use when auditing probe coverage of an existing HUBDesign probe set (e.g., probes/Sepsis FASTA) against annotated bacterial genomes to quantify per-species and per-genus targeting fractions. The goal is de novo probe design rather than auditing an existing probe set — use the HUBDesign pipeline (Clustering, Assignment, Identification, Filtering, Selection) instead Input genomes are unannotated or unannotatable; HUBDesign relies on annotated genomes and probes cannot be designed for unknown genomes The probe set targets non-bacterial diversity (e.g., the 56 RefSeq coronavirus genomes), where the sepsis genome/taxon metadata does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Reanalyzes the HUBDesign sepsis probe set by aligning every probe sequence against BLASTn databases built from the 1,926 annotated sepsis bacterial genomes (81 species, 35 genera) to compute per-species and per-genus probe coverage, confirming that all strains have genus-level probes and 53.3% have species-level probes. metagenomics/v1 10.1016/j.crmeth.2021.100069
skills.summary: Reanalyzes the HUBDesign sepsis probe set by aligning every probe sequence against BLASTn databases built from the 1,926 annotated sepsis bacterial genomes (81 species, 35 genera) to compute per-species and per-genus probe coverage, confirming that all strains have genus-level probes and 53.3% have species-level probes.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is de novo probe design rather than auditing an existing probe set — use the HUBDesign pipeline (Clustering, Assignment, Identification, Filtering, Selection) instead Input genomes are unannotated or unannotatable; HUBDesign relies on annotated genomes and probes cannot be designed for unknown genomes The probe set targets non-bacterial diversity (e.g., the 56 RefSeq coronavirus genomes), where the sepsis genome/taxon metadata does not apply

skills.description: Use when you need to determine the minimum RAM/CPU allocation for efficient alignment of a fixed-size sequence set (e.g. 50,000-sequence FASTA files) against a large local database (~6 GB nr Bacteria), or to find where added memory stops paying off.
skills.name: sequence-alignment-benchmarking
skills.search_text: sequence-alignment-benchmarking Use when you need to determine the minimum RAM/CPU allocation for efficient alignment of a fixed-size sequence set (e.g. 50,000-sequence FASTA files) against a large local database (~6 GB nr Bacteria), or to find where added memory stops paying off. The input is a completed abundance/annotation summary table rather than raw sequence files to align The reference database already fits comfortably in available memory, so a memory-scaling benchmark would only measure constant overhead The goal is accuracy benchmarking of the aligner (e.g. fast vs. sensitive mode) rather than resource-scaling benchmarking http://edamontology.org/topic_0091 http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 A benchmarking skill for measuring how sequence-annotation runtime scales with allocated compute resources (RAM at fixed CPU), using SAMSA2's DIAMOND annotation against a local, DIAMOND-indexed reference database as the workload. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: A benchmarking skill for measuring how sequence-annotation runtime scales with allocated compute resources (RAM at fixed CPU), using SAMSA2's DIAMOND annotation against a local, DIAMOND-indexed reference database as the workload.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is a completed abundance/annotation summary table rather than raw sequence files to align The reference database already fits comfortably in available memory, so a memory-scaling benchmark would only measure constant overhead The goal is accuracy benchmarking of the aligner (e.g. fast vs. sensitive mode) rather than resource-scaling benchmarking

skills.description: Use when raw metatranscriptome reads (e.g. FASTQ) must be assigned organism or functional annotations by aligning them to a local protein database, and speed or reproducibility rules out BLAST and web services like MG-RAST.
skills.name: sequence-annotation-database-mapping
skills.search_text: sequence-annotation-database-mapping Use when raw metatranscriptome reads (e.g. FASTQ) must be assigned organism or functional annotations by aligning them to a local protein database, and speed or reproducibility rules out BLAST and web services like MG-RAST. Reads are unfiltered ribosomal sequences — SortMeRNA filtering must come first since rRNA alignments are discarded regardless High accuracy is required and compute/memory budgets do not allow DIAMOND --sensitive mode's significantly increased memory requirements Analysis goal is de novo assembly or genome annotation rather than direct read-to-protein-database mapping http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Annotation of metatranscriptomic reads by direct alignment against local, DIAMOND-indexed protein reference databases (NCBI RefSeq, SEED Subsystems, or custom databases such as CAZy) using DIAMOND within the SAMSA2 pipeline, replacing slow BLAST or web-service (MG-RAST) annotation. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-018-2189-z
skills.summary: Annotation of metatranscriptomic reads by direct alignment against local, DIAMOND-indexed protein reference databases (NCBI RefSeq, SEED Subsystems, or custom databases such as CAZy) using DIAMOND within the SAMSA2 pipeline, replacing slow BLAST or web-service (MG-RAST) annotation.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are unfiltered ribosomal sequences — SortMeRNA filtering must come first since rRNA alignments are discarded regardless High accuracy is required and compute/memory budgets do not allow DIAMOND --sensitive mode's significantly increased memory requirements Analysis goal is de novo assembly or genome annotation rather than direct read-to-protein-database mapping

skills.description: Use when benchmarking alignment-based marker retrieval (e.g., Patchwork/DIAMOND) against a known set of reference USCOs and you need percent identity, query coverage, and a combined pidentical,cov score per marker.
skills.name: sequence-coverage-metrics-computation
skills.search_text: sequence-coverage-metrics-computation Use when benchmarking alignment-based marker retrieval (e.g., Patchwork/DIAMOND) against a known set of reference USCOs and you need percent identity, query coverage, and a combined pidentical,cov score per marker. References are not near-USCOs — the article recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences, which would invalidate coverage/identity comparisons Query and reference are the same species with expected near-perfect recovery — use the same-species benchmark (815/815 retrieved, 95.9% identity) rather than the divergent-reference metric You lack a defined set of homologous reference USCOs to restrict evaluation to, since the metric is only meaningful against known homologs http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 Compute the combined retrieval-quality metric pidentical,cov = nmatch/naligned x cov used by the Patchwork benchmark, where cov is total recovered marker length divided by total reference USCO length, to quantify marker retrieval accuracy across divergent species pairs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Compute the combined retrieval-quality metric pidentical,cov = nmatch/naligned x cov used by the Patchwork benchmark, where cov is total recovered marker length divided by total reference USCO length, to quantify marker retrieval accuracy across divergent species pairs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: References are not near-USCOs — the article recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs to avoid chimeric sequences, which would invalidate coverage/identity comparisons Query and reference are the same species with expected near-perfect recovery — use the same-species benchmark (815/815 retrieved, 95.9% identity) rather than the divergent-reference metric You lack a defined set of homologous reference USCOs to restrict evaluation to, since the metric is only meaningful against known homologs

skills.description: Use when you need to characterize or validate the asymptotic runtime scaling of a clustering or search tool by measuring wall-clock times on nested random subsets of a sequence database.
skills.name: sequence-database-subset-sampling
skills.search_text: sequence-database-subset-sampling Use when you need to characterize or validate the asymptotic runtime scaling of a clustering or search tool by measuring wall-clock times on nested random subsets of a sequence database. You want clustering quality or sensitivity benchmarks rather than runtime scaling — this skill only measures wall-clock time versus input size The tool under test cannot complete on the smallest subset within your compute budget, since nested-subset fitting requires runtimes at every scale point You need exact worst-case complexity analysis; fitted exponents are empirical approximations ('very roughly quadratic') valid only near the tested identity threshold and hardware http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0623 Empirically measure how sequence-clustering runtime scales with input set size N by clustering nested random subsets of a database (e.g., UniProt 2016_03) and fitting a power law T = a*N^b in log-log space, as done in the Linclust paper to demonstrate linear O(mN) scaling. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Empirically measure how sequence-clustering runtime scales with input set size N by clustering nested random subsets of a database (e.g., UniProt 2016_03) and fitting a power law T = a*N^b in log-log space, as done in the Linclust paper to demonstrate linear O(mN) scaling.
skills.when_to_use_negative: You want clustering quality or sensitivity benchmarks rather than runtime scaling — this skill only measures wall-clock time versus input size The tool under test cannot complete on the smallest subset within your compute budget, since nested-subset fitting requires runtimes at every scale point You need exact worst-case complexity analysis; fitted exponents are empirical approximations ('very roughly quadratic') valid only near the tested identity threshold and hardware

skills.description: Use when a metagenomic sample contains closely related strains (e.g. the HIV lab mix) and the goal is to recover per-strain sequences from a de Bruijn assembly graph rather than settling for a single consensus contig.
skills.name: sequence-graph-gfa-extraction
skills.search_text: sequence-graph-gfa-extraction Use when a metagenomic sample contains closely related strains (e.g. the HIV lab mix) and the goal is to recover per-strain sequences from a de Bruijn assembly graph rather than settling for a single consensus contig. When the goal is a single consensus assembly for coverage/contiguity benchmarking rather than per-strain sequence recovery — consensus assemblers are sufficient and strain graph walking adds unnecessary complexity When the sample has low strain-level diversity and no local variation signatures exist in the assembly graph, leaving no graph branches to resolve When no per-strain reference genomes are available for BLAST-scored branch selection or dnadiff validation http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Reconstructs strain-specific contigs from MetaCortex's sequence-graph (GFA) output by performing per-strain BLAST-scored graph walks, capturing intra-species variation that consensus metagenomic assembly collapses into a single contig. Applied with dnadiff to validate that strain-specific paths are more accurate per strain than the consensus contig. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad020
skills.summary: Reconstructs strain-specific contigs from MetaCortex's sequence-graph (GFA) output by performing per-strain BLAST-scored graph walks, capturing intra-species variation that consensus metagenomic assembly collapses into a single contig. Applied with dnadiff to validate that strain-specific paths are more accurate per strain than the consensus contig.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is a single consensus assembly for coverage/contiguity benchmarking rather than per-strain sequence recovery — consensus assemblers are sufficient and strain graph walking adds unnecessary complexity When the sample has low strain-level diversity and no local variation signatures exist in the assembly graph, leaving no graph branches to resolve When no per-strain reference genomes are available for BLAST-scored branch selection or dnadiff validation

skills.description: Use when a DIAMOND BLASTX search of fragmented short-read assembly contigs (or raw reads) against amino acid reference sequences produces multiple scattered hits per marker that must be merged into one continuous sequence for phylogenomic retrieval.
skills.name: sequence-hit-stitching-and-region-concatenation
skills.search_text: sequence-hit-stitching-and-region-concatenation Use when a DIAMOND BLASTX search of fragmented short-read assembly contigs (or raw reads) against amino acid reference sequences produces multiple scattered hits per marker that must be merged into one continuous sequence for phylogenomic retrieval. When the query is a single complete, well-annotated genome where markers can be extracted directly with annotation tools like BUSCO — stitching is designed for fragmented short-read assemblies or reads When references are not (near-)single-copy orthologs — the article warns that chimeric sequences can arise and recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs When a de novo gene predictor or read-to-tree tool like Read2Tree is preferred and no reference-guided stitching is desired http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3293 Merges multiple overlapping or gappy alignment hits (HSPs) from a translated nucleotide-to-protein similarity search into a single continuous query sequence per reference, then trims noncoding stretches and concatenates/realigns remaining regions to recover full-length phylogenetic markers from fragmented WGS data. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gbe/evad227
skills.summary: Merges multiple overlapping or gappy alignment hits (HSPs) from a translated nucleotide-to-protein similarity search into a single continuous query sequence per reference, then trims noncoding stretches and concatenates/realigns remaining regions to recover full-length phylogenetic markers from fragmented WGS data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the query is a single complete, well-annotated genome where markers can be extracted directly with annotation tools like BUSCO — stitching is designed for fragmented short-read assemblies or reads When references are not (near-)single-copy orthologs — the article warns that chimeric sequences can arise and recommends limiting reference sequences to near-USCOs When a de novo gene predictor or read-to-tree tool like Read2Tree is preferred and no reference-guided stitching is desired

skills.description: Use when clustering protein or nucleotide sequence sets at a chosen sequence identity level (e.g. 90%, 70%, or 50%) and the tool-specific parameters — --min-seq-id, -c/-n for CD-HIT, --id for UCLUST — must be matched to that threshold.
skills.name: sequence-identity-threshold-configuration
skills.search_text: sequence-identity-threshold-configuration Use when clustering protein or nucleotide sequence sets at a chosen sequence identity level (e.g. 90%, 70%, or 50%) and the tool-specific parameters — --min-seq-id, -c/-n for CD-HIT, --id for UCLUST — must be matched to that threshold. The task is pairwise sequence search or alignment scoring rather than redundancy clustering — identity thresholds there (e.g. BLAST-style criteria) are configured differently The identity cutoff falls between the validated word-size regimes (e.g. needing a cutoff between 40% and 50% where CD-HIT -n 3 is no longer matched) Exact similarity verification of all candidate pairs is required, since k-mer-prefiltered clustering at low identity is only approximate (Linclust's prefilter is approximate) http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Configures and validates sequence identity thresholds (e.g. 90%, 70%, 50%) when running clustering tools like Linclust/MMseqs2, CD-HIT, and UCLUST, mapping each threshold to the correct word-size/-n and identity-parameter combinations. Correct threshold-to-parameter pairing is essential because runtime and clustering quality diverge sharply between tools as the identity level drops. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-04964-5
skills.summary: Configures and validates sequence identity thresholds (e.g. 90%, 70%, 50%) when running clustering tools like Linclust/MMseqs2, CD-HIT, and UCLUST, mapping each threshold to the correct word-size/-n and identity-parameter combinations. Correct threshold-to-parameter pairing is essential because runtime and clustering quality diverge sharply between tools as the identity level drops.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The task is pairwise sequence search or alignment scoring rather than redundancy clustering — identity thresholds there (e.g. BLAST-style criteria) are configured differently The identity cutoff falls between the validated word-size regimes (e.g. needing a cutoff between 40% and 50% where CD-HIT -n 3 is no longer matched) Exact similarity verification of all candidate pairs is required, since k-mer-prefiltered clustering at low identity is only approximate (Linclust's prefilter is approximate)

skills.description: Use when a merged gene catalog (e.g. ARG sequences from ResFinder, CARD, MegaRes, AMRFinderPlus, ARGANNOT) has been deduplicated and clustered, and you must report or validate the resulting sequence-count and centroid-length statistics.
skills.name: sequence-length-distribution-statistics
skills.search_text: sequence-length-distribution-statistics Use when a merged gene catalog (e.g. ARG sequences from ResFinder, CARD, MegaRes, AMRFinderPlus, ARGANNOT) has been deduplicated and clustered, and you must report or validate the resulting sequence-count and centroid-length statistics. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a curated multi-fasta gene catalog — length statistics of reads do not validate database curation. The clustering thresholds differ from the PanRes parameters (90% identity / 90% coverage); counts and length distributions will not be comparable to the reported 14,078 / 5,280 / 762 bp values. The goal is profiling ARG abundance in metagenomic samples (that is ARGprofiler's role) rather than characterizing the reference database itself. http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_3071 Compute summary length statistics (count, min, max, median) over a curated nucleotide sequence catalog — here the PanRes ARG centroid set — to characterize a merged, deduplicated, homology-reduced database and validate it against published values. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btae086
skills.summary: Compute summary length statistics (count, min, max, median) over a curated nucleotide sequence catalog — here the PanRes ARG centroid set — to characterize a merged, deduplicated, homology-reduced database and validate it against published values.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than a curated multi-fasta gene catalog — length statistics of reads do not validate database curation. The clustering thresholds differ from the PanRes parameters (90% identity / 90% coverage); counts and length distributions will not be comparable to the reported 14,078 / 5,280 / 762 bp values. The goal is profiling ARG abundance in metagenomic samples (that is ARGprofiler's role) rather than characterizing the reference database itself.

skills.description: Use when a metagenomic assembly (contigs/scaffolds in FASTA, e.g. KOW/ZS mine assemblies from MG-RAST mgp80771) is about to be classified by kmer-signature tools such as PlasFlow and contains many short contigs.
skills.name: sequence-length-filtering-of-assembly-contigs
skills.search_text: sequence-length-filtering-of-assembly-contigs Use when a metagenomic assembly (contigs/scaffolds in FASTA, e.g. KOW/ZS mine assemblies from MG-RAST mgp80771) is about to be classified by kmer-signature tools such as PlasFlow and contains many short contigs. Input is raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs (use read trimming tools like sickle instead) Short sequences themselves are the classification target — the PlasFlow authors state results for short sequences are unreliable for kmer-based methods The downstream tool requires an assembly graph and paired reads (e.g. PlasmidSpades or Recycler), which does not use contig FASTA filtered this way http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Pre-classification filtering of metagenomic assembly contigs by length (retain only sequences longer than 1000 bp) before PlasFlow plasmid/chromosome classification, because kmer-based classifiers perform poorly on short contigs. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321
skills.summary: Pre-classification filtering of metagenomic assembly contigs by length (retain only sequences longer than 1000 bp) before PlasFlow plasmid/chromosome classification, because kmer-based classifiers perform poorly on short contigs.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is raw sequencing reads rather than assembled contigs (use read trimming tools like sickle instead) Short sequences themselves are the classification target — the PlasFlow authors state results for short sequences are unreliable for kmer-based methods The downstream tool requires an assembly graph and paired reads (e.g. PlasmidSpades or Recycler), which does not use contig FASTA filtered this way

skills.description: Use when you need to characterize a FASTA reference set (chromosomes, plasmids, contigs) by per-sequence length and %G+C content, then aggregate means by group labels and reproduce published dataset statistics.
skills.name: sequence-length-statistics
skills.search_text: sequence-length-statistics Use when you need to characterize a FASTA reference set (chromosomes, plasmids, contigs) by per-sequence length and %G+C content, then aggregate means by group labels and reproduce published dataset statistics. Input sequences are already short k-mer fragments rather than full-length sequences, since fragment statistics will not match full-genome reference values You need sequence classification itself (plasmid vs chromosome) — use PlasFlow's neural-network prediction, not descriptive length/%G+C statistics http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 A skill for computing per-sequence nucleotide statistics (sequence length and %G+C content) on FASTA datasets and aggregating them by category (e.g. molecule type, phylum) to characterize reference collections, as done for the 1961 RefSeq chromosomes and 7604 plasmids used to train PlasFlow. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkx1321
skills.summary: A skill for computing per-sequence nucleotide statistics (sequence length and %G+C content) on FASTA datasets and aggregating them by category (e.g. molecule type, phylum) to characterize reference collections, as done for the 1961 RefSeq chromosomes and 7604 plasmids used to train PlasFlow.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input sequences are already short k-mer fragments rather than full-length sequences, since fragment statistics will not match full-genome reference values You need sequence classification itself (plasmid vs chromosome) — use PlasFlow's neural-network prediction, not descriptive length/%G+C statistics

skills.description: Use when error-corrected, window-based reads from a ShoRAH run must be collapsed into a minimal non-redundant set before running global haplotype reconstruction (mm.py) and frequency estimation (freqEst).
skills.name: sequence-read-deduplication
skills.search_text: sequence-read-deduplication Use when error-corrected, window-based reads from a ShoRAH run must be collapsed into a minimal non-redundant set before running global haplotype reconstruction (mm.py) and frequency estimation (freqEst). Only local analysis is needed — invoking shorah shotgun or shorah amplicon handles windows and SNV calling without the contain/deduplication step Running ShoRAH2, where global haplotype reconstruction is disabled and deduplication for global assembly is not available (use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global haplotype options instead) http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Extract the set of unique error-corrected reads that are maximal with respect to the substring relation using ShoRAH's contain program, so that redundant reads are removed before global haplotype reconstruction. This deduplication step is the bridge between local error correction and parsimony-based global assembly. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-12-119
skills.summary: Extract the set of unique error-corrected reads that are maximal with respect to the substring relation using ShoRAH's contain program, so that redundant reads are removed before global haplotype reconstruction. This deduplication step is the bridge between local error correction and parsimony-based global assembly.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Only local analysis is needed — invoking shorah shotgun or shorah amplicon handles windows and SNV calling without the contain/deduplication step Running ShoRAH2, where global haplotype reconstruction is disabled and deduplication for global assembly is not available (use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global haplotype options instead)

skills.description: Use when raw FASTQ reads (e.g., Illumina runs from SRA accessions) are about to be classified with a k-mer/LCA classifier such as Kraken and low-quality bases or adapter contamination could distort exact k-mer matching.
skills.name: sequence-read-quality-trimming
skills.search_text: sequence-read-quality-trimming Use when raw FASTQ reads (e.g., Illumina runs from SRA accessions) are about to be classified with a k-mer/LCA classifier such as Kraken and low-quality bases or adapter contamination could distort exact k-mer matching. Input reads are already trimmed (e.g., SRA-supplied reads with adapters and low-quality bases removed) The classifier pipeline requires variable-length or paired-end structure that 'NNNNN' mate-joining would destroy Sequences contain many ambiguous nucleotides you need retained — Kraken ignores k-mers spanning ambiguous bases, so excessive Ns reduce classifiable content rather than being recoverable by trimming http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Preprocess raw FASTQ sequencing reads by trimming low-quality bases and adapter sequences before taxonomic classification, as done in the Kraken paper's Human Microbiome Project saliva analysis (SRS019120, SRS014468, SRS015055). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/gb-2014-15-3-r46
skills.summary: Preprocess raw FASTQ sequencing reads by trimming low-quality bases and adapter sequences before taxonomic classification, as done in the Kraken paper's Human Microbiome Project saliva analysis (SRS019120, SRS014468, SRS015055).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input reads are already trimmed (e.g., SRA-supplied reads with adapters and low-quality bases removed) The classifier pipeline requires variable-length or paired-end structure that 'NNNNN' mate-joining would destroy Sequences contain many ambiguous nucleotides you need retained — Kraken ignores k-mers spanning ambiguous bases, so excessive Ns reduce classifiable content rather than being recoverable by trimming

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how many sequences in a novel catalogue (e.g. 879 ISC insertion sequences in FASTA) have known homologs in a curated database such as ISfinder, and how those hits split by similarity stringency.
skills.name: sequence-similarity-searching
skills.search_text: sequence-similarity-searching Use when you need to quantify how many sequences in a novel catalogue (e.g. 879 ISC insertion sequences in FASTA) have known homologs in a curated database such as ISfinder, and how those hits split by similarity stringency. The catalogue sequences are already annotated against ISfinder and you only need the existing classification You are looking for ISs lacking inverted terminal repeats — Palidis/ISC only contains common DDE-type ISs with ITRs, so results would not represent such elements http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Benchmark a catalogue of predicted insertion sequences against a curated reference database (ISfinder) by sequence similarity search, classifying each element as a strict homolog, loose homolog, or novel based on e-value thresholds. metagenomics/v1 10.1099/mgen.0.000917
skills.summary: Benchmark a catalogue of predicted insertion sequences against a curated reference database (ISfinder) by sequence similarity search, classifying each element as a strict homolog, loose homolog, or novel based on e-value thresholds.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The catalogue sequences are already annotated against ISfinder and you only need the existing classification You are looking for ISs lacking inverted terminal repeats — Palidis/ISC only contains common DDE-type ISs with ITRs, so results would not represent such elements

skills.description: Use when short metagenomic sequencing reads (FASTQ/FASTA) must be encoded as TFRecord with the DeepMicrobes merged 12-mer vocabulary before training a DNN classifier or running prediction on held-out reads.
skills.name: sequence-to-tfrecord-conversion
skills.search_text: sequence-to-tfrecord-conversion Use when short metagenomic sequencing reads (FASTQ/FASTA) must be encoded as TFRecord with the DeepMicrobes merged 12-mer vocabulary before training a DNN classifier or running prediction on held-out reads. The input data are already in TFRecord format produced with the same 12-mer merged vocabulary The downstream classifier is not DeepMicrobes (e.g. Kraken or Kaiju), which consume k-mer/protein databases rather than TFRecord embeddings Reads have lengths and error profiles strongly different from the short Illumina-style reads the 12-mer vocabulary was tuned for (e.g. long-read sequencing) http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Convert metagenomic FASTQ/FASTA short reads into TensorFlow TFRecord format using the DeepMicrobes tfrecord utility, encoding sequences with the paper's 12-mer vocabulary so they can be consumed by the k-mer embedding + BiLSTM + self-attention classification models. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqaa009
skills.summary: Convert metagenomic FASTQ/FASTA short reads into TensorFlow TFRecord format using the DeepMicrobes tfrecord utility, encoding sequences with the paper's 12-mer vocabulary so they can be consumed by the k-mer embedding + BiLSTM + self-attention classification models.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input data are already in TFRecord format produced with the same 12-mer merged vocabulary The downstream classifier is not DeepMicrobes (e.g. Kraken or Kaiju), which consume k-mer/protein databases rather than TFRecord embeddings Reads have lengths and error profiles strongly different from the short Illumina-style reads the 12-mer vocabulary was tuned for (e.g. long-read sequencing)

skills.description: Use when a nanopore raw-signal workflow must be evaluated under truncated sequencing (small random fractions of reads) or when quantifying how many reads a real-time stopping mechanism like Sequence Until consumes before safely halting.
skills.name: sequence-until-subsample-simulation
skills.search_text: sequence-until-subsample-simulation Use when a nanopore raw-signal workflow must be evaluated under truncated sequencing (small random fractions of reads) or when quantifying how many reads a real-time stopping mechanism like Sequence Until consumes before safely halting. The input is basecalled sequence reads (FASTQ/BAM) rather than raw nanopore signals — RawHash and UNCALLED operate on raw current signals The data is r10.4.1 rather than legacy r9.4(.1) — UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data, so the comparison is invalid The goal is adaptive-sampling enrichment of targets on-device rather than estimating how early a run can be safely terminated from an offline read set http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Emulates progressively truncated nanopore sequencing runs by generating randomly shuffled FAST5 subsamples (0.01%–25%) of a relative-abundance read set, then evaluates RawHash vs UNCALLED relative-abundance estimation accuracy and RawHash's Sequence Until early-termination read consumption. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioinformatics/btad272
skills.summary: Emulates progressively truncated nanopore sequencing runs by generating randomly shuffled FAST5 subsamples (0.01%–25%) of a relative-abundance read set, then evaluates RawHash vs UNCALLED relative-abundance estimation accuracy and RawHash's Sequence Until early-termination read consumption.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is basecalled sequence reads (FASTQ/BAM) rather than raw nanopore signals — RawHash and UNCALLED operate on raw current signals The data is r10.4.1 rather than legacy r9.4(.1) — UNCALLED can only be applied to legacy r9.4.1 data, so the comparison is invalid The goal is adaptive-sampling enrichment of targets on-device rather than estimating how early a run can be safely terminated from an offline read set

skills.description: Use when benchmarking how many sequences an overlapping paired-end assembler recovers from FASTQ read pairs relative to a naive perfect-match overlap baseline, or when tuning an assembly quality-score threshold to raise recovery.
skills.name: sequence-yield-quantification
skills.search_text: sequence-yield-quantification Use when benchmarking how many sequences an overlapping paired-end assembler recovers from FASTQ read pairs relative to a naive perfect-match overlap baseline, or when tuning an assembly quality-score threshold to raise recovery. The input is already an assembled or clustered sequence/abundance table rather than raw paired-end reads — yield comparison requires re-running the assembly itself. Read pairs do not contain overlapping regions (e.g. fragment length far exceeds read length), since the yield gain relies on reconstructing the overlap with error correction. http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Quantify how many paired-end Illumina reads survive assembly under different assembler settings (e.g. PANDAseq quality thresholds of 0.9 vs 0.6) and compare recovery against a naive perfect-overlap baseline, expressed as relative percent yield increase. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-13-31
skills.summary: Quantify how many paired-end Illumina reads survive assembly under different assembler settings (e.g. PANDAseq quality thresholds of 0.9 vs 0.6) and compare recovery against a naive perfect-overlap baseline, expressed as relative percent yield increase.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The input is already an assembled or clustered sequence/abundance table rather than raw paired-end reads — yield comparison requires re-running the assembly itself. Read pairs do not contain overlapping regions (e.g. fragment length far exceeds read length), since the yield gain relies on reconstructing the overlap with error correction.

skills.description: Use when hotspot mutation calls from converted nanopore short reads must be qualified by an empirically measured background noise profile and LoD before being trusted for clinical hotspot panels.
skills.name: sequencing-background-noise-evaluation
skills.search_text: sequencing-background-noise-evaluation Use when hotspot mutation calls from converted nanopore short reads must be qualified by an empirically measured background noise profile and LoD before being trusted for clinical hotspot panels. Input is genuine NGS short-read data with random error profiles — the conversion step's non-random nanopore noise is absent, so this noise evaluation is unnecessary Data are destined for Nano2NGS-Meta metagenomic taxonomic classification rather than hotspot mutation detection A validated LoD and background noise profile already exist for the exact same algorithm, pipeline, and platform-matched data http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0092 Measures background noise and limit of detection (LoD) for hotspot mutation calls generated by the Nano2NGS-Muta nanopore-to-NGS conversion framework. Because the framework performs no error correction and different NGS analysis algorithms produce different result features, noise must be empirically characterized on actual data. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nargab/lqac033
skills.summary: Measures background noise and limit of detection (LoD) for hotspot mutation calls generated by the Nano2NGS-Muta nanopore-to-NGS conversion framework. Because the framework performs no error correction and different NGS analysis algorithms produce different result features, noise must be empirically characterized on actual data.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is genuine NGS short-read data with random error profiles — the conversion step's non-random nanopore noise is absent, so this noise evaluation is unnecessary Data are destined for Nano2NGS-Meta metagenomic taxonomic classification rather than hotspot mutation detection A validated LoD and background noise profile already exist for the exact same algorithm, pipeline, and platform-matched data

skills.description: Use when benchmarking how coverage depth affects strain separation quality, e.g. building a Mock3 5x–50x downsampling series of simulated PacBio reads before strain-oblivious assembly and Strainberry separation.
skills.name: sequencing-coverage-downsampling
skills.search_text: sequencing-coverage-downsampling Use when benchmarking how coverage depth affects strain separation quality, e.g. building a Mock3 5x–50x downsampling series of simulated PacBio reads before strain-oblivious assembly and Strainberry separation. The goal is strain separation itself rather than benchmarking depth sensitivity — a single adequately covered dataset (60–80x) suffices Input reads are real experimental data whose coverage cannot be controlled by simulation parameters; subsampling still works but Badread simulation steps are unnecessary The metagenome is high-complexity — Strainberry is designed for low-complexity communities http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 Builds a series of coverage-reduced datasets by subsampling simulated long reads (5x–50x from a 50x Mock3 PacBio simulation) to quantify how sequencing depth affects strain-resolved assembly quality with Strainberry. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-021-24515-9
skills.summary: Builds a series of coverage-reduced datasets by subsampling simulated long reads (5x–50x from a 50x Mock3 PacBio simulation) to quantify how sequencing depth affects strain-resolved assembly quality with Strainberry.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is strain separation itself rather than benchmarking depth sensitivity — a single adequately covered dataset (60–80x) suffices Input reads are real experimental data whose coverage cannot be controlled by simulation parameters; subsampling still works but Badread simulation steps are unnecessary The metagenome is high-complexity — Strainberry is designed for low-complexity communities

skills.description: Use when planning or evaluating 10x Chromium Linked-Read library preparation/sequencing parameters (CF, CR, C, fragment length) and you need to know which combinations maximize contig/scaffold N50 and NA50 for diploid de novo assembly.
skills.name: sequencing-coverage-parameter-sweep
skills.search_text: sequencing-coverage-parameter-sweep Use when planning or evaluating 10x Chromium Linked-Read library preparation/sequencing parameters (CF, CR, C, fragment length) and you need to know which combinations maximize contig/scaffold N50 and NA50 for diploid de novo assembly. The goal is simulation for metagenomics with unequal species abundances without supplying the two-column abundance flat file (sequence name and abundance summing to 1) that LRTK-SIM requires Assemblies are from long-read (PacBio/ONT) or other barcode-based technologies (CPTv2-seq, stLRF) rather than 10x Linked-Reads, since the parameter map was derived for 10x data Input is a single haploid simulation where diploid phase-block and NA50 metrics from Hap=2 diploid simulation are not meaningful http://edamontology.org/topic_0196 http://edamontology.org/topic_3673 Systematically vary 10x Linked-Read coverage parameters — total coverage C = CR × CF, physical fragment coverage (CF), read coverage per fragment (CR), and fragment length (Mu_F / WμFL) — by simulating libraries with LRTK-SIM and/or sequencing real libraries, then assembling with Supernova2 to map assembly quality onto the parameter space. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giz141
skills.summary: Systematically vary 10x Linked-Read coverage parameters — total coverage C = CR × CF, physical fragment coverage (CF), read coverage per fragment (CR), and fragment length (Mu_F / WμFL) — by simulating libraries with LRTK-SIM and/or sequencing real libraries, then assembling with Supernova2 to map assembly quality onto the parameter space.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The goal is simulation for metagenomics with unequal species abundances without supplying the two-column abundance flat file (sequence name and abundance summing to 1) that LRTK-SIM requires Assemblies are from long-read (PacBio/ONT) or other barcode-based technologies (CPTv2-seq, stLRF) rather than 10x Linked-Reads, since the parameter map was derived for 10x data Input is a single haploid simulation where diploid phase-block and NA50 metrics from Hap=2 diploid simulation are not meaningful

skills.description: Decision support for choosing between 16S+PICRUSt prediction and shallow shotgun sequencing: use when paired 16S OTU tables and HUMAnN-annotated KO tables from the same samples are available and the question is accuracy as a function of sequencing depth.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-accuracy-convergence-analysis
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-accuracy-convergence-analysis Decision support for choosing between 16S+PICRUSt prediction and shallow shotgun sequencing: use when paired 16S OTU tables and HUMAnN-annotated KO tables from the same samples are available and the question is accuracy as a function of sequencing depth. The shotgun metagenomes are deeply sequenced (near or above ~72,000–10^5 reads per sample), where sequencing accuracy converges and PICRUSt no longer outperforms it The community is dominated by organisms with high NSTI (no closely related reference genomes), since PICRUSt accuracy depends on availability of related reference genomes The sample contains substantial viral or eukaryotic metagenome components, which PICRUSt's bacterial/archaeal marker gene framework does not infer http://edamontology.org/topic_3941 http://edamontology.org/topic_0084 Rarefies paired 16S-derived PICRUSt metagenome predictions and shallow shotgun metagenomic KO profiles over a matched depth series and compares them by Spearman rank correlation to find the read depth at which PICRUSt outperforms sequencing. This formalizes the trade-off between prediction error and metagenome sampling depth. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/nbt.2676
skills.summary: Rarefies paired 16S-derived PICRUSt metagenome predictions and shallow shotgun metagenomic KO profiles over a matched depth series and compares them by Spearman rank correlation to find the read depth at which PICRUSt outperforms sequencing. This formalizes the trade-off between prediction error and metagenome sampling depth.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The shotgun metagenomes are deeply sequenced (near or above ~72,000–10^5 reads per sample), where sequencing accuracy converges and PICRUSt no longer outperforms it The community is dominated by organisms with high NSTI (no closely related reference genomes), since PICRUSt accuracy depends on availability of related reference genomes The sample contains substantial viral or eukaryotic metagenome components, which PICRUSt's bacterial/archaeal marker gene framework does not infer

skills.description: Use when pairwise metagenome distances must resolve communities differing in sequencing depth, dominant-organism abundance, or genetic composition, and MinHash sketches (Mash) or presence/absence metrics (Simka Jaccard) compress or saturate those differences.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-normalization-comparison
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-normalization-comparison Use when pairwise metagenome distances must resolve communities differing in sequencing depth, dominant-organism abundance, or genetic composition, and MinHash sketches (Mash) or presence/absence metrics (Simka Jaccard) compress or saturate those differences. Input is already a k-mer feature table or abundance matrix rather than raw read files (Libra indexes reads directly) The analysis requires presence/absence or MinHash-sketch semantics only, and abundance-resolution of depth/abundance gradients is not the goal (Mash or Simka presence/absence metrics suffice) Datasets are too large for a single machine and no Hadoop/CyVerse infrastructure is available, since Libra relies on a Hadoop MapReduce architecture http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 Compare metagenomic samples with Libra's Cosine Similarity k-mer abundance distance, choosing NATURAL (raw-abundance) or LOGARITHM weighting to control how sequencing depth and dominant-organism abundance influence all-vs-all pairwise distances, as validated on simulated 454 mock-community series (mock 1–4). metagenomics/v1 10.1093/gigascience/giy165
skills.summary: Compare metagenomic samples with Libra's Cosine Similarity k-mer abundance distance, choosing NATURAL (raw-abundance) or LOGARITHM weighting to control how sequencing depth and dominant-organism abundance influence all-vs-all pairwise distances, as validated on simulated 454 mock-community series (mock 1–4).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already a k-mer feature table or abundance matrix rather than raw read files (Libra indexes reads directly) The analysis requires presence/absence or MinHash-sketch semantics only, and abundance-resolution of depth/abundance gradients is not the goal (Mash or Simka presence/absence metrics suffice) Datasets are too large for a single machine and no Hadoop/CyVerse infrastructure is available, since Libra relies on a Hadoop MapReduce architecture

skills.description: Use when validating a longitudinal differential-abundance method against sequencing-depth bias: you need negative-control data with no true time effect but varying library sizes, or must quantify FPR inflation from compositional normalization.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-rarefaction-control
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-rarefaction-control Use when validating a longitudinal differential-abundance method against sequencing-depth bias: you need negative-control data with no true time effect but varying library sizes, or must quantify FPR inflation from compositional normalization. Data contain genuine time/treatment effects — this skill is a negative-control design assuming all features are truly null (zero effect size), so FPR is the only meaningful readout Sequencing depth is approximately uniform across time points, so depth-driven confounding is not the validation target Analysis targets absolute-abundance or already-rarefied data where compositional normalization bias (TSS on non-rarefied counts) does not apply http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_2269 A negative-control validation skill that simulates longitudinal microbiome count tables with zero true effect but systematically varying sequencing depth (SparseDOSSA2), then contrasts rarefaction + LongDat's negative-binomial count pipeline versus TSS normalization + linear models to expose false positives driven by depth differences. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbad063
skills.summary: A negative-control validation skill that simulates longitudinal microbiome count tables with zero true effect but systematically varying sequencing depth (SparseDOSSA2), then contrasts rarefaction + LongDat's negative-binomial count pipeline versus TSS normalization + linear models to expose false positives driven by depth differences.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Data contain genuine time/treatment effects — this skill is a negative-control design assuming all features are truly null (zero effect size), so FPR is the only meaningful readout Sequencing depth is approximately uniform across time points, so depth-driven confounding is not the validation target Analysis targets absolute-abundance or already-rarefied data where compositional normalization bias (TSS on non-rarefied counts) does not apply

skills.description: Use when planning or justifying sequencing depth for shotgun metatranscriptomes (e.g., human gut stool samples), or when asked to demonstrate via subsampling how many annotated reads are required to reach a target accuracy for low-abundance transcripts.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-saturation-analysis
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-saturation-analysis Use when planning or justifying sequencing depth for shotgun metatranscriptomes (e.g., human gut stool samples), or when asked to demonstrate via subsampling how many annotated reads are required to reach a target accuracy for low-abundance transcripts. Input data has not been annotated yet (raw FASTQ without MG-RAST or DIAMOND annotation results) — subsampling requires annotated reads, not raw sequences The analysis goal is differential expression between control vs experimental groups (use the SAMSA R/DESeq2 scripts instead of depth saturation analysis) Only very few reads are available overall — a shallow pilot sample cannot serve as the full-sample reference for stratifying high/medium/low abundance classes http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 A rarefaction-style saturation analysis that subsamples annotated metatranscriptome reads at increasing depths to find the minimum sequencing depth needed for accurate abundance measurement, especially for low-abundance transcripts. In the SAMSA paper this established that 5-10 million annotated reads (40-50 million raw reads) yield >90% accuracy. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-016-1270-8
skills.summary: A rarefaction-style saturation analysis that subsamples annotated metatranscriptome reads at increasing depths to find the minimum sequencing depth needed for accurate abundance measurement, especially for low-abundance transcripts. In the SAMSA paper this established that 5-10 million annotated reads (40-50 million raw reads) yield >90% accuracy.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input data has not been annotated yet (raw FASTQ without MG-RAST or DIAMOND annotation results) — subsampling requires annotated reads, not raw sequences The analysis goal is differential expression between control vs experimental groups (use the SAMSA R/DESeq2 scripts instead of depth saturation analysis) Only very few reads are available overall — a shallow pilot sample cannot serve as the full-sample reference for stratifying high/medium/low abundance classes

skills.description: Use when you need to quantify how a viral metagenomic classifier/reconstruction pipeline (e.g. VirMAP on VMC reads) degrades as sequencing depth is reduced, or to compare retention of a reconstruction pipeline against a standard read-classification baseline at shallow depth.
skills.name: sequencing-depth-sensitivity-analysis
skills.search_text: sequencing-depth-sensitivity-analysis Use when you need to quantify how a viral metagenomic classifier/reconstruction pipeline (e.g. VirMAP on VMC reads) degrades as sequencing depth is reduced, or to compare retention of a reconstruction pipeline against a standard read-classification baseline at shallow depth. The question is a single full-depth taxonomic profile of a virome sample — run VirMAP once rather than a subsampling sensitivity sweep The goal is quantitative abundance estimation — random subsampling to 0.1% depth destroys read-count proportionality and only supports detection/retention robustness claims The dataset is not viral-focused (e.g. host-genome or bacterial mock communities) — VirMAP filters contigs to the viral superkingdom, so non-viral sensitivity is out of scope http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 A robustness benchmark that randomly subsamples a viral mock community (VMC) FASTQ dataset to 10%, 1%, and 0.1% depth (ten trials each), reruns VirMAP on every subsample, and reports detection rates of the seven mock constituents plus viral-base retention relative to the full-depth run. metagenomics/v1 10.1038/s41467-018-05658-8
skills.summary: A robustness benchmark that randomly subsamples a viral mock community (VMC) FASTQ dataset to 10%, 1%, and 0.1% depth (ten trials each), reruns VirMAP on every subsample, and reports detection rates of the seven mock constituents plus viral-base retention relative to the full-depth run.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The question is a single full-depth taxonomic profile of a virome sample — run VirMAP once rather than a subsampling sensitivity sweep The goal is quantitative abundance estimation — random subsampling to 0.1% depth destroys read-count proportionality and only supports detection/retention robustness claims The dataset is not viral-focused (e.g. host-genome or bacterial mock communities) — VirMAP filters contigs to the viral superkingdom, so non-viral sensitivity is out of scope

skills.description: Use when exact-overlap-based read recruitment (e.g., TAR-VIR overlap extension with an overlap cutoff) is planned downstream, since raw sequencing errors would break exact overlap matching between reads.
skills.name: sequencing-error-correction
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-correction Use when exact-overlap-based read recruitment (e.g., TAR-VIR overlap extension with an overlap cutoff) is planned downstream, since raw sequencing errors would break exact overlap matching between reads. The downstream pipeline tolerates mismatches (e.g., seed-based mapping alone with Bowtie2/BWA) and does not rely on exact read overlaps Reads are already processed through a correction step; re-correcting can degrade assembly quality (PEHaplo expects raw corrected inputs, not double-corrected data) http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Correct substitution, insertion, and deletion errors in NGS metagenomic reads (e.g., simulated MiSeq 250 bp paired-end reads) with Karect before overlap-based viral read recruitment, so that exact read-overlap detection in TAR-VIR's overlap extension module works reliably. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/s12859-019-2878-2
skills.summary: Correct substitution, insertion, and deletion errors in NGS metagenomic reads (e.g., simulated MiSeq 250 bp paired-end reads) with Karect before overlap-based viral read recruitment, so that exact read-overlap detection in TAR-VIR's overlap extension module works reliably.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The downstream pipeline tolerates mismatches (e.g., seed-based mapping alone with Bowtie2/BWA) and does not rely on exact read overlaps Reads are already processed through a correction step; re-correcting can degrade assembly quality (PEHaplo expects raw corrected inputs, not double-corrected data)

skills.description: Use when you must generate simulated shotgun metagenomic FASTQ benchmarks at prescribed mean depths with an instrument-specific error model (NovaSeq) for validating variant-discovery tools.
skills.name: sequencing-error-model-configuration
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-model-configuration Use when you must generate simulated shotgun metagenomic FASTQ benchmarks at prescribed mean depths with an instrument-specific error model (NovaSeq) for validating variant-discovery tools. When the goal is to analyze real (non-simulated) metagenomic FASTQ data — this skill only generates synthetic benchmarks When the target sequencing platform is not NovaSeq — using --model novaseq would produce unrealistic quality/error profiles for other instruments When single-end reads are required — the benchmark prescribes paired-end 151 bp per mate http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 http://edamontology.org/topic_3697 Configure InSilicoSeq (iss generate) with the --model novaseq error model to simulate paired-end 151 bp shotgun metagenomic reads, per-sample read counts computed from prescribed mean depths (3x–35.5x) so benchmark datasets faithfully mimic NovaSeq error profiles for evaluating MetaQuad. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/bioadv/vbae030
skills.summary: Configure InSilicoSeq (iss generate) with the --model novaseq error model to simulate paired-end 151 bp shotgun metagenomic reads, per-sample read counts computed from prescribed mean depths (3x–35.5x) so benchmark datasets faithfully mimic NovaSeq error profiles for evaluating MetaQuad.
skills.when_to_use_negative: When the goal is to analyze real (non-simulated) metagenomic FASTQ data — this skill only generates synthetic benchmarks When the target sequencing platform is not NovaSeq — using --model novaseq would produce unrealistic quality/error profiles for other instruments When single-end reads are required — the benchmark prescribes paired-end 151 bp per mate

skills.description: Use when gene-calling on unassembled metagenomic reads from error-prone platforms (e.g. 454 with homopolymer-run indels), where frameshifts in raw reads break standard gene predictors.
skills.name: sequencing-error-modeling-gene-calling
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-modeling-gene-calling Use when gene-calling on unassembled metagenomic reads from error-prone platforms (e.g. 454 with homopolymer-run indels), where frameshifts in raw reads break standard gene predictors. Input is already high-quality assembled consensus sequence with a low residual error rate, where explicit error modeling adds computation without benefit The task is standalone sequencing-error correction or base calling rather than gene prediction — Glimmer-MG models errors only to keep gene predictions in frame Computational cost is the binding constraint, since Glimmer-MG is more computationally expensive than existing gene prediction software http://edamontology.org/topic_3308 Model insertion, deletion, and stop-codon-introducing substitution errors directly during metagenomic gene prediction (as implemented in Glimmer-MG) so that predicted coding frames can track through raw error-prone reads, e.g. 454 homopolymer-run indels, without requiring prior error correction. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkr1067
skills.summary: Model insertion, deletion, and stop-codon-introducing substitution errors directly during metagenomic gene prediction (as implemented in Glimmer-MG) so that predicted coding frames can track through raw error-prone reads, e.g. 454 homopolymer-run indels, without requiring prior error correction.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Input is already high-quality assembled consensus sequence with a low residual error rate, where explicit error modeling adds computation without benefit The task is standalone sequencing-error correction or base calling rather than gene prediction — Glimmer-MG models errors only to keep gene predictions in frame Computational cost is the binding constraint, since Glimmer-MG is more computationally expensive than existing gene prediction software

skills.description: Use when assembling overlapping Illumina paired-end reads (e.g. 16S rRNA amplicons in FASTQ/SAM) where naive perfect-match overlap discards ~40% of reads due to uncalled or miscalled bases.
skills.name: sequencing-error-probability-modeling
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-probability-modeling Use when assembling overlapping Illumina paired-end reads (e.g. 16S rRNA amplicons in FASTQ/SAM) where naive perfect-match overlap discards ~40% of reads due to uncalled or miscalled bases. Reads are non-overlapping paired-end (no shared amplicon region), so no overlap likelihood can be computed Input is already a merged contig or a feature/OTU table — assembly modeling no longer applies Sequencing technology has a high probability of gap-inclusion, since PANDAseq exploits Illumina-specific properties including the low probability of gap-inclusion http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0622 Probabilistic error modeling of paired-end Illumina reads that converts ASCII quality values into base-error probabilities and computes the likelihood of each candidate overlap, so the overlap maximizing Pr[F,R|c] corrects uncalled (N) and miscalled bases during assembly (PANDAseq approach). metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-13-31
skills.summary: Probabilistic error modeling of paired-end Illumina reads that converts ASCII quality values into base-error probabilities and computes the likelihood of each candidate overlap, so the overlap maximizing Pr[F,R|c] corrects uncalled (N) and miscalled bases during assembly (PANDAseq approach).
skills.when_to_use_negative: Reads are non-overlapping paired-end (no shared amplicon region), so no overlap likelihood can be computed Input is already a merged contig or a feature/OTU table — assembly modeling no longer applies Sequencing technology has a high probability of gap-inclusion, since PANDAseq exploits Illumina-specific properties including the low probability of gap-inclusion

skills.description: Use when you have parent sequences and their one-mismatch children from amplicon fastq data and need to estimate the Illumina substitution error rate or verify that one-mismatch child accumulation follows a Poisson process.
skills.name: sequencing-error-rate-estimation
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-rate-estimation Use when you have parent sequences and their one-mismatch children from amplicon fastq data and need to estimate the Illumina substitution error rate or verify that one-mismatch child accumulation follows a Poisson process. Your goal is variant calling itself rather than error-rate characterization; HashSeq's own inference uses a normal distribution with LOESS regression for background error instead of the Poisson model Data come from long-read technologies such as PacBio, where the assumption of rarity of multiple-mismatch sequences may not hold You need indel error modeling; HashSeq does not explicitly model insertions or deletions and treats indel events as separate parent sequences http://edamontology.org/topic_0632 http://edamontology.org/topic_3168 Fits a single-parameter Poisson model to the fraction of all possible one-mismatch children observed per parent 16S rRNA sequence versus parent abundance, yielding a per-nucleotide sequencing error rate (approximately P = 10^-4 on Illumina MiSeq zymo mock community data). This quantifies the background error process that HashSeq uses to infer true sequence variants. metagenomics/v1 10.1128/msystems.00697-21
skills.summary: Fits a single-parameter Poisson model to the fraction of all possible one-mismatch children observed per parent 16S rRNA sequence versus parent abundance, yielding a per-nucleotide sequencing error rate (approximately P = 10^-4 on Illumina MiSeq zymo mock community data). This quantifies the background error process that HashSeq uses to infer true sequence variants.
skills.when_to_use_negative: Your goal is variant calling itself rather than error-rate characterization; HashSeq's own inference uses a normal distribution with LOESS regression for background error instead of the Poisson model Data come from long-read technologies such as PacBio, where the assumption of rarity of multiple-mismatch sequences may not hold You need indel error modeling; HashSeq does not explicitly model insertions or deletions and treats indel events as separate parent sequences

skills.description: Use when error-prone NGS reads (e.g., 454 Titanium pyrosequencing of HIV-1 subtype B pol) from a genetically heterogeneous sample must be error-corrected before estimating haplotype frequencies or clone prevalence.
skills.name: sequencing-error-rate-quantification
skills.search_text: sequencing-error-rate-quantification Use when error-prone NGS reads (e.g., 454 Titanium pyrosequencing of HIV-1 subtype B pol) from a genetically heterogeneous sample must be error-corrected before estimating haplotype frequencies or clone prevalence. The sample is expected to be clonal or only a consensus sequence is needed — Sanger-style consensus would suffice and low-frequency variants are not of interest Global (full-length) haplotype reconstruction is required with current ShoRAH2 — global mode is disabled there; use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global haplotype options instead The goal is strand-bias-aware SNV detection alone without read error correction — shorah snv addresses SNV calling separately from the error-correction clustering http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 http://edamontology.org/topic_0199 http://edamontology.org/topic_0625 Quantifies and corrects sequencing errors in mixed deep-sequencing samples by clustering overlapping reads per genome window with ShoRAH's Dirichlet-process mixture (diri_sampler), reducing the residual error rate five-fold (0.25% to 0.05%) so low-frequency variants become quantifiable. metagenomics/v1 10.1186/1471-2105-12-119
skills.summary: Quantifies and corrects sequencing errors in mixed deep-sequencing samples by clustering overlapping reads per genome window with ShoRAH's Dirichlet-process mixture (diri_sampler), reducing the residual error rate five-fold (0.25% to 0.05%) so low-frequency variants become quantifiable.
skills.when_to_use_negative: The sample is expected to be clonal or only a consensus sequence is needed — Sanger-style consensus would suffice and low-frequency variants are not of interest Global (full-length) haplotype reconstruction is required with current ShoRAH2 — global mode is disabled there; use ShoRAH1 v1.1.3 or V-pipe's global haplotype options instead The goal is strand-bias-aware SNV detection alone without read error correction — shorah snv addresses SNV calling separately from the error-correction clustering

Input consists of assembled, high-quality contigs where indel/substitution error rates are negligible and frame tracking is unnecessary The goal is platform-independent classification or abundance estimation rather than gene prediction on error-prone reads http://edamontology.org/topic_3174 http://edamontology.org/topic_0080 Model platform-specific sequencing errors (454 homopolymer-run indels and Illumina stop-codon-introducing substitutions) so that metagenomic gene prediction can track coding frames across error-prone raw reads, as implemented in Glimmer-MG. metagenomics/v1 10.1093/nar/gkr1067
